The Indian actor Nana Patekar, who has died of a heart attack aged 75, first broke through in Mira Nair’s Salaam Bombay! (1988), and the Bollywood hits Parinda (1989) and Krantiveer (1994). These early credits established Patekar as a performer of rare versatility: he and Irrfan Khan remain the only performers to have won Filmfare’s best actor, best supporting actor and best villain awards (considered India’s “oscars”). Yet the question of whether Patekar was better suited to heroism or villainy lingered unresolved: allegations of sexual harassment and intimidation first made by his former co-star Tanushree Dutta in 2008 kickstarted India’s #MeToo movement when she raised them again in 2018.
Until that point, Patekar’s rougher edges had mostly been celebrated. As an actor, he demonstrated a baggy-eyed naturalism that spoke more to Bombay streetlife than Bollywood fantasy. He was given to writing out his dialogue until he had internalised it, and his growling line readings were both idiosyncratic and much imitated. Satyajit Ray counted among the actor’s most illustrious admirers, but apparently could not find a suitable project for him; Patekar instead had Nair to thank for launching him to international prominence in Salaam Bombay! as Baba Golub, the brutal pimp and drug dealer lording over an army of street children.
Yet the Bollywood studios also made good use of his grouchy grit. He was commanding as the kingpin Anna in Parinda, Vidhu Vinod Chopra’s inventive relocation of On the Waterfront, for which Patekar won two best supporting actor awards; he was appointed an honorary captain in the Indian territorial army after undergoing three years of army training for Prahaar: The Final Attack (1991), a film he also ended up directing. He crossed paths with the emergent megastar Shah Rukh Khan in Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (1992) and was momentarily in the running for Subhash Ghai’s blockbuster Khalnayak (1993), losing out to Sanjay Dutt.
Relations between Patekar and Dutt deteriorated further after the latter was linked to the 1993 Bombay bus bombings in which Patekar’s brother was killed. (Patekar’s wife, the Marathi actor Neelakanti, was also due to board one of the targeted vehicles.) Even after Dutt’s comeback, Patekar remained defiant: “I have not worked with [Dutt] in 22 years of my career. I will not work with him in the future.”
A comparable rage powered Krantiveer, in which Patekar played a dissolute gambler reviving his fortunes via social activism. Heart problems meant he shot his final scenes with a doctor on standby; while distributors thought Patekar a commercial risk, the film struck a chord, becoming one of that year’s biggest Hindi hits.
Born Vishwanath Patekar in Murud-Janjira, Maharashtra, Nana was one of the three sons of Dinkar Patekar, a textile painter and businessman, and his wife, Nirmala. He was educated at the Samarth Vidyalaya and the Bandra School of Arts in Bombay (now Mumbai), supporting his family after his father’s business collapsed by painting zebra crossings and cinema posters. He went on to the Sir JJ Institute of Applied Art, where he also joined the drama society.
After graduation, he briefly worked as a police sketch artist before joining the Marathi theatre group Rangayan. Switched on to films by his friend the celebrated Indian actor Smita Patil (“I was happy doing theatre, but she insisted”), he made his screen debut in the 1978 social drama Gaman, starring Patil.
A string of supporting roles followed: two years before Salaam Bombay!, he played Gandhi’s assassin Nathuram Godse in the Emmy-winning TV miniseries Lord Mountbatten: The Last Viceroy.
Despite his success in Krantiveer, for which he won several best actor awards, Patekar was not always the easiest fit with the studio system. He was replaced on Raja (1995) after spending two days hectoring his co-stars Madhuri Dixit and Mukesh Khanna with acting notes. And he paused his career during the Kargil war of 1999 to enlist with the Maratha Light infantry, serving 60 days and earning a promotion to the rank of major.
Back on civvy street, he landed a signature role as Inspector Sadhu, the dirty cop who becomes the hero of Ab Tak Chhappan (2004), and swept India’s best villain prizes as the underworld don Tabrez Alam in Apaharan (2005). He then switched into a lighter mode for the knockabout comedies Welcome (2007) and Welcome Back (2015).
Elder statesman status beckoned: he played Mumbai’s police commissioner in The Attacks of 26/11 (2013), voiced Shere Khan in the Hindi dub of Disney’s The Jungle Book (2016) and enjoyed a major success with the Marathi film Natsamrat (2016), playing an acclaimed actor unravelling in retirement. He was awarded the Padma Shri and the Raj Kapoor special contribution award in 2013; in 2015, he set up the Naam Foundation with fellow actor Makarand Anaspure to help drought-hit farmers.
Then came Dutta’s 2018 interview with the Hindu, where she repeated an earlier accusation that Patekar had first sexually harassed her while shooting a dance sequence for Horn “OK” Pleassss (2009), then, when she fled the set, sent hired thugs after her. Footage of the incident aired on Indian TV showed a mob surrounding her car, her windscreen smashed and tyres being flattened. Patekar denied the allegations. The Mumbai police opened an investigation; while no formal charges were brought, the incident sparked renewed concern about the treatment of women in Bollywood.
After a spell in industry purdah, Patekar recently attempted a comeback. There were supporting turns in the propagandistic The Vaccine War (2023), limp comedy Housefull 5 (2025) and the streaming-bound Subedaar (2026), though the actor did lend a wry centre to Vishal Bhardwaj’s Shakespeare riff O’Romeo (2026).
He married Neelakanti in 1978, and they had two sons, the first of whom, Durvasa, died in 1980, aged two. Patekar is survived by his wife and his second son, Malhar.

Linköping University professor Peter Jonsson is set to have his work presented in two weeks’ time at one of the most prestigious conferences in theoretical computer science. As of Monday, much of that work is “dead,” he says, after AI showed that a 27-year-old hypothesis underpinning it is wrong.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic claimed this week to have disproved the exponential time hypothesis (ETH). Vast swaths of theoretical computer science research on complexity and algorithm design have been built on the premise that the effort it takes to solve certain problems increases exponentially with the size of the problem.
Jonsson expects his predicament will be “very common” at the IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, where his work will be presented by one of his coauthors. “People will start the talks: ‘ETH is false, half of my paper does not work,’” he says. It’s a vexing problem, Jonsson says, “but at the same time, we learn a lot from it. And this is what science is about.”
Researchers haven’t independently verified, let alone had time to fully understand, the AI-produced proofs, which both firms have published on GitHub in both natural language and its machine-checkable Lean format. OpenAI has asked the UC Santa Barbara computer scientists who originally proposed the hypothesis, plus an MIT academic who has refuted a version of ETH, to rally researchers to unpack the proofs. So far, this effort includes a Google form asking for volunteers and feedback, and a commitment from OpenAI to fund a conference on the topic.
UC Santa Barbara professor Daniel Lokshtanov plans to join the effort, as he estimates the result—if confirmed—will render him “galactically wrong” and make around 50 of his published papers either “pointless” or in need of a revisit.
“It’s just a giant bomb dropped into the middle of the field,” he says. “It’s really cool and terrible at the same time.”
Thore Husfeldt, head of the algorithms research group at the IT University of Copenhagen, had spent most of this year thinking about one single problem in his subfield. “As far as I can tell, it’s now all irrelevant,” he tells WIRED. Having first formulated a version of the hypothesis now disproved by OpenAI, he has been writing calculations on his blackboard to figure out what other parts of his work might have become obsolete due to the “once-in-a-generation result.” Unlike the ennui that has gripped math researchers who have faced similarly field-upending proofs generated by AI models, though, Husfeldt expressed enthusiasm about the new results.
The finding is “fantastic,” he says. “Being a mathematician is a lot like stumbling about in a completely dark room,” he explains. “It's like somebody just illuminated an entire subfield in floodlights of knowledge, and now we just run around like overexcited bunnies and look at all the nooks and crannies that we can suddenly explore. So it’s a super exciting time.”
For centuries, science has advanced through making hypotheses and proving them wrong. It also isn’t unusual for an academic to be scooped or have their work otherwise undercut by another research group. But AI has accelerated this, obliterating whole research programs and spooking researchers in specific fields of math and science who wonder where they stand now that machines can outperform them.
“The last few months have been really tough. It's a lot of doom and gloom, because every week, or every second week, the results announced by AI just annihilate the ongoing research projects of many people,” Husfeldt says. “That is psychologically taxing for many people,” he says, adding that his department has considered hiring an occupational psychologist because “some people are really depressed and really sad.”
Researchers have also been overwhelmed by the volume of content now being produced, thanks to AI, including slop-level results. Midway through the interview, Husfeldt receives what he suspects to be an AI-generated 17-page paper on the consequences of the ETH result from a random Gmail account. He won’t read it: “Reading math is a very big investment of cognitive time,” he says.
OpenAI has directly contributed to this; earlier this month, it dumped 722 manuscripts on 400 problems on GitHub, to the annoyance of academics, who complain this makes it difficult to digest the results. Adding to the frustration were several documents that contained errors, reflecting what some mathematicians saw as a hasty rollout designed to juice the company’s planned initial public offering rather than moving the field forward. This time around, OpenAI’s 60-odd-page paper on ETH seems to be written better than the companies’ past publications, academics tell WIRED.
They are now scrambling to unpack the paper and find what other results they can quickly deduce from it.
If ETH is false and it doesn’t, in fact, take exponentially more time to solve problems as they become more complex, that’s “exciting,” says Victor Lagerkvist, an associate professor at Linköping. He plans to return to problems he had previously given up on under the assumption ETH was accurate.
OpenAI’s finding could also have impacts on the cryptography that underpins web security, which is based on the assumption that certain mathematical problems take an impractically long time to solve. While this particular result doesn’t directly affect cryptography, “it should definitely scare some cryptosystem designers,” says Lokshtanov.
That’s why continued human and AI-assisted work in theoretical computer science is important, Husfeldt adds: “We want the open scientific process to identify our misunderstandings about computation, in particular because lots of modern digital infrastructure is built on assumptions about computation.”
As for Linköping’s Jonsson, he plans to revisit both his own and others’ papers that hinge on ETH being true, and believes his conference paper may eventually be salvageable through another method. He’s excited to look into the details of OpenAI’s proof and see what he can learn from it and apply it to new problems. Even though it undoes the assumptions underpinning his work, having a verdict for ETH is something he could only “dream of” before, he says. “These are exciting times,” he adds. “Most people would never experience anything like this in their career.”
“I don’t care if it's a human-written proof, or it's written by AI, or if an alien transmitted this proof to us. If it’s true, then we must simply use it in the future.’’

Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
- Published
Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.
During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."
Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.
The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.
After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.
Goodbye Raila
BBC Africa Eye investigates the killing of three mourners at Raila Odinga’s national farewell
Watch on iPlayer
In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.
Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.
Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.
Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.
Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.
Within hours, he was dead.
His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.
As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.
"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.
"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."

- FromSoftware has temporarily taken Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 servers offline across all platforms due to a server issue.
- The developer has not revealed what caused the outage or when the online services will return.
- The shutdown brings back memories of the 2022 security exploit that kept the games' PC servers offline for months.
FromSoftware has temporarily taken the servers for Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 offline across all platforms. This is due to an issue affecting the games’ online services. FromSoftware announced the shutdown on October 30, 2026, leaving players unable to access the online features of both games.
In the announcement through its official FromSoftware support X account, the developer didn’t specify what the server issue is, but apologized for the inconvenience. It confirmed that it would share a separate announcement once it determines when the server would go online.
At the time of writing, FromSoftware has not provided any details about the nature of the server issue or how long the shutdown will last. Interestingly, DS2 and DS3 also underwent scheduled server maintenance on October 28 and October 21, 2026, respectively, across all platforms. However, it remains unclear whether the current issue is connected to that maintenance or involves a separate technical or security problem.
The biggest concern is that the current shutdown could be similar to the shutdown in 2022. Back then, FromSoft discovered a serious Remote Code Execution exploit that allowed hackers to take control of players’ PCs. The shutdown lasted 275 days for DS2, 214 days for DS3, and 290 days for DS Remastered.
The timing of the shutdown has also raised some questions, as several major gaming companies have also faced security incidents. Bandai Namco confirmed a data breach on October 28. Just a few days earlier, Capcom also confirmed a major data breach affecting millions of records. Sony also faced various security concerns recently.
While these incidents highlight the growing security concerns in the gaming industry, there is no confirmation that they are connected to the current Dark Souls server shutdown. FromSoftware has also not indicated that the issue involves a security vulnerability.
For now, we can only hope that the problem is a relatively minor technical fault that the developer can resolve soon, and not take months

China elevates a military general to Politburo, seeks to strengthen party discipline
China's top leaders have elevated the only remaining general of the body that oversees the country's military to its Politburo, the Communist Party's top governing body
BANGKOK -- China's top leaders on Thursday elevated the only remaining general on the commission that oversees the country's military to the Politburo, the top governing body of the Communist Party.
The leaders also adopted a resolution on strengthening self-governance, discipline and anti-corruption in the party, as they seek to extend their grip on power.
During a four-day closed-door meeting, top Communist Party leaders deliberated on and adopted resolutions that will guide the party in the coming years. The meeting comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party’s leader.
The party elected Gen. Zhang Shengmin, who currently serves as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, to the Politburo. Xi had earlier purged two of China’s top generals, leaving Zhang as the commission’s only member besides Xi himself.
The party said in a summary of the resolution that the tasks facing it were “increasingly arduous,” such as “uniting and leading the people to safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests.”
It said it must step up its self-governance, which involves rooting out corruption and maintaining ideological purity.
The party should “with an eye on enhancing its long-term governance capacity, maintain its progressive nature and purity, and its close, flesh-and-blood ties with the people,” according to a summary of the resolution from the official Xinhua News Agency. “The Party must remain unswerving in its commitment to a rigorous tone, improve the system for full and rigorous self-governance.”
Xi has championed anti-corruption since coming to power in 2012, and has sustained a crackdown on officials going for more than a decade. However, analysts say the focus now also includes underperforming officials.
Party members also reviewed the earlier purges of top members and military officials, confirming the personnel changes.
Zhang also holds a position overseeing internal discipline for the military, serving as deputy secretary of the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection.

People living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine were evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.
The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River, opposite Kherson, has suffered months of serious food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including about 50 children.
The humanitarian convoy, including 25 buses and ambulances, had arrived in the city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine.
The localised ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region allowed for the roads out of Oleshky to be de-mined, making evacuation possible.
While Ukrainian territory lies just 3 miles (5km) from Oleshky, evacuees will need to travel to the southern Russian city of Anapa and on to Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.
Davyd Arakhamia, a lawmaker with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party – who was part of the delegation to Oleshky – confirmed the evacuation of some people who were travelling to Anapa.
“From there, they will fly by plane to Belarus, and then travel by bus to their homes,” he said.
Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an online post: “At this moment, the humanitarian operation is under way in Oleshky.” Budanov is not part of the delegation in Oleshky.
While earlier reports had suggested more than 500 people wanted to move to Ukrainian territory, it was unclear how many people travelled in the convoy.
Kyiv’s delegation reached the city late on Friday morning to prepare for the evacuation, with footage on social media showing tearful residents embracing delegation members as they gathered in heavy rain to wait for the main evacuation convoy to arrive. Several hundred people, mainly older people, have chosen to stay.
Asked if she was packed and ready to leave by a member of the Ukrainian delegation, a woman who identified herself as “Anna” was shown on video saying: “Yes, we are on bus 20, my son is on bus 17. To Ukraine.”
Oleshky’s population has declined to about 2,000 since the star of the war, according to authorities and volunteers, and many of those who stayed have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads to get food and water.
Some say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild plants added.
“We’ve been through so much here in these five years,” one woman said in a report broadcast on Ukrainian TV. Another older woman, preparing to evacuate, said: “If we had our health, maybe we’d stay there a bit longer, but that’s it. We just want to be with our children.”
Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with people there, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city.
“They are currently checking empty houses and, in some cases, moving into them,” she told the Associated Press. “They are also pressuring local residents to evacuate to Russia, rather than to Ukraine,” she added.
The convoy arrived under a ceasefire in the area, which the US first lady, Melania Trump, claimed to have helped broker – a rare example of cooperation between the warring sides.
On Friday, the Kremlin, however, described it as a special case that was “difficult to extrapolate” to the wider search for a peace settlement.
Oleshky was seized by Russian troops during the first days of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
It has suffered extensive damage and was badly flooded after the destruction of the huge upriver Kakhovka dam in June 2023.
“The problem is that a lot of people are staying,” one woman told Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who was on the ground to coordinate the operation with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.
“I’ve been told that it’s their own choice,” Lubinets replied. “At the very least, we’ll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through.”
He added: “This is the first time since 2022 that a ceasefire has been established across such an extensive stretch of the frontline and has been maintained for such a significant duration.”

GELEPHU (BHUTAN) A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) in Shintapu Tsho in the Laya area of northwestern Bhutan’s Gasa district on Thursday night (October 29, 2026) triggered flooding along the Mochhu, damaging roads, bridges and public infrastructure in two districts.
Officials on Friday (October 30, 2026) said no human casualties have been reported, but there are growing concerns over a large artificial lake formed near Taktsemakhang, about 2,000 feet downstream of Laya. The accumulation of water at the confluence of the flood-affected channels of Mochhu (river) has raised fears of another sudden outburst, which could be disastrous for downstream areas.
Officials said they could not immediately assess the GLOF impact on Thursday night (October 29, 2026). Royal Bhutan Army personnel stationed at Taktsemakhang and people near Gasa Tshachu, a hot spring, were instructed to evacuate to a safer location.
“Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay is in Laya to assess the artificial lake at Taktesakhang, while Industry, Commerce and Employment Minister Namgyel Dorji is monitoring the situation in Punakha,” a Department of Local Governance and Disaster Management official said.
Punakha and Thimphu districts are south of Gasa, which borders the Tibetan Autonomous Region. These and other neighbouring districts were put on high alert for potential danger from the GLOF-induced artificial lake.
According to disaster management officials, Gasa Tsachu, one of Bhutan’s popular hot spring destinations, suffered extensive damage due to Thursday’s (October 29, 2026) GLOF. Floodwaters washed away almost all public facilities in the area.
This was the second flood-related damage at Gasa Tshachu since August 26, 2021, when the swollen Mochhu changed course towards the area.
The GLOF also damaged two vital roads in Gasa district and swept away a Bailey bridge in Punakha district. The bridge was constructed in 2022 with support from the Government of India.
Melting Himalayan glaciers endanger all of South Asia
In Assam, Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said the State government was closely monitoring the possible impact of the Bhutan GLOF. “The vulnerable revenue circles in (western Assam’s) Dhubri and Kokrajhar districts have been put on high alert,” he said.
Shintaphu Tsho (Lake), located at the source of the Mochhu, is among Bhutan’s 17 glacial lakes identified as potentially dangerous. The Mochhu, considered female, and Phochhu (male) meet in Punakha district to form the Punatsangchhu, which flows along the Assam-West Bengal border as the Sonkosh River.

Breeders' Cup: Sun Goddess in class of her own with Juvenile Fillies Turf win at Keeneland as Libertango takes Juvenile Turf Sprint
Sun Goddess capped off a memorable two-year-old season with a fourth success at the top level with a scintillating display in the Breeders' Cup Juvenile Fillies Turf on a winning night for the European raiders at Keeneland; Libertango won the opening Juvenile Turf Sprint
Friday 30 October 2026 22:08, UK
Sun Goddess confirmed herself as a two-year-old out of the ordinary with a clear-cut win Breeders' Cup Juvenile Fillies Turf at Keeneland.
Seen by many as the banker of the two-day meeting, she already had three Group Ones in Europe to her credit but she had to contend with the journey to America and stall nine.
However, Ryan Moore got her out of the stalls sharply and across to the inside in the perfect position just behind the leader whereas her main market rival, Francis-Henri Graffard's Amusingly, had to settle at the rear of the field.
As soon as Moore kicked clear early in the straight the race was over as a contest and once again it was left to Joseph O'Brien's Green Empress to chase her home, the fourth time she has been second to the winner this year.
- Sun Goddess dazzles in the Breeders' Cup Juvenile Fillies Turf
- Libertango and Billy Loughnane storm to Breeders' Cup success
Johnny Murtagh's Curracloe ran a fine race to finish third while Amusingly made late gains under Colin Keane for fourth. Joseph O'Brien's Alwaysanangel finished fifth in a clean sweep for the Europeans.
It was Aidan O'Brien's 22nd Breeders' Cup winner, meaning he has now had more winners at the meeting than anybody else, having been previously tied with Bob Baffert.
O'Brien said: "She was just really natural all the way from day one.
"She obviously had a run or two before Royal Ascot and she's taken everything in her stride.
"We could have taken in the Fillies' Mile in Newmarket on the way, and the lads just decided this with the view to next year. They wanted her here, so that's why she's here.
"Whether it's six furlongs, seven or even a mile now it all comes alike to her.
"Ryan just lets her come out and he lets her get comfortable in the first half and in the second half she comes home really well.
"I suppose a worry today was we all know what she can do when there's a strong pace on in front of her. He thought that he was going to end up a lot more forward than usual on her because he wasn't sure what was going to take her. So that's exactly what he did.
"I thought he gave her a beautiful ride. It was all very clean cut, no chances. The filly had a lovely day out.
"We usually start this kind of filly in the Guineas, I'd imagine the English Guineas is where she will start and there's a chance she might stay further."
Moore said: "What she's done this year is very unique, that is her fourth Group One from nine starts, that was her first over a mile though and the first time round a bend.
"There was a lot new to her but she was able to sit just off the pace and the pace was very ordinary really, we felt like we went a lot slower than we normally do in Cup races over a mile here.
"She was in front a long way from home and she was only idling really. It's hard to know where the bottom is for her. Hopefully she can continue next year."
Co-owner Michael Tabor said: "To win wherever the Breeders' Cup is held is very special because it's great competition and the crowds make it.
"I love American racing but it's tougher (to win) out here. Paul Shanahan buys so many of our horses and the irony of it is that this is maybe the cheapest (£120,000) he's bought but probably the best."
O'Brien went on to notch his 23rd Breeders' Cup success when Haffner claimed the Juvenile Turf.
Libertango delivers for Boughey and late sub Loughnane
Libertango came with a sustained late run under substitute jockey Billy Loughnane to win the Breeders' Cup Juvenile Turf Sprint at Keeneland.
In the days leading up to the race new UK champion jockey Loughnane had resigned himself to not taking the mount as her weight of 8st 7lb was 3lb lower than he had ridden at all season.
Loughnane could not face the prospect of seeing someone else take the mount, though, and having made a concerted effort in recent days to keep the weight off, one final stint in the sauna saw him meet the required point on the scales and trainer George Boughey was only happy to stand by his stable jockey.
Flavien Prat was the unlucky man to miss out, but bar meeting a slight but of trouble on the turn for home behind Andrew Balding's Moonrise, everything else went to plan.
Wesley Ward's Ruiva was the one to catch before Harper's Corner briefly hit the front only for Libertango to swamp them all. Adrian Keatley's Hell Of A Spin ran a massive race to get up for second.
Loughnane said: "I don't know what to say. I've ridden this filly in every single race and in every piece of work she's ever done and I thought I was going to have to give up the ride on her today.
"I've watched my weight for the last two weeks, obviously condolences to Flavien but I managed to just get enough off in the sauna and I'm sat on the smallest saddle I've ever ridden on. It's good to be able to get the weight off.
"It was awful thinking someone else was going to ride her but big thanks to George and all the team, it was literally 45 minutes before the race it was confirmed.
"She has such a good racing brain, she went to sleep. There was interference on the turn but she didn't even break stride and when I moved her out she hit the wire fantastic.
"I'm riding at 8st 10lb later on so I'd been aiming for that and I'd never been down to 8st 5lb all the time I've been riding, but it's a massive advantage having saunas here, we don't have them in England."
Boughey said: "Credit to Billy I didn't think he would do the weight but the saunas helped and it's the stuff of dreams. All credit to Billy as that was some ride.
"Flavien was meant to ride and it was a very late decision. Billy had ridden her all year and he text me when he got to the track saying he weighed in a lot lighter than he expected. I'd like to apologise to Flavien because he'd been booked a while and it was probably one of his better mounts of the day.
"The race look mapped out for her even from Royal Ascot. That was the plan to come here and for her to train as well as she did through the last few races, it wasn't a huge surprise that she was able to put in a performance like that today.
"The Breeders' Cup for me is as good as it gets. She's been ridden so beautifully by Billy all year. To say he wasn't riding her until 55 minutes before the race, he's just an extraordinary talent."

Erin Patterson is set to find out if she could face a longer prison sentence or a new trial, as Victoria’s highest court hands down its decision on two appeals regarding her triple murder case.
The court of appeal is set to rule on the two appeals from 10am on Friday, after justices Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd heard arguments from her legal team and prosecutors in August.
Patterson, 52, is not expected to attend the appeal decision in person.
She was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.
Patterson was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.
She has appealed against her convictions, while the director of public prosecutions appealed against Patterson’s sentence, arguing that it was manifestly inadequate.
In August, the court heard Patterson should have been given no possibility of ever being released from prison, or a non-parole period so lengthy that she was likely to die behind bars.
Her lawyers argued seven grounds for her appeal, including that allowing jurors to stay in the same hotel as police and the prosecution while they deliberated over their verdicts in the triple murder trial represented a “catastrophic” failure of the justice system.
Richard Edney, for Patterson, said the failure to properly separate the jury during their deliberations was a fundamental irregularity that had denied her a fair trial.
“What we say has occurred here in the applicant’s trial was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure of a process,” Edney told the court in August.
They also argued that the trial judge Christopher Beale erred in ruling that photos and videos related to mushrooms and found on an SD card in Patterson’s home was inadmissible, as it tended to support her evidence that she foraged for mushrooms.
During the hearings, Brendan Kissane KC, the DPP, said that even though Patterson would be aged in her 80s by the time she was eligible for parole, her sentence was still too lenient.
When asked whether a longer non-parole period would essentially damn Patterson to dying behind bars, and had “some artifice of it being life with life”, Kissane told the court: “It has its harsh aspect to it, of course, we accept that.”
“But in our submission that is not a matter that is outweighed by the seriousness of the offending.”
There are several possible outcomes to Patterson’s appeal: leave to appeal is not granted; leave to appeal is granted, but her appeal dismissed; leave to appeal is granted, her appeal upheld and a retrial ordered; or her leave to appeal is granted, the appeal upheld, and acquittal entered.
If either of the final two decisions are handed down, there will be no need to rule on the DPP’s sentence appeal.
If not, either the appeal fails, or it succeeds and Patterson is resentenced by the court of appeal.

Indian shuttler P. V. Sindhu made short work of her Round of 16 opponent Rosy Oktavia Pancasari at the Hylo Open 2026 in Saarbrücken, Germany, on Thursday.

The two-time Olympic medallist comes into the Super 500 tournament on the back of a runner-up finish at the French Open Super 750, where she lost to World No. 1 An Se-young in the final.

She will take on compatriot Unnati Hooda for a spot in the final four.
Earlier in the day, Malvika Bansod lost to Canada’s Wen Yu Zhang 11-21, 17-21 in the round of 16.

ఫ్రాన్స్ నిరసనల సందర్భంగా, నిరసనకారులను ఎదుర్కోవడానికి ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్ను సిద్ధం చేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ఫ్రాన్స్లో నిరసనకారులను అడ్డుకునేందుకు పోలీసులు ‘పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్’ను సిద్ధం చేయడాన్ని చూపుతున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఇది కృత్రిమ మేధ (AI)తో సృష్టించిన ఫేక్ వీడియో. ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు అలాంటి స్క్వాడ్ను ఏర్పాటు చేసినట్లు ఆధారాలు లేవు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, ఈ విషయం గురించి ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతకగా, నిరసనల కోసం ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు ఇటువంటి పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్ను సిద్ధం చేయడం గురించి ఎటువంటి విశ్వసనీయ వార్తా కథనాలు లభించలేదు.
ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, ఇందులో ఉన్న మనుషుల ముఖాలు, అక్షరాలు అస్పష్టంగా, అసహజంగా ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. దీని ఆధారంగా, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోని కృత్రిమ మేధ (AI) ఉపయోగించి సృష్టించి ఉండొచ్చని తెలుస్తోంది.
దీని ఆధారంగా, ఈ వీడియోను AI వీడియో డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్తో(ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పరీక్షించగా, ఈ వీడియోను ఏఐతో రూపొందించినట్లు స్పష్టమైంది.
అలాగే, ఈ వీడియోను ముందుగా ‘Jaranor films’ అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీ అప్లోడ్ (ఆర్కైవ్) చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియో AI ద్వారా చేయబడిందనే లేబుల్ ఇందులో ఉంది. ఈ పేజీ వివిధ ఏఐ వీడియోలను రూపొందిస్తుంది. గతంలో కూడా ఈ పేజీలో అప్లోడ్ చేసిన ఈఫిల్ టవర్పై పాలస్తీనా జెండా వీడియో గురించి మేము రాసిన ఫాక్ట్-చెక్ కథనాన్ని ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, నిరసనకారులను ఎదుర్కోవడానికి ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్ను సిద్ధం చేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక AI వీడియోను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
- Published
The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.
Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey.
Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.
The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.
On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.
The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.
Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.
But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".
Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."
Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.
The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.
A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.

A chill in the air and leaves tumbling to the ground means Halloween must be approaching, bringing a holiday season full of spooky decorations, bone-chilling movies and more candy than is reasonable for any human to eat.

Update | Oct 30, 19:55 IST The Competition Commission of India (CCI) has cleared Prosus' investment in Navi to acquire a minority interest in the IPO-bound fintech company. "The Target is the holding company of the Navi Group, which offers financial services accessible through a single consumer-facing mobile app. The Target offers transparent, user-friendly financial products through its subsidiaries, all accessible via mobile devices," the CCI said. Original | Aug 19, 18:54 IST Global VC firm Prosus has invested $100 Mn (over ₹955 Cr) in Sachin Bansal-led fintech startup Navi, marking the latter’s first institutional capital raise. The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals, including clearance from the Competition Commission of India (CCI), Navi said in a statement. The fintech startup did not disclose the valuation at which Prosus is making the investment, the stake the investor will acquire, or how it plans to deploy the fresh capital. “My association with Naspers and the Prosus Group dates back more than a decade, making this partnership particularly meaningful. Their investment is a strong endorsement of the institution we’re building at Navi,” cofounder and executive chairman Bansal said. In a statement, Navi said that it is entering its next phase of growth with strong operating momentum across its businesses. Ashutosh Sharma, head of Prosus India investments and M&A, said the investor was backing Navi on account of its large user base, multiple business lines, and technology-first approach. “We believe the team has executed extremely well in the last 12 months despite a tough macro environment, which makes the company well-positioned to capture significant opportunities in the sector in times to come,” Sharma added. During FY26, Navi UPI claims to have strengthened its position as digital payments platforms, while Navi Finserv continued to scale its lending franchise responsibly with AUM crossing ₹13K Cr. The company also said the Navi Group achieved consolidated profitability in the fourth quarter of FY26 but did not disclose the financial figures. NBFC arm Navi Finserv’s standalone net profit increased 32% YoY to ₹292.2 Cr in FY26, while its operating revenue rose 8% to ₹2,461 Cr. However, its consolidated net profit declined 46% to ₹93.3 Cr during the year, even as operating revenue grew 17% to ₹2,691.5 Cr. Navi’s IPO Plans The investment comes at a time when Navi is reportedly looking to revive its public listing plans. Recent reports suggested that the fintech startup could refile its draft IPO papers with the SEBI by December this year. Navi is said to be eyeing a fresh issue of around ₹3,000 Cr and has appointed JM Financial, Kotak Mahindra Capital, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan as advisers for the proposed offering. This would mark Navi’s second attempt to go public. The startup filed its draft papers with SEBI in 2022 for a ₹3,350 Cr IPO but later shelved the plan amid adverse market conditions. Founded by Bansal and Ankit Agarwal in 2018, Navi offers financial products across lending, insurance, mutual funds, and UPI payments. Bansal stepped down as the startup’s chief executive in February 2025 and took over as its executive chairman. Navi said its UPI platform retained its position as India’s fourth-largest third-party application provider by transaction volume during FY26. Meanwhile, the assets under management of its lending arm, Navi Finserv, crossed ₹13,000 Cr.

Nearly 2 out of 3 teens and tweens use AI chatbots, new research shows
Artificial intelligence chatbots are increasingly becoming a regular part of life for American youth. Two new surveys show that nearly two-thirds of tweens and teens use AI chatbots. While most kids use the technology for help with school work, and for companionship and emotional support, certain uses were linked with worse mental health symptoms.
One survey, done by the online safety advocacy group, Common Sense Media, found that AI use starts early – years before kids hit the minimum age of 13 on most popular chatbots. Nearly half 9-to-12-year-olds have used an AI chatbot or companion. By the time kids are 13 years old, nearly three-quarters of them have used chatbots.
The other survey, done by the mental health advocacy group JED Foundation, found that 90% of the 5,500 9-to-17-year-olds in schools across the country have used an AI chatbot. Nearly two-thirds use it both for schoolwork and as companions, or when they are stressed, lonely, anxious or overwhelmed.
The findings are "remarkable" in showing how dramatically AI use by children and teens has changed in a short time, says developmental psychologist Anne Maheux at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, who wasn't involved in the surveys.
"It seems like just a few years ago, no one was using" the technology, she says. "And now it seems like roughly the same number of kids using it for homework are using it to get emotional support or help with coping."
"I use it to make myself practice sample questions – sample test questions that I will answer with my own work," says 15-year-old Arjun Sharda, in Round Rock, Texas. "I use it to understand concepts outside of the classroom."
He uses both OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, he says, although he prefers the latter lately.
In Raynham, Mass., McKenzie Craig, 17, has been using chatbots since she was in eighth grade. "I use it typically if I'm overwhelmed with a bunch of tasks I have," she says. "I'll have it help me prioritize the tasks."
She also uses it for help with assignments. "If I write an essay, I'll run it through either Grammarly or ChatGPT and have it graded, so to speak," says Craig. "It gives me feedback, and then I can edit accordingly."
Sharda says he and his friends also turn to chatbots when they are stressed and anxious.
"With tests, for example," he says, "I was so scared of failing one of my first chemistry tests on conversions and moles that I kept asking ChatGPT 'Will I be OK? Will my GPA still be fine?'"
Some chatbot uses are linked to worse mental health
Researchers at the JED Foundation also surveyed students on symptoms of overall well-being and mental health.
"We were able to look at how young people are using AI and then how that correlates separately with indicators of well-being, history of suicidal ideation and attempts, and poor mental health," says psychologist Kayla Anderson, vice president of research and evaluation at the JED Foundation.
"When young people are using AI, when they're in emotional distress," she adds, "they're more likely to report poor mental health and well-being outcomes." They also report a greater history of suicidal thoughts and attempts.
But the data don't suggest a causal link, cautions Anderson.
"It's unclear, based on these data, whether AI use is contributing to poor mental health and well-being, or whether students who are already in distress in certain ways are more likely to turn to AI," she explains.
But preliminary data collected by other researchers suggests that the link between chatbots and poorer mental health symptoms in young people might go both ways, says Maheux.
"So kids who do have worse mental health are seeking out AI to help them," she says. "But that AI use may be exacerbating those mental health challenges instead of helping."
In a soon-to-be-published study of middle schoolers in one state, Maheux and her colleagues at UNC found that students who use chatbots for companionship grew lonelier over time.
They found similar results in another study of young adults. "We see that people who are using AI more for companionship or feeling like they're overreliant on AI to solve various emotional or cognitive problems, are developing worse mental health over time."
One potential explanation for this effect, she says, is that AI is easing people's emotional distress — loneliness, anxiety, stress — in the immediate moment, but that reliance on the technology is preventing young people from developing the skills to tolerate and navigate normal daily stresses.
That, she explains, "can lead to worse mental health."

India is set to launch its next-generation navigation satellite, NVS-03, aboard the GSLV-F18 rocket today, Friday, October 30, at 11:51 pm IST, in a mission aimed at strengthening the country’s indigenous satellite navigation capabilities.
The launch from Sriharikota will be the GSLV rocket's 20th flight and marks another attempt by India to strengthen its own satellite navigation system, NavIC, which helps people and services determine their location and track time accurately.
The launch comes at a challenging time for NavIC, as several of its existing satellites have stopped working properly, while attempts to replace them have also faced setbacks.
The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has scheduled the GSLV-F18/NVS-03 mission for October 30, 2026, at 11:51 pm Indian Standard Time.
The 51.7-metre-tall GSLV Mk II rocket will lift off from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota.
Its primary task will be to place the 2,232 kg NVS-03 satellite into a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO).
Space enthusiasts can follow the launch through ISRO's official digital platforms.
Viewers should check ISRO's official website and YouTube channel for the live broadcast and mission updates.
NVS-03 is the third satellite in ISRO's new-generation NavIC programme, which aims to improve and strengthen India's home-grown navigation system.
The satellite will carry an Indian-made atomic clock along with other clocks sourced from outside the country. It will also introduce support for an additional signal, which could help more smartphones and navigation devices use NavIC.
With these improvements, India hopes to make its navigation system more reliable and useful for everyday needs. NavIC is designed to cover the whole of India and areas extending up to 1,500 km beyond its borders.
Atomic clocks play a crucial role in helping navigation satellites pinpoint locations accurately. Even a tiny error in timekeeping can affect how accurately a phone or other device identifies where someone is.
By developing its own atomic clocks, ISRO hopes to rely less on imported technology and give India greater control over its satellite navigation system.
NVS-03 will also support an additional signal, known as the L1 band, alongside the existing signals. This is expected to make NavIC more compatible with smartphones and other navigation devices, while allowing it to work more effectively alongside systems such as the US-based GPS.
NavIC has been facing several problems in recent years, with a number of its older satellites developing faults or becoming unusable. Some stopped working because of failures in their onboard clocks, while others could not reach the right orbit.
The system suffered another setback in January 2025, when ISRO's NVS-02 satellite failed to move into its intended orbit because of a problem with its thrusters. As a result, it could not begin providing navigation services as planned.
The situation became more difficult in March 2026, when the last working atomic clock aboard another satellite, IRNSS-1F, also stopped functioning. This left NavIC with only three satellites capable of supporting navigation services, fewer than the four needed for the system to work fully.
ISRO is now looking to rebuild the network with NVS-03, followed by two more satellites, NVS-04 and NVS-05. Together, these launches are expected to help make India's navigation system more reliable.
ISRO has also made changes to avoid a repeat of the problem that affected NVS-02. For the new mission, the space agency has decided to keep certain valves open before launch to prevent a similar technical fault from occurring.
The successful launch of NVS-03 would be an important step towards making India's own navigation system stronger and more dependable. It could also reduce the country's reliance on foreign systems such as GPS, which are widely used for navigation and other essential services, including banking, transport and telecommunications.

I am scheduled to die on August 10, 2060, at the age of 74.
So says my iPhone screen, where Death Clock, an AI-powered longevity app that predicts life expectancy based on your medical habits and lifestyle, has produced an image of a smiling grim reaper to celebrate my expiration date. There he was one September morning, looking especially thrilled about the reveal, gesturing with a peace sign as he reclined in a doughnut-shaped pool inflatable under that giant number: 74.
I have never resented getting older, but I suppose that’s younger than I’d like to be when my time is up. In the last four years—years that brought the passing of my grandmother and aunt within 18 months—I’ve become hyperaware of how finite my days are. Since turning 40 in January, I’ve also experienced daily reminders of aging: inexplicable pains that rotate between my back, neck, and hips. Spiritually, I feel young; physically, my body screams otherwise. Aging is natural, but I had a creeping suspicion I could buy myself more time.
Our collective obsession with life extension has given rise to a multitrillion-dollar longevity industry, bolstered by wannabe prophets like Bryan Johnson. Threats like climate change and AI doomerism only seem to have intensified existential fears, even as LLMs promise a new era of personalized medicine to address any health issue. Track enough pieces of data, the thinking goes, and algorithms can help you hack your own demise.
All of which led me to Death Clock, an app launched in 2024 aimed at tracking users’ health habits in an attempt to prolong their lives. In February, the company announced a new feature that lets you order biomarker panels. For a $69 subscription, you can get a basic blood panel that measures things like cholesterol, blood sugars, inflammation, vitamin D, and blood and organ health. There are also nine additional tests—assessing everything from hormones and micronutrients to your thyroid—that, altogether, cost $780. I opted for the routine blood panel and added the “stress” test ($29). Maybe some new insight could help me get a handle on it.
In an attempt to be more than another morbid countdown gimmick, Death Clock says it’s trained its AI on 1,200 longevity studies, actuarial data from life insurance companies, and life expectancy tables. Based on your results, its algorithms create a detailed prevention plan intended to help extend the time you have left.
Frankly, I was skeptical that anything meaningful would actually come from this. I was also, I can admit, a little fearful that I’d learn something I didn’t want to, a fact that might dissolve the little sanity I had left in a year that had already brought its share of unexpected problems.
After filling out an initial health questionnaire, a notification buzzed, forewarning my demise. There are three ways I will likely perish, it said: cardiovascular disease, a sleep disorder, or cancer (it doesn’t specify which type). This means, according to the app, I have already “completed” more than half of my existence on this mortal plane. A few days later, when I noted that my family has a mild history of diabetes, the app updated my age of death from 74 to 73.
And just like that, I lost a year.
I know I won’t live to be 100; people in my family generally croak in their early eighties. But was it possible to extend my lifespan by 10, even 15 years, with a hyperpersonalized plan? “You have two paths,” a message from the app exclaimed. “We are here to help you achieve the longer one.” I made an appointment with Quest Diagnostics, one of the two labs the company has partnered with, and willingly gave Death Clock my blood.
There’s no shortage of products that aim to reshape our relationship to our bodies. My inbox overflows with emails from longevity zealots pitching the latest anti-aging fads: salmon sperm scalp injections, a platelet-rich plasma treatment “Hailey Bieber swears by.” It’s almost too much, this urge to cheat the natural order of time.
“That’s a fool errand,” Death Clock CEO Brent Franson tells me one afternoon. He says advocates like Johnson—whose mantra “Don’t Die” reads more like a rejected Nike slogan than a wellness-oriented affirmation—“have to be really careful about inferring immortality when you have something to sell. That’s a dangerous place to be. The reality is we’re all going to die. It’s a question of when.”
Over Zoom, all I can think about is what Franson is trying to sell me.
The longevity market is projected to reach $8 trillion by 2030, meaning the future of health care may be shaped less by traditional treatment and more by personalized AI health services. With Doctronic, a HIPAA-compliant platform that works like a personal AI doctor, people can refill prescriptions without the need to see a human physician, while apps like Superpower and Lifeforce (similar to Death Clock) offer membership-based health insights and clinician-reviewed recommendations. Twin Health purports to create an AI replica, whatever that means, of a person’s metabolism. All of it is meant to help us live a little longer, though it’s unclear exactly how and at what cost.
Mike Ludkovski, a professor of statistics and applied probability at UC Santa Barbara whose research focuses on longevity analysis, says mortality awareness platforms like Death Clock “sell the illusion that individual lifespan is a linear process” that can be hacked. A 2024 Aging Cell study likewise suggested that an aging clock shouldn’t be treated as a measure of someone’s overall biological age. “Ultimately, individual-level triggers precipitating death are inherently random and will never be truly forecastable,” Ludkovski says.
I ask Franson if we’re actually getting healthier or just growing more anxious about being unhealthy. “I think both,” he says. “There’s a very unhealthy obsession with self-optimization—tracking everything, trying to control everything.”
Wasn’t Death Clock, in part, also guilty of that?
When the blood panels returned a week after I gave my sample, the results were mostly what my doctor had warned me about earlier this year. I’ve got borderline high cholesterol and blood sugar levels “creeping toward prediabetic range.” Shockingly, I have “optimal liver health” and normal cortisol levels. Videos from so-called wellness influencers had convinced me that a string of recent sleepless nights were the result of high cortisol, but, it turns out, the algorithm isn’t always right.
Based on my results, the app kept feeding me more tasks. Increase my vitamin D3! Schedule a DEXA scan for bone density! Discuss a prostate-specific antigen screening with a specialist! Despite Franson’s claim that he wants Death Clock to eventually be a replacement for primary care physicians, the app kept nudging me to discuss my results with a doctor.
Ultimately, I started to realize, tracking health data can only do so much. There is a belief, says Gretchen Terry-Leonard, author of Your Second Prime: Does Aging Suck, or Do We Suck at Aging?, that being able to measure something means it can also be managed. Death doesn’t work that way, she says, “so the measuring starts to serve a different need: the need to feel less afraid.”
Terry-Leonard is also the cofounder of the Center for Deeply Human Leadership, an independent research institute studying AI’s effect on brain health. She’s skeptical that consumer-facing longevity apps can lead to positive behavioral shifts on their own. “Facts don’t change minds,” she says. People understand that certain activities are unhealthy, but they do them anyway.
Keeping death in view is one of the oldest practices we have, and what seems to matter is whether a person feels they have the personal agency to make the necessary adjustments in their life. Researchers who study how thoughts of death shape health choices find that people move toward healthier behavior when they also have the confidence and resources to act, which not everyone does. “And without those,” Terry-Leonard tells me, “the anxiety tends to go into protecting how we feel about ourselves rather than into our health.”
While researching her book, Terry-Leonard found that older adults with more positive attitudes about aging lived an average of seven and a half years longer than those with negative outlooks. An app with a death countdown “can quietly teach us that aging is loss,” hindering longevity rather than promoting it.
In the month that I used Death Clock, this was the fact I couldn’t completely escape. I became a meticulous steward of my bodily functions, logging “daily habits” with the verve of an accountant manically calculating numbers just before tax deadline. In a single day I added 5.8 years to my life by earmarking that I’d completed at least 30 minutes of strength training, abstained from alcohol, brushed and flossed my teeth, gotten consistent sleep, spent time in the sauna, and drank more than eight glasses of water. But even as I labored to improve my death date, the clock was always there, counting down. It was an albatross that moved in a single, uniform direction: tick, tick, tick. Time became a burden I was being forced to optimize.
It makes sense that people are preoccupied with the very thing they are trying to escape. The need for control is addictive. But instead of assuaging my anxieties and questions about the great beyond, Death Clock only seemed to amplify them.
As the image of the life I want to build sharpens in my mind, a life that has already unfolded in deliciously unforeseen ways, I realize it has less to do with how I will make things happen and has everything to do with who I want them to happen with. Life isn’t about adding more time, but making it count when we can. I silenced Death Clock’s notifications on my phone and texted a friend: “Let’s meet at 7.”

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."
