Welcome to Edition 9.17 of the Rocket Report! It’s been a while since an American company announced plans for a medium-lift new launch vehicle, but that’s what happened this week when a startup named Cowboy Space revealed specs for its Big Iron rocket, named for the classic country-western song by Marty Robbins. I’m a huge fan of the name. Maybe Cowboy Space is striking while the iron is hot as the space industry frets over demand for launch outpacing supply. However, Cowboy Space lags far behind so many other launch providers nearing the launch pad with their medium-class rockets, and the company didn’t have much hardware to show at this week’s big reveal. In other words, don’t mistake style for substance. But we’re rocket fans at Ars, and we wish them luck.
As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Virgin’s new rocket plane reaches home port. The first of Virgin Galactic’s new Delta-class rocket planes left its Arizona factory Wednesday for a trip to Spaceport America in neighboring New Mexico, where it will undergo preparations for a test campaign culminating in suborbital flights to the edge of space, Ars reports. Virgin Galactic expects the craft’s first commercial spaceflight to take place “early” in the second quarter of 2027, but like every other projected date in aerospace, this should be taken with a grain of salt. Virgin Galactic halted commercial flights of its previous vehicle, VSS Unity, in 2024.
More to do … The company also revealed the rocket plane’s name: Apeiron. Engineers and technicians at Spaceport America will complete work on the vehicle’s avionics equipment and flight software. Following additional ground tests, Apeiron will be mated again to its carrier aircraft for captive carry tests, followed by a drop test and ultimately a powered test flight above 80 km. With Blue Origin’s retreat from the suborbital spaceflight market and SpaceX’s planned retirement of the orbital-class Dragon spacecraft, Virgin Galactic is the only company with a realistic chance of flying paying commercial passengers to space anytime soon.
ESA’s reusable rocket testbed seems cursed. The European Space Agency’s Director of Space Transportation, Géraldine Naja, said on October 22 that she was uncertain whether the agency would be able to complete the first flight of its Themis reusable rocket demonstrator before the end of the year, European Spaceflight reports. The single-stage rocket hopper has completed two countdown rehearsals at Esrange Space Center in Sweden, but the harsh Scandinavian winter may prevent Themis from taking flight this year.
Missed schedules … ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher said in January that the Themis rocket’s first hop test would happen in the first quarter of 2026. Delays are nothing new for Themis. Officials originally expected the rocket’s first low-altitude hop test to occur in 2022. The rocket is powered by a reusable methane-fueled Prometheus engine. ArianeGroup, the company behind Europe’s Ariane rocket family, is the main contractor on Themis, which is supposed to test technologies for an eventual reusable replacement for the expendable Ariane 6.
Rocket Report
Keep up with the latest in space exploration and rocket launches.
Cowboy Space unveils new rocket. Cowboy Space on Monday released the first details about the launcher that it plans to loft before the end of 2028, Aviation Week & Space Technology reports. The rocket, named Big Iron, will be 282 feet (86 meters) tall and about 15 feet (4.7 meters) in diameter. Cowboy Space is developing a methane-fueled engine named Clydesdale. Nine of them will power the first stage, and the second stage will fly a single Clydesdale. Big Iron’s payload capacity will be up to 18 metric tons (39,700 pounds) to low-Earth orbit.
Let the horses run … Baiju Bhatt, the billionaire co-founder of Robinhood, started his space company, originally named Aetherflux, in 2024. He rebranded the company as Cowboy Space earlier this year. Bhatt is chasing the market for space-based AI led by SpaceX. After launching into orbit, the upper stage of the Big Iron rocket will form the core of Cowboy Space’s data center spacecraft, with five racks of GPUs, six inter-satellite laser links, and solar arrays stretching the length of one-and-a-half football fields.
More good news for Stoke Space. The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital announced Monday a conditional commitment to provide a $150 million loan to Stoke Space for construction of a second launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, GeekWire reports. Stoke Space is well along in construction of its first launch pad at Cape Canaveral for its reusable medium-lift Nova rocket. The second pad would accommodate an upgraded Nova Block 2 vehicle for heavier payloads.
Swimming in cash … The $150 million government loan is subject to financial, legal, technical, and due diligence requirements. It follows Stoke Space’s $1 billion Series E fundraising round in September, bringing the company’s total amount of capital raised to $2.3 billion. Stoke aims to launch its Nova Pathfinder rocket next year, followed by Block 2 in 2029. The company’s reusable upper stage, the most innovative segment of the rocket, is now undergoing qualification testing at Moses Lake, Washington.
Industry execs forecast launch crunch. The US government may have moved too quickly to conclude that the commercial launch market could support its growing military needs, industry executives warned at a conference this week, Space News reports. The Space Force’s launch strategy, which is designed to broaden competition by tapping commercially developed rockets, has expanded the number of companies eligible to compete for military launches. But executives speaking at the 2026 Silicon Valley Space Week conference questioned whether enough capacity will be available as national security demand rises and SpaceX begins a long-planned transition from its workhorse Falcon 9 to its next-generation Starship rocket.
Pertinent quotes … An executive at Stoke Space, one of the companies seeking to break into the military launch business, said it “may have been a strategic error” for the government to assume the launch problem had been solved. Devin Papandrew, Stoke’s vice president of business development, said the government should consider additional funding, along with relief from regulatory and infrastructure constraints. The head of government relations at United Launch Alliance, the military’s leading launch provider after SpaceX, said the launch supply crunch should ease as new rockets enter service. When might that happen? “2030-ish is the best I would hope for right now,” Hunt said.
SpaceX no longer needs NASA. In a comprehensive feature story this week, Ars reports on the fraying relationship between SpaceX and NASA. For the last decade and a half, NASA has relied upon Elon Musk’s space company to resupply the International Space Station, end US reliance on Russia for crew transport, and develop a critical piece of the puzzle for beating China back to the Moon. But Musk is now all-in on AI, and SpaceX’s clear priority today is focusing on how to rapidly deploy compute on Earth and in space.
The signs are there … SpaceX continues to work on a human-rated lander for NASA’s Artemis Moon program, but there are signs of a partial breakup looming. SpaceX wants to end flights of the Crew Dragon spacecraft by 2030, and is already winding down its remarkably successful Falcon 9 rocket in favor of the company’s much larger but relatively unproven Starship. And Starship’s launch capacity will be filled by SpaceX’s internal demand for Starlink and Starmind, the company’s orbital data center constellation. SpaceX now seems increasingly disinterested in the US government for most contracts outside of data services, such as Starshield for military communications and observations.
ULA to develop upgraded Centaur for SLS. During a lengthy news conference on October 23, NASA provided a detailed overview of how it plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface as soon as 2028 as part of its Artemis program, Ars reports. The changes include revised architectures for getting astronauts to the lunar surface on landers provided by SpaceX and Blue Origin. On the launch front, NASA confirmed it will contract with United Launch Alliance to develop an upgraded version of its Centaur V upper stage to fly on the Space Launch System rocket.
LLO or bust … The “extended” Centaur V is a larger version of the upper stage that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Incorporating the extended Centaur onto the SLS rocket will allow the Orion spacecraft to reach low-lunar orbit, a capability it does not have with the current SLS upper stage. In fact, NASA officials said the extended Centaur will be higher-performing than the costly Exploration Upper Stage the agency originally planned to develop as an SLS enhancement. “Getting Orion to low-lunar orbit means solving propulsion and spacecraft integration problems that were left unaddressed for far too long,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said.
Vulcan’s return-to-flight mission has a launch date. United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company’s 2026 launch schedule into oblivion, Ars reports. The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval.
An important mission … The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. In both cases, the rocket overcame the nozzle failure and completed its mission, but officials at the US Space Force, ULA’s primary customer, lost confidence in Vulcan. It’s also important for the Space Force and Amazon, which have staked much of their future satellite fleets on the success of the Vulcan rocket.
Space Force says America needs a new spaceport. US Space Force leaders want a new spaceport up and running by 2030, adding a third heavy-lift launch site to relieve pressure on bases in Florida and California that have launched rockets into orbit for nearly 70 years, Ars reports. The obvious problem with that ambition is that 2030 is four years away, and Pentagon officials have not determined where the new spaceport should go or how to acquire land for it.
All options on the table … “We need this capability by 2030, but I’m also a pragmatist,” said Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, head of Space Systems Command. “That is not an inconsequential demand to build a spaceport when you factor in orbital regimes, safety, access to commodities, the Americans that live near it. In many ways, it’s much like an airport, but even louder. So there’s a lot of consideration.” Officials haven’t decided where to put a new spaceport. Garrant later said all options are on the table: a public-private partnership, a new military base, state land, or commercial land.
Next three launches
October 30: GSLV Mk.II | NVS-03 | Satish Dhawan Space Center, India | 18:21 UTC
October 31: Falcon 9 | Starlink 15-18 | Vandenberg Space Force Base, California | 03:48 UTC
November 2: Electron | QPS-SAR-20 | Māhia Peninsula, New Zealand | 08:45 UTC
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

Punjab, Odisha and Tamil Nadu are the frontrunners to host the 2030 FIH World Cups for both men and women, Hockey India secretary general Bhola Nath Singh confirmed to PTI.
This development confirms that India is eyeing the hosting rights for the next edition of the showpiece events.
Odisha has hosted the men’s World Cup twice, while Tamil Nadu organised the men’s Junior World Cup last year in Chennai and Madurai.
Punjab, regarded as the cradle of Indian hockey, has never hosted the mega event. The state is currently hosting the men’s Asian Champions Trophy, its first international hockey tournament in 17 years. The last international hockey event hosted by Punjab was the Gold Cup in 2009.
“Odisha, Tamil Nadu and Punjab are all in the race. If Odisha gets the Hockey World Cup, it will be a big achievement for the state. Odisha will be the first preference,” Bhola Nath said.
READ: Asian Champions Trophy 2026: Harmanpreet, Sukhjeet star in India’s 5-2 win over China
The HI secretary general said his primary focus since taking charge had been to take hockey to every corner of the country.
“I want to take hockey to every corner of the country. Tamil Nadu has produced many Olympians, and we took the Junior World Cup there last year. Punjab is now an example. We are now taking the Women’s Asian Champions Trophy to Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh. No international tournament has been held in Madhya Pradesh so far. The women’s ACT will be held from November 19 to 28 in Bhopal,” he said.
“The purpose of taking hockey to every part of the country is to build infrastructure of international standards.”
Bhola Nath said Punjab was chosen to host the ongoing Asian Champions Trophy because of its rich hockey legacy and the significant number of players from the state in the national squad.
“When I became the secretary general of Hockey India, I saw that most of the players in the team were from Punjab. When I spoke to the boys from Punjab, they used to say that they had played in countries across the world, but their parents had never seen them play an international match. So, I wanted to organise an international tournament in Punjab,” he said.
“The talks were going on, and one day I met Bhagwant Mann (Punjab Chief Minister) and discussed this with him. He said he was ready and would do it.”

Some of the health harms of climate change grew faster in the decade since the Paris Agreement entered into force (2016-2025) than in the previous decade (2006-2015) as climate action fails to keep pace, according to the 10th Lancet Countdown Report on Health and Climate Change.
The report, which was released on Wednesday, said the annual average heat-related deaths rose by nearly 36% globally after the Paris Agreement was introduced.
"In 2023 alone, heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths with more than 70 per cent of that toll attributable to human-caused climate change," it said.
The analysis represents the work of 146 multidisciplinary researchers from more than 100 institutions across more than 30 countries. It tracks 54 indicators of the health impacts of climate change and the health effects of climate action.
The report highlights that cleaner energy, more resilient health systems, more health-protecting legislation and growing scientific evidence have brought real health benefits to local communities since the Paris Agreement, but these gains are still too slow, too insufficient, and too inconsistent to offset the growing risks.
"Rising overall energy demand and slow system change means fossil fuels still supply over 80% of the world's energy, and climate-heating emissions reached a record high in 2024," it said.
The report added that despite gains in some countries, fossil-fuel air pollution still kills an estimated 2.8 million people a year worldwide.
Moreover, adaptation funding is falling far short of what's needed.
According to the report, the health adaptation needs quantified so far by developing countries put the minimum cost at $3.3 billion a year, based on data from only 48 of the 79 countries that have completed these estimates.
However, only around a third of this declared need, $1.1 billion, was committed in 2024.
"This substantial financing gap is reflected in countries' ability to translate adaptation priorities into action, with finance and human resourcing identified as the top barriers to implementation of Health National Adaptation Plans," said the report.

Elon Musk has enjoyed a cozy relationship with top Texas brass for years. And in recent weeks, as the midterm elections approach and Musk’s financial support of the Texas GOP has become virtually limitless, that relationship has gone under the microscope.
While polls suggest that a number of races in deep-red Texas are looking dizzyingly close, Federal Election Commission filings show that Musk has given at least $158 million to super PACs supporting Texas attorney general Ken Paxton’s bid for Senate, and last week Musk explicitly endorsed him in a post on X. “The fate of Texas and America is at stake,” Musk wrote. “Vote for @KenPaxtonTX today.”
Newly released state campaign filings also show that Musk also donated $5,000,000 to Governor Greg Abbott’s bid for reelection, making him his single largest donor.
Abbott’s relationship with Musk has been the subject of public interest for years. State representative Gina Hinojosa, who is running against Abbott, recently sued to view, in full, 1,400 pages of the governor’s correspondences with Musk. Abbott has been trying to block their release for some time; his office has described the communications as too “intimate and embarrassing” to be made public. This week, a judge ruled that Abbott had illegally “obstructed and continues to obstruct” Hinojosa’s right to inspect the documents in her capacity as a state lawmaker and ordered their release to her. Abbott has since appealed; a hearing is scheduled for November 2, one day before the election.
State representative James Talarico, who is running against Paxton for Senate, has campaigned on his opponents’ checkered past. As attorney general, Paxton has been indicted on felony securities fraud charges (which he settled without a plea), was accused by whistleblowers of using his office to benefit the financial interests of a political donor, and was impeached (though later acquitted).
And at a campaign event on Monday in El Paso, Talarico raised questions about Paxton and Musk’s relationship. “Ken Paxton has the ultimate megadonor,” Talarico said. “Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat.”
But Musk’s business dealings in Texas politics didn’t start with the midterms. For years, he has enjoyed lucrative state contacts, tax breaks, and allyship from Texas leaders. In 2021, Musk moved Tesla’s corporate headquarters from Palo Alto, California, to Austin, and SpaceX’s headquarters from Hawthorne, California, to Starbase, Texas, in 2024.
Musk’s initial relocation to Texas coincided with a shift in operations inside the Texas Attorney General’s office. In the past, lawyers would prepare notices of investigation (administrative subpoenas known as CIDs) based on public complaints or evidence collected, then send them up the chain for approval.
Sources tell WIRED that from about 2021 onward, lawyers were increasingly instructed by Texas’ executive branch—which included Paxton and Abbott—who and what they were going to investigate, despite internal efforts to steer resources toward more “legitimate” issues. For example, in 2022, eyebrows were raised internally when, the same day Musk sent a letter to Twitter threatening to abandon a $44 billion acquisition agreement over Twitter’s alleged misrepresentation of the number of bots on the platform, Paxton’s office issued a statement asserting that his office would be launching its own investigation against Twitter.
A year later, Paxton once again appeared to use his office to benefit Musk. Musk sued the progressive watchdog Media Matters for defamation after it published an investigation showing that X, under Musk’s ownership, had been placing ads from major brands next to white-nationalist content. Moments after he filed his suit, Paxton’s office announced its own investigation into Media Matters. (Media Matters sued Paxton, asserting that his investigation was brought out of retaliation for its coverage of Musk and X.) In 2024, after Musk filed an antitrust lawsuit against the World Federation of Advertisers and major brands, accusing them of a conspiracy to pull revenue from X, Paxton announced his own investigation into the organization, accusing them of a “potential anticompetitive scheme to withhold advertising dollars from certain social media platforms.” (He did not mention X by name.)
And when the Department of Justice’s Public Integrity Section wrote a letter to Musk warning that his America PAC million-dollar sweepstakes program ahead of the presidential election could violate federal election law, Paxton intervened by filing a FOIA request, accusing the government of “intimidation of businessman Elon Musk.”
This summer, Musk’s activities in Texas didn’t slow down: Texas legislators called for an audit after the Texas Broadband Development Office allocated $110 million in grants to Musk’s satellite internet company Starlink; Texas’ Office of the Comptroller recently announced that “Terafab,” Musk’s proposed 100-million-square-foot chip manufacturing facility in Grimes County, was the recipient of a $1.66 billion tax break; and SpaceX has also received around $30 million in state grants.

MrBeast has found his first CMO, Business Insider exclusively learned.
The top YouTuber's company promoted Michelle St. Jacques to the role. St. Jacques has led consumer goods, including Feastables, MrBeast's snack and candy company, since February.
In her new role, she'll add marketing duties for Beast Industries, the star's holding company, while continuing to oversee consumer goods. She's based in Chicago.
Beast Industries started the search earlier this year, a move that reflected the company's growing ambitions. It's been expanding far beyond its core YouTube channel and seeks to become a Disney-style entertainment giant.
Beast Industries CEO Jeff Housenbold said in a memo to staff, viewed by Business Insider, that he considered external candidates for the CMO role but decided St. Jacques was the best person for the job.
"In her time at Beast, MSJ has shown she can set clear strategy and deliver strong execution for our products and partners," he wrote. "She has served as both CMO and Chief Commercial Officer and built iconic consumer brands like Dove, Heinz, Miller Lite, and Coors Light. She's also a world-class people leader who knows how to build high-performing teams."
St. Jacques joined the company following a slowdown in Feastables' growth.
Housenbold wrote that St. Jacques' remit would involve defining the MrBeast brand and making sure everything the company does ladders up to the same positioning; leading marketing for MrBeast and partner brands; and overseeing the viral marketing team. He said that he saw an opportunity to lean into e-commerce and performance marketing to drive customer acquisition and retention.
St. Jacques steps into a role overseeing a brand that's looking to lessen its reliance on its famous founder. Her job requires someone who can do everything from getting people to theatrical releases — Donaldson lent his voice to "Angry Birds Movie 3," which is scheduled for a December release — to selling snacks and toys in stores, or pitching fans on phone plans and financial products.
Beast Industries has made a string of big hires to bulk up its executive suite. Along with Feastables, the company has begun to move into financial services with the acquisition of the Step app and has planned a mobile phone service.
The company is also laying the groundwork to expand into ad and marketing services for brands and additional services for other independent content creators like MrBeast, and has teased a membership program.

Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
- Published
For the last three decades, Novaya Gazeta has been one of the most high-profile independent news outlets in Russia.
Now it's shutting down - and it has accused the Russian authorities of the "murder" of a newspaper.
"They've killed us," reads a statement on the Novaya Gazeta website.
"The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."
Novaya Gazeta has received an eviction order. Crucially, at the same time, the system that had allowed the paper to receive donations from readers was disabled.
That leaves no way to fund the publication.
Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.
The paper said that over time six journalists connected with the paper were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty." Those reporters include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block 20 years ago this month. Among the subjects she had reported on were the wars in Chechnya.
In the statement announcing its closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities, claiming the newspaper was the victim of a "coordinated act" and blaming "the repressive state apparatus".
"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime," the statement said.
"The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing.
Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the so-called "special military operation", new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.
Novaya Gazeta itself and its staff had been facing a multitude of problems.
The authorities had already revoked the newspaper's licence and blocked access to its website. Several of its journalists and contributors had been designated "foreign agents", a label often used by the Russian authorities to punish critics.
Earlier this year there was a police search of the editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information".
In connection with the case, the newspaper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, was recently taken in for police questioning and his home was searched.
Despite increasing pressure, Novaya Gazeta had managed to continue operating, albeit in a reduced form.
Loyal readers used virtual private networks to circumvent official blocking of the website and access content. But the loss of its licence and other restrictions dealt a major blow.
One of the founders of Novaya Gazeta in the 1990s - and for many years its chief editor - was journalist Dmitry Muratov, external. In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".
The award didn't stop the authorities from declaring him a "foreign agent" in 2023.
At the offices of Novaya Gazeta, they've already started packing.
The end of this newspaper is very much the end of an era.
In an increasingly authoritarian Russia, it's also a sign of the times.

NPR special: 5 takeaways from a year of listening to swing voters
Every election, there is a crucial sliver of voters who help determine which candidates win.
These are voters who bounce from one side to the other — the rare swing voters.
And all throughout 2026, NPR has had a front-row seat to how these folks think, listening in as voters in different swing states reflect on President Trump, the political issues that matter to them, and who they might vote for going forward.
In this case, these voters supported Joe Biden in 2020 and then swung to backing Trump in 2024.
They all participated in the Swing Voter Project, which hosts online focus groups every month. They are run by messaging firm Engagious and market research recruiting firm Nelson Recruiting. NPR is a partner on the project.
So just ahead of Election Day, what have we learned from swing voters this year? Here are five takeaways:
- These Biden-to-Trump voters quickly soured on the president
- Voters are able to draw a direct line from Trump's decisions to their feelings about the economy
- It's not like Democrats are popular either!
- There appears to be a convergence among voters on the left and right in support of economic populism
- There's broad concern about artificial intelligence and the proliferation of data centers
Click the audio player above to listen to a special, hour-long discussion about these takeaways and the voters.
This special — "Swing voters and the issues that matter" — was edited by Ben Swasey and produced by Lexie Schapitl.

In September, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. fired the two vice chairs of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. This move was both unsurprising and troubling. The task force is a critical advisory body to HHS, reviewing scientific evidence to provide recommendations on whether private health insurers should be required to cover services like cancer screenings at no cost to patients. Congress created the task force as part of the Affordable Care Act and require by law that it be staffed by people with “appropriate expertise,” and “to the extent practicable, not subject to political pressure.”
These firings are the latest chapter in a vast project of eliminating, ignoring, and replacing scientific advisory committees. In 2025, the Trump administration terminated 151 advisory committees at scientific government agencies, including 75 in HHS. It has altered or ignored those that are left. In 2025, Kennedy fired the entire Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which provides public recommendations on vaccines. His replacements are, to varying degrees, sympathetic to his unscientific views, and a majority lack substantial expertise in vaccines and immunology.
At the Food and Drug Administration, agency leadership has largely ignored the standing advisory committees that have historically weighed in on new drug approvals. The FDA convened a record low number of advisory committees in 2025. Instead, it hosted a handful of pseudo-scientific look-alike meetings called “expert panels.” Panelists were handpicked and invited for a single meeting to share their own data, analysis, and conclusions, unmoored from any semblance of collaborative consensus and, too often, scientific rigor.
Expert advisory committees matter for two reasons. The first is obvious: Agency policymakers need high-quality, independent advice to improve the quality, credibility, and legitimacy of agency decision-making. Agencies can’t possibly have the internal expertise to handle every question. This is especially true after staffing cuts to agencies like the EPA, FDA, and CDC.
The other reason is accountability: When a legitimate expert advisory committee makes a recommendation about what an agency should do, it leaves a public record that enables us to hold our government accountable if it declines to follow that advice.
Over the past few decades, courts, Congress, and the public have come to rely on these public recommendations — in congressional oversight, judicial review, and science journalism — to better understand the choices expert agencies make.
This is what happened when the FDA approved the Alzheimer’s drug aducanumab in 2021 despite the near-unanimous vote of the advisory committee (which included one of us) against approval. The committee noted conflicting evidence on the drug’s efficacy and clear safety risks, including brain bleeds, in large numbers of patients.
The negative vote anchored the debate that followed. Critics pointed to it as evidence that the FDA had made a terrible mistake, and payors and hospital systems used it to justify not paying the outlandish price set by the manufacturer. Patients largely avoided drug, with the whole episode culminating in investigations by the media and Congress that demonstrated improper pressure by the manufacturer on the FDA leading to the approval decision.
Advisory committees don’t just provide recommendations to agency policymakers. They enable us to literally hold the agency to account for its decision — to explain why it thinks its advisers were wrong. With no advisory committee to create a record, policymakers can more easily evade hard questions about unscientific or politically motivated decisions.
The dismissals at the USPSTF follow a Supreme Court decision in 2025 stating that the secretary of HHS can remove members at will. The court reasoned that the secretary has the power to appoint them, and “no statute restricts [their] removal.”
But Congress can, and should, change this. It has an array of tools at its disposal. Depending on the circumstance, it could enact for-cause statutory removal protections, staggered terms, formal expertise and qualification requirements, and enforceable conflict of interest rules. It could require that advisers be chosen more transparently and according to stricter criteria. It could even vest the power to choose advisers in another body entirely, akin to how independent redistricting commissions draw state electoral boundaries.
These reforms would likely survive constitutional scrutiny because advisers do not actually make policy. Their advice is nonbinding. The Supreme Court’s recent decision striking down statutory removal protections for agency heads depended on the idea that the agency head was exercising executive authority that must ultimately be accountable to the president. But independent expert scientific advisers do not exercise authority; they merely speak authoritatively. And when they speak, they are heard by those of us — courts, Congress, the press, and through them, the public — to whom public policy must ultimately be accountable.
This evisceration of scientific advice is untenable. If Congress is committed to the idea that evidence, science, and expertise should guide public policy, then it needs to act by insulating expert advice from arbitrary political control.
C. Joseph Ross Daval is a research specialist at the Program On Regulation, Therapeutics, And Law (PORTAL) at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School and a former lawyer in the FDA’s Office of the Chief Counsel. Aaron S. Kesselheim is a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, director of PORTAL, and a former member of the FDA’s Peripheral and Central Nervous System Advisory Committee.

Lucknow, Oct 30: Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Friday said the BJP would implement the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in Uttar Pradesh, expressing confidence that the party would return to power in the state after assembly elections next year.
Addressing the party's state working committee meeting here, Shah targeted the Samajwadi Party and other opposition parties over the Ram temple issue and alleged voter list irregularities.
"This time, when the government comes to power, UCC will be implemented in Uttar Pradesh. UCC has already been implemented in many states," he said.
Shah kickstarted the daylong meeting at the Dr Ram Manohar Lohia National Law University auditorium. It was chaired by BJP state president and Union Minister of State for Finance Pankaj Chaudhary.
Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, Deputy Chief Ministers Keshav Prasad Maurya and Brajesh Pathak, BJP state in-charge Vinod Tawde and national general secretary Smriti Irani were among those present.
Shah said the BJP in Uttar Pradesh could not be dislodged as the government has firmly established itself in the state.
"The BJP government in Uttar Pradesh is like Angad's foot. Nobody can move it. The BJP is going to form the government again. There should be no doubt about it," he said.
Claiming that the Samajwadi Party would remain out of power in the state, he said, “ (SP president)Akhilesh babu, mark my words, your party will not form the government in Uttar Pradesh for the next 30 years. The people will not forgive even your third generation.”
Referring to the events of October 30, 1990, when police opened fire on kar sevaks in Ayodhya, Shah targeted the Samajwadi Party and its leadership over the Ram temple issue.
"I want to ask them, on what grounds do they talk about forming a government? They ordered firing on Ram devotees, while we have built the Ram temple," he said.
Shah also attacked opposition parties over their allegations of vote theft, and compared their complaints to a team blaming the umpire after losing a match.
"After losing the match, they are blaming the umpire and alleging vote theft. The BJP is ready for a discussion in Parliament. Let them come today and convene a special session. We are ready to answer every question. Let there be a discussion in Parliament," he said.
Earlier, the Union minister lit a ceremonial lamp to start proceedings of the meeting, and paid floral tributes to portraits of party ideologues Syama Prasad Mookerjee and Deendayal Upadhyaya.

Leh, Oct 30: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk said the protest against the new liquor policy in Ladakh was suspended after the administration agreed to all demands and sought a week's time to formalise the agreement.
Women-led protests began last week in Ladakh, driven by a newly introduced liquor policy, demanding a complete rollback of the policy and for Ladakh to be declared a dry Union territory.
"Ladakh women leaders suspend their protest against liquor. After the UT administration agreed to all demands and sought a week to finalise the agreement. Let's hope that their trust and faith in the system will be respected," Wangchuk said on X on Thursday.
The four organisations on Thursday suspended their dharna planned from October 29 to November 5 following a written assurance from the UT administration.
The assurance was conveyed through a letter issued by the Home Department on October 29, signed by Special Secretary Tashi Dolma, accepting in principle all the points and recommendations submitted by the organisations on the liquor policy.
The Ladakh Buddhist Association Women Wing, Anjuman-e-Imamia Women Wing, Anjuman Moin-ul-Islam Women Wing and Christian Community Women Wing have objected to the liquor policy.
In a press release, the organisations said the UT administration has sought a week's time to finalise the agreement in the spirit of dialogue and cooperation.
Respecting the request, the women's organisations have agreed to temporarily suspend their dharna, giving the administration an opportunity to fulfil its commitment and formalise the agreed points in writing, it added.
The organisations said the suspension of the protest should be seen as an expression of their faith in the administration's assurance and thanked the people of Ladakh for their overwhelming support.
The protest was launched against the expansion of liquor availability, including the issuance of recent bar licences and wine shops. The organisations have been demanding measures to safeguard the future of youth, protect the social fabric and preserve Ladakh's cultural and spiritual values.
The organisations reiterated their long-term commitment towards a healthier and alcohol-addiction-free Ladakh.

లెఫ్టినెంట్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా, చైనా అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోని అసఫిలా, లాంగ్జు, తక్సింగ్ సర్కిళ్లను తన ఆధీనంలోకి తీసుకుందని, ఈ విషయంలో కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం తగిన చర్యలు తీసుకోవడం లేదని చెబుతున్నట్లు ANI లోగోతో ఉన్న ఒక వీడియోను సోషల్ మీడియాలో షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. ఈ వీడియోను ఇదే వాదనతో సోషల్ మీడియాలో (ఇక్కడ) షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన వాదనలో నిజమెంతుందో ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: లెఫ్టినెంట్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా, చైనా అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోని అసఫిలా, లాంగ్జు, తక్సింగ్ సర్కిళ్లను తన ఆధీనంలోకి తీసుకుందని, కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం ఈ విషయంలో తగిన చర్యలు తీసుకోవడం లేదని తెలిపిన వీడియో.
ఫ్యాక్ట్: వైరల్ వీడియోను డిజిటల్గా ఎడిట్ చెయ్యబడింది. అందులోని ఆడియో డీప్ఫేక్. ANI 2023 అక్టోబర్లో ప్రచురించిన అసలు వీడియోలో, మేజర్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా జమ్మూ కశ్మీర్లోని నియంత్రణ రేఖ (LoC) వెంబడి చొరబాటు ప్రయత్నాల గురించి మాట్లాడారు. ఆయన అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోని ప్రాంతాలపై చైనా నియంత్రణ గురించి మాట్లాడలేదు. ఈ వీడియో డీప్ఫేక్ అని భారత సైన్యం ఫ్యాక్ట్ చెక్ విభాగం, ANI కూడా స్పష్టం చేశాయి. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన వాదన తప్పు.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేమ్ల రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, 2023 అక్టోబర్ 27న ది స్టేట్స్మన్ ప్రచురించిన అదే వీడియోకు సంబంధించిన పూర్తి వీడియో లభించింది. ఈ వీడియోలో లెఫ్టినెంట్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా, నియంత్రణ రేఖ (LoC) వెంబడి పాకిస్థాన్కు చెందిన ఉగ్రవాద బృందాలు పదేపదే చొరబడేందుకు ప్రయత్నించడం గురించి మాట్లాడారు. గత ఎనిమిది నెలల్లో భద్రతా దళాలు 10 చొరబాటు ప్రయత్నాలను అడ్డుకున్నాయని, ఈ ఘటనల్లో 27 మంది ఉగ్రవాదులను హతమార్చాయని తెలిపారు. అలాగే, ఆయుధాలు, ఇతర యుద్ధ సామగ్రి, మాదకద్రవ్యాలను స్వాధీనం చేసుకున్నట్లు చెప్పారు. ఈ వీడియోలో ఎక్కడా అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్ను చైనా ఆక్రమించిందని ఆయన ప్రకటించలేదు.
అంతేకాకుండా, ANI కూడా ఇదే వీడియోను 2023 అక్టోబర్ 27న తన Xలో పోస్ట్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఎనిమిది నెలల్లో 10 చొరబాటు ప్రయత్నాలను భద్రతా దళాలు అడ్డుకున్నాయని, ఈ ఘటనల్లో 27 మంది ఉగ్రవాదులను హతమార్చి, ఆయుధాలు, మాదకద్రవ్యాలను స్వాధీనం చేసుకున్నాయని ANI తన పోస్టులో పేర్కొంది.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని ఆడియోను Hiya AI, Resemble AI టూల్స్తో విశ్లేషించగా, అది కృత్రిమ మేధస్సు (AI) ద్వారా రూపొందించిన డీప్ఫేక్ ఆడియో అని గుర్తించాం.
భారత సైన్యం ఫ్యాక్ట్ చెక్ విభాగం, ANI కూడా ఈ వీడియోను డిజిటల్గా మార్చారని స్పష్టం చేశాయి. లెఫ్టినెంట్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా చేసినట్లుగా చూపిస్తున్న వ్యాఖ్యలు కల్పితమైనవని తెలిపాయి.
చివరిగా, అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోని కొన్ని ప్రాంతాలపై చైనా నియంత్రణ సాధించిందంటూ లెఫ్టినెంట్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా వ్యాఖ్యలు చేసినట్లు చూపిస్తున్న ఈ వీడియో డీప్ఫేక్.

Namit Malhotra’s Ramayana has a special connection with Yash and Radhika Pandit’s family, as the film reportedly marked the first movie experience of their children, Ayra and Yatharv. The siblings watched the film at an early premiere in Los Angeles, making the occasion a personal milestone for the family.
Yash’s children Ayra and Yatharv watch Ramayana at LA premiere, marking their first movie experience
Yash and Radhika’s children, Ayra, seven, and Yatharv, who turns seven on October 30, experienced cinema for the first time with the upcoming mythological epic. While details of their experience have not been shared publicly, the occasion carries an added significance given Yash’s involvement in the project. The actor plays Ravana in the film and is also associated with its production through his banner, Monster Mind Creations.
Yash and Radhika Pandit have previously spoken about their children's names
The occasion also brings attention to the meanings behind the children's names. Yash and Radhika have previously shared the thought behind choosing their names. Ayra draws inspiration from Airavathi, a name associated with Goddess Lakshmi, while Yatharv means 'complete'. The couple has also spoken about how Yatharv's name brings together elements of the names of Yash, Radhika and Ayra.
With Ramayana becoming their first movie experience, the film now has a personal association for the family beyond Yash's role in the adaptation. The actor will be seen portraying Ravana in the two-part cinematic adaptation of the epic.
Produced by Namit Malhotra's Prime Focus Studios and co-produced by Yash's Monster Mind Creations, Ramayana is scheduled to release on November 5.

Indian drug regulators ordered Sun Pharmaceutical Industries to stop manufacturing, selling and distributing ophthalmic products made at its Assam facility after finding failure in its quality management system, documents reviewed by Reuters showed.
The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation and the office of Drugs Controller Assam ordered the shutdown on August 20 after a joint federal-state inspection of the facility identified lapses in the system meant to ensure product quality and safety, following Sun Pharma’s move in July to voluntarily recall about 11 eye-care brands.
India’s drug quality standards have come under increased scrutiny at home and overseas in recent years after locally made cough syrups were linked to the deaths of children in India and also in countries including Gambia and Uzbekistan.
The regulatory agencies’ move marks an escalation of the action against Sun Pharma, India’s biggest pharmaceutical firm, which will be unable to continue ophthalmic drug production at the Assam factory until it submits a satisfactory compliance report. Sun Pharma said previously the site was expected to become one of its largest manufacturing hubs for sterile products in a business identified as a key global growth driver.
The regulator sought more information on the recall of 332 batches of ophthalmic suspension products — liquids used to treat eye conditions — the documents showed.
In an internal notice sent to stockists at the time, the company said it was withdrawing the products as a “precautionary measure.” It remains unclear whether all of the recalled products were contaminated.
Sun Pharma did not publicly disclose details of the recall.
The company has submitted a compliance report in response to the order, which is being reviewed by the regulator, an official familiar with the matter told Reuters on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
“We voluntarily initiated a temporary cessation of manufacturing activities and informed the regulators,” Sun Pharma said in a statement on Friday (October 30, 2026), adding that remedial measures have been put in place.
It did not respond to a request for comment on the recall. The company says on its website it follows a single global quality standard.
Recall could involve hundreds of thousands of bottles
Some of the recalled products included Lotepred 1% 5ml eye drops, Nepalact OD eye drops, Nepalact-Z, Brinzotim eye drops 5ml and Depopred 2ml. The eye drops are used to treat eye inflammation, infections and chronic eye diseases, according to doctors.
It is unclear whether these eye products were exported from India or whether any patients reported any adverse effects.
Reuters found that, based on the product packaging, most of the recalled products were manufactured at the Assam state facility in Kokjhar village. Reuters could not independently verify whether the 332 batches cited by regulators were related only to the 11 identified brands in the recall notice or included additional brands.
The affected batches could translate into hundreds of thousands of eye-drop bottles, according to industry experts, who declined to be identified because they were not authorised to speak publicly.
Ophthalmology contributes about 3% of Sun Pharma’s domestic revenue, according to its 2025-26 annual report. It is also one of its key areas for the U.S.
The company reported a drop in second-quarter profit on Friday (October 30) weighed down by a one-time charge related to its acquisition of U.S.-based Organon.
The eye product recall coincided with a patient-safety advisory issued in June by the All India Ophthalmological Society (AIOS), an independent body of eye specialists, warning that certain batches of Predmet eye drops appeared to be contaminated.
“There were some adverse cases of infections reported in patients who used Predmet and we got sealed bottles investigated and found it was contaminated,” Santosh Honavar, a doctor and secretary of AIOS, told Reuters, adding that Sun Pharma had also recalled those Predmet drops.
Sun Pharma did not respond a request for comment on the AIOS advisory.
The regulators issued a show-cause notice to Sun Pharma on August 10, citing the quality management system failures, the documents showed.
Dissatisfied with the company’s response, the regulators ordered a halt to the manufacturing, sale and distribution of all ophthalmic products from the facility.
Indian regulators did not respond to requests for comment. The agency did not issue a public health alert after the recall.
It is not the first time Sun Pharma’s sterile manufacturing facilities have faced regulatory scrutiny. Last year, the U.S. FDA halted the company’s shipments from Gujarat’s Halol plant after inspectors cited shortcomings in contamination controls.

The CZUR ET Max makes digitizing hundreds of books faster and easier with overhead scanning, foot-pedal capture, automatic curve flattening, and ABBYY OCR. It supports searchable PDFs, 180+ languages, and non-destructive scanning, though you still need to turn pages manually.
Digitizing physical books and documents offers many benefits. The most noticeable benefit is that you can store them forever in different formats and search them easily. In this AI era, you can submit them to an AI assistant to quickly summarize them and find the information you need.
Digitalizing physical copies isn’t that hard in 2026. You just need a smartphone with a camera and a physical copy of a book or documents. You can instantly convert it into a digital version and convert it into multiple formats. However, digitizing hundreds of books or documents is a complex job to do with regular phones or regular scanners.
This is where the CZUR ET Max makes it easy to scan and digitize hundreds of books and documents. It is an overhead scanner with foot-pedal capture, curve-flattening software, and OCR support. You still turn and position each page by hand.
Because it uses an overhead camera, you don’t need to press the book against the scanner glass as you do with a flatbed scanner. CZUR says its automatic curve-flattening software straightens curved pages and corrects their alignment.
Table of Contents
How the CZUR ET Max Is Designed To Make Book Digitization Easier
All these features are designed to make scanning hundreds of books or documents easier. Let’s go through each feature in detail and explain why this product might be the right fit for you.
Fast scanning with foot-pedal capture
One of the most time-consuming parts of regular scanning is manually turning each page, aligning it perfectly, and then pressing the scan button. Even with phone apps that have an auto-capture feature, scanning a 500-page book is still very hard.
With the CZUR ET Max, you place the book on the base and turn each page manually. The computer preview lets you check how the pages are positioned before capturing them.
CZUR advertises a capture speed of 1.5 seconds per scan. That is the manufacturer’s stated capture speed, not the total time needed to turn, position, and process every page. Pages may still need repositioning between captures.
The included foot pedal lets you trigger a scan with your foot while keeping your hands available to position the book.
Support for automatic curve flattening
Another feature CZUR lists for the ET Max is curve flattening. According to the company, its software detects the book’s central curve and the curvature of its pages, then corrects their shape and alignment.
This is the most common issue many of us face with regular scans or even capturing with a smartphone, where you will see a middle line if you capture two pages at once.
And since it is a top-down scanner, you don’t have to force the book to lie completely flat or manually straighten each scanned page either. It automatically detects the shape and curvature of the pages, divides them, and converts them into regular documents. The company also has patented laser-based curve flattening technology.
Support for ABBYY OCR
One of the biggest benefits of converting physical books into digital is the ability to instantly find content.
CZUR says the ET Max’s ABBYY-powered Optical Character Recognition (OCR) supports more than 180 languages and converts captured documents into searchable PDF, Word, and Excel files.
This can be especially useful for students, lawyers, journalists, academics, and authors, who can quickly search for words, copy passages, and reuse information directly without using a separate OCR function.
Overhead non-destructive scanning
One primary benefit of overhead scanning is that you can scan books without pressing them flat against the scanner glass.
You turn the pages manually, as you would while reading, and use the foot pedal to trigger each capture. Overhead capture avoids pressing a bound book against flatbed glass; it does not eliminate page handling.
CZUR lists the ET Max with a 38-megapixel camera and support for documents up to A3, helping capture detailed prints without losing detail.
Anti-glare lighting and image correction support
Another issue that we most commonly face while scanning glossy pages like magazines is reflections.
For instance, if you scan a glossy magazine, you will see a reflection in the scan. However, the CZUR ET scanner addresses this with anti-glare lighting and image correction support. It includes built-in LED lighting and an additional side light to reduce reflections, plus adjustable brightness and automatic finger removal from scanned pages.
The CZUR ET Max combines overhead capture, manual page turning, foot-pedal triggering, curve-flattening software, and OCR. These features are intended to simplify repeated book scanning and searchable-document creation, but their accuracy and real-world throughput have not been established through our own testing.
If you are struggling to digitize your documents, even with current scanning methods, try the CZUR ET Max overhead scanner, which fixes these issues and lets you digitize physical books quickly and conveniently. It comes in multiple variants, and the prices range from $377 to $799 depending on the model, which is expensive compared to regular scanners; however, it solves the biggest problems standard scanners currently have and is especially great for people who want to digitize physical books frequently.

Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
- Published
Riot police have been deployed at Poland's Constitutional Court amid an escalating stand-off between the government and the court's top judges.
The row pits the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk against his predecessors from the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS).
The police intervention came after Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said he had requested stripping the court's President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański of their immunity from prosecution to bring criminal charges against them.
Tusk has vowed to depoliticise the judiciary, and on Friday defended the move as PiS supporters gathered outside the court premises in Warsaw in protest.
Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.
In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.
"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.
In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, ordered his plane be turned back to Warsaw on his way to Senegal to attend the Summer Youth Olympic Games.
The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.
Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.
The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.
Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.
Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.
One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.
Justice Minister Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.
Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.
Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.
But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.
Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons".
"Today's action at the Constitutional Court, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media.
"Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Court by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.

In 1904, two scientists, Henry Wheeler and Treat Johnson, synthesised a variant of cytosine, one of the building blocks of DNA, in the laboratory.
The variant they synthesised contained a chemical tag called a methyl group (-CH3) attached to cytosine, so they called it 5-methylcytosine. Their motivation for doing so was based on the observation that two other building blocks of DNA and its chemical cousin RNA, called thymine and uracil, differed only by the presence of a methyl group.
So Wheeler and Johnson figured that a methylated version of cytosine might also exist in nature.
In 1925, Johnson, while working with another scientist named Robert Coghill, finally discovered 5-methyl-cytosine in the DNA of the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. Two more decades later, Rollin Hotchkiss found 5-methyl-cytosine in the DNA of cows. Soon, scientists found that it existed in nearly all animals.
However, nobody knew why it existed — or why some of the cytosines in DNA were methylated while others were not.
Genes on and off
That insight came in 1975, when Robin Holliday and John Pugh proposed that the methylation of the cytosine could be a way for the body to use the information stored in DNA.
DNA is segmented into genes, and each gene contains the information necessary to make a particular protein. These proteins perform their specific functions in the cells. Since every cell in the body has two copies — one from each parent — of all human DNA, all cells technically have the blueprint to make a whole organism.
However, cells also have specialised functions. A brain cell will not need the genes for the proteins used to digest food. So Holliday and Pugh suggested that chemical modifications such as the methylation of cytosine could help establish and activate genes that a cell wants while silencing those it does not.
This idea, that cells could use chemical tags on DNA to control which genes were active, has come to be called epigenetics. (The British biologist Conrad Waddington had actually coined the term in 1942 itself.) Soon, scientists found enzymes that could add and remove these chemical tags to and from DNA.
Today, we know that cells use many other chemical tags, not only on DNA itself but also on the proteins around which DNA is wrapped like a vine around a stick.
Together, all these chemical marks help control which genes are switched on or off. Problems in this system can lead to changes in gene activity, which in turn can lead to diseases like cancers.
Functional cure
Now, according to a paper that appeared in Nature Biomedical Engineering on September 21, scientists have used this epigenetic control to treat a hepatitis B infection.
This is a remarkable development because, instead of targeting the virus directly, the work silenced the viral DNA. This is promising because current treatments rarely eliminate the DNA, which allows the virus to rebound. By silencing this residue, the treatment could offer a path to a lasting functional cure for hepatitis B.
The hepatitis B virus mainly infects liver cells. After entering a cell, the virus’s DNA serves as the template to make new viral particles. In many people, the immune system clears the infection, but if it does not, the viral DNA can persist for years or even decades in the host’s liver.
In this time, the virus can remain silent, meaning the viral DNA is still present in the cell but its genes are not active to produce new viruses. This allows the virus to ‘hide’ from the immune system. Then, at a later point, the virus can activate again and produce new virus particles.
And studies have shown that one of the mechanisms by which the virus stays silent is by methylating the cytosines.
Locator and effector
The authors of the new study have reported a new experimental therapy called CRMA-1001, which, they have claimed, can silence the DNA of the hepatitis B virus by selectively adding methylation marks to the viral genome.
The study is innovative because it uses several different technologies to overcome three major challenges. To epigenetically silence viral DNA, scientists first need to be able to target the virus’s DNA without methylating any of the cytosines in the host’s DNA. Then, the silencing mechanism must switch off the virus’s DNA effectively. Finally, all of this should happen without causing any unwanted side-effects to the host.
The study authors solved the first two problems by combining two substances called a ‘locator’ and an ‘effector’. The locator used the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool to find and bind to a specific DNA sequence: in this case, that was a sequence within the viral DNA. This allowed the CRISPR system to take the ‘effector’, the methylation machinery, to the correct location. The effector had proteins that could add methyl groups to nearby cytosines in the viral DNA and proteins that help switch off genes.
Finally, the researchers packed the entire system and delivered it on an mRNA platform (similar to the mRNA vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic). This made the system transient: once a cell had read the instructions to make the required proteins, it degraded them, stopping the production of those proteins too.
Novel therapy
The researchers gave mice infected with hepatitis B virus either a single dose of CRMA-1001 or three doses, one month apart, and regularly tested them for six months for the signs of infection. They reported that after one dose, the levels of several hepatitis B virus markers, including the viral DNA and two viral proteins called HBsAg and HBeAg, dropped significantly. When they tested the viral DNA, they found new methyl groups, suggesting that the treatment was working as intended. The effect was even stronger after three doses: six months after the first dose, as many as 90% of the animals had less viral DNA than could be detected.
CRMA-1001 is not a cure in the traditional sense of the word. The hepatitis B virus DNA is still present in the liver cells. Instead, the study demonstrated a functional cure: when the virus is not necessarily eliminated but is kept so thoroughly suppressed that, for all intents and purposes, the patient has no active signs of disease.
In this study, the team followed up with the mice for six months after treatment, and the researchers found sustained suppression of the virus in that period. However, the study did not establish whether the virus could eventually become active again after those six months, since the viral DNA was still present.
Further studies are needed to examine the long-term effects of CRMA-1001, including whether the silencing effect can persist over many years and whether the virus can ever become active again after treatment. An ongoing phase I/II clinical trial includes these among other questions.
If CRMA-1001 is eventually approved as a therapy for the market, it will represent a novel way to tackle a viral infection: where instead of fighting the threat, the cell ignores it.
Arun Panchapakesan is an assistant professor at the Y.R. Gaitonde Centre for AIDS Research and Education, Chennai.

Health officials hoping to boost adoption of artificial intelligence in health care have been moving behind the scenes to address brewing conflict between states and the federal government over the technology.
The Trump administration has sought to alleviate regulatory burden on companies developing health AI and created new ways to pay for the technology. But there remains a key problem: The federal government and states have overlapping jurisdiction over AI that performs clinical work, like writing prescriptions.
States regulate the practice of medicine and issue licenses to doctors and other clinicians. If AI performs these tasks without human supervision, that would likely push those products into the jurisdiction of the Food and Drug Administration, which regulates medical devices.

The European Union and Canada announced a new alliance of “ever-closer association” designed to bring together like-minded countries to address common challenges.
Canadian prime minister Mark Carney said on Friday he and his European counterparts would define the scale and scope of a "new form" of European Union membership over the coming months, and that Canada would become its first "associate member."
They will define by a 2027 summit what the association would entail exactly, Carney said.
In a post on X, Carney said that what he called an “Alliance for the Future” would not only be open to Canada and the EU, but to “other countries that share our views to address common challenges and strengthen our collective power.”
Donald Trump last month threatened trade sanctions in response to von der Leyen's proposal to create a new status for the EU-Canada relationship.
The US president has adopted a more transactional approach to foreign policy and has repeatedly attacked multilateral institutions.
Carney called Canada “the most European of non-European countries” early in Trump’s trade war. This week, it was reported that discussions regarding trade between the US and Canada had seen only modest advancement.
On Thursday, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said the EU and Canada continue to explore the North American nation becoming the union's first "associate member," a term so divisive among member countries that it does not appear in the final statement.
Carney said the alliance between EU and Canada, announced at a summit in Montreal on Friday, would focus on resilience in areas including AI, energy and critical minerals.
"We are working towards the deepest possible partnership, short of accession," he said, adding that this would result in "Canada becoming the European Union’s first Associate Member."
The associate member term, which Germany and several other EU countries oppose, has no legal meaning.
In a joint statement released to mark the end of the summit, Canadian and EU leaders cited an “unwavering commitment to effective multilateralism, democracy and to the rules-based international order."
The statement said Canada and the 27-nation EU would work to resolve the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East and deepen security ties elsewhere, including in the Arctic.
It added talks had been concluded on a digital trade agreement that would complement the existing trade agreement between Canada and the EU.
Carney also said he had accepted the European Council president's invitation to attend meetings in Europe next June, where he said talks on the deeper relationship would be concluded.
"We are building the industries and infrastructure that underwrite our collective security," Carney said.
"This is only the beginning."

Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
- Published
Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.
Óscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.
"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.
The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.
Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.
A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.
In January a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people in Adamuz in southern Spain.
Wednesday's tragedy was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Puente said on Wednesday a computer failure at about 08:30 that morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the crash.
Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Puente had said that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".
The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".
Meanwhile, Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.
On Friday Puente said he was "not going to use any worker as a shield".
But he said "many questions" arose as a result of the tragedy and he wanted to look at them "one by one".
"If the investigation shows there is human error we will act in consequence of that," he said.
The conservative People's Party joined calls for Puente's resignation after trade union CSIF called for the same earlier this week.
But Puente said on Friday he would not budge from his position.
"The easy thing for me would be to leave, but neither that fits with my character nor is it what the Prime Minister has asked me to do," he said.
"I feel immense pain and immense sadness for the victims and their relatives... I cannot let this pain paralyse me though. We have to find solutions to this problem."
The country is observing three days of mourning, as the families of victims and the survivors of the crash struggle to comprehend how it could have happened.
A 24-year-old athlete and a former government minister are among the victims of Wednesday's disaster, but many families are still waiting for information from authorities about their loved ones.
Esther San Emeterio, whose 54-year-old brother Pepe is still missing, told reporters in Toledo, near Urda, that officials were forcing families to wait in "uncertainty".
"We went to bed crying, outraged and full of shame," she said. "We are desperate and I want all of Spain to know. How can they keep us like this?"
