Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.
Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.
The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.
There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.
Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.
“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”
Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable.”
Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”
On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.
In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.
She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.
To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.
An informal security council poll earlier his month had placed the former Costa Rican vice-president Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.
At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”
Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”
Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

Everything you need to know about Googlebooks
Despite good initial hardware, the Googlebook OS still needs a lot of work.
It's somehow been almost two and a half years since Google said it would migrate its laptop operating system from ChromeOS to Android, and the results of that effort are finally out in the wild. Google and its hardware partners officially launched Googlebooks earlier this month with the promise of tight integration between your Android phone and this new, Android-powered laptop OS, plenty of AI-powered tricks and premium hardware.
As someone who has used and tested ChromeOS extensively over the last decade (!), I've been wondering what exactly would differentiate the Googlebook OS from ChromeOS. Google's initial Googlebook introduction in May didn't give us a ton of information, but a big demo event and several weeks of testing has given me a better idea of what the company is shooting for. And after my time with Googlebooks, I can say that while there might be benefits internally for Google (as well as third-party developers) to move from ChromeOS to Android, the upside isn't fully there for potential buyers yet — particularly when you consider how expensive Googlebooks are.
A quick word on hardware
This isn't a formal review of one Googlebook but rather an evaluation of the operating system Google is pushing. But it's worth talking quickly about the Googlebook hardware launching alongside the OS. Most of my testing was done on the $1,299 ASUS Googlebook 14, an extremely thin and light laptop that weighs in at only 2.2 pounds. It features an OLED touchscreen with Corning's Gorilla Matte glass, which significantly cuts down on reflections. From a specs standpoint, it runs on an Intel Core Ultra 5 chip with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage. It's a really lovely laptop, as it should be at that price point. I also did some testing on the Acer Googlebook 14 and HP's Googlebook 14, the latter of which runs on the Snapdragon X Elite X1E-80-100 processor. Performance felt similar whether using the Intel or Qualcomm models, though I anecdotally feel like battery life was better and fans kicked in less frequently on the HP.
The Googlebook introduction positioned these new devices as premium computers, and indeed they are priced to match that claim. The least expensive Googlebook out there, Acer's Googlebook 14, starts at $899 — and that's the only Googlebook under $1,000. And while various manufacturers (including Google itself) have released premium, expensive Chromebooks over the years, Acer's $899 Googlebook is more expensive than nearly all the Chromebooks on the market.
Eventually, Googlebooks will fully replace ChromeOS, so I expect a future wave of devices will focus on affordable options. But for now, Googlebooks are strictly a premium experience with a price to match, and that'll be a big part of my evaluation of the OS. It's always been easier to forgive any limitations you might find on a Chromebook when they were priced at $400 or $500, but it's a lot harder when we're in the $1,000 range where you can get a more versatile Mac or Windows PC.
Out of the box
Setting up a Chromebook isn't hard — you generally just log in with your Google account. But Google is emphasizing the ties between your Android phone and Googlebook right from the first step, where you're prompted to set up with an Android device or even an iPhone or iPad. When I selected Android device, a notification popped up on my Pixel 11 asking me if I wanted to use it to set up my Googlebook. The laptop, meanwhile, had a QR code for scanning at the ready.
After scanning that code, my Googlebook connected to Wi-Fi and then asked me if I wanted to use the Google account from my phone. After that, I just confirmed my name and profile picture, set a login password and added a fingerprint to unlock the device. Finally, it asked if I wanted to copy apps and data from my phone, which didn't take long at all. I don't think all that much was shared, but there's a customize option for those who want to be specific about what moves over. Finally, I got a quick tour of some of the Googlebook's Gemini-powered features like Magic Pointer, the Quick Insert key and using voice chat with Gemini Live.
I was also prompted to set up the connection between my phone and the laptop so I could do things like see notifications and files from my phone on my Googlebook. That involved giving some services permission on both devices, but it didn't take long nor was it too complicated for the average user.
Once everything was set up, I was greeted with a desktop that, unsurprisingly, was quite similar to ChromeOS. There's a taskbar along the bottom with shortcuts to apps like Chrome, Gemini, Gmail and a handful of other Google services, and there are also some shortcuts on the desktop that are organized in folders for productivity (apps like Docs and Drive), media (voice recorder, PDF viewer and camera) and messaging (Gmail, Messages and Meet). Wisely, the Googlebook also booted up with an in-depth walkthrough for things like accessing quick settings, changing your wallpaper and screensaver, finding files, managing your windows and all the initial things you'll want to be able to do on a laptop. I definitely appreciated the tutorial — not that the system would have been unfriendly to use without it, but having some guidance for tips and tricks in a brand-new OS is smart.
While it's easy to mistake the Googlebook UI for ChromeOS, there are a few subtle differences here. The taskbar is exclusively for apps; the time, date, notifications and quick access to system settings are in a thin strip at the top of the screen now. I'm hit or miss on that change. On the one hand, the ChromeOS taskbar feels pretty cluttered now, but on the other I don't love giving up vertical pixels to the info bar at the top of the screen.
Unfortunately, Google also removed a few handy features that were in the ChromeOS taskbar, as well. For example, clicking on the date and time would bring up a calendar and anything on your Google Tasks list, but that integration is no longer present. ChromeOS also has a little button where you can pin files and see ones you've recently opened. I think Google expects you to replace those features with widgets that you can add to your desktop, a feature that Chrome OS doesn't support.
When Chrome isn't quite Chrome
Google's Chrome browser is not perfect, but it's the most popular browser in the world and basically every site works well on it. That was perhaps the biggest selling point for ChromeOS: Many people do the vast majority of their computing in a browser, and a Chromebook offered a great browsing experience. Naturally, Chrome was the first place I started on my Googlebook, as I planned to open the various saved tab groups I had set up on my Mac and continue my work.
Those tab groups simply did not appear. Even though you can sync tab groups across the desktop, Android and iOS versions of Chrome, those groups don't show up on a Googlebook. I find it hard to put into words how bad it is to have such a baseline, crucial feature missing from a brand-new product that's ostensibly meant to replace Chromebooks. Google says it'll be added in a future update, but it's not here now and that's a shame.
Similarly, I initially was unable to install web apps on my Googlebook. On ChromeOS, you can take something like the web version of Slack (which is identical to the desktop app) and have it open in its own window, with a dedicated app icon in the taskbar rather than have it as a tab in a crowded Chrome window. For the first week or so I was using a Googlebook, I was only able to save shortcuts to my desktop that would open apps like Slack and Trello in my main Chrome window as tabs. This was fixed with a subsequent Chrome update, so now I use those apps in their own windows. But between the lack of tab group syncing and this initial web app issue, I was left feeling that my Googlebook wasn't fully baked.
The app situation
Just as on Chromebooks, Googlebooks give you two main options for apps: web-based tools or Android apps from the Google Play Store. It's been about 10 years since Google first put the Play Store on Chromebooks, and it was a pretty big deal then to expand the laptop beyond its "just a browser" reputation. Ten years later, though, and on a new platform, many of the same issues persist.
The biggest issue by far is that Android developers have never embraced building apps for larger screens. That situation has improved over the years, as many apps can dynamically adjust to fill a bigger display. But too many apps just stretch a view that works on a phone over a much bigger space without taking advantage of it.
Going back to Slack again, I considered using the Android app when the web app wouldn't install properly. But while the desktop version of Slack has a multi-column view that's essential for keeping up with a busy workplace, the Android app only shows you one view at a time, regardless of how big your screen is. Slack supports a much better large-screen view on the iPad, so there's no reason they couldn't do so here as well. It's just that Android tablets and Chromebooks have never gotten attention from developers. As long as that's the case, chances are good your favorite Android app won't feel quite at home on a Googlebook.
To be clear, though, the situation is definitely better than it was a decade ago. Google used its launch of the Pixel Tablet in 2023 to revamp its core set of apps for bigger screens, and now many of those apps feel right at home on a Googlebook. Android versions of Keep, Google Home, Calendar, Photos, Google TV and numerous others work well after you install them.
Google is also doing its best to push people towards web apps when they're better suited. Installing Google Chat from the Play Store sets up the web-based app, for example, and the Gmail shortcut in the taskbar opens your account in its own window but with the same familiar Gmail web interface. It's always been a bit confusing to know whether you should install an app from the Play Store or use its web-based counterpart — but in the case of Google's own apps at least, the Play Store knows which kind is best to install for a Googlebook.
And while many third-party apps don't take advantage of larger screens, there are also plenty that do. Todoist and Spotify are native to the Googlebook and display multiple columns of info, while Adobe Lightroom pulled up my library quickly and synced edits I made on the Googlebook back to my Mac without any hiccups.
But of course, there are likely apps you use on Windows or Mac that won't be available here. There might be substitutes, but you won't be able to install things like Adobe Premiere or Logic Pro here. And while most people can do most things through a browser or via the Android apps you can get on a Googlebook, the question remains what the benefits are for moving your workflow to a totally new platform that might not have all the apps you need.
Native gaming, of course, is a bit of a non-starter as well. Sure, you can install games from the Play Store — I checked out Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge and Limbo, and they ran without issues. Shredder's Revenge even had keyboard controls already mapped out. But these aren't exactly new or cutting-edge titles.
One nice perk that Google is including with Googlebooks is a year of GeForce Now "Fast Pass" access. GeForce Now lets you stream games you own from storefronts like Steam and the Epic Games Store, and the "Fast Pass" here provides up to 50 hours of gaming per month. There are also no ads like you get in the normal free GeForce Now tier, and it gives you priority access as well (hence the name). Obviously, this doesn't replace a proper gaming PC, but it does provide you with an option for playing on a Googlebook as long as you have an internet connection.
Android integration
So if a Googlebook's app support isn't all that different from what you could get for years on a Chromebook, what really sets the new platform apart? Integration with your Android phone, at least that's how it seems from the way Google is pitching these laptops. It's not an illogical strategy: Android is used by billions, and the smartphone is the most important device in most people's lives. And as someone well versed in Apple's ecosystem, there's no doubt that the close ties between an iPhone and a Mac (or iPad, or Apple Watch) are a major selling point.
There are a few key parts of this integration, the most prominent of which is probably casting apps from your phone. In the taskbar, next to the "G" icon where you can find all your installed apps is another little icon that looks ilke a smartphone. Clicking that brings up all the apps you have on your phone, and picking an app opens it in its own window, as if it is running on your Googlebook itself. Rather than Apple's iPhone mirroring approach, casting apps works independently from what's happening directly on your phone. But in both cases, it's a good way to quickly check on things that started on a phone, like calling a Lyft, adjusting playback to Sonos speakers or checking on a delivery order you placed in DoorDash. Once I had things set up on both devices, casting apps worked reliably. Interestingly, the apps aren't limited to being in a vertically-oriented phone-sized window — you can expand and resize the window and the app will adjust accordingly.
Transferring an app from my phone to a Googlebook didn't feel quite as useful to me, but it can be handy in a pinch. If you have a tab open in Chrome or are composing an email in Gmail on your phone, for example, you'll see a little icon on the right side of the taskbar for the corresponding app. Clicking it opens up what you're doing on your phone directly on your Googlebook. So if you're in the middle of typing out an email and want to do it on a big screen, one click will pick things right up in your draft.
It took me a little while to understand the behavior that triggers this transition. In Gmail, you need to be composing an email, whether it's a new message or a reply. If I was just reading an email, I wouldn't get the icon in the taskbar to read it on my laptop. But in Google Keep, just looking at a specific note on my phone was enough to get a shortcut to that content in the Googlebook taskbar. I also ran into a handful of occasions when the shortcut for whatever app I had open on my phone just wouldn't show up, even if it had worked previously. I'd say that this feature is still a work in progress, between the inconsistencies I experienced and the need for third-party developers to enable it in their own apps.
The last notable connection between your phone and Googlebook is simple and straightforward. Your phone shows up in the Files app as a drive you can browse. So if you have anything saved on your phone you want to get on your laptop, it's a simple process. The most obvious use case I can think of is transferring photos, but Google Photos can already back up everything you shoot on your phone to the cloud. If you prefer to manually deal with files, though, you can easily access them as if your phone is just another drive connected to your computer. It's also handy for grabbing things like screenshots or voice recordings.
Finally, while Google obviously is positioning Googlebooks as a close companion to Android phones, I was shocked to discover a nod to iPhone users as well. One of the apps pre-installed on Googlebooks is called "Link to iOS," and after scanning a QR code and enabling a few settings on an iPhone, you can get messages from an iPhone on a Googlebook. This works for SMS, RCS and iMessages, though the experience leaves a bit to be desired. Group chats don't work at all; instead, messages from people in a group chat just show up in their individual threads. But having one-on-one conversations works well enough, though it doesn't sync a full message history and images (or basically anything besides text) aren't supported. It's not nearly as full-featured as using the Google Messages app with an Android phone, but it's something!
The Magic Cursor and other Gemini tricks
Google made Gemini features a big part of the Chromebook Plus initiative it launched a few years ago, so it's no surprise to see many of those features migrating over to Googlebooks as well. A few of those tools, like the Quick Insert key that brings up a contextual menu with AI-powered suggestions, has been around for a while now. But Magic Pointer is the most significant addition to the Googlebook and its AI-focused feature set.
In Google's demos, wiggling the cursor will turn your normal pointer into the Magic Cursor, but Google is good about making sure users opt into AI-powered features for the first time. So you'll start by clicking the little pointer in the upper right corner of the screen, next to the notification alert. After enabling permissions, you'll get a little tutorial on the Magic Pointer, and then any time you vigorously wiggle your finger on the trackpad you can access this new Gemini tool.
Essentially, Magic Pointer lets you select a section of your screen to take actions on with Gemini. One thing that's pretty handy is that you can make multiple selections and have Gemini analyze them together. It's kind of like a super-charged screenshot tool, and it's smart enough to automatically highlight sections of your screen as you mouse over them. For example, moving your cursor across some text will suggest you clip a full paragraph, or it'll know when you hover over an image that you probably want to grab the entire thing. You can specifically choose a selection, but I really like the way it automatically highlights coherent sections of the screen.
Once you've selected part of your screen, Gemini will offer proactive suggestions — if it recognizes a date and location, it'll ask you if you want to add the event to your calendar. You can also type your own prompt or decide to add more sections to the selection. In that scenario, you could capture your calendar and a workout training schedule and ask Gemini to schedule those workouts at times you're free.
As with most of Google's AI tools, I can see the use case in the tightly-scripted demo examples the company gives, but I don't often see an easy or obvious way to work it into my daily workflow. It's entirely possible I'm just not clever enough to think of places where this would make my life easier. I've even been training myself to try and use the Magic Pointer for capturing things I want to act on rather than just taking standard screenshots, but it's not second nature yet. That said, this is an AI feature that I like at least at a conceptual level and it's one that I'm going to continue trying to use and see if it becomes second nature to me over time.
Rambler is another headline AI feature that came to the Pixel 11 series earlier this year. Just as you can on those phones, you can use your voice to dictate a message on your Googlebook and Rambler will clean it up. It'll remove things like "um" and if you change your mind about what you're saying, it'll recognize that and clean up your speed.
So "what are the best coffee shops, um, never mind, I mean, what are the best bakeries in the Hartford area?" became "what are the best bakeries in the Hartford area?" I don't often find myself talking to my laptops at this point, but I still think Rambler is a smart inclusion — especially for people who might get used to using it on their phone and want to try it on a Googlebook.
Another Android feature making its way to Googlebooks are home screen widgets; more specifically, you can ask a Googlebook to "create a widget" for you. There are suggestions to get you started with this, like one for the Files app that analyses and groups different documents together for quick access. I asked for one to keep my local weather up front and it worked fine, except it said the sun would set at 9:51PM or so in Massachusetts, where the sun is going down before 6PM right now. As with all things AI, make sure you check your work.
Are Googlebooks ready to be your primary computer?
At this point, it's time to get into the value proposition here. As I mentioned at the top, Googlebooks are not cheap computers. All five Googlebooks are very well made with nice screens, good performance and relatively attractive industrial design. Strictly from a hardware standpoint, the $899 Acer is asking for its first Googlebook feels appropriate given its build quality and specs. Dell's $999 XPS Googlebook is also intriguing given its extremely compact size without skimping on performance, while HP's $1,199 Googlebook 14 is a premium laptop through and through, and it feels nearly as nice as most MacBooks.
But at these prices, particularly once you're over $1,000, you can spend a little more and get similarly nice, well-equipped Windows PCs or a MacBook Air — both of which run a far more useful set of software than a Googlebook. The promise of improved connectivity between your Android phone and laptop could absolutely be beneficial, but I'm not convinced it is in anyone's best interest to choose Gemini's AI features over the much more robust and battle-tested experience you'll get using a Mac or Windows computer.
That said, I'm looking forward to the evolution of Googlebooks. While the OS might not be fully baked yet, the fact that Google has both its desktop and phone platforms now running essentially the same software would make things a lot easier for development, as well as making the two categories of devices work even more seamlessly together in the future. Just as it did with Chrome OS, Google is offering a platform that could cover the basics for a lot of users in a relatively simple, straightforward package — if we get hardware at a wider range of prices and a more mature OS, that is.

Ruling Janata Dal (United) on Friday (October 30, 2026) celebrated its 23rd foundation day of the party and credited the party’s President and former Chief Minister Nitish Kumar leadership for the Bihar’s development.
JD(U) working president Sanjay Jha wrote a message on social media account X asserting that with the trust of the people, the dedication of its workers, and the resolve for good governance, the JD(U) has carved out a distinct identity in Bihar’s politics.
“Under the leadership and guidance of our esteemed national president, Nitish Kumar ji, the party has played a pivotal role in advancing Bihar’s development, social justice, good governance, and inclusive growth. On this special occasion, heartfelt congratulations and best wishes to all senior leaders, dedicated workers, and supporters of the party,”Mr. Jha wrote.
He added that we should come together to strengthen the resolve for public service and continue working tirelessly for Bihar’s progress and prosperity.
JD(U) State president Umesh Singh Kushwaha also extended greetings on the party’s foundation Day and said that the 23-year glorious journey of the JD(U) under the leadership of Nitish Kumar is dedicated to the values of social justice and good governance.
Speaking to the media, he called Mr. Kumar as the party’s undisputed leader and his son Nishant Kumar who is also the Health Minister of Bihar as future leader of the party. Mr. Kushwaha said that the JD(U) was founded on October 30, 2003, drawing inspiration from the ideals of the Father of the Nation, Mahatma Gandhi, Dr. Baba Saheb Bhimrao Ambedkar, Loknayak Jayaprakash Narayan and Jannayak Karpoori Thakur.
“Since its inception, the party has remained committed to advancing the principles of social justice, good governance, and social harmony throughout its 23-year journey. When Nitish Kumar took the reins of Bihar in November 2005, he ushered a new era for the state,” Mr. Kushwaha said.
He added that Mr. Kumar introduced a transformative model centred on “development with justice,” good governance, and women’s empowerment that fundamentally altered both the destiny and the image of Bihar.
JD(U) State president pointed out that while the term “Bihari” had become synonymous with contempt and neglect before 2005, Nitish Kumar, through his efforts, restored honour and self-respect to Bihar and its people.
In his congratulatory message, Mr. Kushwaha asked all the party workers and leaders to take a resolve to move the JD(U) to unprecedented heights of success in days to come.
“We shall further strengthen the hands of the party’s future and our popular Health Minister, Nishant ji. We shall reinforce our commitment in taking the socialist principles of our leader, Nitish Kumar, as well as the contributions he has made toward the development of Bihar, to every household and every individual,”Mr. Kushwaha said.
Also, JD(U) has decided to organise a programme titled Sushasan Diwas: Nitish Samvad (Good Governance Day: Dialogue with Nitish) across all districts of the State on November 24, 2026.
Senior leader and minister Leshi Singh, has been appointed as the ‘State Coordinator’ for the execution of this programme.

When Nisha Panwar,30, was diagnosed with lupus in December 2013, she felt relieved. After months of recurrent fever, rashes and worsening symptoms, she finally had an explanation for what was happening to her body. Before the diagnosis, she says, several doctors had told her she had no disease and that it was “all in my head” and was referred to a psychiatrist.
For Tabassum Sultana, 28, a Bengaluru-based content creator, the diagnosis of mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), with features of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), in 2024 was followed by another setback. She developed avascular necrosis of the right hip and underwent surgery in September 2025. Her recovery was slow, she became dependent on her mother for everyday activities and had to stop working. Recurring flare-ups continue to affect her mental health.

Bucking the age-old trend of films, both big- and mid-budget, relying heavily on weekend collections, several recent titles with positive word-of-mouth have managed to draw significant audiences through the working week, according to theatre owners and trade experts.
While big films such as Dhurandhar: The Revenge and Border 2 have shown that large-scale cinema can continue to perform exceptionally well on weekdays, mid-budget Hindi films such as Welcome To The Jungle, Bhooth Bangla and Main Vaapas Aaunga have also seen steady weekday footfalls across multiplexes.
Theatre owners say audiences are becoming more selective about what brings them to cinemas. Films that earn their trust can sustain footfalls rather than rely solely on a strong opening. Cinemas, meanwhile, are increasingly treating weekdays as a distinct opportunity rather than simply an extension of the weekend. Weekday pricing, food and beverage (F&B) combos and loyalty offers are being designed to make a Tuesday or Wednesday outing more compelling. Showtimes and screen allocation are also becoming more dynamic, with cinemas responding to actual demand through the week rather than relying only on opening-day performance.
“We are seeing a very encouraging shift in the way audiences are coming to cinemas beyond the Friday-to-Sunday weekend. They are no longer deciding purely on opening-day hype. When a film connects, word-of-mouth takes over and gives it a much longer and healthier theatrical life,” said Sanjeev Kumar Bijli, executive director, PVR INOX Ltd.
“The biggest change is that audiences have become more deliberate about the films they choose. The opening weekend is often driven by star power, marketing and the initial excitement around a release. But the weekday audience is driven much more by whether people genuinely enjoyed the film and what they are hearing from others. That word-of-mouth brings in working professionals and families who may prefer a quieter weekday evening over the weekend rush,” Bijli added.
The company is closely tracking weekday demand and using it to fine-tune screen allocation and show timings, Bijli said. The weekday has become the real test of a film, he added, as it shows whether the initial buzz can translate into genuine audience connection.
The trend has played out across regional cinema as well, with Tamil films Gatta Kusthi: 2nd Round and Idhayam Murali, Punjabi film Carry On Jatta 4 and Malayalam film I, Nobody showing strong weekday holds.
Rohit Dalmia, chairman and managing director of entertainment financing platform CineNow, said Main Vaapas Aaunga actually grew through its first Wednesday and Thursday after a modest opening, while Telugu film Lenin also held strongly during the week. The trend remains title-specific, but good word-of-mouth is giving smaller and regional films longer theatrical runs, he added.
Sameer Munshi, chief operating officer, Miraj Entertainment Ltd, said theatre operators are moving away from a one-size-fits-all weekday strategy towards a more location- and city-specific approach to pricing, programming and showtimes.
“We use local audience behaviour, advance bookings and occupancy data to optimize shows and respond quickly to films showing stronger weekday legs,” Munshi added.
Agreeing that films which open small and then build through the weekdays are no longer the exception, Ashish Misra, head of commercialization, Cinépolis India, said the way films are marketed has also changed. The marketing push no longer stops on the day of release. Production houses now sustain their social media campaigns well beyond opening day, leaning into audience reactions as they come in and allowing that momentum to carry into the second and third week.
Pricing is another lever, according to Misra. The company's Blockbuster Tuesday ticket offering is designed to address this, taking the price question off the table on Tuesdays.
“Weekend ticket prices can be quite high, so many viewers, especially middle-class families and working professionals, prefer a Tuesday or Wednesday show when it is more affordable. People are also more careful about what they spend on now. They often wait for the first reviews and audience reactions before deciding if a film is worth watching in a theatre,” said film producer Anand Pandit.
At the same time, filmmakers are making more genre-specific films for particular audiences instead of trying to please everyone. Such films may start slowly but pick up as the right audience finds them, Pandit added.
“I do think we are seeing signs of greater staying power among certain films, although I wouldn’t call it a uniform trend just yet. What is particularly encouraging is that some of the strongest examples are coming from mid-sized, story-driven films, suggesting that sustained audience interest isn’t necessarily limited to big Hindi or pan-India tentpoles,” said Ashish Saksena, chief operating officer - cinemas, BookMyShow.
The platform is seeing audiences plan theatrical outings around their individual schedules, with working professionals, college students and families increasingly finding weekday slots that work for them, Saksena added. This creates an opportunity for films with strong audience appeal to build steadily across the week, even after the initial marketing-led hype has died down.
Lata writes about the media and entertainment industry for Mint, focusing on everything from traditional film and TV to newer areas like video and audio streaming, including the business and regulatory aspects of both. A journalist for over a decade, she has extensively covered relatively underexplored aspects of what is seen as a glamorous business—from the death of single-screen cinemas in small towns to unreasonable star fees and demands eating into film production budgets and eventually inflating ticket rates. She was early to spot what are now established and ongoing trends such as the slowdown in the OTT business and the surge in the popularity of southern movies, which she continues to spotlight. A regular writer of in-depth, long-form features, her best-read work ranges from critical profiles of companies like Netflix, JioHotstar and Prime Video to takes on sexual harassment and mental health in the entertainment industry. She spends a lot of time watching content, particularly the old-school way in movie theatres, to make sure her writing is embedded in on-ground experience, since she believes the best stories often come from the travesties of directly engaging with and paying for the content that she writes on, and not from celebrity tweets, company releases or listings. A graduate of the Columbia School of Journalism, she has also authored a book on the business of entertainment.

'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
- Published
The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.
Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones.
"Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed."
"I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."
Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."
The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.
For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.
But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" – which some American journalists will be invited to witness – the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week.
"They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.
Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.
Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."
Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.
No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said.
"This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive."
On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."
This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson – an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable.
"Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.
Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.
Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".
Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.
On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."
The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.
Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground.
"An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.
Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon.
But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.
But the clock is ticking.
The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said.
"We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months.
"These few days showed us how it could be if it all finally ended."

You know that phone addiction has become a big issue when even Google and Apple are bundling time management tools into their handsets—Digital Wellbeing and Screen Time, respectively. There are now also a plethora of apps looking to help you cultivate a healthier relationship with your device.
One of the newer ones, which takes a slightly different approach to the norm, is Oh My Hours for iOS. (There's no sign of an Android version yet.) Rather than giving you a mass of menus and options to wade through, it simply splits each day into blocks of hours that you can either waste or use productively, then puts a black mark next to the hours during which your phone has distracted you.
It's simple, it's effective, and it just might work. Rather than seeing how long you spent on X and Instagram, you see the hours you've lost to social media algorithms and the infinite scroll. Here's how Oh My Hours works on your iPhone, plus some other apps to check out if you’re looking to develop healthier phone habits.
Moments Lost
You can get started with Oh My Hours for free on iOS. But to really make the most of it, a $10-per-year or $20 lifetime payment is required. This lets you customize what counts as a “lost” hour or day, and it gives you access to month and year views, which provide the best insights into how you're spending time on your phone.
Here's how it works. First, you indicate which apps you consider distractions, either by category (social media apps and games, for example) or by selecting apps individually. If you use any distracting app for a certain amount of time—this can be customized in settings—then that hour of the day is marked as “lost.”
The main interface shows each day as a straightforward series of circles representing hours. Every circle that’s filled in black is an hour you’ve lost to an app that has pulled you away from something more worthwhile.
It’s quite a brutal and minimalist approach, but I like it. It really brings home how much time you can spend on apps that aren’t really all that good for you, especially when you start looking at your progress (or lack of it) over entire weeks or months. However, I did find that once I’d lost a particular hour, my brain wanted to cram in as much absent-minded scrolling as possible during the rest of that hour.
By default, an hour is marked as lost if only if you spend seconds inside a distracting app. It's quite a harsh approach, but it needs to be—otherwise I think there would be the temptation to use up any allotted free time after every hour resets. You can extend this threshold period through settings, if you pay for the app.
Another handy feature here is the ability to set designated quiet hours. These are times when you really, absolutely do not want to look at your phone unnecessarily: Any use of a distracting app here blackens the boxes for all the hours in the quiet zone, not just one. Again, this can be customized, whether or not you’re using the app for free.
There’s one more option here, which is to reset an hour if you think it’s been marked incorrectly. (Maybe your finger slipped and you really didn’t mean to launch Instagram.) It’s all very simple and easy to use, and there’s an export tool here that gives you a CSV file of your stats if you want to do more with them.
Other App Picks
As I’ve already mentioned, if you’re in the market for an app that’ll gently nudge your habits toward spending less time on your phone, there are abundant options that look at the problem from a variety of angles. These are in addition to the Digital Wellbeing (Android) and Screen Time (iOS) tools you’ll find on your phone, which can be accessed from the Settings screens.
One Sec for Android or iOS takes a simple approach to phone addiction. For the apps you specify, it will load up a breathing exercise for you to complete before giving you the choice to continue to the app or back out. It’s a small tweak, but it’s surprisingly effective, and it’s backed by science. You can get started for free, while $20 a year gets you more features, including full app blocking and more advanced time tracking.
Then there’s Forest, for Android or iOS, which I’ve found to be useful whenever I’ve wanted to try to encourage myself to spend less time on my phone. The longer you ignore your handset, the bigger your virtual forest grows, and the app developers invest in real tree planting to further incentivize you. The main focus timer can be used without paying, while upgrades like customizations and allowed lists will set you back at least $6 a month.
ScreenZen, available for Android or iOS, is comprehensive and completely free (though you can donate to the developer if you find it helpful, which I’d recommend). You can set up a variety of barriers between you and your distracting apps, depending on your preference, including customized pauses (with motivational messages) and math challenges. Conventional app and timer blocks are also included.
One of the most thorough options here is Roots, though it’s available only on iOS. You’re able to schedule phone-free periods, block specific apps, and set up phone detox challenges that you can take on with friends and family. Like Oh My Hours, the app is also really good at giving you a breakdown of how much time you’ve saved by staying out of certain apps. Basic blocks and limits are free, with more advanced customizations available for $10 a month.
Also worth considering is Brick, which combines the free Android or iOS app with a small physical device that’ll set you back $59. The Brick itself is an NFC transmitter (it works like tap-to-pay), and when you want some distraction-free time, just press your phone against it to block (or unblock) specific apps. The controls are all managed in the Brick app. It’s incredibly simple, and that’s what makes it effective.

India's biggest telecom giant, the Meta and Google-backed Jio Platforms, is set to make its stock market debut on Wednesday.
Despite a bruising spell for Indian markets, its historic $3.2bn initial public offering (IPO) - the country's largest ever - has drawn overwhelming demand from top global fund managers, domestic institutions and mom-and-pop retail investors.
Bids outstripped the shares on offer within hours of subscriptions opening on 21 October.
Owned by Asia's richest man, Mukesh Ambani, Jio is one of India's most consequential companies, with half a billion people subscribing to its cheap mobile data. But its meteoric rise has also been dogged by controversy.
The company burst onto India's crowded telecom scene in 2016, offering throwaway tariffs that got millions of Indians hooked to the internet.
But its launch led to a huge disruption in the telecom sector. A market once crowded with 17 operators shrunk to an oligopoly of just three, with critics accusing the deep-pocketed company of waging a price war that pushed rivals out of business.
More recently, Elon Musk criticised Ambani, calling him the "real boss of India", suggesting that Jio was trying to thwart Starlink's entry into India. Reliance dismissed the allegations saying it welcomed competition from Musk.
For all the scrutiny it has faced over the last decade, Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution, spawning a huge digital economy and democratising online payments, food delivery and e-commerce in Asia's third-biggest economy.
Within three years of its launch, customer data usage rose fifty-fold and data prices crashed.
This aggressive discounting helped Jio rapidly amass some 553 million mobile subscribers by 2026. It also cemented its dominance in other segments, capturing 50% of the wireless broadband market and more than 40% of fixed broadband.
Jio also carries 60% of India's wireless data traffic and boasts of the largest 5G subscriber base outside China, according to brokerage Emkay Global, which has described the company as the "digital engine of India".
But analysts say its stock market debut - which will see its promoters dilute their shareholding by about 3% - could mark a turning point in Jio's pricing strategy, potentially bringing an end to years of ultra-cheap tariffs.
"The era of Jio using cheap tariffs as a market-share weapon is drawing to a close," said Nitya Shah, co-founder of KamayaKya Wealth Management.
"A listed Jio must answer to minority shareholders… which structurally reduces its incentive to keep pricing suppressed."
Jio's future growth will no longer be driven primarily by adding subscribers through discounted plans. Instead, it will depend on "earning more per subscriber - through the migration to 5G, successive tariff revisions, and the extension of fixed wireless broadband into homes fibre has never reached", brokerage company Motilal Oswal said in a note.
The listing could also pave the way for Jio's competitors to raise prices, as fears of being undercut by a cheaper rival begin to recede.
"The biggest beneficiary of this shift could be Vodafone Idea," says Shah. "It is a moment the sector's weakest balance sheet gets its strongest tailwind".
For Indian consumers, any further increases would come on the heels of an industry-wide tariff hike a few years ago. Analysts say another round of price rises could trigger a fresh churn in the market as price-sensitive customers switch to the cheapest plans available.
While consumers may have to brace for higher bills, Jio's IPO offers investors a bet on India's seemingly insatiable appetite for data - and the growing ecosystem of digital services the company offers across entertainment, cloud computing, gaming and financial services.
India has emerged as the second-largest consumer of mobile data in the world, driven by lower tariffs and rising penetration of smartphones.
Jio's monthly data use per customer has climbed from 28.7 GB in 2024 to 42.3 GB in 2026 - up by 52% in two years. As per some estimates, usage is expected to surge further to 65GB by the end of this decade as disposable incomes rise.
All of this will give a tailwind for Jio to drive long-term growth in average revenue per user.
"Penetration of most digital services remains well below China and the US, which leaves significant headroom [for growth]," according to Emkay Global.
The listing is also likely to enhance transparency and provide investors with a "clearer market valuation" for the company, according to Moody's rating agency, as Jio is currently part of Reliance Industries, which has businesses spanning oil refining and retail.
But as much as its central and growing role in India's economy has excited investors, the buzz about the IPO also comes from the fact that this is the first share sale from the Reliance conglomerate in over two decades.
The company - which started as a small spice and polyester yarn trading venture in 1958 before expanding into textiles, petrochemicals, refining and eventually to retail, telecom and digital services - is known for its track record of long-term wealth creation, and enjoys legendary status among mom-and-pop investors.
Dhirubhai Ambani, the founder of the Reliance empire, is said to have played a foundational role in popularising equity investing and taking it beyond the preserve of traders and wealthy families in the 1980s and 90s.
In its early years, Reliance built a vast base of individual shareholders by turning its annual general meetings into grand spectacles of big announcements, dividend payouts and celebrations of public share ownership. Over time, this helped forge a fiercely loyal investor base, many of whom developed a deep emotional bond with the company.
And while Reliance Industries' stock has fallen nearly 20% over the past year, its longer-term track record continues to inspire confidence.
"The company has given average annualised returns of around 30% consistently for thirty years," Kranthi Bathini of Mumbai-based WealthMills Securities told the BBC.
"That's why there's anticipation that the same magic can be replicated with the Jio IPO."

Harley-Davidson's electric motorbike brand has 'substantial doubt' about its future
LiveWire cited 'recurring operating losses' despite an 80 percent US market share in its segment.
Harley-Davidson's electric motorcycle spinoff LiveWire has raised "substantial doubt" about its ability to continue as a going concern, the company said in its latest financial report. LiveWire cited "recurring operating losses, negative cash flows... and limited liquidity resources" as contributing factors to its determination. The warning comes despite a rise in LiveWire's sales this quarter and its 80 percent market share in the 50+ kW on-road EV segment.
To address those issues, LiveWire said it has formed a "special restructuring committee" to explore financing, a sale, restructuring, strategic partnerships and other options. It withdrew previous guidance projecting a 2026 operating loss in the $70 million to $80 million range. (Harley-Davidson held a 74 percent stake in LiveWire when it spun the company off into a separate unit by a SPAC merger in 2022.)
The warning comes just as LiveWire is releasing its LiveWire S4 Honcho series with a starting price under $5,000. The company said it has delivered the first units of that model to the US market with the S4 Honcho Trail, and plans to ship the S4 Honcho Street version to dealerships in October. Livewire recently revealed a new model called the Dust Spur as well.
The electric motorcycle market has grown steadily over the last five years, with sales reaching a record 10.17 million units in 2025. However, ICE motorcycles still dominate market share with nearly 88 percent of sales (2024), according to Mordor Intelligence. Much of the market growth is concentrated in southeast Asia and Africa, regions that saw 83 percent and 86.9 percent growth, respectively, in 2025. The North American market expanded by 27 percent last year.
LiveWire's struggles are unfortunate, given Harley-Davidson's legacy as an American icon. The company's new, cheaper e-motorbikes could help it expand in other territories and boost cash flow, provided it can navigate its current financial troubles.

Former Bachelor star Sam Wood will remain in custody while he awaits trial on domestic violence charges, after he was refused bail for a second time.
Wood, 46, from Melbourne, has been held in custody since his arrest on 4 October at Noosa.
 
On Friday supreme court justice Patrick McCafferty said Wood posed “an unacceptable risk” of further offending, meaning he will remain in the high-security Wolston correctional centre until his trial, which the court heard might not take place until 2028.
Wood was previously remanded over allegations he choked and assaulted his wife, Snezana Wood, while the family was holidaying on the Sunshine Coast.
He is charged with two domestic violence offences: assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting.
His legal team have indicated he will fight the charges and he has not yet entered a plea.
During an initial bail hearing, a court heard Snezana was supportive of the charges, that she was allegedly choked and that “there was a cessation of breath”.
“She articulates [in a video-recorded statement] the banging of her head on the floor. She couldn’t breathe,” police prosecutor Jeanette Grigoris told the earlier hearing. “She thought she was going to die.”
The more serious charge, related to strangulation, placed him in a “show cause” position where there is a presumption against bail unless he can demonstrate he does not pose a risk of re-offending. McCafferty said that Wood had not satisfied him that proposed conditions could ameliorate that risk.
 
During Friday’s bail hearing, the Supreme Court heard claims that Wood used drugs and alcohol, engaged in a “party lifestyle” and that he “struggles with anger”.
  
On Friday Wood’s lawyer, Paula Morreau KC, said that there was no suggestion Wood “suffered from addiction” despite crown submissions that he used drugs and alcohol use and engaged in a “party lifestyle”.
Morreau said that if granted bail, Wood proposed to reside in Tasmania, where his father lives, and that he would agree to the condition “to not enter Victoria” where Snezana lives. At the earlier application, Wood had sought bail to reside in Melbourne.
Morreau said Wood had been suffering “significant stressors” and that he “struggles with anger” but that in such situations “he usually leaves and takes time”.
“He shows he has the capacity for self-control,” she said.
Wood’s legal team proposed he undergo a “men’s behavioural change” course if released on bail.
Crown prosecutor Jessica Guy said there were “serious features” to allegations that Wood assaulted and strangled his wife.
“[Wood] didn’t desist. [The] violence extended beyond the application of force to her neck, to the banging of her head to the floor of the skirting boards.
“[It occurred] in the presence of an adult witness and the close proximity of young children.
Wood is now being held at the high-security Wolston correctional centre near Brisbane. He was not brought to the court for the hearing on Friday.
The bail hearing continues.

Canadian Crime Stoppers Association advises chapters to accept tips by phone only
Public asked to call 222-TIPS to submit tips anonymously
The Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) is advising its local chapters to solely accept tips by telephone instead of online, it said in a statement to CBC News on Friday.
The "interim telephone-only approach … will allow participating local programs to receive tips without using Navigate360’s P3 platform," reads the statement, referring to the third-party U.S. company's tip management platform that suffered a massive data breach in March.
It appears to be a shift for the not-for-profit organization, which had previously issued guidance to local programs that if members of the public asked about the breach, they should express their confidence in Navigate360's security improvements and say the platform "remains secure and appropriate for continued use."
In the Friday statement, the CCSA asked that the public now call 222-TIPS to submit tips anonymously. For programs that have been paused, there will be local announcements about when telephone reporting will resume, it said.
"Local programs will keep new information under their control and share it securely with law enforcement," reads the statement from CCSA president David J. Forster.
"This change cannot undo the exposure of information already taken. We will continue pressing Navigate360 for answers while working to rebuild trust in a program that has long helped communities prevent and solve crime."
The extent of the breach was revealed in a CBC investigation published last week, which found that over 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years had been hacked.
To date, more than 40 local Crime Stoppers chapters and police agencies in five provinces have temporarily paused their intake of anonymous tips or their partnerships with the organization. Meanwhile, the privacy commissioner is investigating the breach, focusing on Navigate360 and its security safeguards at the time of the hack in March.
"It's hard to imagine [Crime Stoppers] ever getting back to where they were in terms of trust," said Randy Lippert, a criminology professor at the University of Windsor in Ontario, in an interview with CBC News before the Friday statement was released.
At least 13 programs not accepting tips in any form
Before receiving the CCSA statement, CBC had attempted to contact all 64 Crime Stoppers chapters we identified as having compromised tips. (Six do not have publicly listed contact information.)
To date, 13 Crime Stoppers programs in Ontario and Saskatchewan said they would no longer accept anonymous tips.
The latest addition to the list was Ontario's Brant-Brantford Crime Stoppers chapter, which made the announcement on its Facebook page.
Three Crime Stoppers chapters explicitly confirmed they were still accepting anonymous tips: New Brunswick and the districts of Thunder Bay and Sault Ste. Marie and Algoma.
The latter two programs both have statements on their websites — published before the Friday statement — stating that they were unable to accept tips intended for their local police services, which had paused their participation in Crime Stoppers. But they said they would still accept tips for "other participating police services in our region."
CBC News has reached out to the three chapters about whether they will reconsider the decision, in light of their national organization's new guidance.
OPP 'pausing the promotion' of program
CBC also contacted the biggest municipal police departments in the country that hadn't yet commented on the breach to ask them if they intended to suspend their use of anonymous tips as a policing tool. Crime Stoppers sends tips to law enforcement when deemed necessary, but it works independently of the police.
At least 29 police units across Ontario, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and British Columbia said they had suspended their partnership with the Crime Stoppers program.
However, some, such as Calgary and Charlottetown, said they would continue accepting Crime Stoppers tips and that their use of the program "has not been paused."
Meanwhile, the Ontario Provincial Police confirmed that it was pausing the promotion of the Crime Stoppers program. However, people can still use it if they prefer to, a spokesperson said in a statement, and the agency will assess the information "as appropriate."
The RCMP did not explicitly confirm whether it was still using anonymous Crime Stoppers tips for active investigations. Instead, it said it was aware that several chapters had paused their tip intake, and advised any potential tipsters to avoid sharing any identifiable information in their reports.
Lippert said that there could be long-term implications from police agencies' distancing from Crime Stoppers, going beyond the use of anonymous tips in policing, due to the program's "strong overlap" with law enforcement.
"It's just hard to imagine Crime Stoppers being able to survive without a lot of the support," he said.
For example, while Crime Stoppers' reward money does not come from the police, many agencies do give their local chapters funding for other matters, such as special events or marketing campaigns, he said. Some have provided their chapters with physical offices, or have even assigned officers to serve as program co-ordinators and help investigate tips.
CCSA previously insisted on 'continued operations'
The CCSA previously appeared take a different approach to how it addressed the breach and its relationship with Navigate360, even with the fallout after CBC's initial investigation.
In an internal memo to local programs dated Oct. 22 and obtained by CBC News, president David J. Forster had advised them to direct all media inquiries to the national association, saying one of its key messaging points would be that Navigate360's "security improvements support continued operations."
The memo, which was sent the day after Toronto Crime Stoppers paused accepting tips, included a suggested response to potential questions from the public about why other local chapters continued to accept tips: "We continue to receive tips because of our confidence in the technical work completed by our third-party software provider, together with stronger procedures for handling information within Crime Stoppers."
CBC News has reached out to Navigate360 for comment on the Friday statement.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

A federal judge on Thursday rejected the federal government’s new definition of “medical frailty” and ruled that states did not have adequate time or resources to overhaul their eligibility systems, injecting new uncertainty into the imminent rollout of Medicaid work requirements across the country.
Judge Richard D. Stearns of the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts ruled that federal regarding who is considered too sick to work was overly restrictive, and said that the suit from over two dozen states successfully demonstrated that implementation of the Medicaid work requirements, as written, would cause “irreparable harm.”
“Because enforcement of an unlawful definition of ‘medically frail’ may lead to the disenrollment of otherwise eligible vulnerable individuals relying on Medicaid coverage for continuity of care, the States (and public) face potential for great hardship in the absence of an injunction,” Stearns wrote in his order.
