For people living with peripheral artery disease (PAD), walking even short distances or doing routine household tasks can become difficult because of leg pain. The condition develops when arteries supplying blood to the legs become narrow, usually because fatty deposits build up along their walls. With less blood reaching the muscles, walking can cause pain, cramps or heaviness that ease with rest. In advanced cases, pain may persist even when a person is sitting or lying down, and poor circulation can lead to wounds that do not heal.
Treatment can be challenging too because movement is an important part of managing PAD, while pain makes it difficult to stay active. Structured exercise, medicines and control of risk factors such as smoking, diabetes and high blood pressure can help manage the condition. When blood flow is severely reduced, procedures may be needed to prevent damage to the feet and legs. PAD can also affect overall cardiovascular health, increasing the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Managing pain
Pain, cramps, heaviness in the calf or thigh that develop during walking and ease with rest are known as intermittent claudication. This happens when narrowed arteries cannot supply enough blood to meet the muscles’ increased needs during activity.
Venu S., consultant vascular surgeon, Prashanth Hospitals, Chennai, says structured walking programmes can help patients gradually increase the distance they can walk. Patients are generally advised to walk until the discomfort becomes moderate, rest until it settles and then resume walking. Sessions commonly last 30 to 45 minutes and take place several times a week, with supervision where possible.
He says patients who follow a structured programme for about three months may be able to walk twice as far, or more, before pain begins. The pace and duration should suit each patient’s ability. Those who find walking difficult may need an adapted exercise programme under medical supervision.
Balaji V., senior consultant, vascular surgery, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai, says quitting smoking, eating a healthy diet, staying physically active and controlling blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol are also important parts of treatment.
Exercise should not mean pushing through severe pain. Pain that does not settle with rest needs medical assessment. Pain in the feet or toes while resting, particularly at night, can indicate a serious reduction in blood flow and requires prompt medical attention.
Diagnosis and treatment
Diagnosis usually begins with a review of symptoms and medical history, followed by an examination of the legs and feet, including checking the pulses. Doctors may measure the ankle-brachial index (ABI), which compares blood pressure at the ankle with that in the arm, to assess blood flow. A Doppler ultrasound scan can help identify narrowed arteries and assess circulation. In patients with severe symptoms or wounds that do not heal, a CT angiogram may be needed to locate the blockage and plan treatment.
Medicines aim to relieve symptoms, slow the progression of arterial disease and reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke. Antiplatelet medicines such as aspirin or clopidogrel help prevent blood clots. Statins lower cholesterol and help stabilise fatty deposits in artery walls. Medicines to control blood pressure and diabetes are also important. Cilostazol can help some patients with walking-related pain walk farther before symptoms begin, but it is not suitable for people with heart failure. Select patients may need additional medicines to reduce cardiovascular and limb-related risks.
Experts say treatment often needs to continue long term, even when symptoms improve. Patients should not stop or change prescribed medicines without consulting their doctor.
Diabetes can damage nerves and reduce sensation in the feet, allowing cuts and wounds to go unnoticed. It can also affect smaller arteries, making some blockages harder to treat. High blood pressure and cholesterol contribute to arterial damage and the build-up of fatty deposits. Kidney disease can cause calcium to build up in artery walls and delay wound healing. Heart disease can occur alongside PAD because both may result from the same underlying process.
During follow-up, doctors assess changes in walking distance and symptoms and may repeat ABI measurements or Doppler scans to check blood flow. Blood tests can help monitor cholesterol, blood sugar and kidney function.
Preventing complications
When symptoms remain disabling despite medicines and exercise, doctors may consider a procedure to widen the narrowed artery. The decision depends on the location and extent of the blockage, the severity of symptoms and the patient’s overall health.
Angioplasty uses a small balloon to widen a narrowed artery. A stent may be placed to help keep it open. Experts say newer techniques can also help treat complex blockages.
Intravascular lithotripsy uses shock waves delivered through a specialised balloon to modify heavy calcium deposits in the artery, making it easier to widen the vessel. Atherectomy devices can remove fatty deposits in selected cases, while thrombectomy devices are used to remove blood clots. The appropriate method depends on the type and location of the blockage.
For extensive disease, bypass surgery creates an alternative route for blood to reach the affected part of the leg. The choice between a procedure performed through a blood vessel and surgery depends on the blockage, the patient’s condition and the likely benefits and risks.
Pain at rest, wounds that do not heal or gangrene can indicate that the leg is at risk and require urgent medical assessment. A wound that has not healed within two weeks, a cold or discoloured foot, or a black patch on a toe or heel should not be ignored. Sudden, severe leg pain accompanied by paleness, coldness, numbness or weakness is a medical emergency because it may indicate a sudden blockage of an artery.
Regular foot checks are particularly important for people with diabetes, who may not feel an injury developing. Recognising worsening symptoms and seeking timely care can help preserve mobility and prevent serious damage to the feet and legs.

Alberta separatist Jeff Rath kicked out of governing United Conservative Party
In an email, the party said he had 'made clear' he did 'not support' party
Separatist leader Jeff Rath, who rose to prominence in the lead-up to the Alberta referendum in his white cowboy hat, has had his membership revoked by the governing United Conservative Party.
In an email sent to Rath on Thursday and viewed by CBC News, Dustin Van Vugt, the party's executive director, said that Rath's "words and actions have made clear" that he does not support the party or its objectives.
"Your public conduct in relation to our party and leader has not met the basic standard of decency we expect of our members when they disagree or otherwise."
His membership was revoked immediately, Van Vugt wrote.
In a phone call, Rath said he knew why he was being singled out.
"Because I'm a very loud and effective critic of Danielle Smith," he said.
"She obviously does not want free speech in the party."
Rath said he also received an email from the UCP notifying him the party had refunded the $239 he paid in order to attend next month's AGM.
Rath and Smith have publicly sparred over their differing views on Alberta’s place in Confederation, and their debates have occasionally veered into more personal territory.
Earlier this week, Rath accused Smith of colluding with federalist leader Thomas Lukaszuk in a text exchange he posted online. When NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi questioned Smith about it, the premier noted Rath’s prior financial contributions to the Opposition party.
Speaking to reporters Friday, Smith confirmed the party's executive director had pulled Rath's membership.
"He’s never supported me ... He never supported me during the leadership, he never supported me in my time in office, and he certainly doesn’t support me now," she said.
"That’s irrelevant," she added. "What is relevant is that he has said publicly things like he wants to come to the AGM to turn the UCP into an independence party. And we are not an independence party."

Elephants, monkeys, tigers, and reptiles once lived on a corner of a South Florida beach, where I found empty cages covered in graffiti and greenery.
The Crandon Park Zoo opened in 1948 as Miami's first zoo, according to the Miami Herald. Then a hurricane in the 1980s left it in shambles. The park closed, and animals that survived the hurricane were moved to a larger area. In 1991, the zoo ruins reopened as gardens.
I visited the park in October 2021 to see what remained of the abandoned zoo, and I found a natural wildlife sanctuary.
The first thing I noticed was a sign at the entrance warning visitors that crocodiles were present.
According to Atlas Obscura, the ruins are also home to wild alligators, iguanas, and peacocks.
The walkways through the park made me feel as if I were in a zoo — one where the animals were free.
Parts of the park were paved, while others felt wild. Some of the land was once a coconut plantation, according to the Miami Herald.
In one shaded area, I spotted what appeared to be an abandoned animal cage embedded in the rocks.
I thought it looked like it could have been a unique, immersive attraction and wondered what animals may have lived there decades ago.
Some of the abandoned structures were fenced off and covered in graffiti.
I peered over high, chain-linked fences and spotted remnants of vandalized structures.
But one large structure remained accessible.
It appeared to once house multiple cages.
Around the back, I noticed caged doors that looked as if they were used to feed the animals inside.
I was able to see inside a few of the animals' quarters, which were now empty aside from some leaves, branches, and overgrown vines. The doors were still locked.
The view inside the structures was somewhat haunting.
Peering inside made me think about the animals that might have gotten stuck inside as hurricane waters filled their enclosures.
I tried to imagine what kind of animals could live in these spaces. Based on their size, maybe monkeys, I thought.
I left the park thinking it's probably a better home now for the wildlife that has taken over.
After my visit, the zoo celebrated its 75th anniversary of serving the community in November 2022.

Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent media outlets, has announced it will permanently close next month. The newspaper, whose former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov won the Nobel peace prize in 2021, cited intolerable pressure, including being stripped of its newsroom, its donation platforms and its legal right to publish.
“This is not just our own story; it is the story of a country and a society that are being systematically crushed,” wrote its editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, on the newspaper’s website.
Launched in the 1990s and for many years partly funded by the late Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, Novaya made its name through dogged, long-form reporting on corruption, rights abuses and social issues. Over the years, six of its journalists have been assassinated, including Anna Politkovskaya, who was gunned down in the stairwell of her Moscow apartment block in 2006.
While Novaya always swam against a tide of repression, the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made independent reporting almost impossible and decimated the Russian media landscape. Novaya was one of the last critical voices still operating from inside the country.
“For nearly five years of ***, we managed to keep working while being completely encircled by the security services. Now it’s over. We have found ourselves in a ‘kill zone’,” wrote Sokolov. The stars were used in place of the word “war”, as under Russian law, journalists must refer to the war in Ukraine as a “special military operation” or face consequences.
The newspaper’s first response to the invasion was to put out a special bilingual Russian-Ukrainian edition in the days after Vladimir Putin launched the invasion. It described the war as “madness” on its front page. Soon after, the Kremlin implemented draconian new censorship laws, which forced media outlets to publish only the Russian official narrative about the conflict.
“We said it’s not journalism and we’re not going to do that,” said Nadezhda Prusenkova, the head of Novaya’s press service. The newspaper published blank white spaces instead of euphemisms and false information, to provide a visible reminder of the censorship laws.
By the end of March 2022, Novaya decided to stop publishing its print edition altogether, but the threats and pressure only increased. In April that year, Muratov was doused with red paint while on a train, an attack that damaged his eyesight and that US officials say was carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence agencies. In September that year, the newspaper’s official licence was taken away and soon after their website was blocked in Russia.
Novaya’s journalists, long used to operating in a hostile environment, found ways to circumvent the bans. Many left Russia, and a number of exiled former employees set up Novaya Gazeta Europe, a legally distinct outlet. Muratov and a core team stayed behind and continued to publish a series of magazines with a print run of 999 copies, taking advantage of a law that means magazines with under 1,000 copies do not require an official licence. Novaya’s website continued running, too, although the Russian state hit the outlet with various new legal threats.
“The fact Novaya kept working for this four and a half years after everything that happened was a miracle, but it was not just a miracle, it was also the daily choice of people who continued to go to work even when it was very scary,” said Elena Kostyuchenko, a former Novaya journalist who spent 17 years at the newspaper. “Today I feel very inspired by my colleagues, but also very painful and sad for them, and for all of us.”
In recent months, Prusenkova said the pressure had become intolerable. In April, the journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”. He is under house arrest awaiting trial and last month Sokolov’s home was searched as part of the case.
This month, the newspaper’s landlords informed Novaya staff that they must vacate their longstanding office premises in central Moscow by 9 November. The newsroom has been the hub of the newspaper for decades and houses a memorial museum to Politkovskaya in the former office of the murdered journalist. Prusenkova said the exhibits would be taken down and put into storage, for now.
On top of the eviction notice, all the outlet’s donation platforms have been shut down, leaving the paper without any source of funding. The court case, combined with the eviction and the lack of funds, gave the newspaper no choice but to close, said staff.
“Sometimes it happens that your enemies win. At this moment in time, it seems like they have won, and we have no options left,” said Prusenkova. But she said it was probable Novaya’s journalists would try to find some way to continue their work. “After all, we don’t know how to do anything else,” she said.

It is officially the flu season with winter and monsoon seasons creeping in on large parts of the world. There is a need to take precautions and be aware of the risks of the season, particularly at a time when we are hearing of old viruses resurging, or new, never-before heard pathogens rearing their heads, even known microorganisms that cause disease among humans, after a zoonotic spillover.
As in the case of the Shamonda virus. Last week France reported the first human Shamonda virus case, a virus usually circulating amongst livestock. The severely immunocompromised patient died, spurring global public health concerns. While France said there was no health risk as a result of this, there are definitely problems when a new pathogen crosses the barrier. For everything we currently know about the Shamonda virus, read Athira Elssa Johnson’s explainer, here.
She also writes on Melioidosis in India: a potentially deadly infection that may be going undetected. Melioidosis caused by B. pseudomallei which is found in soil and water in tropical and subtropical regions, can cause pneumonia, bloodstream infection, skin and soft-tissue infections, abscesses in organs such as the liver and spleen, septic arthritis and bone infections. It can also affect the kidneys, muscles and prostate.
Meanwhile, as the second patient in Nigeria, a relative of the first case of death from Ebola in the nation, also died of Ebola, some hopeful news came from DR Congo where the Ebola vaccine trial began for the Bundibugyo strain.
In the U.S., where an early U.S. flu season has set in, doctors warned that the current strain may signal a higher risk for younger people; and urged them to get shots.
Talking of the weather, it is also time to discuss pollution and climate-related health effects. Nikhil M. Babu writes that air pollution in Delhi-NCR has come ahead of winter.
In Mumbai, Yohaan Varghese says another crisis is brewing, as attention remains on the northern States. Mumbai recorded 231 days of ‘good’ or ‘satisfactory’ air quality in 2026. The BMC has been forced to unveil a winter pollution action plan.
Geetha Srimathi interprets a global report that claims: Extreme weather, harmful chemicals escalating health risks among food workers.
As a bellwether State for healthcare in the country, what happens in Kerala affects the entire nation, in some way. The Spinal Muscular Atrophy controversy, currently brewing in the southern State too could contain lessons for the nation.
First do read C. Maya’s explainer on what this controversy is all about, here. After the government switched the drug in its SMA programme from branded to generic, parents of children living with SMA have been asking for a switch back to the branded version; meanwhile the label on a drug bottle has sparked concerns, and political parties have now latched on to the issue.
Meanwhile, experts have opined that the Row over SMA drug distribution in Keralam is unwarranted and a hospital rejected charges of ‘clinical trial drugs’ given to children. Further a doctor at SAT Hospital said Parents were actually counselled about the generic drug that was to be used ahead of administration.
We are sure to be following up this story until it reaches its logical conclusion.
Further on the regulation scenario in the health care/medical sector, the issue of prices of drugs was top of the agenda after the recent Supreme Court judgement. Devyanshi Bihani looked at data and found that ₹8,447 crore in medicine overcharging claims remain outstanding as SC seeks wider price controls.
Bindu Shajan Perappadan wrote on the concerns over the National Medical Commission withdrawing the 2023 Rules on medical education standards. While the government claims this has been done to eliminate duplication and multiple overlaps, it has raised questions about how violations by medical colleges will be penalised, and how compliance with prescribed standards will be verified under the remaining regulatory framework.
She also recorded the disability lobby’s demand that the Centre classify communication aids as essential products.
Dr. C. Aravinda explained what the National Medical Commission’s new guidelines say about advertising in medicine, while Afshan Yasmeen reported a Lancet review that called for clinical assessment over routine scans for back pain.

This recent UK-Chennai collaborative study showed that good-quality diets are associated with better cholesterol levels even among those with a genetic predisposition.
Jacob Koshy wrote about a study that claimed Plant-based meat yielded a higher share of absorbable protein than traditional meat, and on the side of plants, still, Vasudevan Mukunth asked if theCentre’s new fortified potato variety the Centrecan address India’s hidden hunger or undernutrition problem.

A three-year long study in Bengaluru of over 10,000 frontline workers has brought to light reduced lung function among BMTC bus drivers, traffic police, pourakarmikas and construction workers — sections most exposed to polluted air.
The study, done by the VAAYU Occupational & Environmental Respiratory Illness Clinic (VOERIC), screened 4,517 BMTC drivers, 3,285 traffic police personnel, 2,169 construction workers and 379 pourakarmikas.
Vulnerable sections face highest health risk
All the groups that were screened showed higher-than-normal prevalence of early lung-function abnormalities.
Among the occupations, pourakarmikas were found to have the highest proportion of workers with the PRISm pattern, an indication of reduced lung capacity. Around 45% of them showed indications of reduced lung function.
BMTC workers and traffic police followed, with 29.5% and 28%, respectively, showing reduced lung function. Among construction workers, 15% showed a PRISm pattern.
Around 2.6% of BMTC drivers, 2.3% pourakarmikas, 2.1% construction workers, and 1% traffic police personnel reported signs of obstructive airflow.
The survey also found that 88.2% of the BMTC drivers never used a mask, as was the case with 55% traffic police, 37.9% construction workers, and 16.3% pourakarmikas.
Comorbidities
The subjects were also analysed for comorbidities, and the results revealed a grim situation, with high levels of obesity reported among the sections.
Pourakarmikas had the highest proportion at 62%, closely followed by BMTC drivers, 60.7% of whom were found to be obese/overweight. For traffic police, the figure stood at 51.3%.
The figures are much higher than the India reference figure of 28.6%.
The study also flags that diabetes prevalence among BMTC drivers was 18.2%, higher than the Indian average of 11.4%. Among traffic police personnel, the prevalence was 14%.
The physically active nature of the work and the relatively young demography among the construction workers translated to lower prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases. The average age of construction workers was found to be 31.3± 10, 98.3% of whom worked for more than 8 hours daily.
The concerns with higher incidences of diabetes, uncontrolled blood pressure, overweight and obesity across occupational groups has reinforced the need for a comprehensive approach to worker health including cardiometabolic screening
“While the findings demonstrate a significant burden of health abnormalities, further longitudinal research is required to establish the extent to which occupational exposures contribute to specific respiratory and cardiovascular outcomes. VOERIC plans to start this as cohort along with government support,” a statement from VOERIC said.
“Air pollution is considered the new tobacco. It is an emerging risk-enhancing factor for heart attack and brain stroke,” said C.N. Manjunath, leading cardiologist and Bengaluru Rural MP, at a round table where the results from the study were published.
Speaking about the importance of reducing traffic congestion, scientific garbage disposal and adoption of necessary measures during road construction to reduce dust, in tackling air pollution, he acknowledged the importance of policy intervention backed by data.

Kenya's Health Ministry announced the country's second Ebola death on Friday (October 23, 2026), saying a 65-year-old woman who was a close relative of the first patient died after developing symptoms while in quarantine.
The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago and began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.
The Ministry said medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life", but she died on Friday (October 23) evening.
Her family was notified, and the Ministry said it would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.
The remaining seven Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities. No new infections were reported.
Kenya announced its first ever Ebola case on October 6 after a 40-year-old Kenyan man who was living in Congo travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3. He was driven by a relative to Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for Ebola on October 5 and died the same day.
Authorities have identified some 135 contacts of the first patient, placing 118 in quarantine. Eight tested positive while in quarantine, including four health workers and four close family members.
The Health Ministry said some contacts who completed the 21-day quarantine period without developing symptoms would be released starting Saturday (October 24).
'Nigerian patient did not travel to Congo'
In Nigeria, authorities said on Friday (October 23) that they were yet to verify how the country's first Ebola patient contracted the disease. The woman tested positive for the virus upon her return to Nigeria's capital of Abuja from Uganda.
The woman — married to a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria whom she had been travelling with — did not visit Congo and "is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda", Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, or FDFA, told The Associated Press on Friday (October 23).
Her husband has not shown any symptoms and remains in isolation, the FDFA added.
Nigeria's Health Minister Muhammad Pate told reporters on Friday (October 23) that the Nigerian patient "appears to be closely related" to the first case in Kenya in terms of the nature of their infection. "That may or may not change the understanding of the route of transmission given that the virus itself takes time to change," Mr. Pate said.
The Africa CDC earlier said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3.
U.S. introduces new protocol for all travellers
United States health officials this week said that all passengers boarding an international flight to the U.S. — no matter from where — must sign a statement attesting that they have not been in Congo in the previous 21 days. The US has been screening travellers from Ebola-affected countries during the current outbreak.
Travellers who were in Congo in the three weeks leading to their trip will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations, including Americans, the U.S. CDC said on Thursday (October 22).
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing. Congo is experiencing its deadliest outbreak, with at least 4,000 deaths since May.

After years of following the strict, unyielding codes of the Indian Army as the Aide-de-Camp (ADC) to President Droupadi Murmu, Major Rishabh Singh Sambyal (Retd.) has now ventured into the commercial fashion industry.
Swapping his crisp olive-green uniform, the polished combat boots, and the weight of the stars on his shoulders for streetwear fashion, the 30-year-old former Special Forces officer is reinventing himself as a fashion model.
Major Rishabh Singh Sambyal took a premature retirement from the Indian Army in August 2026 after 12 years of service.
According to a Business Today report, Sambyal has officially partnered with the popular homegrown clothing brand Bonkers Corner on a new youth-focused streetwear collection.
The campaign, which features Sambyal modelling alongside television actress Anushka Sen, marks a highly unconventional leap from the rugged, high-stakes environment of the armed forces to the glamorous, fast-paced world of urban fashion.
For Major Rishabh Singh Sambyal, the transition is not just about changing clothes but about translating military discipline into a new cultural space.
According to the brand's official website, the collaborative streetwear line—launched under the title "MAJ RISHABH (RETD.) X BONKERS"—heavily incorporates the slogan “Earned, not borrowed.”
Brand representatives noted that this messaging reflects themes of genuine achievement, individuality, and leadership, which align closely with the former officer's real-life trajectory.
Industry observers and fashion commentators have quickly taken note of his unique aesthetic, noting that his military background brings a rare level of gravitas to the studio.
“This is a compelling, unexpected fusion of two distinct cultures—military discipline and urban fashion,” an industry commentator noted on the brand's launch platform. “It is an inspiring transition showing how a veteran can channel his discipline, leadership, and vision into creative entrepreneurial spaces like homegrown fashion.”
The collection is available on the Bonkers Corner website, where consumers can browse all the items featured in the special section dedicated to Major Rishabh.
Commissioned into the Indian Army in 2014, Major Rishabh Singh Sambyal previously led the Jat Regiment contingent at the 2021 Republic Day Parade and later earned the prestigious Balidaan Badge with the elite 4 Para (Special Forces) before his high-profile, widely recognised stint at Rashtrapati Bhavan.
While he has traded his combat uniform for designer collections, the core of his identity remains fundamentally unchanged.
By stepping into the limelight of the fashion world, Major Sambyal continues to command attention, proving that a strong, disciplined presence can lead the way, regardless of the attire.

The State government has released ₹9.86 crore for the modernisation of 16 drug de-addiction centres functioning in government hospitals across Andhra Pradesh, with a focus on strengthening medical treatment, counselling and rehabilitation services for people suffering from substance addiction.
The funds have been released by the Prohibition and Excise Department to upgrade infrastructure and provide advanced medical equipment at the centres.
A statement issued on Friday said the initiative aimed to make de-addiction services accessible at the grassroots level while strengthening specialised treatment and rehabilitation facilities at major regional hospitals. The proposed works include renovation of hospital buildings, restructuring of rooms, installation of glass doors, improvement of electrical systems and provision of modern furniture.
The centres will be equipped with advanced medical devices, including biofeedback machines, breath-testing equipment, multiparameter monitors and ECG machines. Digital information technology facilities will also be introduced to improve healthcare delivery.
Modernisation works will be taken up at 10 government teaching and major hospitals under the Medical Education Department. They include Kurnool Government General Hospital, SVRR Government General Hospital in Tirupati, Guntur Government General Hospital, Srikakulam Government General Hospital, Nandyal Government General Hospital, Rajamahendravaram Government General Hospital, Ongole Government General Hospital, Vijayawada Government General Hospital, King George Hospital in Visakhapatnam and the Institute of Mental Health under Kadapa Government General Hospital.
Of these, Vijayawada Government General Hospital, King George Hospital in Visakhapatnam and the Institute of Mental Health in Kadapa will be developed as specialised Centres of Excellence. These three regional centres will provide advanced medical treatment, specialised addiction care and comprehensive rehabilitation support to people struggling with substance abuse.
Infrastructure at six other district and area hospitals will also be upgraded. They are Anakapalli District Hospital, Narsapuram Area Hospital, Narasaraopet Area Hospital, Chittoor District Hospital, Hindupur District Hospital and Bapatla Area Hospital.
The works at these hospitals will focus on improving buildings and electrical infrastructure and installing modern medical equipment to strengthen de-addiction treatment services.

North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking.
Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.
North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector’s relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.
Kim Jong-un, its dictatorial ruler, controls a stockpile of about 50 nuclear warheads, and has been supplying troops and weapons to help Russia in its war in Ukraine. But North Korea is also extremely poor: 40% of the population are undernourished according to the UN and nearly one in five of its children are stunted.
A UN panel of experts, reporting to the security council, said in the spring of 2024 that it was reviewing “58 suspected cyber-attacks” by North Korea “on cryptocurrency-related companies between 2017 and 2023” worth $3bn.
The panel said the cash was estimated to generate half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. One unnamed country went further with its estimate: the stolen billions fund “40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes”.
The suspected crypto hacks amounted to as many as 17 in 2023 alone: thefts valued at $750m, and disturbingly, the sums involved are only increasing. The world’s largest previous crypto hack took place in February 2025, when $1.5bn was stolen from the Bybit exchange – the work, the FBI said, of TraderTraitor.
Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, argues that North Korea appears to have targeted crypto because traditional banks have developed sophisticated defences that the fast-growing and lightly regulated sector has yet to match.
“Over the last decade, hackers have walked off with nine- or 10-figure sums from crypto hacks on more than 30 occasions. The number of traditional banks who have suffered a loss of more than $100m as a result of a cyber-attack in the same period is zero or one,” Martin said.
North Korea was behind one of the last large cyber thefts on a traditional bank – an attack on Bangladesh Bank in February 2016, where North Korean hackers tried to illicitly move $951m from an account the bank had with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, taking advantage of time differences between the two.
A piece of luck prevented most of the money from being sent to an intermediate account in the Philippines. The corresponding bank was based on Jupiter Street, which shares its first word with the name of a sanctioned Iranian ship, so most of the transfers were held up. In the end, $81m was stolen.
The isolated state has long been accused of engaging in criminal activities to survive, including the forgery of high-quality $100 bills, known as “supernotes” in the 1990s, and the production and trafficking of crystal meth for export in the 2000s.
The UK has been rarely targeted. In 2019, North Korean hackers did try to take control of cash machines linked to 56 financial institutions to make them pay out sums well in excess of normal. British officials spotted what was afoot, alerted the banks and the hack was quietly suppressed with no media coverage.
The irony is that the internet in North Korea is severely restricted, with access denied to the general population. Maths and science are pushed at school, however, and at university some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, such as Lazarus, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.
Hacking is closely tied to the all-powerful state. In December 2014, it emerged, to the embarrassment of Sony Pictures, that film stars Jennifer Lawrence and Amy Adams were paid less than their male counterparts in American Hustle. It was one of thousands of embarrassing emails leaked from the Hollywood studio through a hack.
The attack, by North Korea’s Lazarus Group, was conducted because Sony had funded a film, The Interview: a Seth Rogen comedy that depicted the assassination of Kim Jong-un. Amid the chaos of the revelations, Sony tried to cancel the movie, then had to U-turn on its retreat, releasing it online and to a handful of cinemas, after being criticised for caving in to North Korean pressure.

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has reported a security breach affecting an estimated $6.3 Bn in assets, in what appears to be the largest crypto heist on record. The exchange said it has worked with blockchain partners to freeze around $3 Bn on-chain. Binance has temporarily suspended withdrawals while it completes security checks. It has also revoked the affected address authorisation and engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover funds. Withdrawals are expected to be restored in the next 48 hours, Binance said. The exchange said it would cover all losses through its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds. It also plans to publish updated proof of reserves after completing remediation. Investigation Points To Laptop Binance said its initial investigation suggests that a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer may have allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions. The exchange said it had found no evidence of wallet private keys being leaked. It will publish a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the findings have been verified. Cryptocurrency news platform Watcher.Guru reported that the affected assets included Bitcoin, Ether, Tether’s USDT, Circle’s USDC, and TRON, among others. Its tally put the Bitcoin outflow alone at around $1.45 Bn. In an earlier X post, Binance cofounder Changpeng Zhao said Tether had frozen approximately $971 Mn and Circle around $823 Mn linked to the suspected hack. Those were initial figures: subsequent reporting put Tether’s freeze at more than $1.5 Bn. However, experts are claiming based on on-chain data that the hacker was able to deposit the stolen assets on decentralised liquidity platform Aave before they were frozen, and borrow Ether against them. While stablecoins like USDT and USDC can be frozen due to being controlled by a centralised authority, Ether is more decentralised and hence can’t be frozen on-chain. In response, Aave said it has suspended new deposits and borrowing across its V3 and V4 lending markets. Fallout Reaches Other Platforms Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with a significant presence in India. It restarted operations in the country in 2024 after tightening its reporting rules and registering with the Financial Intelligence Unit. The Binance breach followed a separate incident at prediction market platform Polymarket, where around $2.6 Mn was reportedly drained. Polymarket said a third-party provider had been compromised and promised to reimburse affected users. In light of these developments, Indian cryptocurrency exchange CoinDCX announced that it has halted new trades on its futures desk as a precautionary measure. Separately, the development comes a day after the Enforcement Directorate (ED) announced investigations into alleged unauthorised cross-border crypto transfers worth more than ₹4,940 Cr. The investigations concern alleged violations of the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) involving crypto platforms Mudrex and Saber.money, along with decentralised finance protocol Instadapp and its associated platform Fluid.

Alexander Zverev ensured he would overtake Jannik Sinner in the rankings and become world number one for the first time next week with a 6-4, 7-5 victory over Tallon Griekspoor in the last 16 of the Vienna Open on Thursday.
The 29-year-old, who has enjoyed a stellar season capped by titles at the French and US Opens, will become Germany’s second men’s number one after Boris Becker in 1991 when the new rankings are published on Monday.
Zverev’s victory, which was sealed with an ace, was followed by a ceremony on court when he was joined by his team and Thomas Muster, the only Austrian to have topped the rankings, to mark the feat.
“[It is] very special. To have the feeling to be on the top of the world is amazing,” said Zverev, who will be the 30th man to top the rankings since they were introduced in 1973.
“It’s different than winning a tournament, winning a title, but it’s such a special feeling to know that the number one is going to be next to your name when the new rankings come out,” he added.

“I had to wait, but sometimes you’ve got to wait for the best things in life. So it is how it is. I’m super happy, super thrilled,” he said, adding, “This year, I mean, I have no words for this year. Again, I’m just thankful. I’m happy and all of the above.”

The reminders to vote in Tuesday’s midterms are ubiquitous. Some health scholars have another reminder: that elections, especially divisive ones, can stress the heart.
Studies have found a significantly higher chance of arrhythmias in the weeks just before and after elections, and an increased rate of hospitalizations for heart attacks right after voting day.
“Your political party doesn’t matter to your heart; stress does,” Lindsey Rosman, assistant professor of medicine in the division of cardiology at Northwestern University, told STAT on Thursday. “Your emotional health and your heart health are connected.”
Take the last two presidential elections. Compared to other timeframes, researchers noted distinct changes in early November that aligned with heightened anxiety. Even if transient, higher blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms can turn serious for people diagnosed with cardiovascular disease, or for those unaware of a condition that might make them more vulnerable.
What research on 2016 and 2020 found
To see how elections may stress the heart, Rosman studied people who already had a heart rhythm disorder, taking advantage of data provided by their implanted cardiac devices. Her team found a 77% higher rate of irregular heartbeats during the six weeks around the 2016 election, compared with a control period.
The arrhythmia pattern was similar across age, sex, race, and other health conditions; Democrats and Republicans had similar risk. The retrospective observational study was carried out in North Carolina, when Rosman was at the University of North Carolina. Because it was a swing state in 2016, residents saw an especially heavy volume of political ads and campaign events.
After the following presidential election, Matthew Mefford, a cardiovascular disease epidemiologist and research scientist at Kaiser Permanente Southern California, asked whether hospitalizations for acute cardiovascular disease went up immediately after Election Day, akin to admissions after natural disasters. The answer was yes, with the rate of heart attacks significantly higher compared with the same five-day period two weeks before. The retrospective cohort study looked at people with and without a history of heart disease.
“Stress comes in many forms, including both positive and negative, and the stress impact associated with elections is just one situation that can result in adverse heart outcomes,” Mefford told STAT Thursday. “Being aware of how stress, generally, can impact your body is important especially for those with pre-existing heart disease.”
While stress responses in the body follow the same mechanisms, they’re not the same in all cases. “Not everyone responds to stress in the same way or to the same magnitude that triggers a heart event,” he said.
Other caveats: The two studies can’t establish cause and effect, just an association between health events and exposure to political campaigns.
How does stress play out in the body?
Ten years after Rosman’s study, today’s exposure may be magnified beyond political ads, thanks to the saturation of social media. Whatever the source, the deluge of news can cause acute stress and anger, triggering a fight-or-flight response. Adrenaline rises, the sympathetic nervous system ramps up, and the calming influence of the vagus nerve drops.
These changes can alter the heart’s electrical activity, making abnormal rhythms more likely in someone already prone to them, Rosman said. Stress hormones like cortisol and inflammation may also play a role, as can stress-related behaviors, such as sleeping poorly, skipping medications, eating more foods high in fat or salt, or drinking more alcohol or caffeine.
Her findings apply most directly to people at higher cardiac risk, she said, but she pointed out that nearly half of U.S. adults have some type of cardiovascular disease, including high blood pressure.
“People with existing heart disease are more vulnerable to arrhythmias triggered by emotion, but these events can also happen in people without known heart disease,” she said, citing reports of more heart attacks and cardiac events after 9/11, earthquakes, and World Cup matches. “Chronic stress is also an established risk factor for heart disease over time.”
Next up for Rosman is using wearables to study acute stress events. She hopes a larger, nationwide follow-up study looking at the 2020 and 2024 elections will offer some answers before the next U.S. presidential election.
What’s a voter to do?
In general, acute stress raises heart rates and blood pressure readings in the short term. But for people with uncontrolled hypertension or coronary disease, spiking stress adds strain.
Rosman suggests setting limits on news and social media, especially before bedtime. Focus on sleep and physical activity. Take your medications. Both Rosman and Mefford recommend meditation or yoga, taking a walk, hiking in nature, or engaging in exercise.
“Listen to your body,” Mefford said.

The Hindu Group, in association with the Cancer Institute (WIA), Adyar, launched Cancer 360: Overview of Detection, Treatment, Palliation, a book examining cancer care from prevention and early detection to treatment, rehabilitation and palliative care. The book was launched at The Hindu office in Chennai.
N. Ram, director of The Hindu Group, launched the book alongside Suresh Nambath, editor of The Hindu. Mr. Ram handed over the first copy to E. Hemanth Raj, executive vice-chairman of Cancer Institute.
Speaking at the launch, Mr. Ram emphasised the importance of making advanced cancer care accessible and affordable. He highlighted the institute’s work in providing treatment to those who need it most and stressed the need to ensure that advances in cancer care reach patients facing barriers to treatment.
Dr. Hemanth Raj spoke about the need to translate advances in cancer research, much of which takes place in the West, into practical interventions in local settings. He also highlighted the institute’s charitable programmes, supported by donations, to help patients access treatment and facilities, and its plans to expand cancer care to reach more patients.
Arvind Krishnamurthy, professor of surgical oncology at Cancer Institute, stressed the need for continued research to improve cancer care and develop better treatments.
The book also addresses care beyond treatment. Mahalakshmi Rangabashyam Shetty, ENT surgeon and lecturer in the Department of Surgical Oncology at the institute, spoke about individualised treatment plans developed through multidisciplinary consultations. She also highlighted the need to tailor exercise and nutrition regimens to individual patients, alongside supportive services such as hospice care.
Surendran Veeraiah, professor and head of the Department of Regional Cancer Centre (RCTC), Cancer Institute, emphasised the importance of psychological support and allied services. He said the book could help make technical information on comprehensive cancer care accessible to more people.
The book features contributions from experts across oncology and allied disciplines. Its chapters cover multidisciplinary tumour boards, psychological care, onco-physiotherapy, palliative care, cancer research, speech and swallowing rehabilitation, early detection, precision treatment, pathology, nutrition and healthcare quality.
The book is available free of cost to The Hindu subscribers at https://www.thehindu.com/premium/ebook/

Following the increase, government employees will receive arrears for the nine-month period from January to September in three equal monthly instalments. The enhanced DA will be paid in cash along with the October salary, payable in November.

The revised Maximum Retail Price (MRP) list of anti-cancer medicines published by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) raises serious concerns about excessive pricing and the exploitation of patients, noted medical health activists on Wednesday (October 28, 2026).
Editorial | Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
The NPPA, under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, has released a list of 543 brands of anti-cancer medicines with their revised MRP that will be effective from November 9.
“The revised price list reflects the information submitted by companies up to October 27, 2026, and it will be updated as and when manufacturers submit their revised prices of non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs,” said a release issued by the Union government on Wednesday (October 28, 2026).
On October 17, the NPPA had announced Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) of 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs in public interest to address excessive trade margins, make cancer treatment more affordable, and improve access to anti-cancer medicines. Manufacturers were instructed to submit their revised list to NPPA.
The 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs include immunotherapy medicines used in the treatment of over 20 types of cancer, Denosumab used by breast and prostate cancer patients, Pegfilgrastim used to prevent neutropenia in cancer patients, and Bevacizumab, which is approved for the treatment of colon, ovarian and cervical cancers.
Curbing profiteering
Stating that cost-based price control can further reduce medicine prices and curb excessive profiteering, Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India (JSA India), an organisation working for accessibility of medicines, said that controlling trade margins alone is insufficient. Life-saving cancer treatment must be affordable based on medical need, not a patient’s ability to pay.
In their statement, the group explained: “For example, the reported MRP of one brand of palbociclib fell from approximately ₹40,421 to ₹2,720 per pack, while thiotepa fell from approximately ₹80,072 to ₹7,150 per vial. Such drastic reductions raise serious questions about the pricing practices of pharmaceutical companies, including major Indian manufacturers of generic cancer medicines that have reportedly offered substantial trade margins while patients continued to face unaffordable prices.’’
It added that, several patented cancer medicines remain exorbitantly priced. The Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) policy has failed to ensure affordability, while excluding medicines supplied free under Patient Assistance Programmes from its calculations has further limited its potential impact on patients, said the group.
“The policy’s formula is also deeply flawed. Allowing a 42.8% markup over the Price to Stockist [PTS] legitimises excessive margins, particularly in a supply chain often involving only one or two intermediaries or direct sales to hospitals. A substantially lower markup, comparable to the 16% margin applicable to scheduled formulations under the DPCO framework, could have delivered greater benefits to patients. A one-time MRP reduction is not enough. Without permanent, enforceable margin caps, regular monitoring and verification by NPPA, excessive pricing can persist or re-emerge,” JSA stated in the release.
The NPPA must also strengthen its collection and maintenance of price data across supply chains and distribution channels, the group said, adding that companies should not be left to calculate and self-report revised MRPs without adequate independent verification.
Tanvi Singh, medical oncologist, MOC Cancer Care, said that cancer is an ailment whose treatment demands are extensive so when drug costs are high, patients may end up delaying treatment initiation, or skipping doses, or even discontinue therapy prematurely. All of these will in turn affect and compromise outcomes.
“Lowering drug costs is an imperative that can improve treatment continuity, reduce financial toxicity, and help patients complete the prescribed course of therapy. However, price caps are not enough on their own. Meaningful and sufficient improvement in affordability can be said to be achieved when price regulation is complemented by wider insurance coverage expansion of government reimbursement schemes, increased availability of quality generic and biosimilar medicines, robust Patient Assistance Programmes (PAPs), and greater access to comprehensive cancer care across the country,” said Dr. Singh.
Sandeep Nayak, chairman of oncology, MACS-Renova Oncology Institute, KIMS Hospital, Bengaluru, said: “The price control introduced by the government is a positive move. But low cost life-saving drugs should remain viable to manufacture and seller.”

22 అక్టోబర్ 2026న, అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్ సరిహద్దు వెంబడి పలు ప్రదేశాలలో భారత సైనికులకు చైనా బలగాలతో ఘర్షణలు జరిగాయని ఇండో-టిబెటన్ బోర్డర్ పోలీస్ (ITBP) డైరెక్టర్ జనరల్ శత్రుజీత్ కపూర్ అంగీకరించారు. చైనా సైనికులు నిర్ధారిత గస్తీ పద్ధతులను పాటించనప్పుడు వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ రేఖ (LAC) వెంబడి పరిస్థితి “అస్తవ్యస్తంగా” మారుతుందని విదేశీ వ్యవహారాల మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ (MEA) ప్రతినిధి రణధీర్ జైస్వాల్ మరుసటిరోజు పేర్కొన్నారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో భారత్, చైనా సైనికుల మధ్య ఘర్షణలకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలంటూ కొన్ని వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉన్నాయి. వీటిలో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: అక్టోబర్ 2026లో అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్ సరిహద్దు (LAC) వద్ద భారత, చైనా సైనికుల మధ్య జరిగిన ఘర్షణలకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోలన్నీ పాతవి లేదా అక్టోబర్ 2026 నాటి ఘర్షణలకు సంబంధం లేనివి. ఇవి 2021, 2024, 2025 సంవత్సరాలకు చెందిన పాత ఘటనలు, జూలై 2026 నాటి అమర్నాథ్ యాత్రకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు. కావున, ఈ వీడియోలు తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉన్నాయి.
వీడియో 1
ఈ వీడియో కనీసం డిసెంబర్ 2022 నుండే ఇంటర్నెట్లో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. అంటే, ఈ వీడియో అక్టోబర్ 2026లో రిపోర్ట్ చేయబడిన భారత్-చైనా సరిహద్దు ఉద్రిక్తతల కంటే ముందే ఉందని, తాజా పరిణామాలతో దీనికి సంబంధం లేదని స్పష్టమవుతుంది. డిసెంబర్ 2022లో ప్రచురితమైన ఒక CNN కథనంలో, ఇదే దృశ్యాలను చూపిస్తూ, ఈ వీడియో సెప్టెంబర్ 2021లో చిత్రీకరించినట్లు పేర్కొన్నారు. ఈ వీడియో వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ రేఖ సమీపంలో అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లో చిత్రీకరించినట్లుగా భారతీయ సైనకాధికారి ధృవీకరించారని ఈ కథనం పేర్కొంది.
వీడియో 2
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలు రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో కనీసం నవంబర్ 2024 (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోకి చొరబడటానికి ప్రయత్నిస్తున్న చైనా సైనికులను భారత సైనికులు అడ్డుకుని దాడి చెయ్యడం ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుందని ఆ పోస్టులు పేర్కొన్నాయి. ఇండియన్ ఆర్మీ ఫ్యాక్ట్-చెక్ విభాగం కూడా ఈ వీడియోను ఖండిస్తూ ‘X’లో చేసిన పోస్ట్ చేసింది.
వీడియో 3
ఈ వీడియోకి సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు కనీసం జూలై 2026 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. వీటి ప్రకారం, అమర్నాథ్ యాత్ర 2026 సందర్భంగా, జమ్మూ & కాశ్మీర్లోని బాల్తాల్ వద్ద ప్రవేశ ద్వారం దగ్గర యాత్రికులు నమోదు చేసుకోవడానికి, RFID కార్డులను పొందడానికి గుమిగూడిన దృశ్యాలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుంది. ఇండియన్ ఆర్మీ ఫ్యాక్ట్-చెక్ విభాగం కూడా ఈ వీడియోను ఖండిస్తూ ‘X’లో చేసిన పోస్ట్ చేసింది.
వీడియో 4

New tvOS 27.2 features to try for an upgraded Apple TV experience
No major changes here, but tvOS 27.2's new features are welcome additions all the same.
Apple recently released iOS 27.2 to the public alongside macOS 27.2 and tvOS 27.2. For Apple TV, this was the first update since tvOS 27 debuted in September, because Apple skipped version 27.1 entirely. Unlike iOS, tvOS updates don't usually come with release notes, but a support document on Apple's website outlines exactly what changed in tvOS 27.2. There aren't any major changes this time, but you'll still find a few new features to try out. From new screen saver options to FaceTime improvements, here's everything new coming to your Apple TV with the latest tvOS.
Screen savers with more variety and FaceTime upgrades
Apple TV probably has some of the best screensavers of any streaming box, and while they aren't its biggest selling point, they're definitely a pleasure to look at. Until now, you had to choose a single category, but tvOS 27.2 changes that.
The update adds a new "Shuffle" option that cycles through Aerials, Memories, Portraits and Snoopy. Now, every time your TV enters screen saver mode, it will show you something different. You can now use your iPhone to choose specific photos for your screensaver without sharing your entire photo library with your Apple TV. This helps a lot if you share your home with others and don't want all your personal photos suddenly appearing on the big screen.
Apple has also updated the FaceTime experience, starting with FaceTime links. These make it easier to join a call directly from your Apple TV, although the call still uses your iPhone as a webcam via the Continuity Camera feature. FaceTime now also lets you add third-party sign language interpreters and live captioning services to your calls. This feature is also available for iPhone, iPad and Mac with their respective updates.
Find My for the Siri Remote and sign language in the player
The new Apple TV 4K comes with a new Siri Remote that improves Find My support and even includes a speaker so you can easily locate it. Although you will need a new device — or at least a new remote — to get this feature, tvOS 27.2 still brings a small improvement to previous Apple TV models. The remote now appears in the Find My app, so you no longer need to open the TV Remote from your iPhone's Control Center to locate it. It's a small change, but it makes the experience more consistent.
Select movies and shows on the Apple TV app now support ASL and BSL, and you can turn them on using the player controls or in Settings. Speaking of the TV app, it finally gained profile support on iPhone and iPad with iOS 27.2, and they now sync with your Apple TV. Apple even added new characters to the profile selection screen. If you share your Apple TV with others or have kids at home, the profile feature is definitely worth trying out. Another small detail in tvOS 27.2 is the new black-and-white Apple Music icon, which matches the one added in iOS 27.2 as part of the platform's new identity.
If you haven't updated your Apple TV yet, you can do so by opening the Settings app, going to System and selecting Software Update. The update is free and available for the second-generation Apple TV 4K (released in 2021) and later models. Note that some new features, such as setting up a surround sound system with two pairs of the new HomePod mini 2 (or HomePod 2nd generation), are exclusive to the new Apple TV 4K with the A19 chip introduced earlier this month.

Any actor will tell you that they'd be lucky to play a character long enough — and iconic enough — to become beloved by generations of fans worldwide.
Patrick Stewart had two.
The acting legend, who died on October 28, 2026, at the age of 86, played Captain Jean-Luc Picard, the captain of the USS Enterprise in the "Star Trek" franchise, for 36 years. He played the character from the premiere of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" in 1987 through three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard," which concluded in 2023.
Of course, that's not the only character Stewart will be remembered for.
In 2000, Stewart was cast as Professor Charles Xavier, aka Professor X, the kind, yet complicated, telepathic leader of the X-Men. He went on to play Xavier eight more times in the X-Men series. He reprised the role for what will now be the final time in "Avengers: Doomsday," which is set for release in December.
In addition to Picard and Xavier, Stewart was a prolific theater actor and was knighted by the Queen in 2010 for his services to drama. He was a Shakespeare devotee, as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company from 1966 to 1982. He also kept many of us sane during the pandemic by reading one of Shakespeare's 154 sonnets a day and posting them on Instagram.
Here's a look back at his 60-year career, onstage and on screen.
Before Patrick Stewart was on TV or in movies, he was a stage actor.
Stewart's first professional acting credit was in 1959 in the play "Cyrano de Bergerac." He then became a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966.
He made his Broadway debut in 1971 in "A Midsummer Night's Dream."
He was nominated for five Olivier Awards, winning three. He was also nominated for a Tony and three Drama Desk Awards, winning one.
His first Olivier nominations both came in 1979. First, for best actor in a revival of "The Merchant of Venice," which he did not win, and second, for Best Supporting Actor in "Antony and Cleopatra," which he did win.
He won twice more: In 1994 for Best Entertainment for his one-man production of "A Christmas Carol" and in 2009 for Best Supporting Actor in "Hamlet."
His Tony Award nomination was in 2008 for best actor in a play for "Macbeth."
His Drama Desk win was in 1992 for his one-man version of "A Christmas Carol."
He appeared in dozens of productions in both London and New York.
It's impossible to list all his theatrical roles, but he was a true giant — so much so that his colleague and future close friend Ian McKellen told him that he shouldn't throw his stage career away to star in some sci-fi TV show.
"'No!' he said. 'No, you must not do that. You must not. You have too much important theater work to do. You can't throw that away to do TV. You can't. No,'" Stewart wrote in his memoir, "Making It So."
Of course, that sci-fi show was his big break.
His big break came in 1987, when he was cast as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on "Star Trek: The Next Generation."
Before "The Next Generation," there had been just one captain of the Enterprise: Captain Kirk, as played by William Shatner. Stewart had some large shoes to fill, but, as he would've said, he made it so.
Stewart played Picard for seven seasons of "TNG," plus an appearance on "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine."
"TNG" became a deeply respected and beloved series, even garnering an Emmy nomination for best drama series in 1994 — a feat that wouldn't have been possible without Stewart's stewardship. He was also nominated for a SAG Award in 1994 for outstanding actor in a drama series.
"Without question, Jean-Luc is the most significant role of my career. And I will be forever grateful to have had the opportunity to be a part of what is now such a historic franchise," he said in 2026.
He played Picard in four films, including "Star Trek: Generations," in which William Shatner passed the torch to Stewart and his crew.
Stewart starred in four "TNG" films: "Star Trek: Generations," "Star Trek: First Contact," "Star Trek: Insurrection," and "Star Trek: Nemesis."
In "Generations," Stewart and Shatner appeared onscreen together, with Kirk giving Picard some advice on holding on to the captain's chair.
Shatner posted a statement on X after the news of Stewart's death, writing, "Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work."
After an 18-year break, Stewart returned to Picard and starred in three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard."
Many "TNG" fans were less than pleased with how we left the crew of the Enterprise in 2004's "Nemesis," which is considered a low point for the franchise.
So, Trekkies everywhere were thrilled when news of "Star Trek: Picard" became public. Stewart reprised his role for three seasons, concluding in 2023.
In 2000, Stewart began playing Professor Charles Xavier in the "X-Men" film series.
The only other role that could rival Captain Jean-Luc Picard is Professor Charles Xavier, the leader of the X-Men.
He appeared in "X-Men," "X2," "X-Men: The Last Stand," "X-Men Origins: Wolverine," "The Wolverine," "X-Men: Days of Future Past," "Logan," "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," and "Avengers: Doomsday" as the telepathic, preternaturally wise mutant.
On set, he befriended his costar and fellow legend, Ian McKellen. The two became fast friends.
The two were so close that McKellen officiated Stewart's wedding to his wife, Sunny Ozell, in 2013.
In addition to playing Xavier and Magneto, the two also acted together onstage in productions of "Waiting for Godot" and "No Man's Land."
Stewart and his costar Hugh Jackman also had a close bond, which was on display when they reunited for the 2017 film "Logan."
Xavier and Logan (aka Wolverine) had a particular bond throughout all the "X-Men" films, and it seemed that continued offscreen.
The two reunited for "Logan," which, at the time, was thought to be their final hurrah as the two mutants. It became one of the best comic-book films of all time, with Stewart even getting Oscar buzz, though he lost out on the nomination.
"We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today," Jackman wrote on Instagram after Stewart's death. "And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."
One of Stewart's other longest-running roles was in "American Dad!" He appeared in over 120 episodes across 22 seasons.
MacFarlane, the creator of "Family Guy," "American Dad," and Ted," among other shows, is famously a huge Trekkie. His shows constantly reference "Star Trek," and he frequently got members of the cast to voice themselves on "Family Guy."
But with Stewart, he took it a step further, casting him as Avery Bullock, the unhinged deputy director of the CIA, on "American Dad."
He also narrated the two "Ted" films.
Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us." MacFarlane wrote on X. "We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet.
Stewart was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his services to drama, solidifying his status as a British national treasure.
"The knights of the theatre represented to me not only the pinnacle of the profession but the esteem in which the profession was held," he said at the time, per the BBC. "To find myself, to my astonishment, in that company is the grandest thing that has professionally happened to me."
He is one of 95 actors who have been bestowed the honor, according to People.
He was also a torchbearer at the 2012 London Olympics.
Being a torchbearer is a huge honor, especially when the games are in your home country.
"I have attended world premieres of big movies that have not had the excitement, and the sense of pleasure and pride that people are exhibiting today," Stewart said. "It was thrilling. I shall never forget today."
In July, Stewart said, "I can't imagine ever officially 'retiring.' I'll always and forever be an actor."
One of Stewart's final interviews was with TV Insider in July 2026, which he did to promote his new audiobook, a recording of Shakespeare's sonnets.
When asked whether he would ever retire, Stewart said no, though he noted that parts for people his age were few and far between. But he did shout out one of his final voiceover roles — and he had quite a varied voiceover career — in the series "Bait," in which he voiced a pig's head.
His final role will be this December in "Avengers: Doomsday."
After playing an alternate version of Xavier in "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," Marvel confirmed back in March 2025 that Stewart would be reprising the original Xavier in "Avengers: Doomsday."
"It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed," Marvel head Kevin Feige said in a statement.

Meta is testing 'Threads Friends' for sharing posts with smaller groups
Twitter Circle, anyone?
Threads is experimenting with a way to more privately share posts with smaller groups of followers. The app said it's testing "Threads Friends" in Ireland, Italy and Japan.The feature is basically like a "close friends" list for Threads. It allows people to opt to share posts with up to 50 friends (or "Thriends" as the app also calls it) without making it visible to anyone else on the platform.
If that sounds familiar, it's also remarkably similar to a feature Twitter introduced back in 2022 called "Circles." Twitter's version of the feature allowed users to limit posts to groups of up to 150. The company killed Circles about a year later.
It seems that Meta is helping users create their initial friends list. The app will automatically suggest followers that you frequently engage with, a Meta spokesperson shared, though the list is customizable. Once a friend list is set up, users are then able to tap a green bubble at the top of their feed to see "Friends' posts that have been shared in the last 24 hours.
The company hasn't shared detailed images of the feature yet, but Laura Javier, product design director for Threads, did show a little preview of what a friends-only post will look like. She also showed off an Easter egg that will change "Threads Friends" to simply "Thriends."
It's not clear if or when Meta plans to expand the initial test, so most users in the US won't have access to it for now. However, if you know someone in one of the test countries, you will be able to see their friends-only posts if they add you to their list.

Street protests sweeping Europe are expected to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Saturday, with police mobilised to stop potential looting and rioting on the fringes of what organisers hope will be peaceful rallies.
Weeks of, at times violent, student demonstrations have rocked Italy, Spain, Portugal, Albania and France, where activists on Halloween have again called for people to make their anger over the cost of living and deficient public services felt across the country.
In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has called for supporters to turn out in more than 30 cities demanding more spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and against any plans to return to mandatory military service.
Alexander Throm, of the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group, wrote in the Handelsblatt business newspaper: “Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs.”
But Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of the opposition Green party, cautioned against attempts to place the youth protests under general suspicion in advance.
“The [CDU’s] rhetoric, which seeks to criminalise these protests pre-emptively and paint them as the work of marauding gangs, may even drive people towards radicalisation,” he told the RND media group.
Berlin’s police chief, Barbara Slowik Meisel, said she would deploy an additional 1,500 officers in the capital, though she had little reason to fear that people or property would come under attack.
“We have no concrete evidence of any coordinated looting operations being planned,” she said.
About 10,000 protesters, mainly pupils, students and their parents, are expected at the Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, with another smaller gathering planned in the early evening in the Mitte district.
Large rallies have also been called in Cologne, Munich, Frankfurt and Hamburg.
The team behind Gen Z regelt has used social media and its website to call on participants to exercise restraint: “Our protest is peaceful, without exception. Violence goes against everything we stand for. Only through peaceful means can we achieve something together.”
By Friday, more than 160,000 people had registered on the website saying they planned to attend the protests.
The federal pupils’ conference, a youth political lobbying group, has distanced itself from Saturday’s demonstrations, saying the initiative’s “unclear” organisational structure made the events unpredictable.
It plans to hold a separate protest in Berlin on 20 November that will include teachers and other youth movements focused on the marked decline in German school performance.
In France, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day, adding that 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the sidelines of the new wave of protests.
Nuñez said late on Thursday that radical groups had called on social media for violent Halloween gatherings and that the biggest threat to public order would probably come after mainstream cost-of-living demonstrations had officially ended.
“We are seeing many calls from the labour movement, the radicalised far left and certain radicalised gilets jaunes [yellow vests], urging people to attend rallies on public streets starting at 8pm in many cities across France,” he said.
The calls were “accompanied by various messages which are quite radical”, Nuñez added, including some demanding “revolution”. He said authorities would “tolerate zero excesses” and promised an “extremely firm” security response.
Measures introduced last weekend to protect shops would be reinforced, Nuñez said, and while peaceful demonstrations would be authorised, most would not be permitted “in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder”.
It is unclear what will happen in Paris. Two separate marches planned by unions and gilets jaunes through the city centre have been banned. Instead, police have authorised a single march in the far south-east. Both sets of organisers are challenging the decision to exclude them from the centre.
The interior ministry has said 410,000 people marched last Saturday, when a strong police presence mostly prevented a repeat of the widespread violence and looting that swept French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October.
Unions and the gilets jaunes movement protesting over low wages, the cost of living and deteriorating public services have joined school and university students calling for better learning conditions, with a nationwide strike called for 5 November.
Government measures to address the students’ demands – including replacing a creaking university admissions platform and providing loans to local authorities for school renovations – did not go far enough, student leaders said.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".
