The Supreme Court on Friday (October 30, 2026) asked the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) to formulate measures against the commercial exploitation of live-streamed judicial proceedings in violation of earlier court orders.
A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant recorded Solicitor General Tushar Mehta’s submission that suggestions from various High Courts and other stakeholders had already been received and forwarded to the Ministry.
Mr. Mehta submitted that the Ministry would consider the suggestions and respond in a few days. He sought listing of the plea for further consideration after the Deepavali vacation.
He also flagged violations of earlier orders and urged the court to consider directing the removal of material uploaded in breach of its restrictions.
The court had recently passed orders banning the unauthorised use and circulation of live-streamed judicial proceedings on social media and digital platforms, saying that anything meant for the public good cannot be exploited commercially for personal gain.
“Necessary measures for taking action against those who fail to comply with the directions will also be incorporated in the policy regime,” the court observed.
Watermark suggestion
Advocate Prashant Bhushan suggested that every official clip released by the court should carry a verifiable digital signature or watermark, enabling the public and digital platforms to distinguish genuine footage from manipulated versions.
He further suggested that all court proceedings should be made available on the Supreme Court’s website in an authenticated and watermarked format.
The court is examining the issue amid concerns over the unauthorised extraction, modification, circulation, and commercial use of video clips of judicial proceedings, often accompanied by misleading captions or representations.

A review of 578 patients who presented with breast-related concerns at the Head & Neck Cancer Institute of India (HNCII), Mumbai, over more than three years found that 82.5% had cancerous conditions and 17.5% had non-cancerous conditions. The diagnoses were confirmed through tissue examination.
The findings reveal patients assessed at the institute and cannot be generalised to the wider population or used to estimate the likelihood that a breast lump is cancerous.
Patients diagnosed with breast cancer ranged in age from 23 to 98 years, with an average age of 52.7 years. Tumour sizes varied, with 35.2% measuring up to 2 cm, 43.3% measuring between 2 and 4.9 cm, and 19.3% measuring more than 5 cm.
The institute also reported that 52% of patients had more than four lymph nodes positive for cancer. Lymph node involvement is one of the factors doctors consider when assessing the extent of breast cancer and planning treatment.
Mastectomy, which involves removing the breast, was the most common surgery recorded.
Recognising unusual breast changes and seeking medical advice can help establish a diagnosis and guide appropriate care. Not every lump requires cancer treatment, but changes should be assessed .

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton could have picked any number of messages for his first Senate campaign ad of the general election back in May. Texans care a lot about cost of living, border security, healthcare, and corruption, among other issues. But Paxton’s very first ad went with something that pollsters don’t generally ask about. He accused his opponent, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, of being “Too Low-T for Texas.” Too low in testosterone. Not manly enough.
Republicans are trying to make the Texas Senate race about “manliness”
Ken Paxton keeps accusing James Talarico of being “low-T.” Do voters care?
Voters generally don’t rank masculinity as a top issue in any race, but Paxton’s opening salvo wasn’t completely out of left field. Young men broke for President Donald Trump by a shocking margin in 2024. During that campaign, Trump played to the “manosphere”, appearing on many a bro-y podcast and leaning on his macho, politically incorrect image for an audience burned out on the politics of Woke 1.
Paxton, whom Trump endorsed over incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) in the primary, is as closely linked to the president as any candidate on the ballot — so it’s not all that surprising to see him attempt the same strategy.
And Texas, after all, has its stereotypes: rugged individualism. Cowboy boots. Smoked meats. Texas Rangers. The list goes on.
Starting with the “Low-T” ad, the Paxton campaign has been all in on exploiting the politics of masculinity and traditional ideas about gender and gender roles to cast Talarico as not man enough to serve as senator — and the rest of the Republican ecosystem has followed suit.
In May, Trump policy adviser Stephen Miller tweeted that “The Democrats made history in Texas by nominating their first transgender senate candidate.” Vice President JD Vance recently walked right up to the line of calling Talarico gay at a rally in the state. Elon Musk’s super PAC has flooded the state with AI slop commercials like this one, in which an adult drag queen in a sparkly jersey dunks on some female athletes. The commercial attacks Talarico for being supportive of trans athletes. Trump himself has also weighed in, accusing Talarico of veganism — fighting words in some Texas circles. (Talarico, 37, is a cis man, says he has a girlfriend, and denies being a vegan.)
Attacks are one thing, though, and an effective political strategy another. To figure out whether Paxton’s masculinity campaign is working, the Today, Explained team headed to Texas.
“People are mad about other things”
At a Paxton rally in Fort Worth, Texas, on a recent Monday night, Jacenta and Susan Sims were riling each other up, seeing who could get the best dig in at Talarico’s manhood.
Susan pointed to her own chest. “My shirt says ‘No Tala-freaking-way.’ Because he is kind of a freak,” she said. She listed some of Talarico’s past comments on gender to support her statement. “Like, how are you talking about God like he’s nonbinary and there’s six sexes?”
Talarico said God was nonbinary during a Texas legislative session in 2021, making what he later described as a “cringey” point about God being above human categorization. Also in 2021, he claimed during a debate over trans kids in sports that there were six sexes. He recently walked that statement back, saying there were only two sexes.
Jacenta Sims at the Paxton rally wasn’t having it: “If you really had to look deep, he’s probably got some lace on his panties. There’s nothing masculine about him.” Susan piped in, “He looks like a little boy. He’s not tough enough.” Back to Jacenta: “And we need masculinity back in Texas.”
Perhaps it’s not surprising that voters who are already all in on Paxton would also be all in on this line of attack. But those are not the voters Paxton needs to convince.
“I don’t care if Talarico’s gay or not. I don’t believe he is, but it wouldn’t matter to me if he is.” Jesse Sandoval said outside the Tarrant County Elections Center in Fort Worth. He’d just cast his ballot in early voting. “I just felt that they were doing that to try to deflect from the real issues.”
Another early voter, Michael, didn’t want to give his last name, and works as a cook at a local restaurant. “I just feel like this whole toxic masculinity thing is so unnecessary,” he said. “I was raised by someone who was very, very aggressive and just a very macho man. And I feel like you have to educate yourself as to why those things are not — why saying stuff like that isn’t okay, you know?”
Walt Thompson, also at the polling place, said, “Because he’s soft-spoken, they feel that he’s gay. And you know, he’s not. He’s just not this big rugged looking guy. They can’t accept that.”
Nate, a 32-year-old construction worker who also declined to share his last name, said 2026 is a whole different moment from the last presidential election. “If this was 2024, those [messages] are effective. But I think this year it’s not gonna be effective,” he said. “People are mad about other things. When people care about gas prices, they can’t run on that.”
In other words, the culture wars hit differently when you can’t afford to feed your family or drive to work.
It’s (still) the economy, stupid
Matt Angle is director of the Lone Star Project, a Democratic research PAC and communications firm. He says these attacks on Talarico’s masculinity are a tell from Republicans.
“What the Republicans are worried about is people staying home,” Angle told Today, Explained. “Those people, they’re mad about the economy, they’re mad at Trump, and [Republicans] are trying to motivate them by playing to their prejudices. … They desperately need fear to be the motivator rather than anger and frustration.”
So far, it doesn’t seem to be working. Most recent polling puts Talarico in the lead. The Cook Political Report is calling the race a toss-up. The last time Texas elected a Democratic senator was 1988, but Talarico appears to have a real shot at breaking decades of Republican dominance.
Angle says Talarico’s laser focus on a message of affordability is breaking through to voters.
“They’re understanding that their salaries aren’t going as far as they should. And they like that somebody’s talking to them about the cost of groceries, the cost of housing, the cost of healthcare,” he said.
Who gets to own masculinity, anyway?
There’s another key factor in how the GOP’s masculinity attacks are landing: the messenger. Paxton, after all, isn’t exactly a paragon of traditionally masculine virtue. (Just ask Trump, who can’t stop needling his hand-picked candidate for the way he dresses, looks, and talks.)
According to Jill Tate, president of the Texas Federation of Republican Women, many of her members had grown skeptical of Paxton’s candidacy. That’s because his wife, Texas state Sen. Angela Paxton, filed for divorce last year on what she described as “biblical grounds.” The actual filing listed adultery as the reason for divorce.
“I’ve been involved in Texas politics over 30 years,” Tate said, “and this is the first time I’ve truly been concerned we could lose a statewide [race] since the Republicans took over in the ’90s.”
Angela Paxton recently did her ex a solid, giving a speech to the Republican women in Tate’s group called the “elephant in the room” speech. She also cut an ad boosting “the Republican ticket,” though not Paxton by name.
“She talked about the fact that while our candidates may fall down and they may do things that are disappointing and morally wrong, it is extremely important to remember that that is the human side. And that’s not what they’re going to do in office,” Tate said of the speech, which urged the audience to vote for the team — for Republicans — rather than on the moral failings of one person.
Tate believes that the speech changed some minds and could push women in the room to vote for Ken Paxton instead of just staying home. But outside of a room of diehard Republicans, that message — vote for Ken Paxton despite Ken Paxton — may not be a compelling one, no matter how much ads try to paint his opponent as less masculine.
“Texas is a knife fight uphill every day for Democrats,” Angle, the Democratic strategist, said. But in 2026, the mix of a weak Republican candidate and anger at the economy might be enough to give Democrats a chance — and help neutralize Paxton’s efforts to turn the race into a referendum on a very specific view of masculinity.
Ryan Rusak, a veteran Texas politics writer, agrees. “I think that where Talarico can use this to his benefit is to turn it around to say, ‘Okay, well, these guys who wear the boots and eat all the brisket are the ones that got us $5 gas. They’re the ones that got us into a war in Iran. They’re the ones that have gotten it to where you can’t buy a house even in a place where we still make it fairly easy to build houses.’”
“Had we not had an environment like this,” Angle said, “I think it might have been harder for James to break through.”

Two suspects have been arrested in connection with the murder of Christina Downer, “Saturday Night Live” writer Jimmy Fowlie’s sister, according to the Los Angeles Police Department.
Delorean Bijon Brandon, 41, Downer’s boyfriend, and Kaylee Nicole Markowski, 34, were arrested Thursday in Highland Park and Tarzana, respectively. Detectives believe Brandon and Markowski were responsible for Downer’s murder and then disposed of her body and concealed the crime.
Downer was reported missing after a welfare check on Dec. 18, 2025, and Brandon claimed she had moved out and left behind her car and dog.
LAPD said law enforcement officials continued to investigate Downer’s disappearance after her cell phone washed ashore on the beach in Santa Monica. Authorities were led to search an Airbnb property in Joshua Tree, located in the high desert several hours from Los Angeles, in connection with her disappearance and conducted an extensive search with K-9 units and the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department.
Downer is “no longer alive,” her brother said on April 29.
“Our prayers for her to be found safely have transformed into prayers for the truth to be revealed and for those responsible to be held accountable,” Fowlie’s post from April 29 read. “We have reason to believe that in the weeks before she went missing, her phone and social media were compromised. The individual(s) in possession of her phone used it to hide the fact she was gone, to ask for money and to create a false narrative that she was going ‘off the grid.’”

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

Markets regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has cleared the ₹450 Cr IPO of consumer appliances company Atomberg today. In its update, the SEBI informed that it had issued its observation letter to Atomberg on October 30, over a couple months after the company filed its draft IPO papers. In SEBI parlance, the issuance of the final observation marks the regulator's formal clearance to a company to proceed with its public offering. As per its DRHP, Atomberg’s proposed IPO could comprise a fresh issue of equity shares worth up to ₹450 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) component of up to 7.65 Cr equity shares. The company plans to use ₹90 Cr from the fresh issue proceeds to repay or prepay certain borrowings, ₹150 Cr towards brand awareness and performance marketing, and ₹100 Cr towards research and development (R&D). The remaining proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes. Meanwhile, its investors like A91 partners, Temasek Holdings, Inflexor Ventures, among others, intend to dilute their stake in the appliance manufacturer via the IPO. Founded in 2012 by Manoj Meena, who was joined by Sibabrata Das as cofounder in 2013, Atomberg builds consumer appliances such as ceiling fans, mixer grinders, water purifiers and cold-pressed juicers. It also manufactures proprietary components, including motors and controllers, for enterprise customers such as Voltas, Godrej and Blue Star through its subsidiary, Atomberg Innovations. The company operates two business segments — consumer appliances and proprietary components. It sells its products through online channels, including ecommerce marketplaces and quick commerce platforms, as well as offline distributors, retailers and modern trade chains. For FY26, Atomberg reported operating revenue of ₹1,293.77 Cr, up 34.8% from ₹959.51 Cr in FY25. Meanwhile, the company's consolidated net loss widened 26.8% to ₹148.9 Cr from ₹117.4 Cr. On the operational front, Atomberg had a network of 626 distributors and direct dealers, with 46,932 retail touchpoints across around 1,600 cities and towns as of March 31, 2026. Its distribution network covered all Indian states, while its after-sales service network extended to more than 18,000 pin codes. Meanwhile, tier II and smaller cities contributed the largest share of its offline consumer appliances revenue at 49.57% in FY26. Metropolitan cities accounted for 30.91%, while Tier 1 cities contributed the remaining 19.52%.

CBSE revises Class 9 scheme 6th time in 7 months; drops 3 planned curricular components
In nearly seven months between April 2 and October 29, the board has issued multiple circulars, notifications and clarifications, including successive changes to its three-language policy
The dropping of three planned curricular components for students currently in Class 9 on Thursday is the latest in a series of changes to the Central Board of Secondary Education’s (CBSE) scheme of studies since the 2026-27 academic year began on April 1.
In nearly seven months between April 2 and October 29, the board has issued multiple circulars, notifications and clarifications, including successive changes to its three-language policy introduced in line with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020.
The latest move came six days after the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) released a 20-hour introductory module on computational thinking (CT) and artificial intelligence (AI) for Classes 9 to 12 on October 23.
In a circular dated October 29, CBSE said Individuals in Society and the CT and AI modules would not be part of the Class 9 curriculum in 2026-27, while Environmental Education would be excluded when the same batch moves to Class 10 in 2027-28. The changes do not apply to the current Class 10 batch.
The circular, signed by Dr Praggya M Singh, professor and director (academics), said the exclusions were intended “to align the introduction of this curricular area with the implementation schedule”. It did not specify when the components would be introduced for subsequent batches.
NCERT’s CT and AI module covers AI in everyday life, machine learning, misinformation, data privacy and responsible use of AI. The council is yet to release the Individuals in Society textbook; the Environmental Education textbook for Class 10 is expected next year.
Also Read:Supreme Court directs CBSE to extend 3rd language policy exemption to Class 6 students
CBSE did not respond to HT queries on the reasons for the changes, and the future implementation timeline. However, People familiar with the development said the latest circular was intended to clarify provisions for the current Class 9 batch as it progresses to Class 10.
“Our foremost priority is to safeguard students’ interests by clearly communicating the academic and examination-related provisions well in advance. The emphasis is on encouraging students to focus on meaningful learning rather than solely the examinations,” one of them said.
From phased language rollout to mid-session mandate
On April 2, CBSE released its revised scheme of studies for Classes 9 and 10, aligned with NEP 2020 and the National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCF-SE) 2023. It proposed a phased rollout of the three-language formula, beginning with Class 6 in 2026-27 and reaching Class 10 by 2030-31. The scheme also planned advanced-level options in Mathematics and Science, vocational education, art education, physical education and well-being, and interdisciplinary learning.
Also Read: CBSE says no to Class 6 exemption from 3-language rule; SC suggests 2027 rollout
Under the original language framework, R1 referred to the first language, R2 to a second distinct language, and R3 to a third language. At least two of the three were to be native Indian languages. R1 and R2 would have board examinations, while R3 would be assessed internally. The initial rollout envisaged R3 progressing one grade each year.
On April 9, however, CBSE clarified that R3 would “not [be] applicable till the academic session 2029-30 at the class 9 level”. It also allowed an optional third language at the R1/R2 level until 2028-29.
Barely five weeks later, on May 15, the board mandated three languages for Class 9 from July 1, with at least two being Indian languages. Acknowledging the change, it said: “Given that the current academic session commenced in April 2026, CBSE has decided to adopt a transitional approach to align its Scheme of Studies with the NCERT syllabus.”
The circular directed schools to use Class 6 textbooks for R3 until dedicated material became available, citing a 75-80% overlap in core language competencies between the middle and secondary stages. It also suggested interim arrangements to address shortages of qualified language teachers.
On June 5, HT reported that the May directive appeared to contradict a recommendation ratified by CBSE’s governing body in December 2025 to continue the existing scheme, particularly for languages, until NCERT released graded textbooks.
On June 29, CBSE granted a one-time relaxation to students in Classes 7, 8 and 9 who had already chosen two non-native languages. They could continue studying those languages while adding an Indian language as their third. The board said: “No student shall be disadvantaged due to this alignment. The focus remains on joyful, meaningful language learning, not on examination.”
The board issued R3 assessment resources on July 2 and detailed implementation guidelines on July 10, retaining the transitional relief for existing batches.
Supreme Court flags implementation concerns
The language policy also became the subject of litigation. On July 15, the Supreme Court sought responses from the Centre on petitions challenging the revised policy, with parents citing shortages of textbooks and teachers. The next day, Justice BV Nagarathna questioned the decision to introduce a compulsory third language in Class 9, saying, “Don’t start a new language in 9th.”
In August, the court asked CBSE to consider transitional relief for the current Class 6 batch and address concerns over teachers and course material. On September 28, it directed CBSE to extend to Class 6 the relief already available to Classes 7 to 9, allowing students to study R3 without a mandatory Class 10 board examination in it.
Also Read: Schools as markers of class and aspirations
While retaining all the clarifications related to language policy till July 10 in its October 29 circular, CBSE has also provided a mechanism to replace a failed language in the Class 10 result. If a student scores less than 33% in either R1 or R2 but passes an additional optional language, the optional language may replace the failed language for result computation. The optional language must be selected from the 45 languages listed by the board and must be different from all three compulsory languages — R1, R2 and R3. This is separate from R3, which remains compulsory and is assessed internally. For subjects assessed through both internal assessment and the Board examination, students must secure at least 33% in the combined marks to pass.
Educationist Keshav Agarwal welcomed the objective of multilingual education, saying learning languages can improve communication, cultural understanding and cognitive flexibility.
“However, implementation will be crucial. Schools will need qualified language teachers, adequate instructional time and clarity regarding the languages available to students,” he said adding that R3 should promote meaningful communication rather than rote learning and examination pressure, while avoiding unnecessary burdens on students preparing for competitive entrance tests.
Nine subjects in Class 9; must pass 5 in Class 10
The October 29 circular requires the current Class 9 batch to study nine compulsory subjects: R1, R2, R3, Mathematics, Science, Social Science, Art Education, Physical Education and Well-being, and Vocational Education. Students may choose one optional subject from 57 listed options; an optional language must differ from R1, R2 and R3. Vocational education remains compulsory. Students can choose Kaushal Vikas, assessed internally by schools, or one of 22 skill subjects, which require a Class 10 board examination. Students passing a skill subject will also receive a certificate under the National Skills Qualifications Framework.
The board’s latest circular in its frequently asked questions (FAQs) also clarified the Class 10 examination and pass criteria. Students must secure at least 33% in each of the five compulsory board-exam subjects, R1, R2, Mathematics, Science and Social Science, calculated by combining internal assessment and board examination marks. A passed skill subject can replace a failed Mathematics, Science or Social Science subject in result computation, but this does not apply to Kaushal Vikas. A passed optional language can similarly replace a failed R1 or R2 language, provided it is different from all three compulsory languages.
Also Read:Bridge course mandatory for Classes 3, 4 and 6
The circular also provides flexibility for Children with Special Needs (CwSN), who must take one compulsory language with a board examination and can choose their remaining four board-examination subjects from a specified list. They may opt for up to two skill subjects, except Automotive; Information Technology, Computer Applications and AI cannot be taken together.
Sudha Acharya, principal of Delhi-based ITL School, said the changes could ease examination pressure.
“Having five compulsory Board-examination subjects in Class 10 can help reduce unnecessary examination pressure and allow students to focus more on learning rather than examinations alone.” She welcomed the flexibility to choose skill subjects and provisions for CwSN as steps towards a more inclusive scheme.

Though the news broadcast is fake, the clip within it showing Trump speaking is real, meaning it is not the product of an artificial intelligence tool. Though Trump did say the words that can be heard in that section of the footage, he was quoting someone else. He was not saying that he, himself, has a husband. The clip featuring the president has been cropped for satirical purposes to omit this crucial context.
In late October, a video spread purportedly featuring a news broadcast showing U.S. President Donald Trump telling his supporters that he has a husband.
Social media users shared the footage on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and X, where one user said (archived), "Trump says he sat down with his husband, they started writing, but ran out of paper!"
At one point in the alleged 15-second news clip, Trump seemingly says, "We sat down and I sat down with my husband and I started writing and I went on and on and in a little I realized I ran out of paper."
Trump says he sat down with his husband, they started writing, but ran out of paper! I ask this often, but I'll ask it again, what is wrong with him? https://t.co/FAHGyIq1xd
— BlueDream (@58bugeye) October 28, 2026
The story spread as the president attended campaign rallies in support of Republican candidates across the country ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
Some users seemed to interpret the rumor as true. Snopes readers also contacted us to check if Trump said he has a husband.
To investigate the claim's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo. If Trump had authentically said he has a husband, journalists at reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters, would have likely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence. That was not the case.
The origin of the claim is a set of social media pages called The BSN Network. Its Facebook bio notes that it posts, "News reimagined through satire," and, "Comedy built from 'real' headlines."
A manager of the network posted a video to Facebook and Instagram on Oct. 28 (archived, archived) seemingly showing Trump saying he has a husband as part of a news broadcast. From two seconds onward, the footage features text that says, "Commentary | Comedy | Cultural Absurdity."
The news broadcast itself is not authentic. It includes an anchor who appears to have been generated using an artificial intelligence tool. It is not clear whether the character is based on a real person.
The BSN Network's video does contain authentic footage of Trump, though. That genuine clip originates from a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, on Oct. 3, during which Trump did say, "We sat down and I sat down with my husband and I started writing and I went on and on and in a little I realized I ran out of paper."
However, that section has been taken out of context for comedic purposes in The BSN Network's posts. An original recording of Trump's speech shows he was quoting a woman who he said was defending his presidential record. From the 1:16:23 mark, he says (emphasis in bold ours):
You know, a woman was on the other day and she was defending me against false charges. Just false crap, you know, political stuff. And she said, "You know, last night I sat down in my kitchen and I started writing out all the things that President Trump has accomplished during the second," this is our second term, probably you could say third term. We just don't, we just don't want the results of the second.
But, "We sat down and sat down with my husband, and I started writing, and I would on and on. And in a little while I realized I ran out of paper. I didn't have that much paper. We went all over the house looking for paper." So many things, it's true.
Snopes contacted The BSN Network for its response to the video being stripped of its "comedy" label in other users' posts and some people mistaking the satirical story as real news. We will update this article if we receive a response.
For further reading, Snopes has debunked similar pieces of media before. For example, we alerted readers to a satirical claim that Trump asked why "we are wasting time counting ballots" when everyone "already knows the Republicans won the 2026 midterms."
Since satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call whether you agree.

In late October, a video spread on social media with claims it showed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu being attacked and seriously injured in Tel Aviv.
"Breaking 🚨 A very dangerous attack on Netanyahu in Tel Aviv it appears he has sustained severe injuries, and an aircraft is being dispatched to transport him to the United States. This is clearly evident from the footage," one X post (archived) captioned the footage.
Other X users also shared the video. Snopes readers searched our website for information about the alleged attack.
The video is authentic, meaning not generated with artificial intelligence or digitally edited. However, it does not show Netanyahu. It shows an attempted attack on Bulgarian politician Ahmed Dogan during a party conference in January 2013. We have therefore rated the claim miscaptioned.
We found no credible reports of such an attack on Netanyahu. He remained politically active following Israel's Oct. 27 election and delivered a speech in Jerusalem the following day.
What we know about the video
On Jan. 19, 2013, Dogan, then the leader of Bulgaria's Movement for Rights and Freedoms party, was giving a speech in Sofia when a man came onto the stage and pointed a gas pistol at his head. The gun did not fire, and Dogan was not injured. Security guards and other people at the conference then stopped the attacker, according to reporting by the BBC and bTV, a Bulgarian broadcaster. The Guardian also shared footage of the incident.
Although a thumbnail attached to the circulating video appeared to show Netanyahu (see screenshot below), the footage of the attack itself didn't.
(X user @AsifAli_Haider)
The video's low quality also made it difficult to identify the person in the footage, which may have made the claim more believable to social media users.
This was not the first time social media users falsely linked the video to Netanyahu. In 2024, Reuters, AFP and Soch Fact Check debunked posts claiming the footage showed Netanyahu being attacked by members of Israel's parliament. Similar claims were debunked again in April 2026. When the video resurfaced in October, fact-checking outlet Lead Stories also investigated it.

Lenovo Googlebook 15 review: Your Android phone's new best friend
Lenovo’s hardware is great, but Googlebook OS still needs some polishing.
The launch of a new operating system presents a lot of challenges, but also the opportunity to install significant upgrades to the status quo. With its new family of notebooks, Google is trying to combine the best features of Android and Chrome OS on a line of PCs that are smarter, easier to use and more mobile-friendly than anything that's come before. However, while Lenovo has done an excellent job of providing premium hardware for the Googlebook 15, Google's latest laptop platform suffers from a number of growing pains you often get from first-gen software.
For die-hard Android fans, some of these issues might be worth overlooking for the increased synergy you'll get between your phone and laptop. But for other users, it's probably worth waiting for a more mature version of Googlebook OS before making the switch.
Design and display: Premium hardware
The design and hardware on this Googlebook is so good I'm actually a little bit annoyed that Lenovo hasn't made a Windows equivalent. It features a 15.3-inch OLED display with 120Hz refresh rate, a typical brightness of 500 nits and HDR True Black 1000 certification. It's bright, it's colorful and delivers pretty much everything you could ask for on a laptop in this price range.
That said, I'd argue the rest of the Googlebook 15's design is even better. Lenovo's chassis is made from a mix of plastic and carbon fiber, with bits of magnesium-aluminum alloy used in certain areas, like its lid, for increased strength and lightness. Then Lenovo covered the entire system in a "silk-touch" finish that makes the whole laptop feel like a piece of unglazed porcelain. It's surprisingly luxurious and comes with the added benefit of reducing the appearance of fingerprints. And despite having a larger screen, the Lenovo Googlebook 15 actually weighs less than a 14-inch MacBook Pro (2.85 pounds vs. 3 pounds).
Elsewhere, Lenovo's Googlebook has punchy up-firing quad speakers with Dolby Atmos flanking the keyboard, a decent selection of ports (2x USB-C, 1 USB-A, HDMI and 3.5mm audio) and a massive haptic touchpad. The keyboard has just enough bounce to make typing quite pleasant, while tweaks like the Google key make performing OS-related shortcuts just a bit easier. There's even a built-in camera with a physical shutter (plus a separate fingerprint sensor) that supports facial recognition, so signing in is friction-free.
The final distinguishing characteristic of all Googlebooks is the lightbar on their lids, which changes color depending on a handful of factors. In normal use, the LEDs are white, but when charging, the light reflects how much charge the laptop has (red means under 20 percent, yellow means 20 to 59 percent, etc.). Alternatively, during startup or when talking to Gemini, you'll get special animations across an assortment of colors. The one issue is that when compared to the Pixel 11 Pro's HiLight indicator, you generally don't interact with a Googlebook when its lid is closed. This makes the Gemini LEDs more useful to someone sitting opposite the laptop than whoever is actually using it.
Performance: More than good enough
One of the nice things about the Googlebook platform is that Google stipulates that all participating systems come with at least 16GB of RAM, so you won't have to worry about running out of memory while doing basic productivity tasks like you do on some budget machines. And when combined with an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 chip and 256GB of base storage, the result is a totally proficient system for handling all of your core computing needs.
The bigger issue for the Googlebook 15 is that because you're encouraged to install the same kind of mobile apps you'd use on a phone, you'll often have more performance than you can really use. It's either that or you'll be faced with apps that haven't been properly optimized to take advantage of the hardware. A good example of this is Photoshop, because the version you download from Google's Play Store is the mobile edition instead of the full desktop app you'd normally install on Windows or Mac PCs. Furthermore a lot of today's Android apps are designed to be run on ARM-based chips instead of silicon with x86 architecture, like the one in Lenovo's machine, which can result in more bugs or stuttery performance. However, at least on tests like Geekbench 7, the Googlebook 15's multi-core CPU score of 9,011 is just as good if not better than what you'd get on a similarly priced PC — like a midrange Dell XPS 13 (7,124 with an Intel Core 5 320 chip).
Software: The next evolution of ChromeOS
The nice thing about being a mix between an Android phone and Chromebook is that Googlebook OS feels immediately familiar and is very easy to use. You get notifications and quick settings in the top right, a row of icons in a taskbar along the bottom and drawer for all your apps. From there, it's super simple to do stuff like side-by-side multitasking — all you need to do is open an app and drag it to the left or the right and let the OS automatically snap the window in place. For general productivity, web browsing or checking social feeds, there's plenty of stuff to like about Googlebook OS' streamlined approach to basic computing.
Where things get even more interesting is with some of Google's special features, the most important of which is cross-device sharing. I'm kind of glad I waited a little bit to do this review because right at launch, a lot of Google's "Better Together" features weren't available with Samsung phones. That changed shortly after release and this collection of tools is the closest thing Googlebooks have to a secret weapon.
Pairing your Googlebook to your Android handset works a lot like the Windows Phone Link app, except that it's better in almost every way. Setup is as easy as scanning a QR using your phone. From there, you can do stuff like transfer things between devices simply by dragging and dropping (via the Files app), seamlessly cast apps from your phone to the Googlebook, sync notifications between devices or pick up where you were last browsing on your phone. In a lot of ways, Google has created the kind of cohesive ecosystem that Mac and iPhone users often say is one of the best things about Apple's family of products, but centered around Android instead of iOS.
That said, there are a number of quirks and limitations that still need work. Transferring files, for example, is currently limited to things under 200MB. For anything bigger, you'll need to rely on the Quick Share tool. And while it works, casting things from your phone to the Googlebook is a bit stuttery and less responsive than I'd like. It's fine for checking messages or apps with a relatively static UI, but if you try to cast a game, there's a noticeable drop in framerate and smoothness.
Some of Googlebook OS' other more unique tools include the Magic Pointer, which makes it easy to select objects so you can ask Gemini about them or transform highlighted pictures into AI-generated drawings. Now, I'll be honest, creating cute stickers or using Gemini to whip up things like party invites isn't something I do regularly, so I sort of had to go out of my way to test these features. But your mileage may vary. Meanwhile, Rambler might be the best voice transcription tool out now, so it's nice to see Google port that over from the Pixel 11 family. And it's so good, there's a dedicated button for it on the laptop's keyboard. You can also use Gemini (and Gemini Notebook) to find, organize and summarize all sorts of different files and docs, but that's sort of par for the course these days.
You can even use AI to create your own custom widgets, but like a lot of machine learning-based tools, the results are hit or miss. At first, I asked the Googlebook to make a basic dashboard showing the live score for all the NBA games, but that didn't work. So then I paired the list down to just a handful of teams and it was able to display the correct scores for various matchups, but the UI remained rather barebones and a bit confusing to look at.
Unfortunately, it feels Googlebook OS still needs a bit of polishing and extra developer support to make it really shine. In addition to often being limited to the mobile version for many apps, the various tiers of app compatibility can get pretty confusing. If you try to install an app from the Play Store, you'll notice that there are five different levels of optimization ranging from "Made for desktop" to "Compatible for desktop" or simply "Better on the website." And if a certain app hasn't been tested, it may be labeled as "Built for mobile."
I do appreciate that all of these tags show up front and center on the listing for each app, but it still results in a lot more trial and error that most people probably want to deal with. Some apps work great, some apps suffer from display glitches and some apps are saddled with smaller issues like awkwardly placed UI elements or not being able to maximise a window to fullscreen. So even though you have a big, beautiful display, you'll still have bits of your desktop wallpaper peeking out from both sides of an app.
Battery life: Fine, but could be better
In a vacuum, the 70Whr battery inside the Googlebook 15 is decently sized. However, because this system has the largest display out of any of the first batch of machines powered by Google's new OS, overall longevity is just okay.
Since there still aren't a ton of desktop-level benchmarks available for Googlebooks at the moment, I decided to perform our usual smartphone battery test on it instead. This involves local video playback to drain the battery from 100 percent to zero, where Lenovo's machine lasted eight and a half hours. That might seem okay until you compare it to something like an XPS 13, which hit 15:56 while running PCMark 10's more demanding Modern Office rundown test. Thankfully, the Googlebook 15 fared a bit better during everyday use, where it survived a full eight-hour workday (including a number of tests and benchmarks) and still had 20 percent left in the tank.
Wrap-up
The Googlebook 15 is a tale of two technologies. On one hand, the hardware Lenovo built is great. It features a vivid 15-inch display with a 120Hz refresh rate, an Intel Core 5 CPU with plenty of performance, surprisingly good speakers, plenty of ports and a huge haptic touchpad. Meanwhile, its design is the icing on the cake, offering a streamlined chassis with a super smooth eggshell finish that begs to be touched. And while its battery life could be a touch better, the rest of the machine is so nice, its merely average longevity is easy to gloss over.
However, the same can't be said for Googlebook OS. The sheer number of different app compatibility levels can be hard to keep track of and, at least right now, a lot of software simply doesn't run as smoothly as I'd really like. So even though the Googlebook 15 is more than capable of serving as a general productivity machine, being limited mostly to mobile versions of apps means the laptop doesn't feel as powerful or versatile as a similarly-priced Windows or Mac alternative. For people wary of first-gen gadgets, that mantra seems to hold doubly true for first-gen OSes.
If you're a hardcore Android user though, there's a lot to like about how well Googlebooks and Google-based phones work together. Handing off tasks and files from your phone to the laptop is a breeze, and the continuity you get between apps and notifications makes bouncing between two devices surprisingly seamless. And while I personally don't get a ton of value out of every Gemini feature, they can come in handy in a pinch. I adore Lenovo's chassis and I think Googlebook OS has a lot of potential, but right now I feel like it's best to revisit this platform once more of its initial kinks have been ironed out.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

Audacious Indian jailbreak saga ends with 17 prisoners recaptured
- Published
A fake medical emergency, an audacious jailbreak and a 36-hour search operation that ended with 17 prisoners being recaptured.
Those are the highlights of a story from India's Tamil Nadu state that has captured headlines across the country.
It began on Monday night after 17 men escaped from a prison in Theni district in the southern state after overpowering guards, and ended almost two days later with police catching them in batches.
The incident has drawn attention to overcrowding in Indian prisons. Police say the Theni prison was housing 334 inmates against a capacity of 200, leaving authorities unable to maintain control once chaos broke out.
The state police said it has suspended nine staff at the prison for alleged negligence in connection with the incident.
All the men who escaped were undertrials - inmates on trial or awaiting one - and 18 of them were in one cell at the prison in Thekkampatti in Theni.
On Monday night at 2230 local time (17:00 GMT), one of the prisoners acted like he was going through a seizure. The other cellmates shouted for help and a jail official responded. He was soon overpowered by the prisoners, police said.
The prisoners then got out of the cell, reportedly attacked two other jail guards and took away keys which they used to open the main gate and flee. While 17 escaped, one returned to the prison immediately.
Several prison personnel were injured in the attack.
Police sources told BBC Tamil that they were examining the possibility of collusion between some prison officials and the escaped men.
Sandeep Rathore, Director General of Police for Prisons in Tamil Nadu, said in a press briefing that the jailbreak was caused by "human error".
"There was a clear breach of security protocol as the prisoners managed to pass through a three-tier barrier manned by security personnel," he said.
On Thursday, he was replaced as the head of state prisons and transferred to a different department.
At the time of the incident, only four guards were on duty, far below the staffing required to maintain the prescribed 1:6 guard-to-inmate ratio recommended by the state - which should have worked out to 34 guards against the approved strength of 200 prisoners.
The police then launched a manhunt, calling forces from across the state.
"Advanced technology, drone surveillance, CCTV footage analysis, and the tireless efforts of police personnel played a crucial role," the department said in a statement on X.
Four men were arrested at a bus station in a nearby village, and the fifth was caught while he was travelling in a tuk-tuk.
A drone search of a forest near the prison led to eight more escaped prisoners being caught. Videos of the arrests showed the men obeying police instructions even as they did not answer questions from reporters who were also seen at the scene.
Two more were captured with the help of drone surveillance, police said, while the last two men surrendered on Wednesday.
News agency PTI reported that all 17 recaptured prisoners have been moved to high-security correctional prisons.
Rathore told media that all prisons across the state would be audited to check if rules were being followed.
The incident evoked memories of one of the biggest jailbreaks in Tamil Nadu in 1995 when 43 suspected militants escaped from a special camp after digging a 153-foot-long tunnel beneath a historic fort. Some of them were never recaptured.
While the investigation is going on, the incident has sparked a conversation on overcrowding in Indian prisons. The National Crime Records Bureau's last Prison Statistics India report from 2023 showed a national occupancy rate of 120.1%.
Data shows that undertrial prisoners - individuals who are detained while they await police investigation or court trials - make up more than 73% of India's total prison population. Human rights groups and legal experts have also raised concerns about delays in investigations and trials that lead to people languishing for years behind bars.

Greetings from Baghdad, where Agatha Christie's old home presents its own mystery
This, according to Iraq's culture ministry, is the one-time home of English mystery novelist Agatha Christie, on the banks of the Tigris River in Baghdad.
Fittingly, the abandoned house has its own mystery: why it's been left to decay over the last century.
Christie made dozens of trips to Iraq, including the one where she met her archaeologist husband, Max Mallowan, in 1930. They Came to Baghdad and Murder in Mesopotamia were two of her novels set in Iraq.
As for the house, it's a heritage property controlled by Iraq's culture ministry. The Iraqi government says it's willing to make the house available to anyone who will restore it. It is padlocked and literally falling down.
When we visited this month, there was a $200 electricity bill stuffed into a hole in the door — apparently reflecting years of unpaid bills in its more recent history.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The Rs 15.78-crore Kalagram project behind Bharat Bhavan has come under scrutiny over alleged construction inside the 50-metre no-construction buffer zone of Bhoj Wetland.
The matter came up before the National Green Tribunal (NGT) on October 28, when the bench expressed displeasure over the applicant's absence and directed that pending formalities be completed within a week.
With the matter still pending, the next hearing has been scheduled for January 5, 2027.
The project, spread across 1.05 acres near the Chief Minister's residence, is being executed by the Madhya Pradesh Tourism Development Corporation for the culture department. It proposes live workshops, an art gallery and an open-air theatre.
The case is pending before the NGT's Bhopal bench in Rashid Noor Khan vs Collector and Others case. A bench of Justice Sheo Kumar Singh and expert member Sudhir Kumar Chaturvedi had heard the matter on October 28 and the written order was uploaded late Thursday night.
On August 3, 2026, the tribunal had impleaded the alleged actual violator as respondent No. 9 and sought a reply within six weeks. Following the applicant's absence at the latest hearing, the tribunal directed the completion of formalities within a week and fixed January 5, 2027, for the next hearing.
JCB excavation, rock-cutting at site
At the site, heavy JCB machines are reportedly being used for excavation and rock-cutting barely 10-15 steps from the lake. Permanent masonry work involving cement and stone is also underway. More than 40 workers and artisans are engaged in the project, while media access to the site has been restricted.
The environment department's order dated March 16, 2022, along with the Wetlands Rules, 2017, and the Ramsar Convention, 1971, have been cited in connection with restrictions on permanent construction and mining within 50-metre zone.

In a major blow to both the terminally online and the criminally horny, the fan fiction website Archive of Our Own (AO3) has temporarily shut down due to a “security incident,” according to an update posted on the site.
On October 29, an admin for AO3 posted that the website was “down for maintenance.” The statement said that it could take up to four weeks for service to be fully restored, though it was possible the site would be back up in a “degraded state” sooner, with some of its features disabled.
Though the original statement did not specify the reasons for the closure, subsequent updates said that a “security incident” had taken place, though “we are still in the early stages of response [and] determining its scope.” While the statement said that AO3 did not believe that its user database had been stolen, it urged users to exercise caution and change their passwords for the site.
Run by the Organization for Transformative Works, a nonprofit dedicated to preserving fandom communities on the internet, AO3 was founded in 2007 in part due to concerns about censorship and corporate interests overtaking fandom spaces. The website has 11 million users, according to a 2026 press release, and hosts more than 18 million original works. The explosive popularity of the gay hockey romance Heated Rivalry TV series generated a surge of new interest last year, resulting in the publication of tens of thousands of stories featuring the show’s main characters, Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov, on the platform.
Those reliant on AO3 for their daily dose of Destiel- or Dramione-inspired smut are not taking the news well. “No ao3 for possibly 4 weeks SOMEONE DO SOMETHING,” one Heated Rivalry fan account posted on X, tagging not just AO3 itself but also the official X accounts for the FBI, the CIA, and, for some reason, Uber Support. Other fans are compiling Google Docs of links to downloaded stories, touting them as “survival guides” for the “AO3 apocalypse” and organizing them by fictional character pairings, or ships. (Be warned, however: One such doc is difficult to load due to “heavy traffic” on the file.)
Others commented on the timing of the outage, pointing out that it coincides with “No Nut November,” the internet-based challenge that encourages people to abstain from masturbation throughout the month. “AO3 taking no nut november a little too seriously,” one person wrote.
A representative for the Organization for Transformative Works did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But the chaos inspired by the site’s shutdown underscores the prominence of fan fiction in everyday lives, driving mainstream publishing trends and generating hundreds of millions of views. It also serves as the engine for the burgeoning vertical video industry, with streaming platforms constantly scouring fan fiction websites for works to adapt.
“All life forms dependent on AO3 are literally withering right now,” one fan wrote. “This is our 9/11.”

Thank you, Brazil, for demonstrating how the far right can be trounced while protection for the Amazon is strengthened. In a world where nature and democracy appeared to be bleeding out in tandem, voters and forest defenders in this global south powerhouse have shown it is possible to staunch the flow. This should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France.
The astonishing comeback victory of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff against his extreme right challenger Flavío Bolsonaro has brought oceans of rapturous supporters on to the streets, while also thrilling conservationists, climate activists and social justice campaigners across the world.
Coming just weeks after the Lula administration announced a record fall in Amazon and Cerrado destruction, they hope Brazil can now go on to achieve its target of zero deforestation by 2030 and continue to support a global transition away from fossil fuels. That would provide a huge boost to flagging global efforts to stabilise the climate and protect degraded ecosystems. It would also set a remarkable example of leadership by the global south.
Big battles lie ahead. In the Amazon region itself, far-right members of Bolsonaro’s party have won the governorships of seven of the nine states and a large number of municipal mayorships. Brazil’s congress is now dominated by agribusiness and mining interests that have set the political agenda in recent years, and will push hard to allow more extractivist industries in indigenous lands, expand road-building, privatise rivers, weaken environmental protections and possibly attempt to impeach the president.
In the regional sphere, Lula, alone among the leaders of main South American nations in not aligning with Donald Trump’s so-called Shield of the Americas, will face pressure from Washington to channel critical minerals and other natural resources to the US, rather than selling to China or Europe, or leaving them in the ground. And, on the planetary level, Brazil faces the threat of accelerating global heating, which is pushing the Amazon ever closer to the point of no return.
So although Sunday’s result will hopefully provide a little breathing space for the Amazon and other crucially important biomes, the joy and hope that Brazil has gifted the world will quickly fade unless it inspires political change in other countries. In that sense, the biggest environmental impact of Lula’s victory may be the lessons it provides for campaigners elsewhere. Here are some initial takeaways:
1 Politics matter. There is no higher environmental priority than defeating the far right, which is a Trojan horse for extractivist – and often criminal – groups to capture states and erode protections for people, democracy and the environment. Just look at the 59.5% surge of Amazon deforestation under the 2019-2022 term of Jair Bolsonaro – the highest level of any four-year presidency in Brazil. Compare that with the 71.2% fall during the Lula administration. Over the past year, forest loss was 3,335 sq km, the lowest level since the start of satellite measurements in 1988. And Lula is not, by any means, an environmentalist. He has approved several destructive projects himself, but he is a people person who listens to the voice of social movements.
2 Don’t give up. Lula was largely written off by the markets and some polls after his first-round defeat. No first-round loser had ever previously come back to win the runoff. Lula was able to do so by securing an extra 10m votes over three weeks. The energy for this came from the streets and the forests. Social movements organised giant rallies in cities. In the Amazon, indigenous, riverine and quilombola groups travelled by hours – sometimes days – to reach polling stations by boats or buses.
3 Mobilise a campaign army. The first round of Lula’s campaign had been stodgy, old-fashioned and defensive – three traits that are also often applicable to environmental campaigns. This was transformed during the runoff, when federal deputy André Janones launched a “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp group that used humorous memes, live streams and algorithmic outreach to seize digital territory that had long been dominated by the right. By voting day, this army had 10m “soldiers”, about 8% of the electorate. Volunteers devoted hours posting stories and spreading messages across social media, speeding up the Lula campaign’s response time and emotional impact. Everyone was instructed not to share or respond to posts by the opposition camp.
4 Go on the offensive against US tech giants. Lula’s campaign accused Meta, which runs the Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram social media platforms, of political favouritism towards Bolsonaro in its algorithms and AI tools. Meta denied bias but acknowledged technical failures. Brazil’s electoral court ordered corrective action. Among the most popular chants of Lula supporters was “Hey Meta, vai tomar no cu!” (Hey Meta, take it up the arse!). Many on the left have blamed US social media platforms for spreading rightwing disinformation and fearmongering, causing recent electoral defeats in Colombia, Chile and Peru. Lula made clear that would not be allowed in Brazil: “We had to overcome foreign interference through digital platforms, which we will have to regulate. We cannot have a monstrously large corporation earning millions and billions paying no taxes to this country and trying to steer our election results.”
5 Reclaim the flag. Brazil’s green, yellow and blue national colours had been associated with Bolsonaro’s movement in previous elections. This time, Lula seized it back by posing in a national football team strip while his “army” launched a campaign called “The green and yellow is ours”. Before voting day, millions of people across Brazil and the world – from Indigenous leaders in the Amazon to Hollywood celebrities and European football stars – flooded social networks with images of themselves in Brazil colours making an L (for Lula) sign with their thumb and little finger extended.
6 Increase social spending. Amazon protection may have galvanised conservationists, but the far greater motivations for many Lula voters were record low unemployment, robust wage growth, a 15% increase in “bolsa familia” poverty relief payments and a promise to raise the minimum wage. The importance of combining social justice with climate and nature action is widely recognised by Brazilian environmental groups. Without it, elections are lost and protests can erupt in the streets – as the world learned from France during the violent gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrations of 2018.
7 Defend sovereignty, democracy and sustainability. Lula and his army called out the interlinked threats posed by the Bolsonaro family’s fealty to Donald Trump (now doubly confirmed by Flávio’s post-election flight to the US). They highlighted the interlinked threats posed by the obsequience to Trump, Bolsonaro’s desire to change the constitution and his promise to open up exploration of the Amazon and other biomes. This reflects a global phenomenon. Now that seven of the planetary boundaries essential for the flourishing of life have been breached, more and more people are affected by business activities that make the situation worse by destabilising the climate, damaging ecosystems and polluting the air, soil and rivers. This makes it harder for extractive companies to secure a social mandate so they become more inclined to either break the law or support extreme politics that override democracy.
The former environment minister Marina Silva pulled these threads together during the victory celebrations, saying Brazil had come together against these threats: “Long live the people who emerged from every corner of Brazil to sow hope for a future that is socially just, sovereign, democratic and sustainable.”
Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action. Now it needs others to follow.

Indian regulators ordered Sun Pharmaceutical to stop manufacturing, selling and distributing ophthalmic products made at its Assam facility after finding failure in its quality management system, Reuters reported.
