Staring down a $40M tariff bill, this American importer is suing Trump to end some tariffs on Canada
Gellert Global Group says tariffs are 'unsustainable,' confident in legal challenge
Inside a sprawling refrigerated warehouse, tucked into an industrial neighbourhood not far from New Jersey's Newark Airport, you'll find a new front in the U.S.-Canada trade war.
It's the headquarters of Gellert Global Group, a third-generation, family-owned food distribution company that is suing the Trump administration over its 50 per cent tariffs on certain Canadian goods and seeking refunds.
In one of his first broadcast interviews since launching the lawsuit, Thomas Gellert, the company's CEO, says he felt he had to do something.
"We can't sustain a tariff like this on these products for much longer," he said during an interview with CBC News on the floor of the warehouse in Elizabeth, N.J.
Gellert Global Group imports roughly $80 million US worth of Canadian cheeses every year, including Celebrity goat cheese produced by Mariposa Dairy in Lindsay, Ont. It also imports a range of Canadian-produced brie and camembert products.
"Customers are not going to take price increases. Everyone is sort of beat down and tired from inflationary pressures," he said, confirming that his company is eating the cost of the tariffs for now.
Thomas Gellert, CEO of Gellert Global Group, stands inside the company's refrigerated warehouse in Elizabeth, N.J. His company is suing the Trump administration over its 50 per cent tariffs on certain Canadian goods. (Katie Simpson/CBC)
Gellert tried to get exemptions for these products in meetings with American lawmakers and diplomats, including U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra. In those conversations, he says he highlighted the fact that American-produced milk is being used for some of the cheese products hit by tariffs, arguing that, in the end, the policy is hurting U.S. farmers too.
Those lobbying efforts were not successful. And with no Canada-U.S. trade deal appearing to be on the horizon, Gellert decided he had to take legal action.
"Frankly we don't have time to wait for things to settle on their own," he said.
"We have a business here to run."
The lawsuit was filed by the Liberty Justice Center, a non-profit, non-partisan legal advocacy organization. It is the same organization that successfully challenged Trump's IEEPA tariffs, which were struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court earlier this year.
"We felt like our job wasn't done if the President keeps putting illegal tariffs on different countries," said Sarah Albrecht, the chair and CEO of the Liberty Justice Center.
Tariff technicalities
The Trump administration imposed this round of tariffs after trade talks with Canada broke down in August.
The duties are applied through Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act, also known as the Smoot-Hawley Act, a Depression-era law that had never been used before for tariff purposes.
The law gives the president the power to impose tariffs of up to 50 per cent on imported goods from a country that has discriminated against the U.S.
The Trump administration has argued that Canada's decision to retaliate against previous rounds of U.S. tariffs amounts to discrimination. It specifically cited the banning of American alcohol products by certain provinces, protections for the Canadian dairy industry and measures related to the auto sector.
In a statement released the day the lawsuit was filed, the Liberty Justice Center said Section 338 cannot be used as an "all-purpose authorization for the executive branch to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises."
Among the arguments the group is making, it says there's a disconnect between allegations of discrimination by Canada and the products Trump is targeting with the tariffs. It also says the Trump administration illegally rushed the implementation of some of the tariffs. And it claims Trump does not have the authority to impose tariffs in this way.
- Trump to swap some tariffs on Canadian goods amid midterm pressure
- Canada scores a dairy win on U.S. soil as farmers grumble about Trump's trade war
"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," Albrecht said.
Initially, the tariffs applied to roughly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods, with targets including cement, road salt, hockey sticks and other items. However, the list has been adjusted twice to remove some products and add others.
Some of the changes were made at the request of Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, as she finds herself in a tough re-election race. She has sought exemptions for products important to businesses in her home state, as the trade war with Canada is proving unpopular there.
Experts mixed on strength of Trump's tariff justification
Since the tariffs were first announced, legal experts have offered varying opinions on whether the measures would survive a legal challenge.
"There's a good chance it could get reversed," said Ryan Majerus, a trade lawyer and partner at King & Spalding International Trade Group.
"I think the administration may have a tough time identifying the reasons why these particular products or these particular actions by Canada are discriminatory."
Lawyers for the Trump administration will have to make the connection, Majerus says, between the alleged discrimination and why the U.S. tariffs offset that discrimination.
"The fact that there have been adjustments [to the product list] since they've been put in place ... I think it may undermine their claim as well," he said.
However, the Trump administration is expected to put up an intense defence.
"I think they can make some creative arguments on how they're able to kind of invoke the authority broadly," Majerus said.
"It's a bit of a blank canvas in terms of how the courts are going to look at this."
A display of Celebrity goat cheese and other Canadian cheese products. Gellert Global Group says U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods are threatening its business and the Canadian producers it works with. (Katie Simpson/CBC)
Fears of losing shelf space
If there isn't a resolution by next year, Gellert says his company will have to reassess how it handles the tariffs and whether it is sustainable to keep importing these Canadian goods.
"If we stop selling a product — to get back on the shelf would be very difficult," he said.
"We don't want to lose shelf space."
He also says that if these Canadian products are not available to U.S. consumers, there aren't readily available American alternatives to replace them.
"There is not enough goat milk in the United States to support demand," he said.
"And the existing goat cheese factories that are here, even if they're importing frozen curd, they don't have the capacity. So that's the reason why we work with our Canadian partners."
The goat cheese issue specifically weighs heavily on Gellert. He says he worked closely with the family that owns Mariposa Dairy and encouraged them to invest in production to grow their business.
"I do feel some sort of sense of personal responsibility to that community, that we've encouraged them to build up infrastructure to help support the business — and now that's at risk," he said.
"If we stop buying, they start culling goats. It's not something that can be brought back again."

Flávio Bolsonaro had hoped that by Sunday night people would be calling him the next president of Brazil.
Instead, the far-right politician’s decision to flee to the US after losing the election and – for 58 minutes – to declare himself “Brazil’s true president-elect”, has made him a laughing stock, with Brazilian newspapers and commentators raining a barrage of scornful adjectives down on the conquered candidate.
“If it served any purpose at all, Flávio’s foolishness liberated the democratic right from a family of coup-mongers, which for far too long held it hostage to their reckless folly and irremediable disdain for Brazil,” the conservative Estado de São Paulo newspaper thundered on Friday.
Bolsonaro fled to Miami on Tuesday night, 48 hours after being beaten by his leftwing adversary, the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, by 4.4m votes. Lula’s victory has been recognised by rightwing leaders from around the world, including El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, not to mention Bolsonaro’s own party and many key allies.
But on Wednesday after landing in the US, Bolsonaro published an outlandish letter – reportedly produced with the help of ChatGPT – in which he declared himself “the true president-elect of Brazil” and made phoney claims about election fraud.
Perhaps most bizarrely, he claimed he would continue to lead Brazil’s opposition from abroad, comparing himself to Charles de Gaulle, who in the 1940s led a French government-in-exile against the Nazis from London, and the 19th-century Cuban independence hero José Martí, who challenged the Spanish empire from New York.
“They were all treated as criminals by the regimes they confronted. History called them something else,” Bolsonaro said, also likening himself to Venezuela’s Nobel laureate María Corina Machado and Rui Barbosa, a Brazilian politician who went into exile in London in the late 19th century after challenging an authoritarian president known as “the Iron Marshal”.
Just under an hour after Bolsonaro’s proclamation was first published on social media, a corrected version was issued, altering his claimed status to “leader of Brazil” – reportedly after he was upbraided by Trump administration officials keen to avoid a full-blown diplomatic split with Brazil’s actual leaders.
The amended letter also updated the out-of-date Brazilian coat of arms that had been used erroneously in the letterhead of the first version referring to the “United States of Brazil” – a name the South American country has not used since 1967.
Bolsonaro’s flight – and his brief but bogus claim to be “president-elect” of one of the world’s largest democracies – prompted an outpouring of opprobrium and ridicule.
“[This letter] seems to have been written by a foolhardy, loony halfwit,” Flávia Oliveira, a prominent political commentator, told the network GloboNews.
The Estado de São Paulo’s leader writers said: “Flávio’s letter isn’t worth the ink of this newspaper, but there’s no way the embarrassment can be ignored,” before savaging a man they called “a con artist of the highest order”.
The Rio broadsheet O Globo said Bolsonaro’s “shameful and sneaky” decision to abscond laid bare the “pathetic” nature of his political movement, Bolsonarismo, while the Folha de São Paulo said it exposed the true nature of the “authoritarian, ignorant, incompetent” Bolsonaro family.
José Casado, a columnist for the conservative magazine Veja, wrote: “The comedy storyline has already guaranteed him a spot in the pages of political satire.”
Merval Pereira, a conservative columnist for O Globo, called Bolsonaro “a madhouse Napoleon”.
Even Silas Malafaia, a pugnacious televangelist who is close to Bolsonaro’s jailed father, Jair Bolsonaro, had harsh words. “Bolsonaro’s kids are jackasses … A bunch of amateur morons,” Malafaia was quoted as saying by O Globo.
Some observers see Bolsonaro’s post-defeat getaway as proof that his dispirited movement is dead. “I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, said this week, calling the result “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying right wing”.
The Estado de São Paulo’s editorial board agreed. “Flávio belongs to the past and will soon vanish into the basement of political irrelevance from which he should never have emerged,” they predicted, urging conservatives to ditch Bolsonaro and throw their weight behind his ally Tarcísio de Freitas, the São Paulo governor.
Others warned Bolsonarismo would remain a powerful political force, even if the Bolsonaro family’s leadership of the far-right movement was now in doubt.
Social media users were also merciless in their reaction to Bolsonaro’s short-lived claim to be “president-elect”. One meme invited supporters to attend his January inauguration – at Cinderella Castle in Walt Disney World, Orlando. Another parodied his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan “God, homeland and family”, which became “Goodbye, homeland and family”.
Donald Trump has declined to publicly recognise the result of an election he has called “a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil”. But a US diplomatic cable obtained by the Folha de São Paulo called Lula’s victory “surprising but definitive”.
Asked if he saw Bolsonaro as Brazil’s “rightful” leader, the US president replied: “I won’t get involved.”

Revolt brews in NC as 19 MLAs seek cabinet overhaul, removal of Omar aides
Nineteen National Conference MLAs adopted a resolution seeking a cabinet reshuffle and the removal of two aides. The move reflects discontent after several senior legislators were overlooked in the latest expansion.
Trouble is brewing within Jammu and Kashmir's ruling National Conference, with 19 disgruntled MLAs adopting a joint resolution seeking a major reshuffle of Chief Minister Omar Abdullah's cabinet and the removal of two of his close aides over alleged interference in party and administrative affairs.
The dissenting legislators have urged the party leadership to drop all ministers who have completed two years in office and redistribute cabinet positions on the basis of merit and balanced regional representation, sources present at the meeting told India Today.
They have also sought the removal of party leader Nasir Aslam Wani and Member of Parliament Shammi Oberoi, accusing the two of interfering in party affairs and administrative decision-making.
19 MLAS MEET IN SRINAGAR, PREPARE RESOLUTION FOR FAROOQ ABDULLAH
The legislators, representing constituencies in both the Kashmir Valley and Jammu region, held a nearly four-hour meeting on Friday evening at the Srinagar residence of MLA Qaiser Jamshed Lone.
While some participants reportedly sought to describe the gathering as a routine lunch meeting, those present discussed their grievances and prepared a formal resolution to be submitted to National Conference president Farooq Abdullah.
According to sources, 19 MLAs attended the meeting, including Abdul Majid Larmi, Hasnain Masoodi, Sajad Shafi, Javid Choudhary, Hilal Akbar Lone, Ghulam Mohiuddin Mir, Farooq Shah, Bashir Ahmed Veeri, Khurshid Ahmed, Mustaq Guroo, Muzaffar Iqbal, Nazir Gurezi and Qaiser Jamshed Lone.
MUBARAK GUL STRIPPED OF GENERAL SECRETARY POST
The internal dissent has also led to action against senior party leader Mubarak Gul, who was removed from his recently assigned position as general secretary.
Gul had attended Friday's meeting and had reportedly declined to take up the organisational post after being left out of the council of ministers during the October 27 cabinet expansion.
His removal comes amid growing discontent among senior legislators who were overlooked during the latest expansion.
CABINET EXPANSION TRIGGERS RESENTMENT
The latest episode of dissent follows the induction of four ministers into Omar Abdullah's cabinet on October 27 - Ali Mohammad Sagar, Shameema Firdous, Mir Saifullah and Altaf Kaloo.
The expansion reportedly triggered resentment among several senior legislators who had expected ministerial positions but were left out.
The demand for a cabinet overhaul and the removal of the Chief Minister's close aides signals a widening rift within the ruling party, with the disgruntled lawmakers now seeking the intervention of its top leadership.

Mourinho and chaos - is Real Madrid boss misunderstood?
- Published
Barcelona fans have long teased Jose Mourinho, with their insult of choice being traductor - Spanish for translator.
It is their way of mocking the Real Madrid manager's humble beginnings.
Learning his future trade while serving as an interpreter for the legendary Sir Bobby Robson, Mourinho followed Robson from Sporting to Porto, before the pair reached Barcelona in 1996.
Four years later Mourinho was the manager of Benfica, the first steps in a coaching career that would lead him to Champions League glory, twice, and success in England, Italy and Spain.
So much more than merely a translator, even while at Barcelona, the Portuguese boss' wide and varied success best illustrates the true qualities that underpin him - diligent, determined, introspective, able to thrive in chaos, and tactically brilliant.
Last weekend, that eager tactical mind was in full force as Real Madrid beat Barcelona 2-1.
As the footballing world praised the tactics Mourinho used, it was an apt moment to reflect on his 26 years in management.
This Clasico featured Real Madrid playing in a 4-4-2 shape with winger Vinicius Jr suspended.
Federico Valverde played at right-back. Bernardo Silva came into the side partnering Aurelien Tchouameni in midfield. Arda Guler and Yan Diomande manned the flanks and Jude Bellingham played up top alongside Kylian Mbappe.
Like he has often done in big games, Mourinho asked one of his more industrious players, Silva on this occasion, to man-mark Barcelona's Pedri. Not an easy task, but it was one that minimised the Spaniard's influence.
1 of 2
Noting Barcelona's intense press and the fact that they converged towards the ball, Real's players drew opponents on to them in wide areas before exploiting space that opened up on the far side – either through impressive dribbling or long switches.
This was particularly noticeable when the ball was played from the right side of the pitch to the left flank as Marc Cucurella snuck behind Lamine Yamal.
After the match, Mourinho broke habit.
Not one to normally dwell on the tactical details of his game publicly, he decided to explain how it was the deep runs from his midfielders that Barcelona found hardest to track.
A master in using news conference as a continuation of what happens on the pitch, perhaps Mourinho revealed his methods in the hope that future opponents of Barcelona would take note.
By running into space behind Barcelona's high line, Real undid Hansi Flick's famed front-footed approach.
1 of 3
Masterminding individual wins in big games tend to garner Mourinho warranted praise, but his wider approach does not always get the recognition it probably deserves.
In recent years, coaches with more clearly defined tactics, patterns of play, or fixed positional references have been lauded as the geniuses of the sport.
Mourinho hasn't taken this approach, opting for one that leans on the quality of his players and tactics that look different depending on the club he finds himself leading.
This less fixed style is more difficult to analyse from the outside looking in, which can result in misunderstanding his work entirely.
Mourinho is a follower of tactical periodisation, a way of football thinking pioneered by Vitor Frade.
While Mourinho was working alongside Robson at Porto in the mid-1990s, Frade was also part of the coaching staff.
Pulling on threads from psychology, sociology, neuroscience, and systems theory, Frade's thinking rejected the common belief that technical, tactical, physical and psychological parts of football should be treated as separate things.
Part of the thinking behind this was that these factors were not drawn on separately in a match but instead all at once.
When Mourinho took charge of Real for this season, the Athletic reported that training sessions had become shorter but more intense, always carrying a focus on the ball.
Even getting players match fit was a job done with the ball at their feet.
In football, coaches seem to veer one of two ways.
Some look to minimise the effect of a match's chaos while others - including followers of tactical periodisation - accept and adapt to it.
Mourinho started his career as impressively as anyone, winning the Uefa Cup and Champions League with Porto, turning Chelsea into a dominant force in England, guiding Inter to a treble and then winning La Liga at Real Madrid.
But between 2019 and 2025, he took jobs at teams with more modest expectations compared to his earlier work.
Since EFL Cup and Europa League success at Manchester United in 2017, Mourinho's only trophy has been the Conference League he won in 2022 with Roma.
During that decade it was the coaches who minimised chaos that thrived.
As fans watched 'chess-like' matches, successful coaches looked to keep lots of the ball, setting their team up in predictable and symmetrical shapes with fixed player roles, such as touchline wingers or inverted full-backs.
Opponents often defended in a zonal manner, as players blocked specific areas of the pitch.
This allowed the attacking team to plan to move players into areas that gave them overloads on the pitch.
In recent seasons, there has been a rise in man-to-man pressing which has removed the ability for teams to find overloads. Pressing puts pressure on the attackers on the ball which hurries their decisions, too.
This has made games look more chaotic, which may be to Mourinho's benefit.
Students of Frade believe chaos is inseparable from the game. By training in a holistic manner, the hope is that players become better equipped to solve problems on the fly.
Perhaps this is why Mourinho's teams have typically thrived in difficult conditions, as underdogs, when the stakes have been high, or when games move away from pre-planned patterns.
Mourinho doesn't seek to control every decision his players make but instead looks to prepare them to find solutions for themselves; with better players, these solutions should, in theory, be better.
It's why, against Barcelona, we saw excellent footballers in Bellingham, Mbappe and Silva excel, all playing in their own unique style, but in a way that came together – when the stakes were highest.
Mbappe attacked the last line and finished moves. Bellingham was combative in duels and elegant on the ball to dribble past players. And Silva slowed down the game under Barcelona's press, before getting the ball to his team-mates higher up the pitch once the opposition had committed.
Mourinho embodies the sequel. He began his managerial career at Benfica, returning 25 years later in September 2025.
He won back-to-back league titles at Chelsea, before returning six years after his departure to win a third. And now, 13 years on from his first tenure at the Bernabeu, a second spell at Real Madrid.
It is fitting, then, that the changing footballing landscape might be offering him another sequel, this time in his tactical approach.

Time is brain, when it comes to the treatment of strokes. But a stroke occurring during sleep may go unnoticed until a person wakes up with symptoms, leaving doctors without a clear timeline of its onset. This is where brain imaging helps doctors identify patients with wake-up strokes and assess the extent of injury to pave the way for prompt treatment. Neurologists underscore the need to seek medical care immediately to ensure timely treatment.
M. Radha, head of department and professor of neurology, Government Kilpauk Medical College (KMC) Hospital, Chennai, said that the prevalence of wake-up strokes is 20% - one in five ischaemic strokes is a wake-up stroke. “This means a person wakes up from his/her sleep with symptoms of stroke. The symptoms include facial drooping, difficulty speaking, sudden vision problems and weakness on one side of the body,” she said.
If a patient arrives at a hospital within 4.5 hours of stroke symptoms, then thrombolysis can be done, she said, adding: “However, in wake-up stroke, we cannot calculate the time of the onset of symptoms. We do not know the window. So, acting fast is important. In case of any symptoms, patients should reach the hospital on time.”
The role of imaging
In wake-up strokes, imaging helps give a clear picture for the doctors. “An MRI brain scan should be taken immediately. If it is not available, a CT angiogram should be taken. The scans help us assess the extent of brain injury and blood flow to different parts of the brain. They can determine whether there is diffusion-perfusion mismatch. The difference may represent brain tissue that is still salvageable and can be potentially saved. Like in regular strokes, ‘time is brain’ in wake-up strokes too, making prompt diagnosis and treatment crucial,” she explained.
Shubha Subramanian, senior consultant - neurology, Kauvery Hospitals, Chennai, said that in ischemic strokes, thrombolysis is used to dissolve the blood clot if a patient presents within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. “In cases involving a large vessel occlusion, mechanical thrombectomy is performed within 24 hours of symptom onset, depending on the patient’s eligibility. In wake-up strokes, we do not know when the stroke started; it could be at night or early in the morning. What we do next is crucial. This is why we rely on imaging techniques,” she added.
“MRI has a lot of sequences. If you compare the diffusion-weighted imaging and FLAIR (Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery) imaging, a mismatch in that shows that the brain tissue is still salvageable. So even if we do not know the time of onset of stroke, we can still go ahead and thrombolyse the patient. In the same way, MRI perfusion or CT perfusion studies will also give us a clue regarding salvageable brain tissue. This will help us in taking crucial decisions regarding thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy or whether to go for conservative management,” she elaborated.
Effective coordination
Under the Tamil Nadu Accident and Emergency Care Initiative and Stroke Care and Rapid Intervention with Plasminogen activator and Thrombectomy (SCRIPT) programme implemented by the Tamil Nadu government and with facilities available at the new JICA building at KMC, patients with with wake-up strokes are regularly treated, Dr. Radha noted.
“There is effective coordination between the administration, the emergency department, radiology and neurology departments. We have a green channel in place. As a result, once the patients with symptoms of stroke enter the Emergency Department, the neurologist is intimated. Our doctor goes to the radiology department which has significantly reduced the door to needle time,” she said.
Awareness is crucial
BE FAST is the acronym to spot the warning signs of stroke, denoting Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech and Time. “We do see that the awareness of stroke symptoms is increasing and the referral system has also improved,” Dr. Radha said.
Dr. Shubha Subramanian said that in wake-up strokes, the person may not realise that he/she has symptoms of stroke when they wake up from sleep. “They may face difficulty in getting up and may also fall as a result. It is important for family members to identify the symptoms and rush for medical help,” she added.

Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
- Published
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.
"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."
The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.
Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.
In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.
But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.
UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.
The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past 
  - Published31 October 2025
Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.
Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.
Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.
The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.
In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.
The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.
The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.
On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.
The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.
But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.
They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.
"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.
Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.
"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."
That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.
The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.
Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.
According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".
In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.
He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.
Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.
The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.
After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.
Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sounded the alarm.
"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, but… the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.
However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.
They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.
Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.
Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.
The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.
Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.
By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.
The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.
Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.
They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.
Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.
In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.
In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.
"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.
Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.
On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.
It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.
On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.
It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.
The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.
"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.
Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.
The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions.
The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.
The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.
"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," Türk said.
Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.
Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.
"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.
"We liberated them," he said.
The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.
"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."
He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.
They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.
"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.
A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.
The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.

A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military’s X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image.
The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force.
The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space.
Lower-resolution views of a Chinese spaceplane showing the vehicle’s general shape were publicly available before the Defense Intelligence Agency assessment. A US Space Force official revealed Maxar’s observation at a 2024 conference in South Korea, but the Pentagon did not release the full-resolution image to the public until Monday, when it appeared in an unclassified DIA assessment of threats to the United States in space.
Catch and Release
The DIA report doesn’t reveal much new about what the Chinese spaceplane does in orbit. China has launched four spaceplane missions since 2020, with durations of up to nine months. The fourth mission is in orbit today after launching in February. It is not publicly known whether China has one or more such spaceplanes in its inventory.
The Space Force has two X-37Bs flying in rotation, with the longest of their eight missions to date running two-and-a-half years from launch until landing. US officials have released photos of the X-37B vehicles, published information about their design and dimensions, and disclosed a handful of experiments they have carried into orbit. Most of the X-37B’s activities in space are classified.
Like the X-37B, China’s spaceplane lifts off inside the payload shroud of a conventional rocket, then operates as a satellite once in orbit. The spaceplane flies like a miniature unpiloted version of NASA’s Space Shuttle and reenters the atmosphere for an autonomous land runway landing at the end of each mission. Ground teams then refurbish it for another flight.
The “enhanced maneuverability” of spaceplanes makes them “more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,” the DIA said in its report. So far, the Chinese spaceplane has only flown in low-Earth orbit (LEO) at an altitude of a few hundred miles. One of the Space Force’s X-37B flights soared to an altitude of more than 24,000 miles before using aerobraking to set up for reentry and landing.
Spaceplanes like China’s and the X-37B can also deploy small satellites from their cargo bay. Most recently, China demonstrated an ability to catch an object in orbit, perhaps using a robotic arm. The vehicle now in space released a sub-satellite in June and recaptured it in July, then did the same thing again in August and September, according to an analysis of open source orbital tracking data by Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist who catalogs spaceflight activity.
A Fleeting Glance
The official name of the Chinese spaceplane is even a mystery. It is often called Shenlong in Western publications, citing reports from the 2000s about China’s development of a robotic spaceplane. Chinese state media only refer to the vehicle as Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, or CSSHQ, which means reusable experimental spacecraft, according to a fact sheet published by the Secure World Foundation.
The DIA did not disclose the exact circumstances of Maxar’s observation of the Chinese spaceplane, such as its timing, location, or distance, but Earth observations often use cameras to view other objects in space as their orbits intersect, an emerging field known as non-Earth imaging (NEI).
NEI allows commercial operators and government analysts to inspect satellites. This is especially useful for gleaning information about classified or proprietary satellite designs, extending a new avenue for international and corporate espionage to the high frontier.
The capability exhibited by Maxar and other commercial companies in the NEI field is distinct from the recent actions of some military spacecraft, such as Russia’s Kosmos 2612, which deliberately maneuvered to approach a US-registered radar imaging satellite earlier this month. Commercial NEI observations come from chance encounters, often at extremely high speed.
Pew-Pew With DEWs
The DIA’s assessment of space threats includes an update on China’s pursuit of anti-satellite technology, or “counterspace” weapons. The intelligence agency reported the Chinese military likely considers directed-energy weapons (DEWs) “ideal counterspace systems” because they can be used to permanently or temporarily disable a satellite. One potential use for lasers in space would be to dazzle a sensor on an adversary’s satellite.
“China has multiple ground-based laser weapons with varying power levels to disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites in LEO,” the DIA said. “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”
The DIA noted China’s testing of ground-based anti-satellite missiles and the country’s historic demonstration last year of satellite refueling in geosynchronous orbit, a regime some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) over the equator, something no other country has achieved above LEO. China has also tested a robotic arm that could snag a spacecraft out of orbit, and now operates a growing fleet of satellites called TJS that routinely approach foreign spacecraft.
The US Space Force also has a constellation of inspector satellites in geosynchronous orbit and recently procured more that could be refueled, overcoming maneuverability limitations. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed last month that the Pentagon has fielded weapons in space, making the United States the first nation to acknowledge possession of orbital weapons.
Russia is pursuing its own orbital combat program, which includes an ambition to deploy a nuclear weapon in space, according to US intelligence officials.
A more conventional Russian weapons system, known as Nivelir, is designed to fire projectiles from one satellite to smash into another. The Russian military simulated an attack using the Nivelir system in 2020. In April, Russia launched a fleet of small satellites into an orbit close to a commercial radar remote sensing satellite owned by ICEYE that provides reconnaissance imagery to Ukraine. One of the Russian satellites moved within “tens of meters” of the ICEYE satellite earlier this month before backing away, US officials said.

Two arrested over fatal hit-and-run Tampines accident; man, 30, to be charged for dangerous driving
The man and his female passenger, 29, were arrested on Friday near West Coast Road, a day after the accident that killed a motorcyclist and his pillion rider, both 24.
SINGAPORE: A 30-year-old man will be charged in court on Saturday (Oct 31) with dangerous driving causing death and other traffic offences following an accident in Tampines that killed a motorcyclist and his pillion rider, both aged 24.
The accident, involving two cars and a motorcycle, occurred along Tampines Avenue 12 at about 10.35pm on Thursday, police said in a news release early on Saturday morning.
The motorcyclist and his female pillion rider were taken unconscious to hospital, where they subsequently died.
A 25-year-old woman who was driving one of the cars was also taken conscious to hospital.
Police said the 30-year-old man, who was driving the other car, did not render assistance and abandoned his vehicle before fleeing the scene with his 29-year-old female passenger.
Through extensive ground enquiries and the use of images from police cameras and closed-circuit television cameras, traffic police officers established the identities of the pair.
They were arrested on Friday in the vicinity of West Coast Road.
Preliminary investigations revealed that the man had driven a deregistered car with a cloned number plate while under disqualification, police said.
He will face nine charges, including dangerous driving causing death, dangerous driving causing hurt, and driving while under disqualification as a repeat offender.
The other charges are failing to stop after an accident, failing to render assistance, using a vehicle without insurance, using a deregistered vehicle, using a vehicle without a licence and displaying a false licence plate.
The offence of dangerous driving causing death carries a jail term of up to eight years.
Police said they take a serious view of motorists who use deregistered vehicles, drive while under disqualification or commit other serious traffic offences.
"Such reckless and irresponsible acts endanger the safety of other road users," they said, adding that they would not hesitate to take firm action against motorists who disregard traffic laws and endanger others.

Seven out of ten women in West Bengal are anaemic, according to the last figures available. The National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019–21) showed the rate to be 71.4% among women aged 15 to 49, the highest in India’s major states, as compared with 39% among men. However, when NFHS-6 released its fact sheets this year, the section on anaemia was omitted. For the first time since the late 1990s, India has a national health survey that does not include an estimate of anaemia, so it is now impossible to tell whether the situation for women in West Bengal has improved or gotten worse.
This more than a minor omission: anaemia in India is a major public health concern, of greater significance in women, since the difference between men and women when it comes to rates of anaemia is generally attributed to biology. This, however, isn’t entirely accurate.
A burden that kept rising
From 2015 to 2016, the rate of anaemia among women of reproductive age increased nationally from 53% to 57%. In West Bengal, the figure rose by approximately 9 percentage points, and for children between 6 months and 5 years, it rose from 54% to 69%. The gap appears early on: nationally, 59.1% of adolescent girls were anaemic as compared with 31.1% of boys, and this difference becomes greater as people go through their reproductive years. Within the State, the severity of anaemia is linked to disadvantage, so that in districts like Purulia and Uttar Dinajpur almost four out of five women were anaemic.
Anaemia prevalence, NFHS-5 (2019–21)
| Anaemia prevalence NFHS-5 (2019–21) | West Bengal | India | 
| Women 15–49 | 71.4% | 57.0% | 
| Men 15–49 | ~39% | 25.0% | 
| Children 6–59 months | 69.0% | 67.1% | 
Source: IIPS & ICF, NFHS-5 (2021). NFHS-6 (2026) did not report anaemia.
Not just biology
The usual explanation given in textbooks is that women lose more iron because they menstruate, carry pregnancies, and breastfeed; this is correct, but it does not explain a 30-point gap or why this gap changes so markedly across districts, castes, and wealth levels. The answer may lie in examining gender rather than biology alone.
It takes four factors to accomplish this. The first of these is time: since women’s duties, both at home and in agriculture, are mostly unpaid, they have little time for rest, for preparing iron-containing meals, or for visiting a health centre. The second is the meal pattern: in many households, food is given to men and children before it is offered to women, so that the women end up eating last and the least of the food from the kitchens that they manage. The third is social norms: it is considered a woman’s responsibility to look after people, and their own health is of secondary importance, and anaemia is regarded as a ‘women’s ailment.’ That stigma has a double effect in that about four out of every five men in West Bengal are anaemic as well, but they are almost never checked or treated. The fourth is money: women who rely financially on others are often unable to act on what they already know about diet.
An anaemia programme that ignores the gender dimension and merely distributes free iron tablets encounters all four of these obstacles and fails to alter any of them. Fieldwork carried out in Bankura in 2025 illustrates exactly what happens in practice. Pregnant and breastfeeding women discarded the fortified (with iron) rice kernels they were given, since they ‘looked like plastic’. They skipped the iron-folic acid tablets, which they did not like, and forgot their doses because of household chores no one else took on. Husbands, who are mostly engaged as migrant labourers, played almost no role in household nutrition. An improved supply chain would not remedy any of this.
The present scenario
The government has, this year, restructured the Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme. In June, the previous 6×6×6 arrangement (six target beneficiary groups, six interventions and six institutional mechanisms) was replaced by a 7×7×7 scheme which includes testing and treatment, a digital ‘T4’ tracking system and a new national centre of excellence for anaemia. On paper, these steps are the correct ones. A digital tracking system broken down by sex could finally show the problem affecting men, a factor kept out of sight because previous messaging had focused only on women.
Yet, in this same year, the country lost its standard for measurement. The official stance is that that anaemia has been omitted from NFHS-6 since blood samples taken from finger pricks are not fully reliable and may have inflated the figures, and also because India had been following the World Health Organization’s cut-offs for anaemia, which may not be suited to the local context. Instead, venous blood sampling was recommended.
All of these are valid concerns, and there is merit in them. The government had also justified dropping the anaemia reading in the NFHS-6 by stating that it would be surveyed more scientifically in the Diet and Biomarkers Survey in India (since renamed the SAMPADA survey), spearheaded by the ICMR-National Institute on Nutrition, and launched in December 2022. Venous blood samples were collected from residents across 183 districts. The problem is, that SAMPADA has not yet released any of its results, despite the survey being completed in November 2025. Until it does, there is no up-to-date national or State figure against which to assess the new programme. It is therefore impossible to verify or alter West Bengal’s status as the most severely affected of the major States, and nobody can tell whether the new framework is having the desired effect.
At present, reform and measurement have become detached from each other, even though they should be closely linked. A programme which is not measurable cannot be held responsible for its actions.
What should follow
There are three issues. The first is that the government ought to make available SAMPADA’s findings on a specific date, breaking the findings down by sex, age and State, and it should ensure that the methods used are sufficiently similar to those employed in the NFHS so that the new figures can be compared with the old ones rather than simply replacing them. An improved measure must not cause the trend to disappear.
The second point is that the new tracking system should regularly provide data by sex, and supplementation for men should be carried out in exactly the same way as it is for women. The third is that counselling and outreach activities must treat anaemia as a problem that affects the entire household, not merely as a problem of women; it is therefore necessary to reach mothers-in-law, since they are often in a position to decide who eats what, and migrant husbands should also be targeted since they are never present in the room.
India is now carrying out a more ambitious programme than before to combat anaemia, and has no current figures with which to evaluate it. Until the data is available, we are facing a problem for which records have been discontinued, and the women who are affected most may be the last to find out whether or not any change has taken place.
(Anurag Telang is a researcher in public health. dranurag225@gmail.com; Karan Babbar is an assistant professor of Economics at XLRI, Jamshedpur. phd17karanb@iima.ac.in)

US and Japan agree to establish a Japanese facility for joint missile production
CEBU, Philippines — The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief said.
It is the latest move by the allies, which have repeatedly expressed alarm over China's growing assertiveness in Asia.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi made the announcement in a news conference Wednesday night in the central Philippine province of Cebu, where he met U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual meeting of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
Koizumi renews concern over China's naval activity
Koizumi raised concern Thursday about China's increasing naval activity in southwestern Japan. He said that three Chinese destroyers and a coast guard ship together crossed the Osumi Strait south of the southern main island of Kyushu and headed east to the Pacific Ocean this week. It was the first such fleet configuration his ministry has spotted, he said.
Koizumi said he cited the incident as "an example illustrating the challenging security environment in the region" in his remark at a session Thursday. His ministry will keep watching the Chinese activity with high level of interest, he said. Japan has been accelerating military buildup in southwestern Japan to deter China.
The annual meetings aim to avert a major regional conflict and strengthen defense cooperation. On the sidelines of the meetings, however, the U.S. and China and their allies have often traded criticisms.
Japan, US to bolster joint missile production capacity
The missiles that will be produced as part of a joint effort called "Operation Supercharge" are essential for the F-35 fighter jets, Koizumi said. The two sides agreed to build a final assembly and inspection plant for the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, in Japan, he said. The U.S.-made F-35s are one of the world's most advanced aircraft and are also used by the Japanese military.
During his brief meeting with Hegseth in Cebu, Koizumi said he "shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before."
"We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means," Koizumi said.
Hegseth reassures US engagement in the region
Hegseth renewed the Trump administration's repeated assurances of commitment to help deter aggression in the region in a separate meeting on Wednesday with ASEAN defense ministers, who were led by the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. Like Koizumi, Hegseth did not mention China by name in expressing his security concerns in the region.
"The approach we're taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear," Hegseth told the ASEAN defense chiefs. "Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves."
His message is "clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners," Hegseth said.
Hegseth has assured the Philippines, the oldest treaty ally of Washington in Asia, that the Trump administration will build a robust deterrence against China's increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea. Beijing claims the busy waterway, a key global trade route, virtually in its entirety.
Australia shows commitment to defend the rule of law in the Pacific
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said his country's forces, along with allies like the U.S., will press on with efforts to defend the rule of law despite China's increasing assertiveness, including in the South China Sea. Australia protested last year after a Chinese J-16 fighter aircraft released flares and passed within 30 meters (100 feet) of an Australian P-8 Poseidon surveillance jet over the disputed waters.
"That doesn't deter us from doing what we need to do and that's essentially asserting the rules-based order here in the end of the Pacific," Marles told The Associated Press in Cebu on Wednesday. "Freedom of navigation on the high seas is profoundly important for Australia."
The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, all ASEAN member states, along with Taiwan, also have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. Confrontations have particularly escalated between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and navy vessels in disputed shoals and outlying waters.
Washington has warned that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships and aircraft come under an armed attack, including in the South China Sea.
Beijing and Tokyo have a separate dispute over tiny Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea, with both sides often accusing the other of infringing on their maritime territory.

Hackers stole approximately $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency from wallets held at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, in what investigators have described as the biggest crypto heist on record. Blockchain analysis firms have attributed the attack to North Korea's elite hacking unit, while Binance has said it will cover all losses and that user funds are safe.
The attack involved the movement of funds across 10 blockchains, with most of the cryptocurrency transferred in about 20 minutes, according to US blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs. As cryptocurrency firms raced to trace and recover the stolen assets, about $3 billion had been frozen by Thursday night in the US, CNN reported.
Binance CEO Richard Teng has since said the attack was more complex than initially described, adding that the exchange has found no evidence of a wallet private key leak.
What happened in the Binance hack?
TRM Labs said an attacker moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets across 10 blockchains.
"An attacker moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said in a blog post.
Binance's initial investigation indicated that the breach involved an engineer's laptop, which allegedly allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.
However, Teng subsequently said the attack was not a simple case of an attacker exploiting one employee's access. "The attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action," Teng said, according to Reuters, adding that it was a more "complicated attack process".
Teng also said the investigation had not attributed responsibility to any individual. The exchange has found no evidence so far that a wallet private key was leaked.
The exchange also said it had "temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed; revoked the affected address authorization; [and] engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds".
Binance said it was working closely with law enforcement to ensure the matter was handled appropriately. Changpeng Zhao, Binance's co-founder and former CEO, also said he expected user funds to be fully covered by the exchange. Zhao, who stepped down as CEO in 2023 but remains its largest shareholder, said on X that the incident appeared to be a hack.
Hackers from North Korea?
TRM Labs attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit, saying its assessment was based on intelligence gathered both on and off the blockchain.
"TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea's elite hacking unit, based on robust on and off-chain intelligence. We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said, as quoted by Reuters.
Other blockchain intelligence firms have also pointed to North Korea. Singapore-based Pangolin Intelligence said its assessment followed an analysis of transactions associated with the hack and comparisons with previous incidents involving the North Korean cyber unit.
"Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]" led to the attribution, an analyst with Pangolin Intelligence told CNN.
Chainalysis, another cryptocurrency-tracing firm, said it was monitoring the stolen funds as they moved across multiple blockchains, including Bitcoin and Ethereum. A Chainalysis spokesperson told CNN the firm had "high confidence" North Korea was behind the attack.
However, the attribution remains an assessment by private intelligence firms and has not been independently established as a confirmed finding by law enforcement.
North Korean hacking groups have repeatedly been accused of stealing cryptocurrency and targeting financial institutions. Current and former US and South Korean officials have described cybercrime as a key source of revenue for the sanctions-hit country.
In February 2025, North Korean hackers were blamed for an alleged $1.5 billion theft from Bybit, another major cryptocurrency exchange. That incident had set the previous record for the largest crypto heist.
North Korean hackers have stolen billions of dollars from banks and cryptocurrency firms over several years, according to reports from the United Nations and private companies.
A 2023 CNN investigation also highlighted efforts by South Korean intelligence officials and private cryptocurrency-tracking experts to seize about $1 million in cryptocurrency stolen by North Koreans from a victim.
Why are cryptocurrency exchanges vulnerable?
Unlike platforms for trading stocks, cryptocurrency exchanges often hold digital assets on behalf of their users. This can make them attractive targets for hackers seeking to steal large amounts of cryptocurrency, particularly in an industry where regulatory oversight varies.
Binance was co-founded in 2017 by Canadian national Changpeng Zhao and became the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform within a year of its launch.
Zhao stepped down as CEO in 2023 after pleading guilty to violating anti-money laundering laws in the US. He was sentenced to four months in federal prison and was pardoned by President Donald Trump in October 2025.
What happens next?
Binance has pledged to cover all losses resulting from the incident using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds.
"Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and company funds," the exchange said, according to Reuters. Teng reiterated the commitment, saying the company was "covering every loss".
In its earlier statement also, Binance said it would "cover all losses" from company funds and its emergency assets fund, adding that "user funds are safe".
Meanwhile, Cryptocurrency firms are continuing to trace the stolen funds and attempt to prevent the attackers from converting or moving the assets beyond recovery.
A Pangolin Intelligence analyst told CNN that the effort to track the stolen cryptocurrency was still in its early stages. "I think the cat and mouse game has barely begun yet," the analyst said, adding that North Korea was likely poised to tap a network of money-laundering organisations to cash out the stolen funds.
The recovery effort will depend on how much of the cryptocurrency can be traced and frozen before it is moved through other wallets or converted into assets that are harder to recover.
Bitcoin and Ether, the two most widely traded cryptocurrencies, fell following news of the Binance breach but recovered some losses. They were trading about 2 per cent to 3 per cent lower by midday Friday in Hong Kong.

Fan fiction website AO3 is down, and it could take weeks to recover
The site's data is reportedly intact, but the cause of the outage is still unknown.
Archive of Our Own (AO3), one of the best-known homes for people who read and write fan fiction online, is currently down for maintenance. The Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit that founded AO3, took the site offline just after 3AM ET and originally planned to keep it down for only 12 hours, per its status page, but now says maintenance could take weeks.
"We estimate that service restoration for #AO3 will take around 2 weeks but it could be up to 4 weeks," the OTW says. "We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved. Please stay tuned for further info."
AO3 hosts millions of transformative fanworks based on existing books, movies, TV shows and more, and likely serves millions more readers who want to read stories about their favorite characters and worlds. The OTW has said the site's data is intact, according to a former AO3 volunteer who moderates r/AO3, which should mean those stories are safe. What's less clear is what caused this lengthy outage.
The OTW logged problems with email notifications, search, history and listings between October 23 and 24, but hasn't elaborated on what issues it's dealing with now. In the last two weeks, two major security vulnerabilities, one found in the PHP scripting language and another found in TLS certificates, have forced some websites to go offline to patch and protect themselves. That includes another OTW site, Fanlore, which was briefly shut down to deal with the PHP flaw. The nonprofit hasn't given any indication it's dealing with those same problems on AO3. Whatever the cause, though, the OTW's engineers are volunteers rather than paid staff, which might make fixes take longer to implement.
Engadget asked the OTW to comment on the outage and share what maintenance work is being done. We'll update this article if we hear back.

A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.
The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.
“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”
The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.
The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)
Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.
Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”
The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.
“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”
According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.
“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”

Kauvery Hospital, Alwarpet, Chennai, has treated a 63-year-old man with severe leakage in his aortic valve using a minimally invasive procedure called transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), the hospital said at a press conference. The patient had a hole in one of the leaflets of his aortic valve and had previously undergone mitral valve replacement.
Aortic regurgitation occurs when the aortic valve does not close properly, allowing blood to flow backwards into the heart. Treating this condition through a catheter-based procedure can be challenging because the valve may not have enough calcium deposits to help secure the replacement valve. The patient’s previous mitral valve replacement added to the complexity.
The HANCHOR valve has a frame that expands with a balloon and a special anchoring mechanism made of nitinol, a flexible metal alloy. This mechanism is designed to hold the replacement valve securely in place by gripping the existing valve leaflets.
The hospital said checks after the procedure showed no remaining leakage through or around the replacement valve and no abnormal narrowing. No significant problems with the heart’s electrical signals were reported. The patient was discharged three days later.
Rajaram Anantharaman, senior consultant interventional cardiologist said the valve’s anchoring mechanism helped address the challenges of positioning the replacement valve in this case.
Asik Ali, senior consultant and clinical lead, Cardiac Imaging Radiology; Mahesh Kumar K., medical superintendent; and Kamal Kanth, consultant cardiologist, were also present at the press conference.
