In a breakthrough for Jamia Millia Islamia (JMI) students, the university on Thursday set May 15, 2027, as the deadline to approve and implement the student union constitution, while appealing to protesting students to call off their agitation. ANI, citing an order issued by the university administration on Thursday, reported that elections will be held within six weeks of the commencement of the next academic session. Following the order, the students called off their protests. The order read, “The approval and implementation of the Jamia Millia Islamia Students’ Union Constitution shall be completed by 15th May, 2027.” The development comes after a prolonged protest began on October 12, with students demanding the restoration of the Jamia Millia Islamia Students’ Union (JMISU), which was dissolved in 2006. The students had also been seeking the announcement of a definite timeline for student union elections. The JMISU was dissolved following recurrent incidents of violent clashes, attacks on teachers and the occasional disruption of classes during that period. The administration also claimed that student representatives had begun interfering in administrative matters and that the union’s activities were affecting the academic environment. On Tuesday, the protest entered its 16th day, with students continuing their hunger strike and demonstrations despite the university announcing that student union elections would be held within 15 days of the union's constitution being approved. Since October 24, the university has also shifted classes online amid tensions linked to the protests, Indian Express reported on Tuesday, with the order extending the arrangement until November 8. The university announced that online classes would continue for all courses, while second mid-term semester examinations would also be conducted online. Tensions further escalated on Monday after scuffles broke out between protesters and paramilitary personnel amid heightened security around the campus. It further stated that after the approval of the constitution, the university would issue a notification to hold elections in accordance with the recommendations and guidelines of the Lyngdoh Committee on student union regulations. The order stated, “The elections shall be conducted within 6 weeks of the start of the academic session, that is, approximately within 6 weeks from 16 July 2027.” On December 12, 2005, the Supreme Court directed the Ministry of Human Resource Development to set up an expert committee, The Hindu reported, adding that the court wanted to examine violence, money and political interference in campus politics. The Lyngdoh Committee recommended that universities and colleges should generally elect their student representatives. Nominations may be used only as a temporary measure when conditions on campus do not permit free and fair polls. Such institutions were expected to establish an election-based system within five years. It allowed institutions to adopt direct, indirect, or hybrid election models. The panel favoured direct polls for smaller, single-campus universities, while suggesting an indirect system for large universities with multiple campuses. Student elections should be held annually, between six and eight weeks after the academic session begins. The entire process, from filing nominations to declaring results, including campaigning, should be completed within 10 days. Most people worldwide could be categorised as having a high genetic risk for three of 28 common conditions, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease and schizophrenia, even if they might not develop them, a new study has found.
Researchers, led by the UK's University of Exeter, described the 'average' human genome, finding that everyone, regardless of their current health status, could be considered at risk for numerous conditions based on their genetics alone.
Every person's genome, or the average human genome, contains around five million variants, or DNA locations that differ between individuals, the findings published in the journal Genome Medicine reveal.
The locations include around 10,000 variants that alter gene sequences, which can have positive or negative effect, ranging from lactose intolerance to drug response, though are often biologically neutral, they show.
Each person also carries between one and three rare variants previously shown to cause serious genetic diseases, and another 50 rare variants that are currently of uncertain clinical relevance, the researchers found.
The team analysed data from two major population biobanks -- the UK Biobank and the US' All of Us -- that include whole genome sequencing, covering nearly one million individuals.
Senior author Caroline Wright, from the University of Exeter, said, "Whole genome sequencing has become such an important tool in diagnosing genetic disease, and we're increasingly moving towards genetic screening for predicting disease."
"Yet most people are unaware of just how much genetic variation is present in every genome. Actually, variation is the norm. For the first time, our study outlines what to expect in the average human genome, which can benefit clinicians and patients across the word in understanding, interpreting and contextualising genomics," Wright said.
The researchers also analysed numerous polygenic risk scores, which consider all known genetic factors to calculate a person's future risk of developing a disease.
"... applying polygenic scores (PGS) for 28 common diseases within UKB (UK Biobank), we estimate that the average person is in the top 10 per cent for (nearly) three conditions, and around one in five people are in the top one per cent for at least one PGS," the authors wrote.
"Importantly, we found that everyone carries a small number of genetic variants linked to disease, although many of these will not actually cause disease in that individual," Wright said.
The senior author added, "It is therefore crucial to consider context when interpreting findings from genetic testing, including symptoms or family history of disease as well as other clinical and environmental risk factors. Our findings also provide important context for professionals who are interpreting genetic testing results or commissioning genetic screening programmes."
Although the studies are large, participation is skewed towards people of Western European origin, and the researchers acknowledged the need for data from more diverse populations to further improve understanding and impact.

During an hourlong earnings call last night, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time talking about the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than he did hyping the company’s still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions.
Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
RJ Scaringe spent nearly half of Rivian’s earnings call hyping self-driving tech. But taking on Tesla’s FSD with custom chips and pricey lidar is an enormous gamble while the mass-market R2 is still scaling up.
But the company faces a crucial test later this year, when it rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature — first to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026, and later to customers in 2027. Following that, Rivian says it will launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber in 2028. In short, the next two years will determine whether Rivian will succeed or fail in its high-stakes quest to become a full-stack autonomy player.
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator,” Derek Mulvey, VP for finance, said during the call.
Success is not guaranteed. Tesla has a huge head start with its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in over 1.7 million active customer cars. But trying to match Tesla’s driver-assist features — while simultaneously designing its own silicon chips, buying pricey sensors, and paying for massive AI computing power — is a huge financial gamble, especially while Rivian is still struggling to build and sell its mass-market R2 vehicles at scale. (The R2 recently became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle by volume, so progress continues.)
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator.”
— Derek Mulvey
But it’s unclear whether Rivian sees the R2 as its make-or-break vehicle or if solving autonomy will be the true decider. That leaves the company in the middle of a difficult balancing act: launching an ambitious, mass-market electric vehicle while simultaneously reinventing itself as a full-stack autonomous driving powerhouse.
Of course, the feature itself needs to work for Rivian to succeed. During the call, Scaringe revealed that he has been using the new point-to-point driving system in his own commute to the office every day, calling it “a wonderful” experience. He continued:
So, our view is that that is going to become a big driver of demand. And I think it’s unclear how quickly the whole — you know, the whole US market and the whole automotive market — starts to shift to really wanting this, and this being a major purchase criterion. But certainly, we’re at the front end of an inflection point where it’s more and more people exposed to what this could do… We do think it’s a really big driver, in the long term, for market share for us.
But Scaringe was cagey about other details. When asked about Rivian’s take rate for its Autonomy Plus package — in other words, what percentage of Rivian buyers who purchase or subscribe to the software out of the total customer base — the chief executive declined to share the exact number. “The take rate on Autonomy Plus has exceeded our expectations,” he said, “and we’re quite encouraged by it.”
Rivian’s execs are no doubt envious of Tesla’s take rates for FSD: Over 75 percent of new Tesla buyers in North America opted to get FSD in the third quarter of 2026, the company recently reported. Meanwhile, Rivian reported $605 million in revenue from software and subscription services in Q3 2026, a 45 percent increase year over year. And Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin.
Rivian will likely spend more money than it brings in as it keeps buying expensive computers and AI systems. On the call, the company pointed out that computer chips, memory, and electronics are getting pricier. It also warned that adding two processors and costly lidar sensors to some R2 models could eat into the profits it hoped to make by building the vehicle in large numbers.
The point-to-point system will face its own hurdles, including edge cases and the complexities of urban driving. A vehicle crash could damage Rivian’s brand and reputation, just as Tesla has experienced many times with FSD. And even though Rivian intends to roll out the feature to require active driver supervision, the company will likely face legal challenges when things inevitably go wrong.
To be sure, Rivian couldn’t afford to sit on the sidelines and concede the autonomous crown to Tesla and Waymo. Self-driving tech could help Rivian post big, software-company-style profits, but paying for expensive AI development while also trying to build the R2 at scale makes the next year or two its riskiest period ever.

Arteta warns Dowman 'we are not in Disneyland' after red card
- Published
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has told Max Dowman "we are not in Disneyland" and that he intends to hold the teenager to the same standards as other first-team players.
Dowman, 16, was sent off in the 85th minute of Arsenal's penalty shoot-out loss to Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday after reacting to a heavy challenge by Harrison Neal and will serve a three-match ban.
A visibly annoyed Arteta spoke to Dowman as the teenager left the pitch, and on Friday spoke about the incident for the first time, saying he warned the attacker before the game about dealing with provocation.
"I haven't seen the reaction to my reaction, whether it is positive or negative. But you need to understand the context and the relationship that I have with him and what we discussed just before we went out," Arteta said of his words to Dowman.
"But, I don't know. You can have another reaction. If you see the reaction of my father and my mother with me some days you might say 'I don't like the reaction'. For me, it was the best reaction to be who I am."
Arteta revealed that he had spoken to Dowman on Thursday and said there were "no issues at all" between the pair. However, he added that he needs to be "very straight" with Dowman and clear of the standards expected.
Dowman was sent off for the England U19s earlier this month where he was also on the end of heavy challenges in a match with the United States.
Of that red card, Arteta said: "They are his age. They are 16 – the same. What is the reaction? That is the level and that is the reaction.
"And whether it is right or wrong, that is the reaction."
Arteta also spoke of the impact the red card had on the team, saying: "And the reaction when I don't win, you want to know what my reaction is? I am [angry] big time.
"So, we need to be ready for that. This is the environment and this is the reality, otherwise we are in Disneyland. We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League and this level.
"We look after him so much that you cannot imagine.
"But at the same time we are going to demand from him, like everybody else, because he needs to earn the right to play. Because the other boys, what are they going to tell me? You need to be fair."
The Gunners did appeal against the red card but the Football Association (FA) upheld the decision. Of that, Arteta said he was "very disappointed", adding "we are lucky today that he (Dowman) hasn't had a broken foot."

The Pentagon inspector general’s office declined a request from US senators to investigate restrictions recently imposed on the Ukraine military’s use of SpaceX’s satellite network.
Ukraine, which uses SpaceX’s Starlink service and the military version known as Starshield, said earlier this month that military drones lost satellite connectivity when traveling above 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour). The limit was removed after about 10 days.
Five Democratic and four Republican senators sent an October 15 letter to Department of Defense Inspector General Platte Moring, asking for a probe into the reported disruptions of Starlink and Starshield. The letter asked, among other things, “whether any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield services were directed, authorized, or implemented by SpaceX, the Department of Defense, or other US government entities; whether such restrictions were consistent with applicable US government contracts, and what actions, if any, the Department of Defense took in response.”
Platte told the senators in a letter Tuesday that the questions should be directed to the US Air Force and Space Force, according to CNN. “They are better suited to address the matters raised in your letter and to coordinate any Department responses to your questions,” Moring wrote.
A spokesperson for the Pentagon inspector general’s office told Ars today, “The Department of War Office of Inspector General (The DoW OIG) answered recent correspondence from members of Congress regarding Starlink… We carefully considered the congressional request and determined that the matters raised were best addressed by the DOW. Should new information come to light, we may reconsider.”
We asked the Department of Defense whether it plans to investigate and will update this article if it responds.

How talking about Man Utd's cycle of doom became an industry
- Published
Manchester United. More a high-volume content farm than a football club these days.
Michael Carrick's starring role in what has become one of the nation's favourite soap operas has been extended for at least another week, with the 45-year-old set to be in charge for Saturday's visit to Chelsea.
Good news - you'd think - for Carrick. But even better news for Amazon's All or Nothing camera crews, who have been given "unprecedented" access to document the behind-the-scenes goings-on at Old Trafford this season.
United fans will presumably be relieved when the football resumes on Saturday, if only to break up the constant stream of opinion for 90 minutes.
But while the wall-to-wall reporting of one of the world's biggest football clubs is hardly new, the unrelenting coverage from former players is a growing phenomenon.
It is easier to name the Manchester United legends who don't have a platform from which they scrutinise the club's every move than those that do - and it begs the question whether the club's demise has been industrialised into a content-creating machine.
'It doesn't really help in any way'
Whether supporters feel comments from ex-players are damaging or not differs from fan to fan, but what cannot be denied is how difficult it is to escape their views.
Sky Sports pundit Gary Neville provided scathing on-air commentary during United's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth last Sunday, before conducting a post-match podcast in the Old Trafford gantry in which he accused some of their players of being unprofessional.
"There's a couple of them... I live in Manchester and they're not that professional, some of them," Neville stated.
"I've got no time for them. There's a few of them that don't go to bed at the right time. Don't eat the right things. Don't think about Manchester United every single minute of every single day."
But it's digital and streaming platforms that are re-defining a new age of analysis.
Neville launched The Overlap in 2021, and its success across video and podcast platforms has seen the channel become one of the most influential outlets in sports media.
On Tuesday, Wayne Rooney appeared on Neville's Manchester United-dedicated YouTube channel 'Stick to United' where he said Carrick's players "need a firework up their a***".
Neville has since hosted his own The Overlap show where he said managers sometimes need to be sacked "for their own good", while ex-United captain Roy Keane said Carrick and his backroom staff are "lucky boys" to still be in jobs.
Neville acquired a network of YouTube channels from United influencer Mark Goldbridge last summer, which has significantly increased the channel's coverage of the club.
Largely known for viral clips of his expletive-laden rants during streamed 'watchalongs' of their matches, Goldbridge's YouTube channels had amassed more than 3.7million subscribers.
Goldbridge - whose real name is Brent di Cesare - now co-hosts the 'Stick to United' show with Rooney, the club's record goalscorer.
But Neville, Rooney and Keane are far from the only ones setting the agenda.
Class of '92 pair Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt co-host their own podcast called 'The Good, The Bad & The Football'.
Before last season's Manchester derby at Old Trafford - Carrick's first home game in charge - Butt said City striker Erling Haaland would "pick Lisandro Martinez up and run with him", while Scholes said the Norway forward would "throw him in the net" after scoring.
United won the game 2-0, with Martinez putting in a stellar performance.
Asked about Scholes' comments after the match, the Argentine defender said: "Honestly, he can say whatever he wants. I told him already, if he wants to say something to me, he can come to wherever he wants. To my house, wherever. I don't care."
Asked during Thursday's news conference how he deals with the 'noise' from former team-mates and ex-players, Carrick said he avoids it as best he can.
"I don't see it really. I see the things that I need to see," he added.
"I don't look for it - it doesn't really help in any way.
"I've said it before, I care about what the supporters think. I care about what it feels like in the stadium, and them travelling to games for us, to come and see us and support us. I care about what we give them, and what we offer them, and what they see. I genuinely don't take any notice of anything else."

  - Published19 hours ago
'Unhelpful' or standard-bearers?
Where once a low rating in a newspaper could anger players, they now have to deal with days of debate after a bad result or below-par performance.
Former manager Erik ten Hag recently alluded to the difficulty his Manchester United squad had dealing with the opinions of people like Neville and Rio Ferdinand, and said former players could be "more helpful" to the club.
"I did nice interviews with them both [Neville and Ferdinand], so it didn't hurt me. Of course, they have podcasts, they have their models," Ten Hag told The Athletic, external.
"Sometimes it's difficult for players. Some of them get affected by it, get annoyed by it.
"They achieved massive successes. But also, they can help the club more, help the players more. There should be two ways that they support it. But I think always the thing you most love, you most criticise."
It is a point Neville agrees with.
Speaking on Ferdinand's podcast, external last summer, it was put to Neville he had been overly critical when covering his boyhood club.
"It's a balance though Rio, isn't it?" he told his former United team-mate.
"It's like, do I want [Manchester] City to win the league? I absolutely don't want City anywhere near the league title."
And he insisted "United are the hardest games I do".
"People might think that I'm more critical of United when they don't play well. Sometimes, over the last maybe 10 years, the balance, maybe I've not got it right," admitted Neville.
But, having won 18 major honours in 19 years at Old Trafford, few are better placed to judge the club than Neville.
"There was a banner in the first half [against Bournemouth] that was held up in the Stretford End - 'standards'. They went a long time ago," he said last Sunday.
Like Neville, Butt also came through United's academy and said former players have the club's best interests at heart.
"When it goes bad, you can't cry and go, 'Oh, they're [ex-players] having a go at us'," explained Butt back in January.
"We love the football club. I've been a Manchester United fan since the age of six or seven, as long as I can remember. I'm not saying it to go, 'Let's stab everybody in the back'. I'm saying it because it is genuinely c**p."
'Hated, adored, never ignored'
While the club would rather be awash with positivity, negative coverage is consumed by a wider base that more regularly includes non-Manchester United fans.
It's difficult to apply a value to the club's popularity but United have remained one of the highest-grossing football clubs in world football since last winning the Premier League in 2013.
Much of their off-field success has been underscored by industry-leading commercial deals, as well as strong matchday revenue. Only Arsenal made more money from matchday revenue last season in the Premier League.
Former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward angered supporters in 2018 when he said: "Playing performance doesn't really have a meaningful impact on what we can do on the commercial side of the business."
Being a constant source of attention is something that the club and supporters have regularly boasted about, too.
The 'hated, adored, never ignored' mantra regularly appears on banners at Old Trafford, while the club even released a clothing range that adorned the slogan.
It's fair to say, then, that the club are as guilty as anyone in capitalising on their global fame and ability to grab headlines.

Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on US military aid decision
- Published
A top Democratic senator has blamed a crackdown on independent journalism in Egypt on a decision by the Trump administration to waive human rights conditions on US military funding to the country.
Chris Murphy, who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, accused the US government of "abandoning" the Egyptian people after it lifted restrictions relating to more than $300m of defence assistance.
Over the last month a series of arrests has taken place of journalists at two of the few remaining independent news outlets in Egypt, where newspapers and TV stations are closely controlled by the authorities.
The US State Department told the BBC it waived conditions on a portion of military aid to Egypt in September due to the country's "importance to US national security interests".
Murphy, speaking at the Middle East Institute (MEI) in Washington this week, said he was in no doubt the two were linked.
"The minute that money was released, the crackdown began in an absolutely devastating way," he said.
On Tuesday a court in Cairo ordered the closure of the news website Madr Masa and fined its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah in what Amnesty International called "a crushing blow to press freedom".
Earlier this month, authorities arrested six journalists at the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh and charged them with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The Egyptian Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

Cairo has remained a close regional ally of the US despite what human rights groups say are widespread abuses under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's government, including torture and enforced disappearances.
Sisi denies there are political prisoners in Egypt. He has previously said stability and security are paramount, adding authorities have promoted rights by trying to provide basic needs such as jobs and housing.
Washington sends Egypt £1.3bn ($1.73bn) per year, making it one of the world's biggest recipients of US military assistance.
US law allows up to £320m of the funding to be withheld, conditioned on Egypt meeting democracy and human rights requirements. But these restrictions can be waived by the administration on national security grounds.
In September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio waived human rights conditions on $320m of military aid in light of Egypt's role since the launch of the US war with Iran, according to a letter addressed to various Congressional committees. Egypt assisted negotiations between the US and Iran.
Exercising the waiver authority was "essential" for the US-Egypt relationship, "particularly in light of Egypt's helpful role following Operation Epic Fury," according to the September 4 memo seen by Reuters which bore Rubio's signature.
Asked by the BBC about the move in light of this month's arrests of journalists, the State Department said the waiver was "due to Egypt's importance to US national security interests, the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States, and the need to maintain that cooperation to address regional security challenges".
It added it maintained dialogue with Cairo on a "full range of issues" but would "not comment on private diplomatic conversations".
Rubio's move followed a similar decision by the Biden administration in 2024, when then Secretary of State Anthony Blinken waived human rights conditions to grant the full military aid allocation to Egypt as the US sought Cairo's role in mediating between Israel and Hamas in the war in Gaza.
Under Biden prior to 2024, the US withheld portions of the annual military allocation over Egypt's human rights record.
Murphy, who chairs a congressional committee on the Middle East and counterterrorism, said he had been a critic of both the Biden and Trump administrations over the issue.
"To the extent that there was any glimmer left of political speech in Egypt, it is gone for one proximate reason: The United States government abandoned the people of Egypt and decided to remove all conditions on our funding," Murphy told the MEI.
"Any hope of a true, meaningful political opposition rebirthing in Egypt has been shattered by this decision," he added.
US military aid to Cairo began after the 1978 Camp David Accords and the peace treaty that followed between Egypt and Israel. Successive administrations have viewed the world's most populous Arab country as a critical US ally in the region.
The group Reporters Without Borders describes Egypt, external as one of the world's biggest jailers of journalists.
The conviction of Lina Attalah and the closure of Madr Masr marked an unprecedented escalation in repression of press freedoms in Egypt, according to Timothy E Kaldas, Deputy Director of The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, a Washington DC-based think tank.
He said both the US and European Union had been prioritising their strategic relations with Egypt over human rights and the rule of law in the country.
"It's been fostering a sense of impunity on the part of the Egyptian authorities that we're seeing play out," he told the BBC.
"Egypt is getting signals from both sides of the Atlantic that human rights and the rule of law are no longer a priority, and they're testing the limits of that."
He added: "The fact that they're not getting more robust pushback reinforces the wrong message."

Reddit will force users to log in as AI is killing search traffic
The company is starting with tests outside of the US.
Reddit will no longer allow logged out users or those without an account to view content on its platform, CEO Steve Huffman shared in an update. The change, which the company said will initially be tested in "select markets" outside the US, comes as the company says that search traffic has declined significantly.
"A key piece of work to retain new audiences is shifting Reddit to a logged-in-only experience," Huffman wrote in a shareholder letter. "Moving to primarily logged-in will ensure our users have the best Reddit experience possible, and can find the content and communities most relevant to them."
The change is the most dramatic shift the company has made as it battles AI scraping and changes to internet search. It will also likely rattle users, some of whom are already frustrated with recent moves like restrictions on Old Reddit. Huffman said that it was a "big change" but necessary for the company.
"It is better for our business because we will have more signals for ads targeting, and being logged-in leads to higher engagement generally," he wrote. "It also allows us to protect access to Reddit's extremely valuable corpus of data, and helps us better adapt to emerging regulations around the world."
Huffman didn't explicitly mention age verification laws, but requiring users to log in would presumably help the company comply with such measures.
Huffman said the company is still working on figuring out exactly when logged out users will encounter a "hard prompt" to log in. "We need to find the right boundary," he said during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "Whether they're coming from a shared link or maybe from search ... there'll be some version of Reddit accessible for those moments before we do that hard prompt."
Reddit's CEO, who has been clearly frustrated with the state of online search and Google's AI overviews for a while, was more explicit in his criticism. "The reality is, the AI mode does not drive traffic, not for us and not to anybody, as far as I know," he said. "So that's just a fundamental shift in how Google works. It used to be a traffic driver, now it's not."
The company reported that search traffic was "down meaningfully" in the most recent quarter, with the company seeing referrals from search drop by more than 1 million each week during the month of October.
Reddit's relationship with Google is also complicated. The company has a licensing deal with the search giant so it can access the platform's data for AI training. That deal is reportedly worth about $60 million a year. More recently, there are reports that Reddit may be reconsidering this arrangement. When asked about it on the call, Huffman said there are "active discussions" but didn't share specifics. "What's most important is that any deal we do needs to advance our long-term strategy, it has to be a fair exchange of value," he said.
Huffman hinted at some other product changes the company is considering to help it grow engagement with logged in users. The Reddit founder said the company is working on adding "more organization" to its main feed to make it "more consistent" and "less grab bag-ey" than it currently is.
He also suggested that an "incognito mode" could be in the works. He speculated that adding "private browsing" could help the company address users who repeatedly uninstall and reinstall the Reddit app.

French prosecutor seeks pretrial detention for suspect in shooting near Paris
France’s national counterterrorism prosecutor has asked for a 39-year-old suspect to be held in pretrial detention over a suspected racist attack in the Paris suburbs
PARIS -- France’s national counterterrorism prosecutor asked Thursday that a 39-year-old suspect be held in pretrial detention over a shooting in the Paris suburbs that killed one person and wounded seven others, saying he targeted people he believed to be Muslim or from Africa.
The suspect, a 39-year-old French national identified by authorities as Kevin T., was arrested less than 20 minutes after the shooting began Friday in Trappes and neighboring La Verrière, a suburban area west of Paris. His last name has not been made public.
An 11-year-old girl was among the injured when a gunman fired from his vehicle at several locations along a 12-kilometer (7.5-mile) route.
The suspect “now acknowledged that the acts were premeditated,” national counterterrorism prosecutor Olivier Christen said. The suspect admitted to “specifically targeting” people he believed to be Muslim or from sub-Saharan Africa or North Africa based on their appearance, Christen said.
Christen added that the suspect said he chose the suburb of Trappes because it is “a haven for Islamists.”
He denied any terrorist intent and said “he had no regrets,” Christen added.
A judicial investigation has been opened into murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, with the aggravating circumstance that the crimes were committed because of the victims’ actual or perceived race, ethnicity, nationality or religion.
Authorities identified the man killed as Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old Black French national. Four other people were seriously wounded, including one who remained Thursday in life-threatening condition. Three others suffered lighter injuries. Authorities have not disclosed details about the identities of those injured.
Christen said the suspect has a history of psychological and psychiatric problems and of drug addiction. Toxicology tests revealed the presence of cannabis and cocaine in his blood, as well as drugs prescribed by a doctor.
A search of his car uncovered a Sten-type submachine gun and investigators found his apartment had been booby-trapped with three gas cylinders and electrical wires connected to a timer.
Investigations have shown he bought several firearm parts last month, Christen said. Two days before the shooting, he deleted all his social media accounts, sold his laptop computer and concealed his phone, but police managed to find it.
Investigators also found Adolf Hitler’s manifesto “Mein Kampf” as well as stickers stored in a drawer with inscriptions including “Long live France," “Proud to be French,” and “RN,” the French acronym for far-right party National Rally.
The suspect told investigators he had himself designed and ordered the stickers. The suspect said he was neither a member nor a supporter of any political party, Christen said.

OfBusiness is heading for the stock market with a business that earns most of its revenue in one place and most of its profits in another. Commerce, which spans raw-material trading, manufacturing and apparel, brings in almost all its sales. Yet its lending business, led by Oxyzo, contributes more than half its segment profits despite being a fraction of commerce’s size. Ahead of the IPO, the question is whether commerce can earn more from its scale, or whether lending will keep carrying the profits. The startup began its journey by helping small and medium enterprises buy raw materials and access working capital. Over the past decade, it has gone from sourcing steel and chemicals for manufacturers to making some of those products itself, expanding into apparel and building a sizable lending business through Oxyzo. Along the way, it has achieved something relatively rare in India’s B2B commerce sector. Not only has OfBusiness built a ₹20,000 Cr-plus profitable business, but both the company and its lending arm Oxyzo have independently achieved unicorn status. That’s a notable contrast with B2B commerce peers such as Udaan, Moglix and Zetwerk, which have struggled with losses. Infra.Market is another exception, having reported ₹220 Cr in net profit on ₹18,472 Cr in revenue in FY25. But as the company prepares for its stock market debut, its FY26 financials reveal an interesting shift. Consolidated operating revenue declined nearly 8% year on year, even as net profit climbed 21% to ₹724 Cr. More importantly, the business responsible for almost all its revenue isn’t the one contributing the most to its profits. Commerce, which includes raw-material trading and manufacturing, generated 93% of OfBusiness’ ₹20,472 Cr consolidated operating revenue in FY26. Yet financial services, led by Oxyzo, accounted for more than half its segment pre-tax profits. The lending-led business generated ₹505 Cr in profit before tax, compared with ₹422 Cr from commerce. The imbalance raises a larger question. Can OfBusiness improve the returns on its commerce business while using lending and technology to earn more from each SME relationship? The answer lies in how its procurement, manufacturing, customer-discovery and financing operations work together. Here’s how the business makes money, and where its economics are changing. The Commerce Engine Is Changing OfBusiness’ commerce business runs on three layers: raw-material trading, manufacturing and finished goods. Trading brings scale, manufacturing helps improve margins, and finished goods open up new markets. The first layer is straightforward. OfBusiness aggregates demand from manufacturers, sources materials and manages pricing, quality and delivery. More than 12,000 SMEs and emerging corporates transacted on OfCommerce in FY26, across a catalogue of 103 products. Its business-discovery platforms help build the pipeline: BidAssist matches companies with government tenders. It had crossed 1.3 Mn subscribers by FY26 and reached 1.7 Mn in October 2026. Nexizo, launched in 2025, offers AI-led buyer discovery, market intelligence and raw-material price insights. These services give the group a way to reach SMEs before they need procurement or credit; neither platform’s standalone revenue is disclosed. But there’s a limitation to this model. Commodity trading is a high-volume, low-margin business, and fluctuations in prices can quickly affect revenue. This was evident in FY26. Metals, OfBusiness’ largest category, saw sales decline 20% to ₹10,434 Cr. Chemicals grew just 4% to ₹3,663 Cr, while food processing and other products fell 55% to ₹1,636 Cr. Part of the contraction was strategic. OfBusiness said it exited lower-return commerce categories and discontinued operations to prioritise margins and manufacturing integration. But the shareholder letter also cites lower mild-steel prices and delays in two mega projects. The disclosures do not isolate how much of the metal’s decline came from deliberate exits versus these headwinds. The second layer, manufacturing, is OfBusiness’ attempt to improve these economics. As cofounder Asish Mohapatra said in September 2026, “As these ecosystems deepen, we are building manufacturing capabilities selectively in categories where we see an opportunity to add value to the supply chain.” Instead of simply buying and reselling materials, it selectively manufactures products where greater control over production can improve quality, supply and margins. In metals, the FY26 annual report identifies six of 26 products manufactured in-house under brands including Noble, Bison and Sangam Steel, with more than 1.1 Mn tonnes of annual capacity. It also reports that structural-steel capacity expanded from 100,000 to 500,000 tonnes a year. Chemicals follow the same logic. The FY26 report identifies in-house manufacturing for eight of 26 chemical products, with annual capacity exceeding 80,000 tonnes, and an expansion in ethyl acetate capacity from 10,000 to 80,000 tonnes. The aim is to capture more value from selected products without abandoning the broader trading catalogue. The strategy is selective rather than a complete shift away from trading. In a September 2026 update, the company described manufacturing capabilities across more than 40 products and plans to expand into herbicides and pesticides. The economics are improving, even as sales contract. Commerce revenue fell 9.7% to ₹19,056 Cr in FY26, but its reported segment result excluding other income rose from ₹303 Cr to ₹527 Cr. In his shareholder letter, cofounder Asish Mohapatra separately reported commerce EBITDA of ₹769 Cr, up 37.9%. The two measures are not interchangeable, and neither reveals manufacturing’s standalone margin. What they do establish is that commerce earnings improved despite lower revenue. The question is whether this improvement can continue as the business invests in capacity, rather than relying on commodity-price recovery or portfolio exits. Apparel Is Emerging As Fastest-Growing Business If metals are OfBusiness’ biggest revenue generator, fashion is becoming its fastest-growing category. Fashion sales surged from ₹376 Cr in FY25 to ₹2,828 Cr in FY26, a more than sevenfold jump. Unlike its traditional raw-material business, OfBusiness’ apparel operations focus on supplying finished products to global brands. It works with smaller manufacturers, manages product development, quality approvals and production, and handles everything from order fulfilment to international deliveries. As of March 2026, OfBusiness had developed capabilities to serve over 70 brands, including Michael Kors, Uniqlo, Adidas, IKEA, GAP and Zara. Its apparel operations spanned 21 processing facilities, with annual in-house manufacturing capacity exceeding 40 Mn units. Acquisitions have played a major role in OfBusiness’ apparel expansion. It acquired footwear manufacturer Alpine Shoes in October 2024, followed by Bengaluru-based garment and home-textile exporter Indian Designs Exports in FY26, which became wholly owned in January 2026. The acquisitions have broadened the product range and manufacturing footprint, but the report does not separate acquired growth from organic growth. In an August 2026 statement, cofounder Vasant Sridhar said, “Apparel has demonstrated how our model scales when we combine manufacturing capability with deep customer relationships and global market access.” The statement describes the company’s strategic rationale, not a separately disclosed measure of apparel profitability. That matters when assessing whether the sevenfold increase can be sustained. For smaller apparel manufacturers, OfBusiness takes on global customer acquisition, certifications, quality approvals and delivery, allowing suppliers to concentrate on production. Unlike commodity resale, this model can capture value through product development, processing and fulfilment. Oxyzo: The Bigger Profit Contributor Oxyzo is the profit counterweight to commerce. In FY26, OfBusiness’ financial services segment, led by the NBFC, generated ₹1,415 Cr in revenue, up 23%, and ₹505 Cr in profit before tax, up 11%. That is nearly 55% of the group’s combined segment PBT from less than 7% of consolidated operating revenue. Oxyzo lends for working capital, raw-material purchases and business expansion. Its advantage is access to SMEs already engaging with OfBusiness’ commerce and business-discovery platforms. A company finding contracts through BidAssist or buyers through Nexizo may later need supplies and credit; that creates cross-selling potential, although the annual report does not quantify conversions or acquisition-cost savings. Its underwriting combines financial and external data with customer information and technology. In an October 2026 company commentary on account management, cofounder Mohapatra observed, “We got there because of sales, but we stayed there because of KAM.” That emphasis on maintaining customer relationships also matters to a model that seeks repeat procurement and financing business. For some purchase-financing loans, Oxyzo pays suppliers directly, offering greater visibility over how the funds are used. That is a structural link between the commerce transaction and the lending product, not simply a referral arrangement. At FY26-end, Oxyzo reported a ₹10,706 Cr loan book, more than 60,000 MSME and emerging corporate borrowers, a 0.74% gross NPA ratio and operating expenses at 2.4% of average assets. These metrics indicate scale and reported asset quality, but do not remove exposure to funding costs and credit losses. Its acquisition of fixed-income distribution platform Golden Pi broadens the financing proposition. OfBusiness held 74.43% of Oxyzo at FY26-end, so the subsidiary’s profits are not entirely attributable to parent shareholders. Management wants to lift Oxyzo’s return on equity from the early double digits to the mid-double digits and diversify funding beyond banks. The challenge is to grow the loan book without requiring disproportionate capital or weakening credit quality. What Lies Ahead For OfBusiness? For OfBusiness, the next phase will be judged less by how much it sells than by what it earns on the capital tied up in commerce and lending. Manufacturing can lift the value captured from each industrial order; BidAssist and Nexizo can help originate customer relationships; Oxyzo can finance their purchases. The opportunity is to make those activities reinforce one another rather than merely add to revenue. Mohapatra’s targets make the test measurable: lift commerce return on capital employed from the late single digits to the early double digits, and financing return on equity from the early to the mid-double digits. The group generated ₹1,256 Cr in operating cash flow, invested ₹881 Cr and reported ₹375 Cr of free cash flow in FY26, with an ambition to fund expansion without shareholder dilution. International sales are also rising. Consolidated revenue from outside India increased 62% to ₹2,058 Cr in FY26, about 10% of operating revenue. Separately, an August 2026 company update described exports exceeding ₹2,500 Cr. US tariffs pressured apparel exports during FY26, even as OfBusiness expanded men’s woven apparel and established a Bangladesh manufacturing footprint for outerwear. Mohapatra has identified European expansion and additional chemicals capacity and marketing presence as priorities for the start of FY28, while flagging West Asian chemical supply disruptions and rising Indian labour costs. Apparel remains much smaller than metals, but its next test is whether growth translates into durable returns. The unresolved question ahead of the IPO is whether better commerce margins, profitable exports and disciplined lending can sustain that cash generation as capacity and credit demand grow.

Three dead after two helicopters collide midair near Oregon airport
- Published
Three people have died after two helicopters collided midair near a small airport in Oregon, officials said.
The collision involving a Robinson R22 and an Airbus helicopter occurred near McMinnville Municipal Airport on Thursday afternoon. Both aircraft crashed in a field adjacent to a highway, the sheriff's office said.
Authorities identified the victims as a 22-year-old flight instructor from Texas and a student pilot from the United Kingdom, who were aboard one of the helicopters. The sole occupant of the other aircraft was also killed.
It was not immediately clear what caused the crash.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) responded to the scene and are leading the ongoing investigation.
The BBC has contacted the FAA for comment.
The flight instructor on the Robinson R22 was identified Maddie Aasbo. The student pilot from the UK has not yet been publicly identified, as authorities work with the consulate and the FBI to notify the next of kin.
The sole occupant of the Airbus was identified as Tyler Delane Sturdevant, 38, of Newberg, Oregon.
One of the aircraft was operated by Jerry Trimble Helicopters, a flight training school based at the McMinnville Municipal Airport, according to a statement from the company.
"Jerry Trimble Helicopters is deeply saddened to confirm that one of our aircraft was involved in an aviation incident this afternoon," the company said, adding that they were fully cooperating with investigators.
Authorities asked the public to avoid the area as they responded to the incident.

Buongiorno! As you put the final touches on your Halloween costumes, here is a spooky story for you: Imagine going to urgent care for something as trivial as a UTI, and getting a bill for $1,756, on top of $211 you already paid at the clinic! Keep reading to learn more.
When urgent care becomes emergency care
Intuitive Health, a private equity-backed company that runs about 50 hybrid ER-urgent care clinics, was launched on the idea that it could offer an alternative to costly hospital visits, providing under the same roof a clinic for uncomplicated issues and an ER in case of necessity.
But for many patients, the opposite has happened: They came in with simple, urgent care-appropriate conditions but were billed for ER services — think close to $2,000 for an UTI or $7,000 ($2,100 after insurance) for congestion and cough. Company officials say every patient should be asked to sign a form before the “upgrade,” but Tara Bannow found in her investigation this was far from standard practice.
A halt to Medicaid work requirements for medically frail people
A federal judge in Massachusetts has rejected the federal government’s definition of “medical frailty,” ruling that states didn’t have enough time to assess eligibility status. The decision overturns an interim CMS rule that substantially limited the pool of people eligible for exemptions to the work requirements, in particular by requiring that medically frail people demonstrate that their condition prevents them from working. The rule also didn’t list conditions that would automatically be exempt from work requirements.
The lawsuit was brought on by states claiming that CMS didn’t have the authority to narrow the definition of medically frail, and that the rule would create red tape for beneficiaries having to demonstrate their status, as well as an additional burden for state workers. Thursday’s ruling complicates the already tangled web of work requirements, and might lead to a delay in their rollout past the beginning of 2027, when they were slated to go into effect. More here.
What RFK Jr. is telling Americans as they head to the polls
At a rally for Zach Lahn, the farmer-turned-unlikely Republican candidate for Iowa governor, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. called Lahn’s opposition to Big Agriculture, a key tenet of his platform, a “spiritual battle.”
“We have to figure out a way to grow food without poisoning our kids, without giving ourselves cancer, without destroying the soils that enrich us and enrich our microbiome that connect our brain and all of our organs. And make us healthy, robust and vibrant people,” Kennedy told the crowd.
Chelsea Cirruzzo, who reported on the rally, also takes a broader look at RFK Jr.’s big talking points, with the midterms around the corner: fighting fraud, doubling down on “medical freedom” in the form of vaccine choice, and pushing MAHA, even as the political future of the movement looks shaky. (Also don’t forget to check out our 2026 midterms roundup for the most important political news.)
Why is colorectal cancer more aggressive in young people? A new database offers clues
People who are diagnosed with colorectal cancer earlier in life, especially younger than 35, often have a grimmer prognosis than people who develop the disease older. Researchers have been trying to understand why. A new “atlas” of 189 colorectal cancer tumors from patients in their 20s to their 90s could help explain the differences in the disease, while controlling for variables that may have confounded previous studies.
“It is devastating to care for young patients diagnosed with often advanced stages of colorectal cancer. These are people in the prime of their life,” Kimmie Ng, the colorectal cancer researcher who authored the database study, told Angus Chen. “That’s what motivates us to do the work, find out what might be causing this, and what unique features we could target so that we can better treat these patients. It’s something that keeps me up at night, and one of the biggest questions facing our scientific community today.”
Ng, who serves as the director of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, discussed in a Q&A what kinds of insights the database might offer, and what her team is learning about the increasing rate of colorectal cancer in young patients.
Men’s health as gender health
A new series in The Lancet argues for the need to investigate a paradox of men’s health: why men experience worse health outcomes than women, even though they hold undeniable privilege. In their approach, the series authors move away from looking at men’s health as an issue of sex, broadening the frame to focus on gender. “Men’s health is defined and shaped by the culturally defined roles, responsibilities, attributes, and entitlements associated with being (or being seen as) a man, as well as power relations between and among women and men,” they write in the introduction.
A first paper proposes a framework that analyzes men’s health through an intersectional lens, focusing on structural determinants of health. A second looks at the available data about men’s life expectancy and burden of disability, trying — with limitations due to the lack of an intersectional perspective in many of the studies so far — to tease out risk factors and causes. The third paper proposes a political strategy that advances men’s health as a contributing factor to the shared public good.
Discussion of men’s health is wont to raise the question of whether it is detracting from women’s. The authors defend their choice. “A gendered approach to health is not a zero-sum game; it can serve to enhance wellbeing for all,” they write.
Helen Branswell, in her own words
This week, STAT Executive Editor Rick Berke travelled to Washington, D.C., to accept in memory of Helen Branswell the Kovler Prize for Trust in Life Science Journalism at the Foundation for the National Institutes of Health dinner. It was an elegant event at Union Station, with 350 luminaries from science and health, including current and former NIH directors.
The highlight of the evening was a video that Helen recorded in late summer to accept the award. She talked about her work and a career she so deeply loved. As readers of this newsletter know, Helen has been a frequent contributor to Morning Rounds over the last 11 years, tirelessly sharing her insights on infectious disease news. (In fact, Helen’s first writings on Covid-19 appeared here.)
Heartbroken as we all are by her loss, I hope you’ll watch and come away inspired but one of the truly greats.

J&K Cabinet minister Sakina Itoo on Friday (October 30, 2026) sought intervention of Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha to end stringent drills during the movement of security forces’ convoys in Kashmir.
Ms. Itoo, who represents a constituency in south Kashmir’s Kulgam, in a post on X, highlighted the inconvenience faced by locals during the movement of security forces. After the Pulwama attack, security forces stop traffic on both tubes of the highway till convoys move.
“While travelling frequently on the Srinagar–Anantnag–Kulgam–Qazigund National Highway, it is deeply distressing to see ambulances stranded, students missing classes and ordinary citizens waiting 15–30 minutes, sometimes even hours, for convoy movement. What fault have our people committed to endure such hardships?” said Ms. Itoo.
She appealed to L-G Sinha and the concerned authorities “to explore practical traffic management measures that uphold essential security protocols while ensuring uninterrupted passage for ambulances and minimising public inconvenience.”
“Security is paramount, but so is the well-being of our people. Security and compassion must go hand in hand. Let governance be reflected not just in policies, but in the everyday lives of citizens through dignity, sensitivity and meaningful relief,” said Ms. Itoo.

Son of Zambian bishop detained in post-election raid fears for his father's safety
The son of detained Zambian opposition politician Bishop Trevor Mwamba has told the BBC he is concerned for his father's safety after the former Bishop of Botswana was detained along with 10 other opposition figures by authorities.
Eno Mwamba said his father, who is leader of the United National Independence Party, has been charged with treason following President Hakainde Hichilema's disputed election victory.
The opposition politicians have been held since a raid by security forces on 14 August.
Opposition leader Brian Mundubile, head of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), had gone into hiding after disputing the election result, but has since also been detained by the authorities.
The government accuses the opposition of planning an armed insurgency and have charged the detained politicians with treason. They have denied the charges.

(Bloomberg) -- The Justice Department is actively working to secure a grand jury indictment against former FBI Director James Comey for allegedly directing the sharing of secret national defense information, a federal prosecutor said in court Friday.
“We are still going to the grand jury very diligently,” Special Assistant US Attorney Dustin Farahnak said in a hearing at the US District Court for the District of Columbia. The proceeding focused on Comey’s motion to toss a criminal information — a charging document — filed in Washington on the eve the statute of limitations was set to expire.
Comey, a frequent DOJ target under the second Trump administration, is accused of being involved in the communication of classified information to the New York Times in October 2016. DOJ said it filed the charging document “to toll the statute of limitations” as it relates to the allegations.
Comey’s attorneys argue the criminal information is untimely and that the statute requires an indictment be filed within the 10 years.
Farahnak told Judge Trevor McFadden that the grand jury process is still playing out, and that DOJ has evidence showing potential additional actions that would fall within the statute of limitations, including as recently as April 2017.
DOJ is attempting to keep the prosecution alive as Comey’s attorneys push for McFadden to not wait for an indictment to toss the case. Ephraim McDowell of Cooley LLP noted in court Friday that FBI agents have been spotted outside his house.
There shouldn’t be an arrest “threat hanging over Mr. Comey’s head,” McDowell said.
The case is USA v. Comey, D.D.C., No. 1:26-cr-00229, 10/30/26.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.
Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.
According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.
“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.
Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.
Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.
The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.
“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”
According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.
Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.
Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.
Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.
“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

If you’ve been waiting for a good deal on Google’s latest smartwatch before you commit, you're in luck. The Google Pixel Watch 5 (the 41-mm model with Wi-Fi) is currently $300, down from $400, marking its lowest price yet. (The larger 45-mm model is also discounted, from $430 to $330.)
This early Black Friday sale means you don’t have to wait until the late-November holiday to score the worthwhile discount—and we recommend you don't. Amazon, Best Buy, and the Google Store are all offering the 25 percent off deal, but I don't know for how much longer. In other words, now is a great time to score this smartwatch for less.
A Record-Low Price
The Pixel Watch 5 is one of the best smartwatches available for Android users. It’s a refinement of an already brilliant wearable, with double the RAM and storage, plus an upgraded Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 processor that makes this edition 20 percent faster than its predecessor. The domed display is gorgeous, comfortable, and easy to read during workouts, and it provides meaningful upgrades for health and fitness tracking.
Beyond being able to track weights and reps, the new Strength Training experience includes a workout builder, audio cues, and rest times. You can build a custom routine in the Google Health app and have the watch guide you through each exercise, and incorporate Gemini AI by asking it to generate a workout based on a photo of your gym equipment. Speaking of Gemini, the Pixel Watch 5 supports certain offline tasks, such as starting a workout, which is nice if you like to leave your watch at home while you exercise.
Google’s new Health Guardian tools include features for monitoring insulin resistance trends, blood pressure trends, breathing emergencies (available only in select countries), and sleep breathing quality. The watch also retains useful features like ECG, skin temperature tracking, and loss-of-pulse detection. It comes with upgraded sleep tracking, too, with Google claiming 15 percent greater accuracy than the Pixel Watch 4.
Google estimates up to 40 hours of battery life, but mine only got to around 36 hours in testing before conking out. Fast charging is the real standout, though; just 15 minutes on the charger delivers up to 15 hours of use. If you’re like me and only remember to charge your watch 20 minutes before leaving the house, this is a lifesaver.
At its original $400 price, the Pixel Watch 5 is a pricey recommendation, especially since many of its software upgrades will also make their way to the previous generation. But at $300, it’s cheaper than the latest Apple Watch Series 12 and other high-end smartwatches. This is the lowest price I’ve seen for the Pixel Watch 5, so if you’ve been eyeing it, there’s little reason to wait for Black Friday.

Apple rarely admits a mistake. But when it unveiled new versions of its operating systems this summer, it came close.
“With all major design updates, there’s a natural process where we take a bold leap forward, and then we continue to iterate,” said Apple's human interface designer, Shubham Kedia, during a predictably sleek keynote video. “Our team really appreciates your feedback, and we considered it deeply as we refined the new design.”
Not quite “Sorry, everyone, we messed up,” but for Apple, practically an apology tour. The subject was Liquid Glass, Apple’s most divisive interface design since at least iOS 7. Apple's Vision Pro mixed-reality headset (which itself flopped) inspired the translucent design language, and the company brought it to millions of other Apple devices.
The result was a mess—at odds with Steve Jobs’ famous line, “Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.” Liquid Glass started obsessed with gloss and effects, despite promises it would bring your content to the foreground. Yet Apple’s own press release showed interfaces with illegible text. Worse, users found constant reflections and flickering color shifts distracting, and a lack of clarity across devices hurt accessibility.
But iOS 27, alongside updates to Apple's other software platforms, signaled a shift in priorities after Kedia’s mea culpa. Kedia spoke of reincorporating design cornerstones in what was, if not quite a U-turn, then at least a rediscovery of a core principle: how it works. Instantly, interface elements across Apple devices gained greater clarity and structure, making it easier to tell apps' components from content. The most obvious change, though, was a slider.
Thinking Differently
Apple said it tuned Liquid Glass to diffuse complex content more effectively, keeping elements legible when above imagery and text. But it also acknowledged that not everyone wants the same thing—some users might prefer a more tinted look, and others “would like Liquid Glass to be even more clear.” You can now decide for yourself with the Liquid Design slider in Settings. For a company known for being opinionated, such bet-hedging was surprising but not unwelcome. Choice isn’t a bad thing, and now users had more of it.
“I immediately pushed that slider all the way to the most tinted setting, and pretty much all the legibility issues vanished,” Ben Rice McCarthy, an indie developer behind popular apps like Obscura and Indigo, tells WIRED. McCarthy has long criticized Liquid Glass. Now? Not so much.
“Liquid Glass introduced a lot of issues without adequate solutions, but this year’s operating systems solved or improved a lot of them,” McCarthy says. “There’s the adaptiveness of the interface. Buttons can grow into menus. Controls merge and divide like cells as you transition between views. Toolbars can expand and contract smoothly as the view changes size.”
Flexibility matters when resizing windows across any device. But while announcing its updates, Apple also dropped major hints that all but confirmed new hardware—it showed iPhone apps running on an iPad or a Mac could resize to a suspiciously specific shape that matched the rumored inner display dimensions of Apple’s upcoming folding phone.
Designed to Flow
When Apple showed off the iPhone Duo, everything clicked. Its passport-shaped display bucks the trend of iPhones and their rivals growing taller over the years. The Duo is wider and almost squat, and when opened, it naturally defaults to landscape, echoing the iPad Mini display.
Apple being Apple, it wanted to avoid the jarring jolt between displays that’s often evident on rival foldables, so it made content appear to move seamlessly from one screen to the other. That begins with the hardware. As Molly Anderson, Apple's vice president of Industrial Design, said at the September keynote: “To achieve this continuity, we designed iPhone Duo around a consistent aspect ratio that is the same across both displays.” But it’s the software—rooted in Liquid Glass—that sells the illusion.
The most arresting element is a fancy animation, which various folks in the Android space are now busy being “inspired” by. It reinforces the idea of a flowing interface. Meanwhile, Liquid Glass freed Apple from being prescriptive about where essential controls live. On the Duo, they sit at the side. When the phone’s closed, that frees up space for content. When it’s open, the controls stay in a consistent spot, so you never have to hunt for them. Reorient the device, and everything settles into the most appropriate place.
That’s form following function, not function being subservient to form. This device and its flexible interface don’t strictly need the Liquid Glass design language, but the two feel made for each other. Liquid Glass finally makes sense on the iPhone Duo—and with Apple’s other refinements, it’s starting to make sense elsewhere, too.
Clarity of Purpose
How much of this is happenstance is hard to say. Given Apple’s lead times, pure coincidence seems unlikely. And even if Liquid Glass wasn’t made with the Duo in mind, it adapts to it.
Liquid Glass feels more considered. It’s increasingly tuned for individual devices rather than governed by a “universal” aesthetic forced onto them all. The result is operating systems that feel solid rather than fragile, with interfaces less likely to fight content for your attention. On Macs and iPads, the Liquid Glass revamp now looks more like a love letter to Aqua—Apple's water-themed interface introduced in 2000. On the iPhone, it’s usable again. On the Duo, it’s a delight.
That’s not to say it’s perfect. “There’s some weirdness that hasn’t been fully resolved, and there needs to be a consistency to all these materials or the metaphors break down,” McCarthy says. “But overall, Liquid Glass is vastly improved.”
And it’s worth remembering that while the Duo is new, Liquid Glass is relatively young, too. As developer Steve Troughton-Smith wrote, “For some iPhone apps, even with keen developers, it will take six months to a year of work to properly support iPhone Duo. A lot of developers are still trying to finish the Liquid Glass transition they started last year.”
A useful reminder that transitions take time. But at least now, Apple’s vision looks clear.

2-day Canada-EU summit winds down Friday in Montreal
Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting European Union leaders in Montreal on Friday as he looks to deepen ties with like-minded leaders in the face of an increasingly protectionist United States.
But the rise of nationalist political forces in Europe could make that more difficult in the years to come.
The 21st Canada-EU summit, which wraps Friday, is aimed at forging a stronger alliance between Canada and the 27-member bloc in the face of an unpredictable and volatile White House.
On Thursday, both Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stressed the two sides' shared values as they pitched an "alliance for the future" based on deeper trade and security ties.
- Carney says Canada is working to become an 'associate member' as he hosts EU leaders in Montreal
- EU dropping associate membership title for its closer alliance with Canada
But shifting political winds on the continent could test that alliance, notably in France and Germany — heavyweights within the bloc.
In France, presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally is leading in polls ahead of the spring 2027 election. Le Pen, an advocate for strict immigration limits, has criticized the EU-Canada trade pact.
While in Germany, the far-right and isolationist Alternative for Germany (AfD) continues to gain ground in regional parliaments and national polls.
Asked Thursday if he has concerns about dealing with a potentially different political makeup, Carney praised the EU's adherence to democratic values.
"One of Europe's strengths is democracy, freedom and a core belief in the rule of law. There will always be different governments, governments of different stripes in Europe," he told reporters.
"Over the course of decades, the European Union has continued to develop, and strengthen, throughout, and be enriched by the national democratic processes of those countries."
Carney also downplayed the notion he was looking to secure commitments with the EU before the French election.
"We're not tying it to any political cycle, but to the fundamentals of what they deliver … for Canadians," he said.
Despite some objections from EU members, von der Leyen has pitched making Canada the first associate member of the bloc. Carney has welcomed a more expansive alliance across the Atlantic.
That appeared to anger U.S. President Donald Trump who said if he interpreted the move as a "hostile act," he might stop trading with Europe "on many things."
Asked earlier this week about the summit potentially attracting retaliation from Trump or right-wing leaders in Europe, a senior Canadian government official told reporters the gathering isn't directed against anyone but reflected deep interests between Canada and the EU.
