A Christian family was allegedly attacked at their home in West Arjunda village, Panskura, East Midnapore district of West Bengal, on the evening of October 26, Monday. An FIR was registered in connection with the case on October 28, Wednesday at Panskura police station.
Parvati Hembram Soren (27) alleged that a mob of around 30 people, including members of their extended family, neighbours and others who associated themselves with the Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP), assaulted her, desecrated Bibles present in their home and threatened them to renounce Christianity and accept Hinduism.
Some of the accused named in the FIR include extended family members of Parvati and her husband, Santu Soren, namely Gorachand Soren, Balaram Soren, Sombari Soren, Mamani Soren, Arati Soren, Arjun Soren, Logen Hansda, Geeta Soren, Kanka Soren and Nera Bou.
Parvati, Santu, and his uncle and aunt had embraced Christianity over a year ago and is associated with Christ the King Mission Church under the Balichak Catholic Parish. Parvati’s sister-in-law had also embraced the faith, but since she is a minor, her conversion certificate has not yet been published.
The alleged assault comes within days of a family in Patlapur village, Paschim Midnapur district, being allegedly subjected to three days of physical assault, sexual harassment, and continuous intimidation by a group of men who identified themselves as belonging to the Hindutva outfit Bajrang Dal.
ALSO READ: Christian families in Bengal attacked, allege ‘rape and death’ threats by ‘Bajrang Dal’ members
‘Dragged, Slapped, Kicked, Clothes Torn’
Speaking to Alt News, Parvati recounted that on Monday evening, she was praying with her husband and their two children while playing Christian religious songs and carols on a speaker. At around 7:30 pm, a group of approximately 30 people allegedly barged into their home. “Initially, they verbally abused us, snatched our Bible and threw it away. Then, they locked my family members in a room and beat me. They slapped, kicked and punched me,” she alleged.
Hearing her screams, Parvati’s other family members tried to intervene but were unable to protect her because of the sheer number of people attacking her, she added.
Further, the attackers allegedly attempted to tear up the Bible and set it on fire. When Parvati tried to stop them, they allegedly grabbed her by the hair, dragged her out of her house and assaulted her again. “Sombari, Mamani, Arati, and Geeta grabbed me by my hair and dragged me out of the house. They also tore of my clothes,” Parvati alleged.
“I have endured several injuries due to this physical assault and have immense pain in my body. Even my sister-in-law was beaten,” she alleged, adding that her husband was spared the physical assault because he was holding one of their children, she said, although he was verbally abused. The assault continued for approximately an hour, after which Parvati became unconscious.
Parvati underwent medical tests at 10:36 pm on Monday. The following morning, October 27, she went to Panskura police station to lodge an FIR. “The police took my written complaint and said that they would do a preliminary investigation and then lodge an FIR,” she said.
Parvati further alleged that her sister-in-law was recording the incident, but the attackers quickly snatched the latter’s phone, deleted the videos and photographs, before throwing the phone to the ground and damaging it. “Later they took all four Bibles from my house, destroyed them and threw them into a nearby pond. The mob also tried to break open my aged uncle-in-law’s home, located next to our house,” she added.
‘Death Threats, Social & Economic Boycott’
Moreover, Parvati told Alt News that the attackers repeatedly demanded that the family renounce their faith in Christianity and return to Hinduism. They allegedly threatened to wreak havoc in their home, harm or kill family members, and impose a social and economic boycott if they refused to comply.
While Santu works as a toto driver, Parvati works on the farmlands. Their neighbours, who were also part of the assault, have allegedly forced them to plant Tulsi and Manasa plants in their courtyard and perform Hindu rituals. “To continue harassing us, they have tied two cows in our courtyard, and the cows keep littering near our water tap,” she claimed. Additionally, the neighbours are allegedly constructing barriers along the local pond’s bank to prevent Parvati’s family from using the pond water.
During the incident, the family managed to contact a local volunteer of Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP) in Monirampur, who alerted the organisation’s legal team. Subsequently, advocate Aditya Tewary contacted Parvati.
However, the lawyer told Alt News that a man answered the phone after the attackers allegedly snatched it away from Parvati. “I called Parvati, but a man answered the phone, who said he was from Vishva Hindu Parishad. He told me, ‘We are here to set things right. We have received information about Christian conversion here’. As soon as I told him I’m an advocate, he disconnected the call,” Tewary said.
Not An Isolated Incident
This is not the first time that the Soren family was allegedly harassed and intimidated for practising Christianity. On October 11 around 6 pm, members identifying themselves as belonging to Bajrang Dal, along with their extended family members, arrived at their home and demanded that they renounce their faith in Christianity and return to Hinduism, Parvati told us, adding that she had then filed a complaint via email on October 12.
Even then, she named members of her extended family in the complaint as she did not know the names of the Bajrang Dal men. However, no action was initiated by the police.
Police Inaction
“When we were trying to call the police [on Monday], they told us that they [the assailants] would call the police themselves,” Parvati said.
However, she alleged that the police did not reprimand the assailants and instead schooled her and her family. “Instead, shockingly, the police told us to perform and practice our religious rituals inside our house and asked us not to use a speaker, claiming it to be an attempt to convert others,” she said. “Our Hindu neighbours keep playing religious songs on loudspeakers. We have never complained. How can playing songs on a small bluetooth speaker convert others?”
Upon being contacted, Panskura police told Alt News that they do not have the authority to brief us on any case and asked us to contact the headquarters. We then contacted East Midnapore Superintent of Police (SP) and Additional SP, but the phone went unanswered.
The FIR has been lodged under Sections 115(2), 3(5), 303(2), 324(4), 329(4), 351(2) and 76 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, pertaining to voluntarily causing hurt, common intention, theft, mischief, house-trespass, criminal intimidation, and assault or use of criminal force against a woman with intent to disrobe her, respectively. Despite the two complaints, no arrests have been made yet.
‘Don’t Give Them Loan’
Meanwhile, Parvati told Alt News that the harassment continued on Wednesday when a representative from a loan agency visited her home to process an application submitted by her and her husband. According to Parvati, her extended family surrounded the representative and allegedly pressured him not to process the loan because the couple had converted to Christianity.
“We bought a toto, but now we do not have enough money to pay the remaining instalments. That is why we had applied for a loan. Today, a person from the loan office visited my house. When he was leaving, my attackers surrounded him and asked him not to give us a loan, because we are not Hindus. If the police do not lodge an FIR and protect my family and me from this daily harassment, then we have to commit suicide,” she said, adding that even though she demanded police protection, her demand went unheeded.

Meta quietly launches an AI fashion app for virtually trying on clothes
For now, it's a limited launch in parts of Asia.
Meta has released yet another AI app with very limited availability. A few weeks ago, it launched Waddle World, a Tamagotchi-like game that the company describes as a "daily journal disguised as a pet," in the Philippines. Now, it has introduced an AI fashion app called Style Sketch in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand on Android and iOS.
The app's existence was first reported by social media consultant Matt Navarra on X. Style Sketch can connect to your Facebook and Instagram accounts to build a virtual closet from photos you've shared on social media. Or you can upload existing photos from your camera roll or snap new pictures of your clothes if you don't want to link your accounts.
From there, you can get outfit combination suggestions from your wardrobe. You can also try on different combinations on the virtual model that matches your body type and skin tone. To get suggestions, you can pick any clothing item in your closet to build outfits around it, tell the app the weather for the day, or ask it to create outfit plans for your trip.
As TechCrunch notes, Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg said earlier this year that the company is releasing many more apps, since AI has made them much easier to develop. These apps will also help the company get more people to use and train their AI systems. Meta isn't the first one to release an AI-powered fashion app or feature, however. Google's AI Search has had a virtual clothes try-on feature since 2025, and it added a "Wardrobe" feature to Photos earlier this year that creates a catalog of your items by scanning your library. More recently, OpenAI also introduced a ChatGPT feature that lets you upload your photos and the clothes you want to try on to see how they look on you.

One of Australia’s most notorious paedophiles is facing hundreds more child abuse charges, including for the alleged rape of children as young as one.
Days after being extradited from Queensland to New South Wales, Ashley Paul Griffith was hit with 202 charges dating from between 2014 and 2017, with police labelling the allegations “deeply disturbing”.
The Queensland man was working at a childcare centre in Sydney’s inner west at the time of the alleged offending, which included dozens of alleged rapes against children between one and five.
Griffith, 48, was jailed for life in Queensland in November 2024 after he pleaded guilty to more than 300 child sexual offences against nearly 70 victims.
The fresh charges from NSW include 68 counts of rape of a child aged less than 10 and 42 counts of aggravated rape of a child aged less than 10 who was under his authority.
Other charges include 69 counts of aggravated indecent assault and 23 charges of producing child abuse material.
Police said the charges pertained to 23 alleged victims aged between one and five.
He was charged while being held in Silverwater Correctional Complex in Sydney.
NSW Det Supt Linda Howlett said charging Griffith with further alleged offending could help potential victims.
“There’s no other word for it, it’s actually horrific,” she said in relation to the allegations.
The child abuse squad commander thanked witnesses, alleged victims and detectives for their work in preparing the challenging but “airtight” case.
Police are extending every assistance to those involved, Howlett said.
Griffith did not apply for bail in a brief court appearance on Friday.
The NSW police assistant commissioner Brett Greentree said the lengthy investigation included collaboration with police across the nation.
“The allegations before the court are deeply disturbing and involve some of the most vulnerable members of our community,” he said.
“Every child deserves to be safe and protected from harm. NSW Police is committed to ensuring those who exploit positions of trust to offend against children are identified, investigated and brought before the courts.”
Griffith arrived in NSW on Wednesday.
In Queensland, he admitted to assaulting and filming young girls over the course of years while working at childcare centres.
His transfer was approved by a Brisbane magistrate earlier in the month, where the alleged victims’ supporters yelled insults at the rapist as he stood in the dock for the decision.
In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

Typhoon Champi was declared the strongest storm of the year so far after recording sustained winds of 185mph last week. From late Thursday to early Saturday, the typhoon battered Taiwan and Japan’s southern islands. Champi approached the east coast of Taiwan before the centre of the storm turned south along the Yilan County coastline, looping offshore and then tracking northwards away from the island. The storm brought gusts of up to 141mph and 48-hour rainfall totals of more than 620mm to parts of Yilan.
So far, the death toll remains at one, with 527 reported injured. There were widespread power outages, with more than 288,000 houses having no electricity at one point, although most had since been reconnected. Champi has been downgraded to a tropical storm as it rapidly weakens to the south-west of Japan’s mainland on Monday.
For the fourth time in October, parts of Greece are at risk of flooding. In the early part of this week, low pressure will bring severe thunderstorms and longer spells of heavy rain to much of the country, and this will be followed by a deep area of low pressure passing across southern areas.
The national meteorological agency issued warnings for Monday, with 30mm-60mm of rain forecast in a 12-hour period across central areas, and50mm-80mm in the north-east Aegean Islands. Forecast models indicate the potential for similar totals in a 12-hour period between Wednesday and Thursday, making further flooding possible.
A low-pressure system developed into a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal this weekend. Cyclone Arnab is expected to move towards the north Andhra Pradesh and south Odisha coast by Wednesday. The India meteorological department has alerts in place for extreme heavy rain, thunderstorms and strong surface winds across the eastern side of the country.
Models are forecasting gusts of up to 85mph, and six-hourly rainfall totals of up to 100mm, as the storm makes landfall, currently expected on Wednesday. From then, the system is set to drift to the north before gradually dying out over north-east India at the end of the week.

CJP's Saurav Das invites some Opposition leaders to Diwali party; Dipke, Ranka likely to attend too
Aam Aadmi Party MP Sanjay Singh and a few other party leaders are expected to join the Diwali party hosted by Das.
In what could be the first meeting between CJP leaders and a section of the Opposition, a few Opposition leaders, including TMC's Derek O'Brien and CPI(M) Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas, have been invited to an exclusive Diwali party on Saturday hosted by CJP leader Saurav Das.
Senior CJP leaders, including Abhijeet Dipke and Ashutosh Ranka, are also expected to attend the gathering. Aam Aadmi Party MP Sanjay Singh and a few other AAP leaders are likely to join the celebrations as well.
A senior Left leader told HT, “Some of us have been invited to the party. Of course, there would be serious political discussions about the current situation.”
The meeting assumes significance amid perceptions that a section of the Opposition is increasingly warming up to the CJP. Over the past few weeks, Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi has sent signals to the CJP leadership, which has also responded to his posts on social media.
The change has been driven by a series of public exchanges, beginning with Gandhi’s assertion that there were no parallel protests against the CEC, followed by his condemnation of the arrest of CJP activists and the group’s subsequent endorsement of the Congress-led INDIA bloc’s November 1 rally.
Gandhi made his support more explicit, condemning the arrest of CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka following their attempt to protest at Jantar Mantar.
“Waving the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice,” he wrote on X.
“Students. Youth. Journalists. The INDIA bloc. Different banners, one cause. All protests are one: citizens demanding their constitutional rights. Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India. We will reclaim it.”
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke responded with a public thank-you, acknowledging Gandhi’s intervention on behalf of the arrested activists. The exchange was significant because the Congress leader had, until then, largely avoided publicly associating himself with the outfit.
On October 28, Dipke backed the Ramlila maidan rally and said, “The Cockroach Janta Party extends its support to the INDIA Bloc’s November 1 rally. Nation above all!”

Climate change must be declared a "global health emergency" to shape governments' policies after heat caused three million deaths between 2016 and 2023, a report in The Lancet said Wednesday.
Published by the British medical journal ahead of the COP 31 climate summit in November, the 10th edition of the report brought together 146 researchers from 30 countries to assess the impact of climate change on the health of the world's population.
It said there were a record 710,000 heat-related deaths in 2023 with more than 70% of that toll linked to human-caused climate change.
Marina Romanello, the executive director of the health and climate research project Lancet Countdown, said there were "three million heat-related deaths globally in an eight-year span since the Paris Agreement" of 2015.
"That's roughly equivalent to the entire population of Wales being wiped out in the space of eight years due to heat," she told a news conference.
And "68% of those deaths are directly attributable to climate change."
The legally binding international climate treaty adopted in the French capital aimed to limit global warming to well below 2C and pursue efforts to keep it to 1.5C compared to pre-industrial levels.
Climate change impact
Romanello said the global health emergency due to climate change should have "an integrated approach so that we're not responding to emergency after emergency".
Instead she called for "a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities, and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies moving forward".
To determine the share of deaths attributable to warming caused by human activity, the researchers compiled the number of heat-related deaths recorded by states, then subtracted those that would have occurred in the absence of climate change, said Professor Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney.
Jay said the intensity and frequency of periods of intense heat were amplified by climate change, pointing out that last year an extreme drought affected more than half of the world's land surface for at least one month.
Economic cost
By reducing worker productivity, warming has cost the global economy more than one trillion dollars per year over the past three years, the researchers said.
Southeast Asia and Africa, the hardest-hit regions, are estimated to have lost the equivalent of 3.9 percent and 3.2 percent of their GDP, compared with 0.2 percent for Europe and 1.5 percent for the Americas.
However there has been concrete progress in some areas.
Since 2016, 56 of the WHO's 194 member states have adapted their health and early-warning systems to anticipate extreme events.
Investment in clean energy reached $2.1 trillion in 2025 -- double that of the amount invested in fossil fuels, which cause climate change.
However fossil fuels still account for 80 percent of global energy, causing air pollution that results in 2.73 million deaths per year, the study said.
Meanwhile, roughly 323,000 deaths have been avoided in "at least" 77 countries where air pollution from fossil fuels has fallen since 2016, according to the report.
Although funding for climate-related medical research has increased sevenfold to reach $316 million in 2024, 84% of these funds go to researchers in wealthy countries, even though the least developed nations are the most affected by the growing climate-related health threats.
Romanello said this year for the first time the researchers' work was complicated by the disappearance of certain data sources, particularly from the United States, such as fossil fuel subsidies, which have not been made public by the US authorities.
And for the past two years, global geopolitical instability has pushed global warming and its health impact into the background, she said, stressing that inaction was exacerbating the situation.

Scientists at the ICAR-Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI) have developed a new potato variety called ‘kufri jamunia’ that has higher levels of anthocyanins, vitamin C, and certain micronutrients than regular potatoes. The Central government has been promoting it of late as a means to address hidden hunger, i.e. when people consume enough calories but still do not receive the necessary nutrients.
Usually, experts who fortify foods, focus on items like rice and iodised salt, which a large number of people in India consume, often throughout the year, thus ensuring the added nutrients are delivered to a significant chunk of the population. Kufri jamunia is however a potato, which people in India generally consume much less consistently than rice or salt, and the micronutrient intake depends on preparation methods and how the body absorbs them.
What makes it different
Kufri jamunia offers nutritional advantages, but they are substantial in some aspects more than others. Questions also linger about its ability to resist disease and retain nutrients through different Indian cooking methods.
The variety reportedly has a mealy texture. In one CPRI assessment involving 64 people, 95% rated its overall acceptability ‘good to excellent’ and 56% said its taste was very good. This study cohort, though, is too small to generalise the results. CPRI researchers themselves have proposed that kufri jamunia can be used in curries, parathas, soups, baked goods, and dehydrated flours.
Importantly, kufri jamunia potatoes also have purple skin and flesh, which could affect consumer interest. Research on other biofortified foods has already shown that while people are generally willing to pay modest premiums — the national average cost of ordinary potatoes purchased wholesale is around ₹17/kg — whether they accept a new variety depends on its appearance, their awareness, taste, and of course local preferences.
How was is developed
The CPRI team developed the kufri jamunia variety by crossing two potato lines, MS/8-1148 and CP4242, in 2015. MS/8-1148 is high in vitamin C whereas CP4242 had purple skin and flesh. The result, formally called MSP/16-307, could naturally accumulate higher concentrations of specific nutrients as it grew. The team then conducted trials, including multi-location testing, in 2021-2023.
Based on the trial data, the Central Sub-Committee on Crop Standards, Notification and Release of Varieties for Horticultural Crops approved the variety in mid-2024 and the government notified it in November that year. The variety’s plants produce 10-12 medium to large tubers each and mature in around 90 days. The purple colour comes from anthocyanins — organic compounds also found in jamun and blueberries.
According to the Press Information Bureau, 100 g of kufri jamunia flesh contains around 42.75 mg of vitamin C (versus 23.15 mg in regular potatoes), 42.05 mg of anthocyanins, 2.28 mg of zinc (versus 0.28 mg), 3.22 mg of iron (versus 0.57 mg), and 161 micrograms of carotenoids. And per the CPRI team’s findings themselves, published in Potato Journal in 2025, 100 g of kufri jamunia was found to have a range of carotenoid levels, from 15.6 micrograms in Kanpur to 298.4 micrograms in Raipur, during the multi-location trials. Kufri jamunia also contains slightly less zinc than kufri neelkanth and slightly less iron than kufri manik; the latter are other coloured potato varieties developed at the Institute.
Anthocyanins are known to have antioxidant properties, although whether the same benefits will accrue when delivered by kufri jamunia potatoes is not known. And in the absence of similar studies, the same caveat goes for iron and zinc.
A 2016 study in Food Chemistry examined purple-fleshed potatoes and reported that steaming and microwaving generally preserved more of the nutritional substances than stir-frying did. However, again, research specific to kufri jamunia is not available.
Cultivation factors
Nutrient availability and delivery constitutes one half of a biofortification programme; the other half is determined by cultivation.
At the Modipuram research station, according to the Potato Journal paper, the team recorded an average yield of 49.01 tonnes per hectare after three months, across three seasons, whereas subsequent multi-location trials, including at Modipuram, recorded an overall mean of 31.96 tonnes per hectare across north (36.77 tonnes), central (33.79 tonnes), and eastern (25.91 tonnes) India.
On the other hand, at these locations, kufri manik yielded 31.52 tonnes per hectare and kufri neelkanth 36.61 tonnes per hectare. Further, kufri jamunia could moderately resist late blight, a disease caused by the water mould Phytophthera infestans, in laboratory conditions but has been reported as ‘susceptible’ in the field. Late blight is a devastator of potato crops and the CPRI team has already recommended that farmers apply fungicide.
Next, the multi-location trials also produced 29.19 tonnes of marketable potatoes per hectare, versus 33.48 tonnes for kufri neelkanth. So if the costs of cultivation were equal, kufri jamunia farmers could need a 15% premium on the selling price to attain the same gross revenue. (A study published by a CPRI in Indian Horticulture in 2020 estimated that, for regular potatoes, the seed material accounted for 40-50% of the production costs vis-a-vis regular potatoes, with a per-hectare seed cost of around ₹60,000-75,000 per hectare.)
Many unknowns
Taken together, there are many unknowns about kufri jamunia at this point to assess its overall cost-benefit ratio, including the cost of seeds and disease management, pricing, its uptake in the market, and how efficaciously it will deliver iron and zinc to the population. It would be premature as a result to deem kufri jamunia to be a proven solution to address India’s hidden hunger.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Some really excellent stories today, including Anil Oza’s profile of Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and the next installment in Bob Herman’s “Out of Pocket, Out of Reach” series.
Also, Andrew Joseph and Adam Feuerstein go live at 10:00am EDT to break down the latest news coming out of Europe’s big cancer conference. You can tune in here.
Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed: RFK Jr. is the ‘most incompetent HHS secretary ever’
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is known for his comical social media videos, his advocacy of “Medicare for All,” and his controversial stance on U.S. policy toward Israel.
One thing that’s been overlooked? El-Sayed would be the Senate’s first epidemiologist. And he plans to use his decades of experience in public health to “grill” health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who he called the “most incompetent HHS secretary ever” during an interview with STAT’s Anil Oza.
El-Sayed is a man with big dreams for how to overhaul the U.S. health care system so it can better serve vulnerable Americans. He has also become a target for many conservative politicians in recent months, including Kennedy, who told a crowd in Michigan earlier this week that “there’s 500 million Arabs in the world and yet they don’t produce science.”
Read more from Anil’s excellent profile, which also dives into El-Sayed’s personal motivations for reducing health disparities and his work to rebuild Detroit’s health system.
Great news, peptide fans…
… federal health officials just made it easier to compound some unapproved peptides.
The Department of Health and Human Services released a policy yesterday that will temporarily allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture some peptide products, increasing access to the experimental wellness therapies embraced by many in the MAHA movement.
The move comes as the Food and Drug Administration weighs broader approval of these compounds. In July, an FDA advisory panel voted to recommend that these pharmacies be cleared to manufacture six of these substances, even though agency scientists cautioned against the move due to the lack of clinical safety or efficacy data.
Read more from STAT’s Margaret Manto.
Martin Kulldorff critiques scientific gatekeepers at NIH lecture
Should academic journals decide what science should be published? Martin Kulldorff, the biostatistician known for co-authoring the Great Barrington Declaration, which advocated against Covid lockdowns, raised that question Wednesday in a lecture on rebuilding trust in science. “Why have journals decide what can be published or not?” Kuldorff, who now serves in a top role at HHS, asked.
Kulldorff made the remarks as part of a larger critique on how gatekeeping in scientific stifles trust. But he did not address the ways that unvetted scientific research, even when debunked after publishing, can sow distrust as well. Numerous polls show, for example, that Americans’ belief that vaccines cause autism has only increased in recent years, despite the fact that the major research making this claim was retracted back in 2010.
During his talk, Kulldorff also insisted that the rise in measles cases being experienced in the United States is the result of missed doctors appointments caused by Covid-19 lockdowns, despite the fact that that claim has been disputed by public health experts. – Nicholas Florko
How employer health care costs are shaping midterm elections
Multiple polls show that Americans are fixated on the high cost of health care even as prices for gas, groceries, and other necessities soar. Voters are asking for the government to intervene and lower prices, and their anger is casting a pall over the midterm elections.
STAT’s Bob Herman is back with the sixth installment of Out of Pocket, Out of Reach, where he has been investigating why health care costs are skyrocketing, even for American workers who get their insurance through their job. As the health care industry sucks up more and more cash, employers are shifting these costs to their workers.
Read more from Bob, or brush up on the rest of the series.
75%
How do you figure out the prevalence of a disease if you can only study it post mortem?
Researchers have struggled for years to suss out an accurate rate for chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a neurodegenerative disease that afflicts National Football League players and other people after repeated head trauma. But a study published yesterday of 2,362 former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 found that 74.5% had CTE, which can lead to worrisome cognitive and behavioral changes.
What does this estimate mean for the quarterbacks and wide receivers who line up every weekend to compete in America’s most popular sport? The researchers are careful to say that this estimate cannot be extended to current players. They suggest the rate could be lower — but it also could be higher.
While the jury’s still out on what these data mean for today’s athletes, I hope Roger Goodell reads Morning Rounds. Here’s the study, if you want to take a look at the data yourself.
The research gap facing trans women and breast cancer risk
The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends cisgender women get regularly screened for breast cancer starting at 40. But what about trans women?
A great story from Rewire News dives into the research gap on this topic, as the most authoritative study on the subject finds only that trans women face less risk than cis women, but more risk than men. That’s 1 in 8 versus 1 in 775.
The few existing guidelines for trans women are based on basically zero data, which is tough to come by for this population. Trans people — including the roughly 700,000 trans women in the U.S. — routinely face discrimination and mistreatment in clinics and hospitals.
My grandmother died of breast cancer at 67. I’m a 33-year-old trans woman. When should I get my first mammogram? For now, science has no answer to that question.

Well ahead of the Black Friday blitz, the Nothing Headphone (1) is steeply discounted, and the CMF Headphone Pro is at its lowest price ever. And when you think about it, there's arguably no better time than now—during the lead-up to holiday-travel season—to gift yourself a pair of high-performing, style-forward headphones to take you through busy airports and long flights.
The Best Nothing Headphone Deals

These earbuds have been coasting at 20 percent off for most of September and October, which is hardly a bad discount, but it's also not the best I've ever seen.
The Best CMF Headphone Deals
CMF is Nothing's sub-brand that focuses on delivering similarly stylish designs at a lower price.
This is the lowest price I’ve ever seen for the CMF Headphone Pro, one of my favorite pairs of cheap over-ear headphones. Frankly, $55 for these is a steal. Sure, they aren’t as premium as Nothing’s models, but they retain the essence: fun, tactile controls; good sound; and access to the useful, reliable Nothing X app, where you can manage settings and tweak an EQ.

Altering copyright law to allow AI companies to scrape music, books and journalism could trigger a constitutional breach, Coalition senators and the recording industry have warned, as they raise new fears it could open Australia to massive legal action and compensation claims from rights holders worldwide.
The attorney general’s department admitted it was “extremely alive” to the issue, and Australia’s leading constitutional expert, Anne Twomey, agreed there was “potentially” a concern – depending how legislation was drafted – that granting AI companies permission to scrape copyrighted material from the internet could amount to an acquisition of property by the government.
In a simmering debate centred on the same legal point as the movie The Castle, the question of acquiring property “on just terms” is emerging as a key concern amid furious lobbying from tech companies and rights holders ahead of a looming federal government announcement on AI.
“We could be liable for ‘just terms’ compensation for acquiring that property for every rights holder on Earth,” Ross Cadell, a Nationals senator, told Guardian Australia.
Michaelia Cash, the shadow attorney general, said the government should not “sell out Australian creators and rights holders in the rush to entice AI investment”.
Labor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of reforms around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material.
Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model which would allow it to scrape content unless a rightholder deployed digital protections signaling an objection.
A fresh concern being aired by sceptics and creatives is that any weakening of copyright to benefit AI could represent a breach of section 51 of the constitution, which allows the commonwealth to make laws about “the acquisition of property on just terms”.
“If they go ahead with an opt-out model, it does raise a real question of whether the government is acquiring the intellectual property rights of others,” said Cadell, a member of the federal parliamentary committee on AI.
“How we support property rights is core to this.”
A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.
Anne Twomey, professor emerita of law at the University of Sydney, said the issue was exceedingly complex and noted no legislative proposal had been aired. She said numerous cases had come before the high court relating to copyright and acquisition of property, including about video games, cigarette plain packaging and cassette tapes, with varying outcomes.
Twomey expected the federal government would be hyperaware of such concerns, but said granting a new right to AI companies to use copyrighted material and diminishing the rights of copyright holders could “potentially” trigger constitutional issues.
“The high court has recognised a number of exceptions to section 51 … One would want to be quite confident before enacting the legislation about whether or not section 51 would apply,” Twomey told Guardian Australia.
She said any change allowing Australia to host AI companies training on international data could potentially create grounds for global rights holders to take legal action here.
Cadell told Guardian Australia he worried about such a development opening the federal government to liability for “the biggest compensation rights case in history”.
Cadell raised his concerns about the constitution in a committee hearing with the attorney general’s department on Friday, in which officials said they were conscious of those issues.
Officials did not directly answer when Cadell asked about international implications and liability for compensation to foreign rights holders.
Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association, claimed any proposal to allow AI companies to scrape data was “clearly an acquisition of property”.
“It’s hard to imagine what kind of compensation would make up for the fact that they’re basically taking our right … and trading it away to the AI companies to then monetise themselves, and that appears to be a clear path to a constitutional challenge.”
Chris Maund, CEO of Mushroom Records, said current copyright law was working and that AI companies should use existing licensing arrangements, noting companies such as Spotify were already making AI-related deals.
He also raised concern about international ramifications were Australia to change copyright law, saying it would not only apply to Australian artists and copyright owners.
“The AI company could do their training here in Australia and circumvent the copyright laws that apply outside of Australia, and that’s why the international creative industries are watching this very closely,” he said.
Maund said international rights holder groups had been urging Labor not to weaken copyright law. Guardian Australia has provided submissions to the Joint Select Committee as a member of Australia’s wider rights holder community.
“The Australian government has been really great to the music industry, particularly Prime Minister Albanese and Tony Burke. They’ve set up Creative Music Australia, which companies like us and our artists have done very well out of, but it feels like they’re out of step with artists and copyright owners on this point,” he said.
Cash said the Coalition welcomed the benefits of AI and wanted investment, but also raised the constitutional concern.
“That is the prime minister’s own test, and the government should be held to it,” she said of compensation to rights holders.
“The constitutional question of property rights and their acquisition on just terms is also a live issue we will be examining depending on what the government puts forward.”
Cadell said while AI had benefits, he worried about its risks.
“There’s lots of talk about what the benefits may be and what may happen. But if we take these rights away, we know what will happen,” Cadell said.
“I don’t want to hurt people for a ‘may’.”

How to come up with a last-minute Halloween costume without spending a ton of money
Tap your creativity (and closet) for the best Halloween costume.
With an October 30 birthday, it’s only natural that Kimberly Murphy takes Halloween extremely seriously. A natural redhead, Murphy has dressed up as iconic crimson-haired characters like the Wendy’s mascot and Chuckie from Rugrats, but once she started dating her now-fiancé, Brian, nearly a decade ago, Murphy’s costumes leveled up. A selection of Murphy and Brian’s greatest Halloween hits: Dexter and Dee Dee from Dexter’s Laboratory, Ms. Frizzle and the eponymous bus from The Magic School Bus, Jack and Sally from The Nightmare Before Christmas, Tormund and Brienne of Tarth from Game of Thrones, and Shaun White and a snowboard.
“We put my snowboard on his back so I could actually ‘ride’ him,” Murphy, who, regardless of the character’s gender, always dresses as the redhead, says. “It gave a funny, experiential element to the costume.”
This October, the couple, both in their early 30s, is getting married and will be depicting Chucky and Bride of Chucky for Halloween. (You can guess who’ll be donning the white dress.)
In childhood, Halloween is one of the few days of the year when you can wear your most imaginative garb to school and to strangers’ doors. As you get older, that sense of youthful creativity might wane, and figuring out what to wear to a costume party becomes another minor conundrum. Whether you dabble in dress-up or are a cosplay aficionado, conceiving of creative, yet approachable, Halloween attire doesn’t need to be a bewildering or expensive experience. Experts in the art of costuming offer their advice for ideating and executing your best guise so you can take home top honors in this year’s costume contest.
Narrow your focus
When every character, celebrity, historical figure, animal, pun, and meme is potential costume fodder, homing in on one idea can feel overwhelming. Limitations and parameters are your best friend. Use your own appearance — is there a person or fictional character who has a similar style as you? Vaguely comparable features? — and the media that interested you this year as jumping-off points. Everything from YA novels and nostalgic ‘90s TV shows to extremely local jokes and gags (public transit, sports mascots) to niche memes (hello, Chris Pine astral projecting) are prime inspo.
Is there an alter ego you’re interested in exploring? Cosplayer and photographer Hope Elmekies often dresses up as characters she feels a personal connection to, like Morticia Addams. “I very much felt like I related to [her] because she’s not fitting in,” she says. “I felt that kinship to that character.”
For all of her costumes, Murphy has let her red hair and the height difference between her and her fiancé (she’s 5 feet tall, he’s 6-foot-2) guide her choices. She thinks back to significant pop culture or historical moments that fall under these categories. For example, Murphy flagged Queen’s Gambit as a potential ensemble, due to its buzzworthiness and the fact that the protagonist had red hair. “I take this formulaic approach to Halloween where if it’s unusually small or redheaded,” she says, “that fits my formula of a potential Halloween candidate.”
For group or family costumes, it can be helpful to focus on one shared interest, accessory, or hobby. If you all met in an adult dodgeball league, maybe you want to dress up as dodgeball players. Maybe your group is composed of three couples and you want to do a Grease-inspired collab.
Then, figure out what effect you’d like your costume to have. Is your goal to make everyone laugh? Be the sexy one? Go all-in on minute details? Incorporate a few friends for a group costume? This can help you zero in on an idea.
The location of your Halloween bash can help further narrow down your options, says custom costume maker Correen Borst-Straub of Correen’s Creative Designs. Think about where you’ll wear the getup to determine what’s appropriate. If you’re going to a party in a small apartment, you probably won’t want to wear a huge Marie Antoinette dress, or you might want to think twice about wearing vampire fangs to a costumed fundraiser with a sit-down dinner.
Buck convention, respectfully
Using popular culture as inspiration may yield a few potential ideas, but if you really want a memorable guise, approach these concepts in an unconventional manner. Many people tend to dress up as the main characters from popular shows, but supporting roles or genre tropes can also be crowd-pleasing attire. For her all-time favorite Halloween costume, Dani Cabot, the manager of New York City vintage boutique Screaming Mimis, dressed up as a virgin sacrifice. “I got bedsheets and a classic cheesy ’70s Roman goddess dress and I got a huge wig, and then a choker that made it look like my throat was slashed,” she says.
Even if you don’t share every physical trait with a character, use your differences to your advantage. Murphy and her fiancé have often dressed up as characters that have historically been depicted as opposite to the couple’s own gender presentation. “Gender is always very subjective,” says Philadelphia-based drag queen VinChelle. “Everyone can express themselves how they want to.” VinChelle frequently performs in looks inspired by Beyoncé and uses the star’s photoshoots as a reference. She’ll then scour fabric stores in Philadelphia or New York City for the garment and works closely with seamstresses to construct the outfit. “Beyoncé’s a glorified drag queen,” she says.
To be clear: This is not an excuse to appropriate other cultures, use makeup to darken your skin, or wear racist costumes. If you’re unsure if a costume is appropriate, run your idea by a few friends first, says Kate Farrier, the wardrobe manager for RWS Entertainment Group, an entertainment and event production company that has produced haunted experiences for the likes of Six Flags Great America, Sea World, and Legoland.
Reference your personal style
Think about ways you can infuse your personality into popular ideas. Say you want to be a witch or a vampire. What can you do to make the costume feel like you? If your one wardrobe staple is a leather jacket, make your witch persona wear a leather jacket. “If you’re always on your phone, maybe you’re a celebrity vampire, social media vampire,” Farrier says. “Try and make it about something that you always have by bringing your personal items into it because that will make it special for you.”
One year, a shopper at Screaming Mimis spiced up their vampire attire by adding ’70s disco accessories. “They did this insane disco Studio 54 vampire look,” Cabot says. You can also take a character who isn’t particularly known for their fashion, like Pac-Man, and make an interesting garment inspired by their aesthetic.
Another way to differentiate is to make subtle changes to tried-and-true depictions. Borst-Straub has a 25 percent rule; she infuses her creativity into well-known designs so the resulting look is 75 percent true to pop culture and 25 percent her own.
Elmekies gets inspiration by searching her costume idea plus “cosplay” on Pinterest to see how others have approached the concept. Don’t worry about being so niche that everyone has to ask you what you are, Elmekies says. “So, what are you?” is a great icebreaker. “Sometimes when I go out as Belle from Beauty and the Beast, people don’t know who I am necessarily because it’s not a Disney knockoff; it’s more built that you can wear every day,” Elmekies says.
Use what you’ve got (or shop secondhand)
Halloween outfits shouldn’t cost a ton of money. Think about the colors, shapes, and silhouettes needed for a costume to help you identify the look’s building blocks. For a gargoyle look, for example, you’ll need a lot of gray apparel and makeup. “Think about the shapes of things instead of the actual items,” says Ryan Walton, the producer of Halloween experiences for RWS Entertainment Group. “[Say] I need a round hoop-like thing. What can I do that’s round and hoop-like that’s not going to cost me a lot of money and then I can refabricate?”
Scour your closet (or your friends’ closets) for pieces you’ll need. If you’re dressing up as a flapper, dig out a slip dress if you have one. Then, let your accessories and props do all the talking. “So things like jewelry, gloves, stockings, headpieces, masks can really transform a basic into something that’s excellent,” Cabot says.
For any pieces you don’t already own, visit a local vintage or thrift store or indie costume shop to get materials. Workers at these stores can offer expert costuming advice, and by shopping in person, you can be sure you’re getting exactly what you want — no online ordering surprises, Cabot says. Shopping secondhand is also far more sustainable than purchasing a polyester outfit from a big-box store. Chances are you can even incorporate aspects of your ensemble into your regular wardrobe, too.
Rock your costume
Ultimately, you’re going to have the best time in an outfit you feel comfortable and confident wearing. Think about how the fabrics and props feel; it’s not worth being constricted by shoes that are impossible to walk in. “You will light up the most when you are wearing something that you love,” VinChelle says. “When I am in my favorite costume, I’m a whole other person.”
Even if you feel like you don’t have the “right” body type for a certain character or look, “you can look at it as this is my character and my character’s just curvy,” Elmekies says. “Realize your character is incredible.”

In July, as supporters of the Cockroach movement took to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, incensed over exam-paper leaks and demanding the resignation of India’s education minister, the rest of the nation realised that for the first time since the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) came to power in 2014, the curse of inertia and the grip of fear had been smashed irrevocably. Prime minister Narendra Modi’s image of invincibility has been punctured.
People in India have been conditioned to believe in an idea of intense slow-burn protests that eventually bring change – but the Cockroaches have shown us that the revolution can be fast-tracked.
This time the Cockroaches are demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, following reports in the Indian Express in late September that he had pushed through a purge of voter rolls. Round one of the Cockroach protests came to an end because the BJP was willing to sacrifice the education minister. Round two does not allow for such scapegoating. If Kumar goes, Modi must go too – it would be an open admission that the electoral system has been compromised.
The response of the BJP so far has been hysterical. The repressive apparatus of the state was out in full force: detentions and arrests of journalists, protesters being roughed up and beaten, an internet blackout in the capital. The Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke’s bravado in announcing his protest plans paid unexpected dividends the first time around. The second time, the continual broadcasting on social media by the three Cockroach leaders seemed like a lack of experience in organising and strategic thinking. Police forces detained them on touchdown at Delhi airport on the morning of the protest. They alleged that thousands of their members faced preventive detention or were not allowed to reach the capital city.
So at protests on 10 October, the CJP leaders were conspicuous by their absence. Only leftwing and Congress-allied student organisations, prominent gutsy young activists (Neha Bora, Aishe Ghosh, Gurmehar Kaur) and their elected political representatives held the ground and faced the worst of the police brutality.
The absence of the Cockroach leadership on the ground notwithstanding, the protests continued in pockets, eventually reaching a crescendo on 12 October. Heeding a call by Rahul Gandhi on behalf of the Congress-led opposition bloc, the streets of Delhi were filled in an act of defiance the like of which I have not witnessed in my lifetime. The state, however, seemed to have got the memo beforehand. The Delhi police and security forces numbered 90,000, 45 metro stations were closed in the inner city and trains to Delhi were cancelled. Student activists travelling to the capital were picked up en route from their railway carriages.
The following day, a small group of Cockroaches were arrested entering Jantar Mantar, which the Delhi police had banned from being used as a protest site. Two of the group’s leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained and subsequently sent to jail for five days.
Despite the high-handed approach of the police, the people are still clamouring for battle on the streets. Every screengrab, every video, every reel reinforces the feeling that we are witnessing a carnivalisation of the protests. The songs, the slogans, the sudden bursts of dancing, the satirical placards, the sheer joy of the crowds: this is Mikhail Bakhtin’s carnivalesque. What is the cause for such celebration? This: the state is evidently in retreat. People have begun to treat power as something to be ridiculed.
One of the most popular slogans has been Jab jab Modi darta hai, police ko aage karta hai (“Whenever Modi is afraid, he pushes the police forward”). The regime’s undiluted dread was most visible at Connaught Place in central Delhi on 16 October, when the CJP had called on people to gather at Central Park for a flag-waving celebration. The New Delhi Municipal Council shut down the park for two days and an elaborate fortification followed. The park was cordoned off, security personnel formed a human chain along the metal railings and 220 companies of the Central Armed Police Forces were deployed alongside the Rapid Action Force and the Delhi police.
Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke and communist student leader Neha Bora were both detained as they made their way towards Connaught Place. Neither was allowed to contact lawyers until late into the night, and lack of knowledge about their whereabouts caused panic online. Neha was released from detention the following morning, and Abhijeet could walk free on conditional bail.
For over a decade, the regime crushed students and dissenters by branding them anti-national and punishing them under the draconian Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The genius of the Cockroach protest lay in something very simple – how could the state frame the waving of the Indian national flag as an anti-national activity? We now have a government that is not confident of its own legitimacy; it views the tricolour as a weapon when it is in the hands of its citizens.
The powerlessness of the state could also be seen in its desperation to police the online space: it summoned Meta officials over the summer and imposed an internet shutdown earlier this month. For a party that coasted to power with post-truth propaganda on WhatsApp, its undisputed dominance on X and heavy investment in keeping social media influencers on its payroll, the algorithms (or their oligarch owners) may well have turned. It is impossible to capture the entire social media ecosystem with threats and purchasing power alone.
For the regime, it is a losing battle against the newfound visual grammar that has defined a wave of protests around the world: nothing is as seductive as young women defiantly clashing with uniformed police, or an opposition leader who climbs the barricades and waves the national flag. The German philosopher Walter Benjamin wrote about the tendency for fascism to lean into the aestheticisation of politics – today, looking at Delhi, he would be pleased to report back that the aesthetic can also be snatched back by the masses.
On 12 October, after the mass mobilisation, Gandhi addressed the media by saying: “This is tandav, Lord Shiva’s dance. There is no planning here”, and “This is the wedding procession of Shiva, anyone can join in”. These references to Shiva are a calculated manoeuvre. It is a nod to India’s majority Hindus who, time and time again, have been sold the lie that their sole protector is Modi.
Modi recently went Bhajan clubbing – a kind of rave setup with remixed Hindu devotional music – in a desperate attempt to establish his gen Z connections. But he may find the rug pulled from beneath his feet. Modi’s base rewarding the BJP election after election for weaponising their faith did not secure jobs for the next generation. And now it is their own children who are at the receiving end of the state’s violence.
Saving India cannot happen without pulling Hindus out from the vicious grip of extremist Hindutva. This is one unforeseen outcome of this protest and the wider movement. Whether it topples the government or not, it has shown it can unite people against the divisive force that is the BJP.
- Meena Kandasamy is a poet and writer based in Chennai

Delhi's Jamia University agrees to students’ demands, sets timeline for union polls
The Jamia university administration has directed that the students' union constitution be completed by May 15, 2027.
Delhi's Jamia Millia Islamia on Thursday agreed to key demands raised by protesting students, including setting a timeline for the implementation of the Students' Union constitution and revoking disciplinary action linked to the protests.
Offline classes are set to resume on Monday, November 2. The university administration directed that the students' union constitution be completed by May 15, 2027, with elections to be held within six weeks of the commencement of the academic session on July 16, 2027.
All disciplinary actions, show-cause notices, suspensions and campus bans linked to students' participation in the protests will also be revoked.
The development comes as the agitation over the restoration of an elected Jamia Millia Islamia Students’ Union (JMISU) entered its 18th day. The union has remained defunct since 2006, and students have been demanding a time-bound plan for holding elections.
Students mark Foundation Day with ‘Inquilabi Mela’
Protesting students marked the university’s 106th Foundation Day on Thursday by organising an ‘Inquilabi Mela’ near Gate No. 7, boycotting the official celebrations, PTI reported earlier. The gathering was held at Gulistan-e-Ghalib, where five students were on hunger strike demanding the restoration of the elected students’ union.
The students -- Ebin Basil, Rehan Khan, Ritik, Altaf and Abuzar -- said the event reflected Jamia’s founding ideals of democratic participation, freedom of expression and respect for dissent. The protesters had also demanded the withdrawal of disciplinary measures against those involved in the agitation, the release of students placed in judicial custody and a clear deadline for resuming regular academic activities.
Students oppose online classes
The university’s decision to extend online classes until November 24 and conduct odd-semester examinations online had triggered further opposition. The administration had cited concerns over the campus situation and the safety and security of students.
Students from the Department of Commerce and Business Studies, through their subject association, submitted a memorandum opposing the move. They said the lack of a firm date for resuming physical classes had created uncertainty over their studies and access to university facilities.
The students argued that those enrolled in regular courses needed classroom discussions, peer interaction and practical exposure, which online teaching could not fully provide. They also highlighted the financial burden on students who had relocated or arranged accommodation near the campus.
A student group claimed that students from more than 100 classes had approached their teachers seeking the restoration of offline classes and examinations. Protesters had also announced a boycott of online classes until the campus reopened.
Under the earlier schedule, online practical, fieldwork, project, viva and minor project examinations were to be held from November 25 to 30, followed by theory examinations from December 1 to 24. Winter vacation was scheduled from December 25 to January 12, with even-semester classes set to begin on January 13.
The administration had initially extended online classes until November 8 before issuing the October 28 order extending the arrangement until November 24.
Disciplinary action adds to tensions
The university’s action against students had become another major point of contention. A show-cause notice dated October 27 was issued to a resident of Begum Hazrat Mahal girls’ hostel over allegations that she had obtained emergency leave on misleading grounds before taking part in the protests.
The hostel’s provost asked her to submit a written explanation within 24 hours, warning that an unsatisfactory response could lead to disciplinary action.
A notice circulated by the hostel’s discipline committee also said residents had been asked to take compulsory leave by November 1 because of the online academic schedule. However, a university official said no official notification directing students to vacate hostels had been issued.

Warren Buffett hasn't had a glass of water since at least the 1970s.
That's what the 96-year-old business icon once told Bill Ackman, the billionaire hedge fund manager recalled during an episode of the Equity Mates Investing podcast that aired this week.
Ackman said that Buffett came over for dinner at his home "years ago," and he'd made sure to stock up on the legendary investor's favorite drink, Cherry Coke.
The Pershing Square founder and CEO said that once they were sitting at the table, he asked Buffett whether he'd like still or sparkling water. Buffett politely declined, opting for his preferred soda instead.
"But I said, you know, 'Don't you drink water?'" Ackman recalled. "And he said, 'Bill, I haven't had water in 48 years.'"
Ackman didn't immediately respond to a request for more detail about Buffett's hydration habits.
Not drinking water might sound unbelievable, but Buffett — who retired as Berkshire Hathaway's CEO after 60 years in charge last December, and as the company's chairman this September — is famous for drinking five cans of Coke daily.
He quipped in 2015 that he was "one-quarter Coca-Cola," as it accounted for 25% of his daily calories.
Buffett's love of soda goes back decades. During Berkshire's 1986 meeting, he declared that after "48 years of allegiance" to Pepsi, he was switching to Cherry Coke, saying it would be the meeting's official drink going forward.
Coca-Cola has also been one of Buffett's landmark investments. Berkshire hasn't touched its roughly 9% stake in the beverage giant since it finished building it in the mid-1990s. The position cost about $1.3 billion and was worth around $28 billion at the end of December — a roughly 21-fold gain.
Coke is only part of Buffett's iconic diet. He's known for grabbing McDonald's for breakfast on his drive to work, and munching on hot dogs, fries, popcorn, cookies, candy, ice cream, and other comfort foods.
His love of fast food and sweet treats extends to his investments. Berkshire counts See's Candies and Dairy Queen among its subsidiaries, and Kraft Heinz among its largest stock holdings.
Buffett's childlike tastes have led to issues in the past, including a disastrous sushi dinner in Tokyo.
Bill Gates and his then-wife, Melinda, went to great lengths to ensure the investor didn't starve when he joined them on a 17-day trip to China in 1995.
They organized for their hotel's chefs to be taught how to prepare hamburgers and fries, and when they climbed the Great Wall, they made sure to have Cherry Coke waiting for Buffett at the top.

The Keralam government will introduce a Bill in the next Assembly session to regulate high medical treatment costs in private hospitals, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan told the Assembly on Monday (October 26, 2026).
He was responding to a question from Communist Party of India (Marxist) MLA K.N. Balagopal on the steps being taken by the government to regulate the trend of some major hospitals, in which global private equity firms now have big stakes, inflating treatment costs.

The Wikimedia Foundation weighs in on the NYT's case against OpenAI
The folks behind Wikipedia say that an extreme decision in either direction could threaten the open web.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
The Wikimedia Foundation has weighed in on the copyright lawsuit launched by The New York Times against OpenAI and Microsoft. The people behind Wikipedia have filed an amicus brief urging nuance in the case, which seeks to decide whether or not OpenAI and Microsoft's use of content published in The New York Times for any purpose, including AI model training, is a violation of copyright law.
The New York Times says that companies like OpenAI shouldn't be given free reign over any of their published content. OpenAI and Microsoft say that training and deploying AI models based on published data is necessary for technological development and would therefore fall within the definition of fair use.
The Wikimedia Foundation, however, is seeking a third way. The amicus brief agrees with Microsoft and OpenAI and suggests that a much more restrictive version of fair use could inhibit tech innovation. However, it also says that a ruling in favor of blanket fair use could lead to a closed web where knowledge is weakened due to a "lack of available secondary source materials."
The platform's alternative position applies fair use to two specific use cases for AI companies. This includes certain model training scenarios and something called retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This is a technique that optimizes the output of large language models (LLMs) by referencing authoritative knowledge bases outside of its training data. However, the organization does not support RAG if an LLM is regurgitating pre-existing articles without attribution.
As for the specifics of model training, the Wikimedia Foundation argues that scraping copyrighted content should be considered fair use if it's being used when "training LLMs that are something new and different from the original sources." It is worth noting that Wikipedia itself is considered one of the highest-quality datasets used to train LLMs.
"A ruling that does not apply fair use principles carefully could threaten the sustainability of free knowledge, and stifle the development of open source technologies, ultimately impacting access to information for everyone in both cases," the Wikimedia Foundation's General Counsel Stephen LaPorte wrote. "The court needs to understand that Wikipedia is created through a collaborative process that requires a strong foundation of open and accessible human knowledge to thrive."
A summary judgment in the lawsuit is expected in the near future. This is just one of over a dozen similar cases working their way through the courts, but it could set an important precedent.

Senators are looking into 'serious privacy risks' with Meta's AI glasses
'Meta's smart glasses have increasingly been implicated in disturbing invasions of privacy.'
US Senators Ron Wyden (D-Or) and and Edward Markey (D-Ma) are investigating "serious privacy and safety risks" around Meta's AI smart glasses. "Meta's smart glasses have increasingly been implicated in disturbing invasions of users' and bystanders' privacy," the pair wrote in a letter to Mark Zuckerberg, adding that Meta launched the product even after identifying risks to bystander privacy.
The senators highlighted multiple incidents of Meta's glasses being used in "disturbing" invasions of privacy. It cited both 404 Media and BBC articles about men secretly filming women with Meta's "pervert glasses" while harassing them, then posting the recordings to social media. It also noted that according to other reports and a lawsuit, Meta's AI contractors said they reviewed footage captured by the eyewear showing people undressing and engaging in sexual activity.
The senators requested that Meta respond to specific questions about accidental camera activation and recording-indicator tampering. They also want to know if the glasses blur faces and license plates for certain AI interactions, like Meta does on Facebook and Instagram. It asked Meta to explain the circumstances that imagery is made accessible to employees or contracts, or when it's used to train AI models. Finally, citing Meta's own documents, it asked the company whether it conducted detailed human rights due diligence and safety testing on its glasses before releasing them. It requested those responses by Thanksgiving (November 26, 2026).
The list of complaints about Meta's glasses is long. On top of the ones cited by Wyden and Markey, users have said that the glasses were recording their conversations without consent following a firmware update. They've also been spotted on ICE agents during raids, and the New York City Police's counterterrorism unit reportedly raised surveillance concerns about the devices in January this year. Earlier in October, California Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed a bill that would have banned people from using wearables to secretly record others in private areas of business.
However, Wyden and Markey seem more determined to hold the social media giant's feet to the fire. "Meta's professed commitment to privacy and preventing intimate image abuse rings hollow if the company cannot demonstrate meaningful steps to prevent its own products and practices from facilitating those harms," the senators told Zuckerberg.

New Delhi, Oct 30: The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has released findings of Independent Drive Test (IDT) conducted across Leh and nearby areas route under J&K LSA, during the month of August 2026, for information of general telecom consumers. The purpose of this drive test is to assess and verify real time quality of mobile network services (both voice & data) provided by Telecom Service Providers (TSPs). During the IDT, TRAI captures performance of TSPs for key Quality of Service (QoS) parameters like Coverage, Call Drop Rate (CDR), Call Setup Success Rate (CSSR), data Download (DL) and Upload (UL) throughput etc., which are then published to inform Consumers and encourage TSPs to improve their services.
These IDTs have been designed to capture on ground mobile network performance of all TSPs across diverse usages environment like cities, hotspots, public transport hubs, etc. In this type of drive testing, live data and voice sessions are established using SIM cards from all TSPs over 2G, 3G, 4G and 5G networks. Multiple advanced test handsets are used, and the sessions are monitored and analyzed in real-time using advanced Software Systems.
TRAI, through its appointed agency, conducted drive tests across City drive – 62.6 Km, Hotspot locations - 07, Walk Test - 1.1 Km, Inter Operator Calling at 01 location and on Highway drive - 396.3 Km during 17th Aug 2026 to 21st Aug 2026 in J&K LSA. These tests were conducted under the supervision of the TRAI Regional Office Delhi. The observations presented in drive test reports represent the performance of the TSPs on the area / route under test on the day / time of conducting the drive test.

Key Parameters Assessed
Coverage Gap: Percentage of samples, for which signal strength observed less than the minimum prescribed signal strength for respective technology (2G/ 3G/ 4G/ 5G).
Voice Services: Call Setup Success Rate (CSSR), Drop Call Rate (DCR), Call Setup Time, Call Silence Rate, Speech Quality (MOS).
Call Silence Instance: Number of call silence instances occurred during the calls.
Data Services: Download / Upload Throughput, Latency, Jitter, Packet Drop Rate.

Industry body Nasscom has urged the finance ministry to defer the implementation of the revised GST rules for ecommerce delivery services to January 2027. In a representation submitted to the ministry on October 28, the industry body sought an adequate transition period for marketplaces to overhaul their technology, accounting and compliance systems in line with the new regime. It also urged the ministry to conduct consultations with ecommerce operators, logistics providers and other businesses impacted by the new norms. It is pertinent to note that the GST rules were notified on October 27 and are scheduled to take effect on November 1, leaving companies only a few days to comply. The changes follow recommendations made by the 57th GST Council on October 8. The new norms introduce a 5% GST rate without input tax credit (ITC) for specified delivery services. The rules also revised the scope of services for which ecommerce operators must discharge tax liability. “While these changes aim to bring greater consistency to GST treatment, their implementation would require significant adjustments across the ecommerce and logistics ecosystem,” Nasscom said. Citing its rationale, Nasscom said that implementing the new framework would require changes to enterprise resource planning (ERP) configurations, invoicing, tax calculations, input tax credit treatment and GST compliance processes. The industry body also noted that marketplaces would need to examine the notified provisions, assess how they apply to different operating models and test their systems before deployment. Based on industry assessments, Nasscom requested a January 1 implementation date to complete the necessary adjustments. The association also called for industry-wide consultation to clarify requirements and address implementation challenges, arguing that coordinated preparation would help prevent avoidable disruptions. At the heart of the development is the revised tax framework, which reduces GST on specified delivery services from 18% to 5% but also removes the eligibility for ITC. This means impacted service providers cannot offset eligible GST paid on business inputs against their output tax liability. As such, a lower headline rate does not necessarily translate into an equivalent reduction in operating costs or customer delivery charges. The impact will depend on each business’s structure and input tax position. The notified wording also replaces “local delivery” with “delivery services, other than postal and courier services”, broadening the description beyond local deliveries. With this, the immediate question for ecommerce platforms is whether the government will extend the deadline and give businesses more time to align their systems with the new regime. Will the finance ministry give in? Only time will tell.

The Madras High Court has issued notice on a public interest litigation (PIL) seeking a detailed investigation into the background and identity documents of Yogesh Sharma, also known as Saurav Das, the National Co-Convenor of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP). A businessman approached the court on Friday, seeking directions to the Union Ministry of Home Affairs to conduct an immediate, detailed and fair investigation into Das and his parents, news agency PTI reported. In his petition, Ganesh Kumar alleged that Das's lineage could be traced to Nepal and argued that the claim required investigation. He contended that if the allegation was found to be true, "he cannot lecture about our government and our judiciary." The petitioner also accused Das of "abusing" the judiciary and sought the cancellation of his passport and Aadhaar card if he was found guilty of the alleged violations. A first bench comprising Chief Justice S A Dharmadhikari and Justice G Arul Murugan heard the PIL filed by Kumar, a resident of Kancheepuram district. The court ordered notice, returnable by six weeks, to the Union government, the Regional Passport Officer and 10 others. Kumar also sought directions to the Ministry of Electronics and Telecommunications to block the Twitter and Instagram accounts operating under the name "Saurav Das". The petition sought to prevent Das from making further derogatory statements against the judiciary and judges of the Supreme Court. It also sought an order restraining him from making allegedly defamatory, browbeating, abusive, vulgar, barbaric and disparaging statements against the judiciary, including personal remarks against judges of the Supreme Court, high courts and lower courts. The petitioner argued that such remarks should not be permitted in the guise of freedom of speech and expression, whether made through traditional media or social media platforms. He further sought to extend the proposed restraint to statements made through Das's friends, colleagues, agents or representatives while the case remained pending. In his petition, Kumar alleged that Das had repeatedly made abusive remarks against the judiciary and claimed that such conduct amounted to an abuse of the Constitution. He further alleged that if information about Das having Nepali roots was true, Yogesh Sharma had deliberately concealed these details and fraudulently obtained an Aadhaar card, Voter ID card and Indian passport. The petitioner sought an investigation into how Das obtained these identity documents and the sources of funding allegedly supporting his activities. He also called for an inquiry into the individuals or entities providing funds to Das and the accounts through which the money was received. Kumar argued that a detailed investigation into these aspects was necessary in the interest of the nation and accountability. The allegations and requests form part of the petition before the Madras High Court. The court has issued notice to the respondents, with the matter returnable in six weeks.
