Potions in Fisch provide temporary boosts that can help you catch fish faster. You can use these potions to increase your luck, lure speed, and even duplicate the fish you catch. In this guide, we will tell you how to get potions in Fisch and how to use them.
List of Potions in Fisch
There are currently four types of potions in Fisch. Every potion comes with different tiers and effects. On the Fisch map, you will find them in multiple areas. Here is a complete list of all Fisch potions, their uses, and how to get them:
| Potion | Tier | Obtainment | Effect | Duration | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All Season Potion | Tier 1 | Personal Aquarium, Challenges | Removes Luck debuffs on fish that are not in their preferred season and grants All Seasons and Lure IV (+20% Lure Speed) | 3 hours | 
| Luck Potion | Tier 1 | Personal Aquarium, Daily Reward, Challenges | Lucky+ II: 1.5x Luck | 15 minutes | 
|  | Tier 2 | Shady Alchemist, Challenges | Lucky+ III: 1.75x Luck | 30 minutes | 
|  | Tier 3 | Shady Alchemist, Friend Quest | Lucky+ IV: 2x Luck | 1 hour | 
| Glitched Potion | Tier 1 | Personal Aquarium, Bloop Cosmetic Crate, Black Market, Angler Quest (3.15%), Daily Reward | Glitched I: 50% chance to duplicate caught fish with the Glitched Attribute | 10 minutes | 
|  | Tier 2 | Shady Alchemist, Challenges | Glitched II: 75% chance to duplicate caught fish with the Glitched Attribute | 15 minutes | 
|  | Tier 3 | Shady Alchemist, Challenges | Glitched III: 100% chance to duplicate caught fish with the Glitched Attribute | 20 minutes | 
| Lure Speed Potion | Tier 1 | Personal Aquarium, Challenges | Lure V: +25% Lure Speed | 15 minutes | 
|  | Tier 2 | Shady Alchemist, Challenges | Lure VII: +35% Lure Speed | 30 minutes | 
|  | Tier 3 | Shady Alchemist | Lure IX: +45% Lure Speed | 1 hour | 
You can also upgrade some potions to higher tiers for stronger effects and longer durations. Combine the potions with the Fisch enchantments and catch fish faster.
How to Get All Potions in Fisch
There are multiple ways you can get potions in Fisch. Some are available as random rewards, while others you can purchase or upgrade.
Personal Aquarium
The Personal Aquarium is one of the best sources of potions in Fisch. You can enter this hub through the “Aquariums” menu at the top of your screen. Here you can display up to 10 fish and earn hourly rewards even when you are offline.
These rewards include C$ (in-game currency), XP, and potions. Here are the chances of receiving each potion from your personal aquarium:
| Potion | Chance | Average Time | Expected Quantity per Hour | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Luck Potion | 1.25% | 0.816 hours | 1.225 | 
| Lure Speed Potion | 1.25% | 0.816 hours | 1.225 | 
| All Season Potion | 1.25% | 0.816 hours | 1.225 | 
| Glitched Potion | 0.25% | 4.082 hours | 0.245 | 
Weekly Challenges
You can check your active weekly challenges from the menu. Completing these tasks rewards you with different items depending on the challenge difficulty.
If you are lucky, you might get multiple quests with potions as a reward.
Daily Rewards
Like most Roblox games, Fisch also gives you a reward every day when you log in. These rewards include in-game currency, relics, and potions. You can claim one reward each day, but missing a day resets your progress to Day 1. After Day 7, the reward cycle starts again. Here is the complete daily reward schedule:
| Day | Rewards | 
|---|---|
| Day 1 | 500 C$ | 
| Day 2 | 1 Enchant Relic | 
| Day 3 | 1 Random Egg | 
| Day 4 | 1 Luck Potion | 
| Day 5 | 1 Exalted Relic | 
| Day 6 | 1 Glitched Potion | 
| Day 7 | 1 Cosmic Relic | 
Fisch Codes
If you regularly redeem the Fisch codes, there is a chance of getting a couple of potions. Yes, the developers give away potions with the other valuable rewards in the codes.
Shady Alchemist
The Shady Alchemist is an NPC located inside The Shady Bazaar, opposite the Hunting Angler. You can visit this NPC to upgrade your Tier 1 potions into stronger versions. However, each upgrade requires a specific number of potions and S$. Here are all the potion upgrades you can get:
| Potions | Tier | Requirements | Stock | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Glitched Potion | Tier 2 | 9 Tier 1 Glitched Potions and 10 S$ | 5 |

| Luck Potion | Tier 2 | 3 Tier 1 Luck Potions and 2 S$ | 6 |

Note: The Shady Alchemist has limited stock, so you may need to check back later if a potion is unavailable.
Once you have the potion, you can place it on your hotbar and press LMB to use it. The buff from the potion is shown on the bottom-left UI.
That was everything you needed to know about Fisch potions. You can now use them to catch rare fish and make money faster in Fisch.

Anderson 'shocked' by Lancs exit and unsure if he will continue
- Published
England legend James Anderson says he is "sad" and "shocked" by his release by Lancashire and has not decided whether to continue his career at another county.
Speaking at length on the Tailenders podcast for the first time since being told he will not have his Lancashire contract renewed, the 44-year-old said the decision made him question whether there is "something fundamentally wrong with me as a person".
Anderson, England's leading wicket-taker and a Lancashire legend, took 50 wickets in the County Championship and served as captain last season but he was told by Lancashire's new hierarchy they want to build an attack for the future.
"I went in for what I thought was a conversation about how the team moves forward," Anderson said.
"It wasn't a great year for the team. Being captain I thought it was chat about that.
"A couple of minutes in I realised it wasn't a conversation. I was being told they thought the best way for the team to move forward was without me.
"I was quite shocked. It was quite brief."
Lancashire's decision was made by their incoming director of cricket Paul Farbrace, who held a meeting with Anderson and Lancashire's new chief executive Richard Kenyon.
Despite Anderson's wickets, the club finished second bottom in Division Two of the County Championship.
In 2024, England also chose to move on from their record wicket-taker in similar circumstances as they attempted to refresh and build an attack for the 2025-26 Ashes in Australia.
"All of the way through the season myself and the head coach were like 'is it something we are doing? Could we be doing more to help the team?'" Anderson said.
"I finished the season thinking 'was it something I did? Was I doing something wrong?' - and then I get this news.
"Now I am thinking that even more.
"I am thinking 'this is happening again. Is there something fundamentally wrong with me as a person?' Your head just sort of races.
"I wanted to see my career out with Lancs.
"I don't know if my career is done, we will have to wait and see, but it would be nice at some point if someone would let me retire."
'I wouldn't have thought so' - Anderson on Yorkshire move
The decision has angered Lancashire members and was criticised for being "pretty disrespectful" by Anderson's former England bowling partner Stuart Broad, who said it showed a lack of leadership given the veteran was not given a farewell.
Anderson first played List A cricket in 2000 as a 17-year-old for the Lancashire Cricket Board against Suffolk.
In addition to his 911 international wickets - an England record and a record for all pace bowlers - Anderson claimed 443 first-class scalps for Lancashire, along with 83 in List A cricket and a further 50 in T20s.
It is understood other counties are interested in signing the bowler, who turns 45 next summer.
He joked he "wouldn't have thought" he could play for Lancashire's historic rivals Yorkshire, but on his future added: "I am still trying to process everything and weigh up the best way forward for me.
"It has been 10 days since it happened.
"I am starting to get excited about the future, whether it is something different or playing cricket again. It is exciting.
"There are exciting challenges ahead. I have to attack it like that and not dwell too much on how or why it finished at Lancs."
He added: "I am sad the way it ended with the club I supported as a kid but now I have thought about it I am quite excited for the future.
"I am always going to support Lancashire.
"I was born there, grew up watching them, had some of my most memorable days out with dad watching them, got to play for them and captain the club, which is something most people dream about.
"I feel like I have a special connection with the club and will always support them."

Police secured Poland's Constitutional Tribunal as dozens of protesters gathered to demonstrate against what they perceive as the wrongful suspension of the top court's president by the current pro-European government.
Police said they detained three people after some protesters breached the tribunal's fence and others threw objects at officers.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki, who was flying to Senegal, said he turned his flight back because of the situation. “At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland. I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning,” he wrote on X.
Poland's top judicial bodies, including the Constitutional Tribunal, have been a major bone of contention between the current pro-European government and the main opposition party, national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS).
Critics in Poland and the European Union accuse PiS, which led the country between 2015 and 2023, of imposing political control over key judicial institutions, including the Constitutional Tribunal. The PiS reforms led the EU to impose fines on Poland.
Old values, new avenues: On India-Poland ties
The pro-European government of Donald Tusk came to power in 2023 with a promise to restore the independence of the judiciary. Since then, the government's efforts have been blocked by vetoes from two successive presidents aligned with PiS, including Nawrocki.
The information about the suspension of the president of the Constitutional Tribunal, Bogdan Swieczkowski, was published on the website of the court around 6 p.m. local time. The website of the Tribunal went down soon after, so The Associated Press could not independently verify the official reasons given for his suspension.
Mr. Swieczkowski became head of the Constitutional Tribunal under the PiS government, and Mr. Tusk has accused him of blocking judges elected by the parliamentary majority from taking up their posts at the tribunal.
“Restoring the rule of law is our obligation," Prime Minister Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening (October 30, 2026). "After years of lawlessness under PiS, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
Speaking about the future of the Constitutional Tribunal at Campus Polska in August, Mr. Tusk said his government had a plan to ensure the tribunal would be staffed again with lawfully appointed judges while acknowledging his methods may not be to everyone's liking.
Politicians from PiS, currently the largest opposition force, have criticised Mr. Swieczkowski's suspension.
“This is a blatant, criminal attack on the constitutional order," former Justice Minister Zbigniew Ziobro wrote on X on Friday evening (October 30, 2026). “That is why I call for resistance that will be loud, firm, solidary and fearless.”

Despite significant economic progress and sustained public health efforts, anaemia — driven significantly by iron deficiency — continues to be one of India’s most pressing public health challenges. Affecting over half of Indian women and almost three-fourths of children, anaemia contributes to maternal mortality, an intergenerational cycle of malnutrition, impaired cognitive development, reduced productivity and substantial economic losses. The Government of India’s 7X7X7 Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, which was launched recently, rightly recognises the multifactorial nature of anaemia through a comprehensive approach spanning prevention, screening, treatment, dietary diversification and behaviour change. Yet, one proven preventive intervention remains significantly underutilised.
The promise of fortification
That intervention is Double Fortified Salt (DFS) — salt fortified with both iodine and iron. Salt offers an unparalleled opportunity to address iron deficiency. Consumed daily by virtually every household across India, in predictable quantities regardless of income or geography, it is uniquely suited to deliver a preventive nutrition intervention at population scale. DFS also addresses one of the fundamental challenges of anaemia control — sustained compliance.
Delivering iron through an everyday food complements interventions such as iron supplementation and dietary diversification, whose effectiveness depends on regular adherence. India already has one of the world’s most successful public health platforms in Universal Salt Iodisation, with around 95% of households consuming iodised salt. Building on this existing infrastructure, DFS is already distributed to an estimated 76 million people across four States through government safety-net programmes. Global and Indian evidence strongly support DFS. A global review has shown that DFS can reduce anaemia by up to 21%. Randomised controlled trials in Bengaluru, Darjeeling, and Punjab, along with large-scale implementation in Uttar Pradesh, have shown improvements in iron status and confirmed that, when manufactured to validated specifications, DFS is acceptable to consumers, reduces iron deficiency, and is highly cost-effective. A DFS standard has been issued by the Government of India’s Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI), and the Government of India actually mandates DFS’ inclusion in the national school feeding programme (PM POSHAN and the national early childhood development programme- Integrated Child Development Scheme, or ICDS).
At an estimated cost of ₹14-₹20 per person annually, DFS represents one of the most affordable population-level nutrition interventions available, with a benefit-cost ratio of 4.2:1 for national DFS introduction, primarily driven by improved health outcomes and subsequent increases in labour productivity. India also possesses the manufacturing capacity to produce high-quality DFS at scale. Established fortification technologies, centralised salt production and existing laboratory infrastructure make quality assurance and regulatory monitoring simpler than for many other fortified foods.
What the barriers are
What has limited DFS from wider adoption? The barriers are now primarily institutional rather than technical. The next imperative is to accelerate its nationwide adoption and ensure last-mile access, particularly the Public Distribution System apart from social safety-net programmes, across all States through a central flagship scheme. Although DFS is recommended under PM POSHAN and ICDS, its integration into the largest safety net programme i.e., the Public Distribution System (PDS) — which reaches around 800 million beneficiaries — remains uneven because implementation depends largely on State governments. Greater policy commitment, dedicated financing, stronger quality assurance, wider commercial availability and consumer awareness are now needed to accelerate nationwide scale-up. These are implementation challenges — not technological ones — and are well within India’s capacity to address.
Like all public health nutrition interventions, DFS should be implemented within a robust regulatory framework. It should complement existing strategies under Anaemia Mukt Bharat, align with India’s sodium reduction goals, and continue to be accompanied by screening for haemoglobinopathies such as thalassaemia and sickle cell disease. These safeguards are well recognised through experience of rice fortification programme and can be readily integrated into implementation and monitoring systems.
The launch of the revised AMB strategy provides renewed momentum to strengthen the preventive pillar of India’s anaemia response and advance the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
Potential to be a global model
India has already shown the world how science, policy, public systems, and public awareness can transform nutrition through Universal Salt Iodisation. By scaling DFS nationally, India can not only accelerate progress towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat but also contribute to global efforts to reduce iron deficiency by demonstrating an affordable, scalable model for other low- and middle-income countries.

The Union Cabinet on 28 October approved a ₹10,000-crore scheme to boost domestic container manufacturing, with an aim to raise India's annual capacity from 70,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) to 7.5 lakh TEUs by FY40. The outlay includes ₹8,891 crore for operating-cost support, ₹859 crore in interest subsidies and ₹150 crore for testing and certification.
Mint explains why India wants to build a domestic container industry and what the scheme seeks to achieve.
Why does India want to manufacture shipping containers?
Containers, the steel boxes that carry freight across the world, are among the foundations of globalization, according to economist and journalist Marc Levinson, author of The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger, first published in 2006.
“What is it about the container that is so important? Surely not the thing itself. A soulless aluminum or steel box held together with welds and rivets, with a wooden floor and two enormous doors at one end: the standard container has all the romance of a tin can,” Levinson wrote in the book's opening paragraphs, before describing containers as a major advancement for the global economy. “The container made shipping cheap, and by doing so changed the shape of the world economy,” he said.
Yet manufacturing remains highly concentrated. China accounted for more than 97% of global container production in FY26, compared with India's 0.5%, according to the FY26 annual report of the National Shipping Board, the highest advisory body on maritime affairs under the Union ministry of ports, shipping and waterways.
Union minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said India aims to capture 15-20% of global container manufacturing by FY40, reducing dependence on a sector where production is concentrated in one country.
Domestic capacity could also help during supply-chain disruptions. During the West Asia war in April, for instance, Indian mango exporters faced a shortage of refrigerated containers and had to rely on more expensive alternatives, alongside higher freight rates.
Why does China dominate production?
The China Container Industry Association reported in April 2026 that China produced about 6.45 million TEUs in 2025, retaining its lead in global manufacturing. India's current capacity is around 70,000 TEUs, Vaishnaw said on Wednesday.
China's advantage rests on an established manufacturing ecosystem. Container makers operate in clusters, sourcing steel, a key raw material, from nearby plants. China is also the world's largest steel producer.
Decades-old relationships with shipping lines, logistics operators and suppliers have strengthened this ecosystem. Its position as a major exporter also supports sustained demand. China exported $3.77 trillion worth of merchandise in 2025, according to the World Trade Organization.
What does the ₹10,000-crore scheme offer?
India had been considering a ₹11,000-crore production-linked incentive scheme for container manufacturing in FY24, Mint reported in July 2024. The Cabinet has now approved a ₹10,000-crore support scheme over 13 years.
The scheme offers support across manufacturing costs, including concessional port lease rates for container makers and partial interest subsidies on capital loans. Most of the outlay, however, will cover operating expenses.
The government has earmarked ₹8,891 crore, nearly 90% of the total, for fiscal incentives linked to production. The support will amount to ₹49,500 per 20-foot container, ₹86,625 per 40-foot container and ₹37,125-74,250 per specialised 20-foot container, according to Vaishnaw's presentation during a press briefing on Wednesday.
Industry executives say the scheme could strengthen domestic supply and reduce vulnerability to shortages.
“During any supply chain disruption, a container shortage occurs. Having a domestic container making industry would certainly reduce the risk of a shortage. Moreover, some of the containers made in India can also be used for local freight transportation, something that imported containers cannot be used for,” said Shankar Shinde, managing director of Mumbai-based reefer service provider Global Express Multilogistics Pvt. Ltd. and former chairman of the Federation of Freight Forwarders' Associations in India.
Which sectors stand to benefit?
The steel industry is a direct beneficiary because containers are made of steel. Trade is another key link: higher exports require more containers. This also supports India's broader push for export-led growth, with trade agreements signed with the European Union, the UK and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), alongside ongoing negotiations for a bilateral deal with the US.
Ports could also benefit. India has 214 ports, including 14 designated major ports, while new deep-water facilities are planned at Vadhavan in Maharashtra and Galathea Bay in Great Nicobar Island.
The scheme is expected to create about 3,000 direct and more than 50,000 indirect jobs across steel, components and logistics, according to a shipping ministry statement on 28 October.
It is also expected to support ancillary industries such as corner castings, specialised steel, wooden frames and paints. The government estimates that the scheme will generate about ₹75,000 crore in economic output by FY40, more than seven times the support provided.

Judge orders an inquiry into potential DOJ misconduct in Trump's golf course case
WASHINGTON, D.C. — A federal judge is launching a formal inquiry into potential misconduct by Trump administration officials in the lawsuit over East Potomac Park, including whether they repeatedly misrepresented the president's plans for the municipal D.C. golf course.
District Judge Ana Reyes ordered Friday's hearing — the third in as many weeks — to seek clarity from government lawyers days after they acknowledged in writing Wednesday that there is a plan to transform the municipal golf course into a championship-level venue, closing it and much of the surrounding park in mid-November.
For months, Justice Department attorneys representing the Interior Department and National Park Service had maintained in court filings and hearings that such a plan was not yet final, despite President Trump's social media statements proclaiming otherwise.
Their abrupt confirmation on Wednesday night prompted Reyes to call both sides back into court, just days after she ordered a halt to tree-clearing and major renovations at the park (which the government promptly appealed).
Reyes opened Friday's hearing by quoting the D.C. Bar Rule of Professional Conduct 3.3, which prohibits lawyers from knowingly making or failing to correct false statements to the court. She asked Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr., who is leading the government's defense, whether there was anything he would like to correct.
"Not to my knowledge," Woodward said, explaining that he hasn't read every transcript in the case. "We have lots of binders," he said, to which Reyes replied: "I bet you do."
Over the next four hours, Reyes grilled Woodward about the timing and status of the administration's renovation plans. She demanded to know whether officials had not been truthful when they told her last Monday that they were not aware of the park closure that Trump had posted about that same morning.
Reyes called the lawyers' claims into doubt for two main reasons.
Government lawyers acknowledged for the first time in their Wednesday filing that the administration is closing the park next month, both for golf course renovations and to address the man-made peninsula's crumbling seawall. And they said in court that they submitted those renovation plans to the National Capital Planning Commission for review on Friday.
Under questioning, Woodward told the judge that the submission had been in the works for several weeks. But, as Reyes fired back incredulously, no one from the government mentioned that in the previous hearings, one of which lasted seven hours.
"Am I to understand that for weeks someone has been putting pen to paper on a submission to design the golf course … while this litigation was ongoing, while Department of Justice employees were representing to me that there was no plan?" she said.
The hearing ended with Reyes announcing that she would "open a formal inquiry into whether agency officials and employees, including agency attorneys and [Justice Department] attorneys, have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated applicable ethical rules."
Reyes said that inquiry may be led by a special master, whom she has not yet appointed but described as a judicial officer with "full investigatory powers." Reyes said if the government rejects her special master, she will conduct the inquiry herself.
Reyes stressed that the opening of an investigation does not mean that the court has found or will find evidence that any government lawyers have violated their professional obligations.
But the relatively unusual move suggests that the judge is finished taking the administration at its word, as she said she has done since local historic preservation advocates and golfers first filed suit in February.
The legal fight kicked into high gear earlier this month when the Trump administration cut down hundreds of trees with less than a day's notice. Officials have denied that the tree-clearing was part of a broader plan to renovate the golf course, but Reyes called it a pretext for beginning work without proper approvals. On Friday, she also ordered the government officials to preserve all relevant documents so the "court can conduct an inquiry without the loss of evidence."
"Trial lawyers sometimes tell juries, 'Trust but verify,'" Reyes said from the bench on Friday. "For months, the court trusted, but did not verify. No longer."
So there is a plan. The judge wants to know where it came from
On Monday, Reyes extended her ban on further tree removal and required the government to provide 10 days' written notice before closing or irreversibly modifying East Potomac, which the administration quickly appealed.
She issued a blistering 70-page opinion in which she said the case had become about much more than golf.
"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president," Reyes wrote.
Within hours of Reyes' ruling, Trump took to social media to double down on his plan to start renovations in November, saying Reyes "has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project."
In response, Reyes scheduled Friday's hearing and ordered the government — including Woodward specifically — to "come prepared to state" whether it continues to maintain that there is no final plan, among other details.
But the reply came even sooner, in a Justice Department filing Wednesday night.
Government lawyers said the National Park Service would submit a plan Friday to the National Capital Planning Commission to review "a rendering designed by Tom Fazio for a World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events."
And they said they would soon "close East Potomac Park south of Buckeye Drive, including the Golf Course, consistent with the President's directive."
The filing says the National Park Service entered into a new lease agreement with the National Links Trust — the nonprofit that operates the golf course — on Wednesday.
Under that new agreement, which was confirmed by the National Links Trust, the organization will continue to operate D.C.'s other two municipal golf courses under a 50-year lease, but cease operations at East Potomac "as of close of business on or before November 15."
But details of that plan were still hazy in the courtroom on Friday. Reyes spent most of the hearing questioning Woodward, the third-highest-ranking official at the Justice Department.
At one point, Reyes accused Woodward of "playing games with words" at last week's hearing and said she refused to do so again. Later, when Woodward characterized Trump's Truth Social announcements as a matter of executive privilege, Reyes erupted: "He posted it!"
One particularly protracted back-and-forth focused on whether Trump's Truth Social posts announcing the golf course's forthcoming closure constituted "plans."
Woodward said that Trump's posts are similar to executive orders, directing an agency to take an action but not guaranteeing it will actually occur. To that end, he said the course is not currently scheduled to close on Nov. 15, but that the government has filed a "notice of intent" to close it in keeping with the judge's order requiring 10 days' written notice.
He said "we would never violate the court's order," drawing laughs from many of the spectators who filled the courtroom.
What's the deal with the seawall? New claims of danger emerge
The East Potomac closure will extend far beyond the golf course, removing public access to recreational areas and much of the three-mile perimeter loop beloved by runners and cyclists.
The administration says the closure is necessary — regardless of the golf course renovations — "as a result of the deteriorated seawall that is currently crumbling into the Potomac River and is a safety hazard in a state of significant disrepair."
Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, said in an official declaration this week that the century-old seawalls have "been compromised" over time. As a result, she said, "large sections of the sidewalk adjacent to the seawall are underwater twice daily" and more often after extreme weather events.
All of that has caused voids in the sidewalk and nearby grassy areas, she said, as well as "significant damage to the trees along the seawall." Bowron said the National Park Service has documented the deteriorating conditions in various reports and photographs in recent years, as recently as mid-September.
Reyes asked repeatedly what specific safety issues the deteriorating seawall posed. Woodward said there were concerns about "people falling into the Potomac [River]" — which made Reyes laugh — but declined to expand beyond the photos in the court filings. The judge agreed that the erosion should be addressed but questioned why the administration officials had not made plans to do so — or even mentioned the topic — at any other point since the lawsuit started.
This week was also the first time that Trump mentioned safety risks associated with the park. His post on Wednesday night focused on the golf course itself, particularly holes in the driving range net.
"Golf balls soar through the holes at high speed and hit unexpecting Golfers — including a White House staffer who was, sadly, hit violently in the chest," Trump wrote. "We will hold the judge, Ana C. Reyes, fully responsible for anybody who is hurt, or killed, on this very dangerous, dilapidated, and unsightly Golf Course."
The Trump administration has made a similar case in its threats to tear down the Kennedy Center — the subject of another heated court battle — if it is not renamed after the president. Its board of directors, packed with presidential appointees, voted in September to close the arts center, citing structural decay that posed safety risks.
Woodward said under questioning Friday that the seawall repairs would cost between $150 million and $400 million, but did not answer how much the overall golf course renovations would cost.
On Thursday, Rep. Jared Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, sent a letter to House and Senate appropriations leaders asking them to block the Trump administration from using any money for the seawall project in order to advance his golf course renovations.
He proposed language they could attach to year-end spending legislation that would block federal money from redesigning or expanding the golf courses, altering roads, removing healthy trees, constructing new buildings or reshaping the land.
"It would be unconscionable to let President Trump direct taxpayers to pay for the most expensive portion of the park's maintenance needs and then take it from them to create a golf course catering to him and his billionaire buddies," Huffman wrote. "Congress must ensure it does not happen."
Congress passed an act designating East Potomac as a public park in 1897, declaring that the land be "forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people." Locals worry the golf course redevelopment would change that.

Amgen's Imdelltra used in combination with AstraZeneca's immunotherapy Imfinzi reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to the Astra drug alone in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, according to data from a study presented at a major medical meeting on Saturday.
Imfinzi is currently the standard of care following chemotherapy for patients with this very aggressive and hard-to-treat disease whose cancer does not worsen after initial chemotherapy.
The study found that those given both drugs lived for a median of 21.1 months, compared with 12.7 months for those treated only with Imfinzi.
"If you give Imdelltra earlier and earlier, you get bigger clinical benefit," said Paul Burton, chief medical officer at California-based Amgen. He called the results "unprecedented in advancing the treatment of extensive-stage small cell lung cancer."
Imdelltra's U.S. list price is about $30,000 per cycle, or over $390,000 a year. Wall Street analysts have estimated annual sales reaching more than $2.5 billion by 2030, according to LSEG data.
The Amgen drug is currently approved for adults in the advanced stages of small cell lung cancer that has worsened despite chemotherapy, based on data showing that Imdelltra reduced the risk of death by 40%.
Full results of the 563-patient trial were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid and published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Amgen had previously announced that the Phase 3 study was successful.
Imdelltra belongs to a dual-target class of drugs called bispecific antibodies designed to pull immune system T cells into contact with cancer cells to destroy them. Imfinzi is an older type of immunotherapy that essentially blocks the mechanism tumors use to hide from immune-system assault.
Most lung cancer cases are non-small cell, while up to 15% are the small cell variety targeted by Imdelltra. About 250,000 new cases are diagnosed worldwide each year, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health.
Very few people diagnosed with small cell lung cancer are candidates for surgery, and most are initially given radiotherapy and chemotherapy, Burton said.
Survival rates depend on when the cancer is diagnosed, but the overall 5-year rate is only around 9%, according to the American Cancer Society.
Amgen said that nearly 80% of trial patients treated with the combination were alive after one year, compared with 53% of those on Imfinzi alone, as patient follow-up continues.
Serious side effects, including low white blood cell counts, occurred in 20.9% of patients on the dual therapy and 10.8% with the single therapy. A potentially dangerous condition known as cytokine release syndrome, an aggressive inflammatory response, was reported in 49.6% of patients who received Imdelltra. But only one case was serious and there were no CRS-related deaths.
Adverse events led to discontinuation of the combination therapy in 5.7% of trial patients and 5.8% of patients given only Imfinzi.

Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper, is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.
For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior.
Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.
“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”
&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.
And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.
The big promise is a future where software runs more reliably with fewer security headaches. But whether AI can bring formal verification beyond the most critical systems at organizations like NASA and Apple and into widespread use remains an open question.
The technology is still in the prototyping stage. Though demand is high, it's unclear how much customers are willing to pay and how they prefer to adopt the technology. Formal verification relies on making assumptions about how computers and people interact with software, and some experts are skeptical about its ability to catch bugs stemming from user error and hardware breakdowns.
Will Wilson, who runs the bug-hunting AI software startup Antithesis, calls formal verification “a trap” for math nerds like himself. Antithesis spent millions of dollars to formally verify some of its cybersecurity defenses, a process Wilson describes as a “pain in the ass.” Yet the startup still uncovered additional errors using its own tool, and Antithesis has also found bugs in software that several of its customers had formally verified. “It can give you some assurance, but only robust exhaustive testing can prove your assurance is true,” Wilson says.
Or as Vitalik Buterin, the engineer known for creating the Ethereum cryptocurrency, put it in a blog post earlier this year, “formal verification is not a panacea.” But he and other proponents of the approach still believe it will be an important defense against AI systems launching cyberattacks and wreaking havoc.
Core Security
Boeing planes, Amazon servers, and more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices contain at least some formally verified software, according to company disclosures. The code in question is typically security-related, and vulnerabilities in it could cause serious harm if exploited.
Byron Cook, a distinguished scientist and vice president at Amazon Web Services, says formal verification has eased customer concerns about cloud security and helped internal teams move faster by squashing big bugs early on.
But several midsized tech companies tell WIRED they have typically verified only one key feature of their products, if any at all. They cite a lack of verification engineers, costs that outweigh the potential risks, and, perhaps most importantly, concerns that waiting weeks for code to be formally verified could slow innovation.
Earlier this year, Apple’s security team said that some of the issues formal verification uncovered in its “corecrypto” library, which is used for encryption, could not have been found any other way. But the company added that it has to be “conservative” when adding new code to corecrypto to ensure it can keep pace with reviewing it.
Two cybersecurity executives at major companies that haven’t formally verified any code say they aren’t sure whether automation will make it worthwhile. But the executives, who weren’t authorized to speak publicly, say they could imagine paying major AI labs for “verified” AI-generated code.
Developers of open source software projects, which are the bedrock of many apps, are increasingly experimenting with AI-aided verification. The nonprofit Beneficial AI Foundation used a grant from Anthropic to validate the same encryption code this year as Sun did at Stanford. Michael Rosenberg, a maintainer of the library known as curve25519-dalek, hopes sustainable funding emerges for ongoing verification efforts. “I have no ideas as to how that’s going to happen, though, and we certainly shouldn’t rely on the goodwill of the AI companies,” he says.
Some of the startups eager to expand verification also aren’t sure whether to deploy their tools directly to customers or through intermediaries like Anthropic. Their general plan is to use AI to automate much of the work involved in defining how a program is supposed to behave. For example, specifications for a data table might require that it contain the same items before and after sorting, just in a different order. Further automation efforts, which may not involve AI, would translate that code into a format that math tools like Lean, Rocq, and Isabelle can use to check whether the code works as intended.
Another recent entrant to the formal verification field is Madan Musuvathi, who left Microsoft Research after more than 20 years to found the startup Truidic. After incidents like the OpenAI hack of Hugging Face, he felt there was an urgent need to commercialize his studies. “AI in the hands of attackers can be extremely powerful,” Musuvathi says, but verification can “make AI safe and secure for everyone, everywhere.”
Proofcraft, one of the few companies that has long offered traditional verification, says growing excitement about the process is translating into a flood of inquiries from potential customers. June Andronick, the company’s CEO, and Gerwin Klein, its chief scientist, say interest easily outpaces what they and their competition can provide.
But both worry that AI-generated specifications could inspire “unjustified trust” in the results. Verifiers are also eager to preserve the joy their work brings them. Klein calls it “pretty addictive, like a puzzle game.” If all goes well, he’ll be doing more solving than ever.

General Motors agrees to pay $220 million to settle multi-state data privacy lawsuit
The automaker sold driver data to insurance companies without permission from 2016 through 2024.
The states that sued General Motors over the whole OnStar Smart Driver program debacle have settled with the company. GM has agreed to pay $220 million to resolve the lawsuit brought by the attorneys general of 35 US states and the District of Columbia.
If you'll recall, The New York Times reported in 2024 that GM had enrolled millions of customers to its Smart Driver program from 2016 through 2024 and then tracked their driving habits. The automaker used Smart Driver to log data on hard braking, late night driving and speeding and then sold the information to data brokers for insurance. As a result, insurance companies raised premiums for people based on information from the program.
GM didn't tell its customers that their data would be sold for that purpose, the attorneys general said. Apparently, a lot of drivers weren't even told they were part of the program. The automaker was incentivizing dealerships with bonuses to sign up as many customers for Smart Driver as possible. Sometimes, dealership employees would allegedly just accept its terms and conditions for customers without their express permission.
In addition, GM didn't always notify customers about their enrollment. The AGs said that more than 370,000 drivers were told that they were not enrolled, even though they actually were. The automaker did unenroll them eventually, but it didn't notify them about the mistake and still sold their data. The data GM collected was "personal, identifiable and specific," the AGs wrote.
GM is required to limit the driving data it collects from customers and protect their personal information going forward, as part of the settlement. The company will also be subjected to mandated internal and external data protection and privacy program assessments, as well as oversight and additional training at its dealerships. Earlier this year, the Federal Trade Commission banned GM from sharing specific consumer data with third parties for five years due to the issue. In May, the automaker reached a separate settlement with California for $12.75 million.

Families hold out hope for loved ones missing after deadly Spain train crash
Families are desperately searching for missing loved ones after two high-speed trains collided in central Spain
TOLEDO, Spain -- Families desperately searched for missing loved ones Thursday, more than 24 hours after two high-speed trains collided in central Spain, killing at least 69 and injuring dozens of others.
“I have my father, and I don’t know where he is. I hope to find him, oh my Lord," said César Vicente, an actor who traveled 495 kilometers (307 miles) from his native Seville to Toledo in search of his father. He spent the night with many other families at a religious center converted into a base for those affected by the disaster.
Vicente was with his mother and his aunt, all of whom were looking for César Vicente, who was sitting in seat 13A on the RENFE train that struck another operated by the private company Iryo, which had stopped on the tracks. The family was among those who braved the cold to take a short walk on a chilly morning.
“I don’t want this to happen to anyone. This is unbearable,” he added. “This is hell.”
Online, relatives and friends flooded social media with desperate appeals for information on the whereabouts of their loved ones, posting photos or describing the clothes they were wearing when they boarded the trains bound for Seville and details about their physical appearance or the seat in which they were traveling.
In a post Wednesday on Instagram, Alejandra Marroquín told her followers that her sister Adriana, who was wearing dark blue clothes, was traveling in car 8 of the RENFE train and that they had been unable to contact her.
“We’re still praying, we don’t know anything,” Marroquín said in a post Thursday morning, as search teams with sniffer dogs continued to look for victims.
“The entire government is working to respond to the victims’ families, shed light on the tragedy, and strengthen security so that this never happens again,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told reporters on Thursday morning.
This was the second high-speed rail disaster this year. In January, 46 people died after one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in southern Spain.
The high-speed rail network has been considered one of Spain’s crowning achievements. It is the world’s second-largest, after China’s. Until this year, it had not experienced a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago.
Life in Urda, a small town of about 2,500 people south of Madrid, was turned upside down early Wednesday.
Residents rushed to help in any way they could: from assisting the injured to preparing sandwiches for the unharmed passengers, many of whom they even carried from the tracks to a nearby sports pavilion in their cars.
David Gómez, a construction worker, was working with his brother and another colleague nearby when they heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.
“People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought until emergency services arrived," he said.
With 180 people injured, including 110 taken to hospitals, authorities issued a call for blood donations.
The response was immediate: in Castilla-La Mancha alone, the region where the collision occurred, more than 2,000 people volunteered in the aftermath.
“I want to express my personal and very sincere gratitude to everyone who has stepped up, starting with the all-time record number of donations,” said the region’s president, Emiliano García-Page, who also thanked the 1,300 emergency service personnel who were mobilized.

Are you an organ donor? Here are some rule changes you may want to know
Organ donation conversations are changing. Critics worry families may feel pressured
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
The U.S. organ transplant system is making a controversial change to a long-standing rule that was designed to protect potential donors. The revision aims to boost donations and reduce errors. But critics worry that the move may endanger patient care.
Under the change, the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network, which runs the transplant system, will relax a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital and the transplantation team standing by to procure patients' organs.
Previously, no one from that team was even supposed to talk to family members until after they had made the heart-wrenching decision to let a loved one go. The rule was intended to prevent pressure that could change the care patients receive. It was also in place to dispel any doubts that doctors aren't doing everything they can to save patients.
But the board of directors for the transplant system voted Aug. 20 to modify that rule as part of a new set of guidelines governing donation following circulatory death. That occurs after life-sustaining care has been withdrawn and now accounts for about half of organ donations.
The new rules, which go into effect Nov. 18, "allow discussions for organ donation to take place once end of life discussions are taking place with the potential deceased donor's agent," according to the new policy.
Why is the firewall previously barring these conversations coming down?
"I think the best way to think about it is that insisting on a bright line without focusing on what's happening on either side of that line is a false sense of security," Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ network, told NPR in an interview.
The new rules aim to prevent disturbing mistakes that have occurred in the past. Those errors have included patients being wheeled into operating rooms to remove their organs when they were still alive.
"That specific line in the policy is part of a suite of improvements to the coordination and communication between the organ procurement organizations and the healthcare team that is caring for these patients in hospitals and the families of the patients themselves. And that really is a marked improvement over the policy that was in place before," Lynch says.
A balance of safety and speed
In addition to allowing donation teams to approach families sooner, the new policies include making it easier to pause organ retrieval if anyone becomes concerned that something is amiss and standardizing other patient protections, including testing for determining death.
"Documentation, clear coordination, deference to the primary healthcare team and consequences — that's what keeps patients safe," says Lynch.
The change in policy is also designed to make sure the organ retrieval team isn't brought in too late to conduct the tests and preparation necessary for families to honor their loved one's desire to be a donor.
When that happens, "the family loses out on that memory" of helping their loved one donate their organs, "the patient loses out on the choice that they made, and the people on the waiting list lose out on the chance to receive a lifesaving organ," Lynch says.
More than 109,000 Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to the Health Resources & Services Administration. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.
Does the change cross an ethical line?
Critics, however, say the change is dangerous. It could subtly pressure families and caregivers to discontinue care and create confusion about who's in the intensive care unit to try to save their loved one and who's there to obtain their organs, which could deepen distrust in the organ donation system.
"It's a very important bright line," says Dr. Lainie Ross, a bioethicist at the University of Rochester. "Our primary responsibility is that patient's well-being and care. And we need a bright line. That's where our focus is, and we're not even going to start thinking about whether those organs are usable until death is inevitable and imminent."
She adds: "When my family member is in that hospital bed, I want to know that we're all on Team Mom and not worried the reason the doctor's really suggesting the treatments aren't working is because they want your organs for someone else."
Ross says she's "horrified to think that families will feel pressured. They'll feel manipulated."
Others also see problems with the change.
"I don't disagree with the desire to have more transplantable organs. I think transplants provide great benefit to many, many people," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network's Patient Affairs Committee. "But people may be pressured to make that decision too quickly. I don't want to interfere with a family's grieving process, and I don't want to interfere with a family's ability to make a decision for their family member at a time when it's correct for them."
Some critics say the change is the latest worrisome development for organ donors.
"This is part of a number of things that are going on in organ donation that are blurring lines," says Lois Shepherd, a professor of law and bioethics at the University of Virginia who opposed the change as a member of the working group that developed the new guidelines. "A lot of safeguards for patients are weakening. And that's a concern to me."
But the change was endorsed by the Association of Organ Procurement Organizations (AOPO), a trade group.
"Families/agents who are considering [withdrawing life support] must be informed about donation and how the donor evaluation process may affect the timing of the [withdrawal of life support]," the group said in its public comments. "Many families have expressed frustration with learning about this timing impact after planning for other family members to be present at the time of [withdrawing life support]. Waiting until the family has made the decision is too late."
The AOPO declined to make someone available for an interview with NPR. But AOPO President Allison Erickson said in a written statement: "Donation depends on public trust, and it is our responsibility to respect and maintain it. Any time there is confusion or concern, [organ procurement organizations] clarify and improve the process. Donor families deserve to fully understand each stage of the end-of-life and donation processes, as well as that their loved ones are cared for by all involved."

Pause on strikes targeting Russia's oil infrastructure could reportedly last deeper into November

Ukraine's military has reportedly paused its strikes on Russian oil refineries until after the US midterms, following weeks of pressure from Donald Trump.
The pause could last deeper into November, sources told the Wall St Journal, and comes despite the fact that Russia continues to target energy and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine.
Ukrainian strikes targeting Russia's oil infrastructure have in part contributed to a sharp downturn in relations between Trump and Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky, with the former blaming them for diesel prices hitting record highs.
Earlier, a Russian drone attack killed 14 people at the main railway station in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, hitting a platform crowded with people boarding a train, officials said.
And both Russia and Ukraine said on Thursday that demining operations around the Russian-held town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine had been completed and that an operation to bring aid and allow residents to leave was ready to begin.
Efforts have been underway for several weeks to organise a relief operation for the acutely deprived town's residents, which Russian forces seized soon after Moscow's February 2022 invasion of its smaller neighbour.
Residents given deadline to return to Ukraine-controlled territory
Residents wishing to leave and return to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government are expected to exit via Russia-controlled Crimea before crossing into southern Russia and being flown to Belarus from where they will be able to cross the border into Ukraine.
By the middle of Thursday, neither Ukraine nor Russia had reported violations of the ceasefire, due to last until Sunday.
Putin says aid is reaching Oleshky civilians due to ceasefire
President Vladimir Putin told a gathering with African nations in Moscow that relief supplies would begin reaching Oleshky civilians on Thursday and Friday, "with the support, incidentally, of the first lady of the United States".
The truce applies only to Oleshky and the wider Kherson region, which has suffered years of near-daily drone and artillery attacks. Some 1,500 of the town's prewar population of 24,000 people are believed to live among the ruins, under regular shellfire amid severe shortages of food and medicine.
Ukraine has long accused Russia of refusing to let aid in or people out. Russia says it is Ukrainian mines on the approach roads and Ukrainian shelling that have prevented the delivery of aid or the safe evacuation of residents.
Ukraine pauses strikes on Russian refineries after pressure from Trump – reports
Ukraine has halted its strikes on Russian oil refineries after pressure from US president Donald Trump, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing people with knowledge of the operations.
Ukrainian units carrying out long-range strikes were told in mid-October that the campaign against refineries was effectively on hold once missions already in motion were completed, the Journal reported.
The unofficial pause is expected to last until after the US midterm elections and potentially deeper into November, it added. Russia has meanwhile stepped up attacks on Ukrainian energy and civilian infrastructure.
The news of a pause comes amid renewed efforts to revive US-backed peace talks to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War Two.
Relations between Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky have taken a sharp downward turn in recent weeks, with Trump growing increasingly frustrated over Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure as diesel prices hit record highs.
Ukraine had refused to halt the strikes, saying its long-range drone campaign is its only viable response to years of Russian bombardment.
That prompted Trump to announce a deal to buy diesel from Moscow and waive sanctions on Moscow authorised by a bill he signed into law in September.
Russia, Ukraine say Oleshky demining operations complete, humanitarian operation to proceed
Russia and Ukraine said on Thursday that demining operations around the Russian-held town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine had been completed and that an operation to bring aid and allow residents to leave was ready to begin.
Efforts have been underway for several weeks to organise a relief operation for the acutely deprived town's residents, which Russian forces seized soon after Moscow's February 2022 invasion of its smaller neighbour.
Both sides have praised US first lady Melania Trump for helping broker a truce in a town where at least one resident who escaped said those remaining feared death by starvation.
"Demining operations of routes have been completed for the humanitarian mission in Oleshky," the two sides said in virtually identical statements issued by Yana Lantratova, Russia's human rights commissioner, and Dmytro Lubinets, her Ukrainian counterpart.
"The humanitarian convoy is ready for departure."
The convoy would head for the district hospital and residents wishing to leave would be permitted to go within a specific time frame. Aid packages would then be distributed, the statements said.
The operation aims to address a crisis in a town marooned inside a war zone since 2022. But it is also part of a diplomatic dance where both sides want to show US President Donald Trump that they back his peace efforts, albeit for different reasons.
Lantratova, Russian human rights commissioner, said she was taking four journalists from the conservative US outlet Newsmax to the area. Lubinets made no reference to specific reporters.
Aid mission set to enter Oleshky as a localized Russia-Ukraine truce holds for a third day
Humanitarian aid is poised to roll into the stricken city of Oleshky, negotiators said Thursday, as a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military units cleared landmines.
Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, but remain otherwise locked in the war that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion more than four years ago. Previous ceasefire talks either failed or the truces quickly fell apart.
“Demining of the designated routes has been completed, and the humanitarian convoy has been assembled and is ready,” ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, who heads Ukraine's negotiating team, said Thursday. He said aid deliveries were due to begin Friday.
Elsewhere, deadly attacks continued and Ukraine's central bank warned that damage to industrial targets could push the country into a recession.
The planned six-day ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky has brought a rare and welcome stillness for civilians in the nearby city of Kherson, which is held by Ukraine and has also been wracked by the war.
Russian and Ukrainian officials head to Oleshky for aid delivery
Both sides thanked Melania Trump for what the White House called her help in brokering the ceasefire so food and medical supplies can be delivered to about 2,000 people trapped in Oleshky. Pope Leo XIV also pressed for a truce.

Udhampur, Oct 30: Launching a scathing attack on the National Conference-Congress government for, what he alleged, “its failure to honour the promises made to the people during the assembly elections”, BJP MLA from Udhampur East, Ranbir Singh Pathania on Friday maintained that the government had reduced governance to a political rhetoric, excuses and unfulfilled assurances, while the aspirations of the people continued to remain unaddressed.
He was addressing the people after inaugurating and initiating a series of important developmental works in the Khandui-Khandra area.
Pathania said that the National Conference had sought votes on the basis of a tall catalogue of promises, including 200 units of free electricity; free LPG cylinders; free travel and one lakh jobs for the youth.
However, even after assuming power, the government failed to translate these commitments into tangible relief for the people, he claimed.
“An issue-less and purposeless government seems to have lost its direction and sense of responsibility. The people were given tall promises and lofty assurances, but what they are receiving in return is disappointment and disillusionment. Political rhetoric cannot substitute for governance, nor can excuses compensate for unfulfilled commitments,” he asserted.
Taking particular exception to what he termed the continued neglect of the Jammu region, Pathania said that the entire region was being left out of the developmental priorities of the present dispensation. “From Doda and Kishtwar to the Pahari belt of Rajouri and Poonch and from Udhampur to Kathua and Samba, people across Jammu region continue to await equitable attention, development and their legitimate share in governance,” BJP MLA alleged.
He said that the people of Jammu region had equal aspirations and equal rights to development and there could be no justification for any discriminatory or indifferent approach towards their concerns. “Elections are not merely about securing votes through attractive promises; they are about delivering on those promises. The real test of leadership lies in the roads constructed, grievances resolved, facilities created and opportunities delivered,” he added.
On this occasion, he also inaugurated and initiated important developmental works in the Khandui-Khandra area, aimed at strengthening rural connectivity, community infrastructure and educational facilities.
A major highlight was the Naddi Talab to Khandra road project, to be taken up at an estimated cost of Rs 12 Cr. He also kickstarted construction of a shelter shed, community hall at Baba Loundna Dev Sthan at an estimated cost of Rs 30 lakh.
Pathania stated that three additional classrooms would be constructed at Middle School Khandui. Timely execution, quality of construction and effective monitoring of all developmental works, he said, would remain central to his approach.

Spacetech startup Manastu Space raised ₹22 Cr ($2.3 Mn) from Gandhi Securities and Investments, the Thacker Legacy Trusts, and a clutch of angel investors in what appears to be an extension of its Series A funding round. It appears the startup intends to raise a further ₹9.2 Cr from Capital A that has yet to be confirmed. The round size can change before its closure. Beyond this sum, the startup also initially issued CCPS worth a further ₹2.5 Cr to Aakash founder Aakash Chaudhry, which were later cancelled. Inc42 accessed the funding details through Manastu’s regulatory filings. Queries sent to the startup went unanswered until the time of publication. “The purpose of the offer is to raise funds for the research & development, growth, expansion, marketing and general corporate activities of the Company,” its disclosures with the MCA read. Notably, the science and technology ministry’s Technology Development Board (TDB) also recently announced that it had committed ₹116 Cr in funding to Manastu in the form of optionally convertible debentures. Founded in 2017 by Tushar Jadhav and Ashtesh Kumar, Manastu is developing a green propulsion system for satellites coupled with its in-orbit refuelling system and debris avoidance technology to reduce the risk of orbital congestion. The startup has developed a proprietary hydrogen peroxide-based fuel that it claims gives 50% higher performance and is less harmful to the environment than conventional toxic propellants like hydrazine. Besides, its debris avoidance systems enable satellites to manoeuvre in orbit, avoid collisions with space debris, adjust trajectories and de-orbit at the end of their operational lives. Until now, it has raised $9 Mn from Capital-A, Capital 2B, Indian Angel Network (IAN), E2MC, BIG Capital, and others. It last raised $3 Mn in another Series A round extension back in August 2025 to commercially roll out its green propulsion and debris-avoidance system. Manastu competes with the likes of Bellatrix Aerospace and Dhruva Space in the global market for satellite propulsion systems, which is projected to grow at 17.6% CAGR to reach $4.7 Bn by 2031.

The brief ceremony introducing the new Macbook Pro this week was as low-key as the presenter, Apple’s new CEO John Ternus. He stepped onto the low stage at a Los Angeles event space with zero fanfare, said hi, and queued up a video showing the first touchscreen Mac. Then he released the modest crowd of journalists and creators to get hands-on with the new laptop and roam between eye-popping demos of music producers, filmmakers, photographers, and fashion designers using the laptop. Ternus, who at 51 is on the younger side of Apple’s top management, has been CEO for less than two months. But this launch and a series of other recent announcements have made one thing clear. With this new guy—if a 25-year Apple veteran could be considered new—it’s all about the products. Perhaps fittingly, the biggest noise of the presentation came when Ternus revealed that the new device restores the illumination to the Apple logo. Maybe that’s a symbol that in the age of AI, Apple is beaming out the message that hardware still rules.
A few minutes after the presentation, I sat down with Ternus, for the second time in two days. Steve Jobs used to grant me an audience after his famous keynotes, too. Ternus isn’t Jobs, of course, nor is he supposed to be. But who is he?
I first met Ternus in 2015, when I spent a day with him at Apple’s Input Design Lab, a testing facility in Cupertino. He’d risen to VP for Mac, iPad, Ecosystem, and Audio Engineering, and he struck me as affable and knowledgeable. (He spent four years right out of college at a virtual reality company, but he’s been at Apple ever since.) The peg to my story at the time was how this unknown manager conducted a Javert-like investigation to fix the weird sound a redesigned mouse made when sliding on a table.
That attention to detail was a legacy of Jobs’ perfectionism, which Tim Cook sustained as the next CEO. In the decade when Ternus overlapped with Jobs, he says he had only “a handful of interactions” with the founder. “But I've always felt like sort of a student of Steve's teachings,” Ternus said. “And then being able to work very closely with Tim, I’ve been very lucky.”
Ternus has so far been defined by his product prowess. “John innately has a great sense for great products, and that’s what Apple is,” says Greg Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of worldwide marketing and a 40-year company veteran. “You can’t teach that.” In one sense Ternus’ ascension is similar to that of Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, another lifer promoted to the top post. But Nadella was called upon to fix a broken organization, while Apple has been on a multi-decade run. Ternus is explicit that he will be an engine of continuity. That word is key to his selection, and above all explains why Tim Cook and the rest of Apple’s board was so comfortable with the choice.
The extent to which Ternus is a deep Apple insider became clear when I probed him on his views on being a corporate leader. I asked him which non-Apple CEOs he admires, and he was stumped. “I haven't really thought about that,” he said. I asked whether any business books had an impact on him. “Not really,” he said. “Of course I’ve read books, but there's so much to be learned from the people I get to work with.” Indeed, every time I tried to pin down Ternus on what mark he wants to make at Apple, he deflected the question and told me how he will continue Apple’s commitment to internal collaboration.
Ternus’ key collaborator is probably Johny Srouji, the architect of the company’s custom silicon, an initiative that’s driven many of the company’s innovations in the past decade. Srouri says that their relationship will be even closer, as Apple has merged its hardware engineering and technology organizations with Srouji at the top, reporting to Ternus. “John is going to be a great CEO,” he said. “He's a product guy at heart, but Apple's secret weapon is the DNA, the culture, which is not going to change. Remember, John has been here for 25 years. It’s not like he's going to come and everything's going to be different.”
Being Apple’s CEO encompasses much more than products—there’s a $100 billion business in services, a huge infrastructure, and the general mishegoss of running a giant corporation. I asked Ternus what it’s like to take on a massively expanded portfolio. “One of the amazing privileges of this job is getting to learn so many new things,” he said. “I have been and will continue to learn and go deeper into different areas. But, you know, I do love product. I'm super passionate about it.”
Like it or not, the CEO of a $4 trillion company has to be involved in policy and politics. It has been widely reported that as executive chair, Cook will still conduct some of Apple’s high-level policy duties, including the equivalent of stuffing gold-plated binkies in the presidential mouth. Ternus implies that the reality is more nuanced. “Tim is available to help wherever I ask him, and it's great to have him in that role,” he said. “He obviously has a ton of relationships he's developed over the years, and of course, I'm building new relationships in this role as well.” One relationship he has yet to build: the president. Ternus has yet to meet Donald Trump.
Then there’s the one thing that could possibly disrupt the way Apple has run its business for the past 50 years. Ternus is taking over the company during what may be the biggest technological shift ever. I suggested to Ternus that history may judge him on how he handles AI. I spelled out for him a couple of narratives people spin about Apple. One is that Apple has been hobbled by a failure to develop its AI product Siri, and even after an update it’s still in catch-up mode. The other is that Apple is smart to avoid the high cost of developing a frontier model and that the strategy of organically putting AI into its products, with a focus on privacy, will pay off in the long run.
“Everyone has an opinion—I really like where we’re at,” he said. “I would hope people recognize that the work we do is building incredible products that make their lives better. We’re absolutely going to leverage AI to do that. We don't want to ship AI for AI's sake. When we're doing it right, people won’t have to think about whether it was AI that made this happen or more traditional software. What matters is, did we build something that they really love?”
That assumes that AI, as powerful as it is, will wind up as a “normal” technology, organically integrated into our current gadget-sphere. Another school of thought is that AI is an apocalyptic disruptor that will shred the current ecosystem. In that vision, all those cool apps Apple supports will be subsumed by AI-concocted agents generated from prompts, or even autonomously. Ternus doesn’t buy that scenario. “That could make life really easy, I suppose, but the creation of products is a deeply human and personal thing, something that we love to do,” he said.
When I asked whether he’s in favor of AI regulation, he replied, “We all read the stories and think about it from a cybersecurity standpoint—clearly these models are very capable of doing things. Our focus is on making sure that our products are secure and safe, and protecting the users' information.”
His non-answer shows that he might well be on the way to mastering political communication. But policy will never be the focus of John Ternus. He is, and probably always will be, the product-guy CEO. Before we ended our conversation, Ternus had one question for me: “What did you think of the logo?”

Ever since my wife and I started dating about eight years ago, we've talked openly about our personal finances.
From the very beginning, we discussed our 401(k) withholdings and emergency funds. These conversations became even more important when we started living together and sharing expenses about a year into our relationship.
As a queer couple, my wife and I have always believed that we can write our own rules when it comes to how we approach our finances.
Our incomes have varied over the years for many reasons, and we've tried several different payment breakdowns before finding what works for us.
Over the years, we've divided our mortgage payments a few different ways to find what feels 'fair'
About a year into our relationship, my now-wife moved into the condo that I had bought on my own. At the time, I was working in tech and earning a higher base salary, as well as annual performance-based bonuses and stock that added to our salary discrepancy.
I knew that my mortgage was higher than the rent on a place we would have chosen together based on our combined income. So, we decided I would pay the bulk of it, but we'd split the costs of groceries, utilities, and internet, as well as shared vacations.
Five years into our relationship, I sold my old condo, my wife increased her hours at her job, and we bought a townhome together.
This time, we decided to split our mortgage payments in proportion to our base salaries, which felt like the fairest thing to compare since annual bonuses and stock awards from my company could vary. This came out to a 60/40 split.
Over the next two years, my wife's base salary got closer to mine as a result of union negotiations at her hospital. Eventually, once our salaries were essentially at parity, we shifted to a 50/50 split.
When I got laid off from my tech job, we had to reevaluate what was 'fair'
Almost eight months into our new system, I was laid off from my tech job.
I had savings in my emergency fund from my years working there and received severance, but I was suddenly in a different financial situation than I'd been before.
For the first time in our relationship, my wife was the higher earner.
We talked about moving back to a proportionate split. My wife reminded me that we were a team, and said she'd be open to covering more of our mortgage and expenses. But between my savings, severance, and bonuses I'd made over the years, I was able to continue splitting the mortgage evenly, and I wanted to.
At the end of the day, reverting to a different split might have been "fair," but it didn't feel fair of me to put the responsibility on my wife to pay more of the mortgage.
I knew that paying a much larger share of the mortgage would bring undue stress on her, and I also knew that I could afford my half, even without my steady paycheck.
Defining fairness on our own terms has felt empowering
It's now been over a year since my layoff, and splitting our mortgage and expenses 50/50 has continued to feel right for both of us.
This isn't to say she's not supporting me during this time. Right now, my wife continues to work full-time while I'm doing freelance and contract work for various clients. She's covering more of our grocery expenses, and I'm also on her health insurance.
We're a team, and I'm learning to accept her help in ways that feel fair to both of us.
We both know that our jobs, housing situation, and approach to personal finance will evolve, especially as we build our careers. What matters to us is having ongoing check-ins about whether our mortgage breakdown feels right and supporting each other equally in other ways, too.
After all, what's just as important is celebrating each other's accomplishments, encouraging each other to learn new skills, and contributing to our household and the labor it takes to run it. Money is only one piece of the puzzle.
