5 unforgettable Patrick Stewart performances as Jean-Luc Picard
Stewart brought emotional ferocity and humanist integrity to bear in his portrayal of the Enterprise captain
Patrick Stewart, who died Wednesday at the age of 86, had dozens of credits to his name on screen and stage over a more than 60-year career, but for many people he will always be Capt. Jean-Luc Picard, of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701-D.
Many Reddit threads and YouTube comments marking Stewart's death are mourning Picard as much as the real man.
"RIP Captain," one Reddit user posted. "You helped change my life for the better."
"Picard was an incredibly well-written and well-acted character that Stewart made real," replied another.
Though Picard had his moments in four movies and on the recent sequel show Star Trek: Picard, the very best moments of the character are all within the 176 episodes of Star Trek: The Next Generation, which ran from 1987 to 1994.
Here are five of Stewart's best Picard performances to seek out. (Warning: Spoilers in the descriptions.)
'Make now always the most precious time'
'The Inner Light,' Season 5, Episode 25
Often argued for as the best Star Trek episode of the almost 1,000 made so far, "The Inner Light" is a Stewart tour de force. 
When an alien probe knocks the captain unconscious, he wakes up as a villager on a dying planet. In what passes for 25 minutes on the Enterprise, the childless Picard lives for four decades as a man named Kamin, aging before our eyes and raising two children to adulthood.
- Star Trek actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86
- Hugh Jackman, William Shatner, Seth MacFarlane among stars honouring the late Patrick Stewart
The entire episode is a masterpiece, but Stewart imbues simple moments of family with a ferocity and humanist integrity that has made many Trek fans weep.
"Seize the time, Meribor. Live now," he tells his adult daughter as they contemplate the imminent end of their planet. "Make now always the most precious time. Now will never come again."
'There are four lights!'
'Chain of Command,' Part II, Season 6, Episode 11
Stewart prepared for this episode, where Picard is brutally tortured, by reviewing tapes provided by Amnesty International, a group Stewart supported and spoke for.
Much of the episode is him alone in a room with another esteemed British actor, the late David Warner. Their scenes crackle with intensity as Cardassian officer (read: space Nazi) Gul Madred attempts to brainwash the captain into thinking there are five lights shining in the room, when there are in fact only four.
The episode offers a brutal depiction of suffering that Stewart throws his full body into. It also contains maybe the biggest "Hell yeah!" moment in the series when Picard refuses to break, yelling, "There are four lights!"
But even better is Stewart's haunted face in the final scene, when he admits the torture had worked, that he would have told his captor anything, and that "more than that, I believed that I could see five lights."
'Shaka, when the walls fell'
'Darmok,' Season 5, Episode 2
Picard is captured on a planet by an alien race that cannot communicate clearly with humans.
Over the course of the episode, Picard and his crew come to realize that the Children of Tama speak entirely in metaphor, using phrases like "Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra" to mean "co-operation" and "Shaka, when the walls fell" to mean "failure."
Stewart shines twice: first, in a campfire scene, where he tells his alien counterpart the story of the Epic of Gilgamesh; second, when he saves the day by communicating with the Children of Tama's ship, speaking an invented language in a way that is nevertheless commanding and affecting. 
Stewart signs a Star Trek: Deep Space Nine banner in Las Vegas on Aug. 14, 2005. Stewart played Picard in that spinoff's pilot. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)
'There is nothing left but dry bones ... dead friends'
'Sarek,' Season 3, Episode 23
This episode features Mark Lenard as the Vulcan Sarek, the father of Mr. Spock from the original 1966 Star Trek series. 
Sarek is dying of the sci-fi equivalent of Alzheimer's disease and Picard joins minds with him so that the Vulcan can carry out one last mission. The mind-meld makes Sarek more stable, but floods Picard with a lifetime of repressed emotion.
In an almost four-minute scene, Stewart screams, rants, smiles, cries, fights, longs, regrets, embodies Sarek as portrayed by Lenard — and finally, crumples. It's impossible to look away.
Stewart in 1998's Star Trek: Insurrection. (Getty Images)
'I would rather die as the man I was...'
'Tapestry,' Season 6, Episode 15
In Star Trek's take on It's a Wonderful Life, a dead Picard is visited in the afterlife by recurring guest antagonist Q, who offers him the chance to do his life over. 
Stewart gets to play Picard as his usual self, as a brash, young ensign, and as an uncertain, middle-management version of himself that happens in Q's alternate reality.
Stewart caps it off by getting stabbed through the heart (as needs to happen in the "right" reality), looking at the blade and laughing. A scene that could have been hokey is not just believable, but exhilarating.
Episodes of Star Trek: The Next Generation are available to stream on Paramount+ in Canada.

When Sarojini Nadimpally was diagnosed with HER2-positive breast cancer in June 2025, the Delhi-based public health researcher was staring at a hidden reality as daunting as the tumour. One dose of the targeted combination drug she had been prescribed would cost around ₹2.7 lakh — and she needed 18 doses.
As someone who works on access to medicines, she closely followed the government’s recent decision to cap trade margins on 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs at 30%, extending a 2019 cap that covered 42. The government claims that the cap, which takes effect on November 9, can save patients about ₹2,500 crore a year.
“Any intervention to lower the prices of cancer drugs is a welcome step,” says Ms. Nadimpally. “But it remains to be seen how this cap will actually reduce what patients pay.”
Survival versus solvency
Cancer is said to be India’s leading cause of catastrophic health spending. India’s out-of-pocket share for cancer care — estimated by various studies to be 50%-80% of direct treatment costs — is far higher than in most high-income systems, where insurance or tax-funded care generally absorbs the bulk of these expenses.
Experts say that drugs make up around over half the costs of cancer care. “High costs of treatments such as targeted therapies and immunotherapy can lead many patients to defer treatment, opt for cheaper but less effective alternatives or give up altogether,” says Vedant Kabra, principal director, surgical oncology, Fortis Memorial Research Institute, Gurugram.
When pills threaten to outrun savings, the standard of care is down to a cruel trade-off between effectiveness and affordability. For example, at about ₹1.25 lakh a month, a lifetime course of osimertinib, the drug of choice in fighting EGFR-mutated lung cancer while reducing the risk of brain metastases, is beyond the reach of many. “These patients switch to gefitinib, which costs only about ₹2,500 a month, but return with brain secondaries and disease progression,” says Narayanankutty Warrier, senior consultant oncologist, MVR Cancer Centre and Research Institute, Kozhikode. “About 30% new-generation drugs are really good,” he says. “The rest are mostly claims. But even a slight improvement in survival means they become monopoly drugs.”
The pricing conundrum
With its latest order, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) is setting a common trade-margin ceiling on a broad range of cancer medicines, including patented, chemotherapy, targeted, immunotherapy, hormonal and blood cancer drugs. Manufacturers are required to report formulation-level information, including brand name, composition, pack size, PTS (price to stockist) and revised MRP.
The order spells out that a drug with a PTS of ₹70 and an MRP of ₹300 can have an MRP of no more than ₹100, excluding GST. Experts argue that the permitted margin — which amounts to 42.8% of the PTS — is a sizeable mark-up, especially for expensive drugs.
In effect, the government is putting a ceiling on the profit, not the underlying price. For example, the actual prices at which hospitals buy drugs, often after steep discounts negotiated for bulk purchases, are hidden from sight. “A cap on trade margins means little to patients if hospitals and dealers do not pass those savings on, and there is no way of knowing whether they do,” says Ms. Nadimpally.
On October 28, the NPPA published a revised price list for the 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs based on data submitted by companies. The MRPs of 37 drugs remain unchanged, offering an early indication of what the final list may look like. The list also reveals margins that manufacturers, including some Indian generic makers, have had. For instance, palbociclib’s MRP for one brand is down from about ₹40,421 to ₹2,720 a pack, and thiotepa’s from about ₹80,072 to ₹7,150 a vial — drops of more than 90%.
The latest order also counts the cap from the PTS, not from the ex-factory price or the landed cost (price paid after discounts and freight), leaving out upstream additions. The mark-up for cancer medicines is unjustified, says Malini Aisola, co-convener, All India Drug Action Network. “With few middlemen involved in the distribution of these high-value, low-volume products, a hospital or distributor gets to keep nearly all the margin. That legitimises profiteering.”
When it comes to patented, mostly imported medicines, we are price-takers, insists Ms. Aisola. “The government is averse to using its legal powers under the Indian Patent Act and TRIPS (Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) — such as government use and compulsory licensing — to increase competition.”
The government, she adds, monitors and controls medicine prices based on a proprietary dataset owned by pharmaceutical companies. “This data,” she argues, “underrepresents or completely excludes institutional sales of cancer medicines because of the way the data are gathered and modelled.”
Besides, freebies under patient assistance programmes (PAPs) are now excluded from the calculation. “Including all PAP volumes would expose the true trade mark-ups to hospitals and force a bigger MRP cut,” says Ms. Aisola.
Beyond medicines
Medicines are only a part of the bill. Cut the margin, and the cost could mimic the cancer in finding another site. Other expensive components of treatment —diagnostic tests, surgery, radiotherapy, hospital accommodation, consumables, consultations, drug administration and associated clinical services — also need to be addressed. “Hospitals have several avenues to recoup the shortfall,” says a healthcare activist.
Running a hospital today is highly capital- and cost-intensive. Industry estimates suggest that each bed can cost ₹30 lakh to ₹1.5 crore, and a hospital needs around two-thirds of its beds occupied just to break even. The bills keep coming even when patients are not, says the COO of a Mumbai hospital. . “Hospitals have long relied on margins because they are legally allowed to,” notes Dr. Warrier.
Optimisation, Dr. Kabra avers, needs to go beyond drugs. “Hospitals and doctors get paid progressively less for the same procedure or disease depending on whether a self-paying patient, an insurer or a government health scheme is footing the bill. This squeeze can make care financially unviable, especially in complex interventions,” he points out. He also asks why caps have not yet been applied to manufacturers. “It seems unfair that manufacturers profit several times their production costs while everyone else is held to 30%,” he says. “Yes, manufacturers take greater risks and often only one of the dozens of drugs they research makes it to the market. But the profits they earn cannot be disproportionate forever.”
The price of exclusivity
Drug patents are another issue, point out experts. While many cancer therapies in India now have multiple generic manufacturers despite patents, generics in India are required to demonstrate bioequivalence — the degree to which they match the reference drug — before they can be marketed, says S. Srinivasan, co-founder of LOCOST, a not-for-profit maker of affordable generic medicines. “Affordability of cancer medicines depends not only on patent expiry, but also on whether generic firms can bear the exorbitant costs of bioequivalence testing,” he says.
Hospitals can add to their troubles. For instance, multinational brands of a targeted cancer medication like palbociclib can cost many times more than their generic equivalents, says a healthcare activist, giving hospitals a significantly bigger margin and thereby, an incentive to push the pricier option. “This only undermines affordable generics and entrenches multinationals,” he rues.
Limits of control
Murali Neelakantan, principal lawyer at advisory firm, amicus, calls price controls a “terrible” solution to a demand-supply mismatch. “It has second order, unintended consequences that are difficult to fix,” he says. “Price control can only be an emergency short-term measure to deal with market failure and catastrophic events that cannot be easily mitigated by market interventions.”
Mr. Neelakantan suggests treating drugs like food grains — not subject to price controls — and releasing government-procured drug stocks to stabilise prices whenever supplies fall short. The government, he says, can intervene by building more government hospitals and by procuring goods and services from private healthcare providers in an efficient manner rather than through fragmented schemes. The scale of procurement gives the government immense economic power to influence demand and facilitate price discovery and stabilisation, he points out. “Coercive regulation of prices will further distort the market and incentivise unethical practices, including evasive tactics by market participants,” he warns.
Trade margin caps are, at best, tokenistic, says Mr. Srinivasan. MRPs of anti-cancer drugs are high even after trade margins. “A better approach,” he suggests, “could be to base the MRP on API (active pharmaceutical ingredient) cost plus manufacturing and marketing expenses, with a 100–200% mark-up to recoup post-manufacturing expenses and trade margins.
The best solution for poor or middle-class cancer patients in India, however, would be free medicines provided by the government.” For now, though, a ‘cheaper’ cancer drug is no cure for exorbitant treatment.
(Harsh Kabra is an independent journalist and commentator. harshkabra@gmail.com)

Lake Ontario, the vast body of water that straddles the US-Canada border, has gone by many names over the centuries: Lac Saint-Louis, Lacus Ontarius, Skaniadorio, Cataraqui Lake. But one thing it will never be called, says the Canadian rock star Bryan Adams, is Lake America.
In his new song Lake Ontario, Adams takes aim at the US president, Donald Trump, accusing him of “breaking the peace” between the people who live on the lake’s shores.
Trump signed an executive order in August directing US federal agencies to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”, echoing his earlier, widely mocked decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico “the Gulf of America”.
The move further escalated a feud with Canada that has strained the longstanding alliance between the two countries. Trump’s decision has largely been met with derision in Canada, with some pointing out that the province of Ontario is named after the lake, not the other way around. Adams’s lyrics emphasise the roots of the name:
 The ‘lake of shining waters’ is what the Iroquois called her
It’s a First Nations name – not an executive order.
Adams’s lyrics also suggest that Trump’s naming stunt was intended to deflect from the president’s other political problems, including the war in Iran and renewed scrutiny of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
 But things weren’t going his way in Iran
So like a baby tossing the toys from the pram
But it feels like another distraction
While the Epstein files were getting traction
The song is part of what Adams described in a recent interview as a broader “love letter” to Canada: a songwriting project that began with an invitation from a film company to write about the Maritimes provinces of Canada and has since morphed into the upcoming album How’s It Goin’.
“After finishing the first song, I moved on to that one, and then moved on to another one, and then started thinking maybe I should just carry on with my theme,” he said.
As well as homages to Canadian heroes, the album also includes 51st State, released on 1 July – Canada Day – as another repudiation of Trump, in this case his efforts to annex Canada.
 You can push us to the brink
But where the open road divides
You’ll find a wall of maple
With us on the other side.
The first time he played the song in public was in the US.
“We weren’t sure how people were going to respond to it,” he said. “But we got a standing ovation every night for it. It made me think: perhaps, finally, the tide’s turning.”

Pandemic preparedness, support for Ukraine, and the fight against superbugs topped the agenda Tuesday as WHO and UK health leaders met in London to discuss their shared global health priorities.
In their first one-on-one meeting, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and UK Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Steve Barclay MP spoke at length about their shared commitment to delivering a pandemic instrument – a new international agreement being negotiated by WHO Member States – to strengthen global collaboration to help protect the world from another pandemic.
Mr Barclay outlined the UK government’s priorities for a pandemic instrument, which include faster and more efficient data sharing between WHO Member States; quicker, more equitable access to affordable vaccines, tests and treatments; and stronger collaboration on scientific research and development.
“The World Health Organization has reached a significant milestone this year in the marking of its 75th anniversary, and I’m proud of the UK’s longstanding relationship with WHO to improve public health,” Mr Barclay said. “The UK is playing a leading role in tackling some of the world’s greatest health threats, including antimicrobial resistance for which we recently announced £39 million for research into new drugs to combat infections.”
In 2022 and in the previous biennium, the UK was the largest contributor to WHO’s Core Voluntary Contributions Account. The account provides flexible funds that WHO can use and allocate as needed within its approved programme budgets. 
Earlier in the day, Dr Tedros joined International Development Minister Andrew Mitchell and Health Minister Will Quince for the annual UK-WHO Strategic Dialogue to discuss how to tackle global health challenges together and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. 
They spoke about effectively responding to health emergencies, preventing the next pandemic and confronting threats to health posed by climate change.
Ministers Mitchell and Quince emphasized the importance of building strong health systems in countries and protecting the health and rights of women and girls. Ministers also cited the importance of reform to strengthen WHO as an organization, expressing support for WHO’s extensive efforts to prevent and respond to sexual misconduct.  
“WHO highly values its strong and impactful collaboration with the UK Government to promote and protect the health of people worldwide,” Dr Tedros said as the meetings concluded. “Today’s strategic dialogue with Ministers Mitchell and Quince, and my productive discussions with Secretary of State Barclay, demonstrated the UK’s commitment to global public health, its support of the World Health Organization, and the great potential and impact of our partnership. I look forward to continuing our joint work to make the world healthier and safer on many fronts, from combatting antimicrobial resistance to supporting the UK and countries around the world to develop a generational accord to prevent and respond to future pandemics.”

The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.
Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.
The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.
Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.
The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.
Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.
At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”
Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.
When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.
In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.
Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.
“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”
Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.
The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.
The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.
In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
KYIV, Ukraine — Like many tech entrepreneurs in Ukraine, Yaroslav Azhnyuk turned to developing drone warfare after Russia's 2022 invasion.
Drones have transformed the way wars are fought. Azhnyuk says artificial intelligence is making drones faster and more capable.
"When the other side has orders of magnitudes higher capabilities, it gives you an asymmetric advantage," he says. "It can make you 10,000 times more effective."
Azhnyuk runs the Ukraine-based defense firms The Fourth Law and Odd Systems. They are among the top companies producing AI-powered drones in Ukraine. Dozens of Ukrainian military units already use their autonomous drone, called the Lupynis-10-TFL-1.
Russia is also deploying AI-enabled drones against Ukraine. AI warfare is part of a high-tech arms race that has many worried, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He has warned that AI could lead decisions on the battlefield as soon as next year.
Azhnyuk told NPR that he acknowledges the concern over destructive weapons but says it's not specific to AI.
"It has been with humanity since the invention of fire or steel," he says. "Any kind of tool can be used for good or for bad. And in the end, it's the human that decides how to use that tool."
Cameras that "fling explosives"
Azhnyuk is 37, a gregarious computer scientist who hails from a family of scholars and scientists. NPR meets him in a conference room in Kyiv; for security reasons he asked us not to reveal much else about the location.
He worked for years in Silicon Valley and started several companies, including Petcube, which makes smartphone-powered cameras that use artificial intelligence to watch and even entertain pets while they're alone.
"These cameras allow pet parents to watch pets when they're not at home," he says, "and fling treats to them and shine a laser toy for them. We sold a million of these devices that are quite popular in the U.S."
After Russia launched its full-scale war, Azhnyuk, by then living in Ukraine, pivoted to the defense space.
"I was like, OK, I've got to move on from Petcube and do something to protect my country," he says. "And so now we're making not cameras that fling treats but cameras that fling explosives at people who came to occupy our land."
The cameras he's talking about are part of an image recognition system incorporated into first-person-view or FPV drones.
"We are leaders in autonomous drones and thermal cameras," he says.
A drone named after a poet
The autonomous Lupynis TFL-1 drone combines a small, affordable FPV drone with an autonomous terminal guidance unit. That means the drone has an onboard computer and AI technology that takes control during the last 500 meters (or 0.3 miles) of the flight.
"But it's very different from, say, the kind of AI that sits on those data centers that power Claude," he says. "Or even the kind of AI that does self-driving for your Tesla."
Azhnyuk says this AI technology uses simple tools to recognize images and make smart software "which then allows you either to navigate autonomously without a human or to choose a target autonomously or to fly toward the target autonomously."
The Fourth Law's autonomous drone is named after the 20th century Ukrainian poet and political activist Anatoliy Lupynis, who endured decades of Soviet imprisonment and psychiatric torture. The company named all its weapons after Ukrainian intellectuals and artists killed or persecuted by Russians in the last century.
"It is important for us to help to resurrect those people," Azhnyuk says. "Their ideas are still with us. And now they're fighting back."
"The drone is doing everything itself"
The Fourth Law teams test the Lupynis TFL-1 drones every day. We meet one team in an overgrown field outside Kyiv. They've set up a fold-out table near a copse of trees and a hornets' nest.
A slight, sandy-haired man stands up from the fold-out table and says he's the head of the test and integration team. He uses the military call sign Stab. The Fourth Law asked NPR not to reveal this location or the identities of those who work here for security reasons.
Stab points to a drone.
"So you see here is our camera, plus the microcomputer inside this 3-D model," Stab says. "All of the mind is here," he adds with a laugh.
The microcomputer inside the drone runs on a deep-learning neural network that uses hours of combat footage to recognize targets.
"Like vehicles, light-armored vehicles, tanks, and flying objects," he says.
The drone begins its flight guided by a pilot, who also asked us to use his call sign, Professor. He navigates the drone with a control stick. He selects a target and checks a video monitor. Then he sees a red flash.
"That means it has locked," Stab says.
The drone has locked onto its target: a dilapidated car an employee is driving along a dirt road. Professor lets go of the control stick. The drone flies itself to the car. The microcomputer inside constantly runs algorithms to keep it on course.
"See, Professor is doing nothing, and the drone is doing everything itself," Stab says.
On the battlefield, the drone would carry an explosive to hit the car. The test drone doesn't have one.
Stab says AI drones are useful because they're hard to jam. He also insists safeguards are in place so The Fourth Law drones won't go rogue. Humans select the target, he says.
Survival vs. the ethics of AI
Back in the conference room, Azhnyuk says his company's AI-powered drones are not killer robots.
"They're very far from a Terminator kind of scenario, right?" he says. "These are just sort of calculators. Like they're no more likely for a Terminator uprising than a warehouse with artillery shells."
He does acknowledge, though, that AI is developing quickly. "It's not unthinkable," he says, "to imagine that some years in the future there will be drones that will be able to make their own decisions on designating targets or not."
That's the future. Right now he is focused on what Ukraine needs today.
"Our adversaries are using the very same technologies, and if they use AI for decision-making in an offensive scenario, and if we refuse to use AI in decision-making in a defensive scenario, we've lost, right?" he says. "Because their systems are capable of making decisions in microseconds, and human control takes minutes, hours and sometimes days."
If Ukraine loses, he says, "there's no way for us to argue about the ethics of AI."
The most important thing, he says, is don't die.
NPR's Polina Lytvynova contributed to this story from Kyiv.

In 2015, biomedical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes was Silicon Valley’s golden girl, lauded as the youngest and richest self-made female billionaire thanks to the company she founded, Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion at the height of its success. Then it all came crashing down when accusations of fraud surfaced about the company’s signature blood-testing device, culminating in a sensational trial. Holmes was convicted on four counts and sentenced to 11 years in prison.
Holmes is back in the headlines thanks to a new film, You Can See Everything, which depicts the final days before Holmes, having exhausted her appeals, went to prison. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, it’s a surreal, absurdist piece that has largely been received with gushing enthusiasm and no small amount of hype, with some declaring it the best film of the year. A few contrarian voices have emerged over the past week with much-needed reality checks, but there’s no denying the film is destined to be an awards-season darling.
Pardon me for joining the buzzkills, but I cannot in good conscience jump on the You Can See Everything bandwagon. Sure, it has its moments, and the second half is highly entertaining, but there’s nothing here to warrant all the breathless hyperbole. For all their much-touted access, Oppenheim and Fielder have produced a surprisingly shallow film that runs in circles, yielding very little fresh or novel insight—into Holmes, personally, or much else.
I get that manufacturing ambiguity is the much-ballyhooed point. I get that much of the film’s appeal lies in how much fun people have afterward vigorously debating their interpretations of key scenes. But there’s no real mystery here. Holmes is still spouting all the same talking points and self-justifications, still playing the victim, dodging accountability, and affixing blame on anyone except herself, just as she did all the way through her trial. The only mystery is why a convicted fraudster is still deemed worthy of our attention.
tl;dr: Elizabeth Holmes is back on her bulls—t, and some people are falling for the act all over again.
(Spoilers below the first gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)
There is already an excellent HBO documentary about Holmes and Theranos by Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney: The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley, a companion piece to journalist John Carreyrou’s 2018 book, Bad Blood. (I reviewed Gibney’s latest, Musk, earlier this month.) Holmes was also the focus of the 2022 Hulu fictionalized miniseries (and associated podcast) The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried as Holmes. None showed Holmes how she clearly wished to be perceived, so she reached out to A24 about making a documentary to tell her side of the story.
You will be shocked to hear that Holmes believes she is innocent and thought all she needed to do was “speak her truth” in order to convince everyone else, too. It didn’t work on a jury of her peers—who deemed her the least credible witness of the entire trial—but apparently it worked on Fielder. At least he’s in good company: Holmes fooled a lot of smart, savvy people for years before a pair of whistleblowers (Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung) exposed her lies.
Fielder, for those unfamiliar with his work, is a comedian, best known for his Comedy Central series (currently streaming on HBO) Nathan for You. Fielder played a fictionalized version of himself as a recent business graduate who “consulted” for struggling local businesses in LA. The gimmick: Fielder’s advice, offered in his trademark deadpan style, was deliberately weird, such as suggesting an ice cream store offer a poop flavor to generate headlines and draw customers. In another episode, he faked a video, which actually went viral, of a pig rescuing a goat at the local petting zoo.
Fielder was also an executive producer on the (excellent) HBO series How To With John Wilson before creating the docu-comedy, The Rehearsal, in which another heightened reality version of Fielder helps people prepare for difficult conversations by re-creating the conditions and environments in which those conversations will take place, frequently building extravagant sets to do so. If cringe humor is your thing (think Sasha Baron Cohen, with whom Fielder has also worked), then you’ll likely find Fielder’s schtick appealing—and you’ll be far more likely to love You Can See Everything.
Still, at first glance, he was a puzzling choice to co-direct this film, as was Oppenheim, who calls himself a “docu-fantasist.” The two men met at some point, became friends, and wanted to work on a project together; Holmes and current partner Billy Evans were Fielder fans. Thus, You Can See Everythingwas born.
Who’s playing who?

Fielder and Oppenheim don’t spend much time rehashing the Theranos debacle and Holmes’ subsequent trial and conviction, which is fine; that has been covered exhaustively elsewhere, including the Gibney documentary, and it’s not what they were interested in capturing. They’re more keen on the vibes than the facts. Holmes and Evans invited Fielder and the film crew to stay with them for the 34 days before her imprisonment, and given the strangeness of their initial interactions, Fielder became a major on-camera presence in the film.
The first half of the film is on the dull side, featuring lots of footage of Fielder and Holmes staring at each other, unblinking, in an attempt to convince each other of their sincerity. (Jimmy Fallon and Jamie Lee Curtis hilariously spoofed this dynamic in a cold open for The Tonight Show.) There is a tiresome segment quibbling over the relative meanings of the words “can” and “could.” Another segment dissects whether or not Holmes is capable of understanding the humor behind the classic “Who’s on First” sketch.
Fielder’s deadpan comedic style is used to good effect. Any laughs in that first half come from his reaction shots, such as his expression when Holmes insists, blue eyes extra wide, that she has never once lied in her entire life. And it’s just innately funny seeing him pop up again and again at the edges of the frame, like an awkwardly diffident stalker.
Much has been made of the scene where Evans insists Fielder film him working out at the gym—including a post-workout shower scene with Evans faux-nonchalantly displaying side-frontal nudity. It’s nothing we haven’t seen before; HBO flashes its viewers all the time. Still, I can never unsee Evans’ flaccid junk, so thanks for that image being burned into my retinas, guys. But it fits the sleight-of-hand theme Fielder and Oppenheimer develop throughout the film. On the one hand, we are literally seeing everything. On the other, it is only the illusion of transparency, because Evans is so relentlessly squirrely and evasive—when not outright combative—about answering Fielder’s questions.
Frankly, Holmes and Evans just aren’t sufficiently interesting to carry a three-hour film, which is why Amanda Seyfried is such a breath of fresh air when she turns up for the second half to help Fielder and Oppenheim work around the physical absence of their primary subject. Seyfried plays Holmes in several carefully staged re-enactments—a fascinating window into the actor’s process—but she also becomes Fielder’s sounding board and (at times) co-conspirator. The film comes to life when she appears, akin to tossing a firecracker into a lackluster dinner party.
Seyfried, for instance, goads Evans into revealing that he has power of attorney and manages most activity on Holmes’ X account. She challenges Fielder about being reluctant to include footage that might show Holmes in a negative light because he’s come to care about her. And the film doesn’t let Seyfried off the hook either, forcing her to confront how her portrayal in The Dropout might have been painful for Holmes, despite clearly being fictionalized to allow for taking a few liberties with the facts.
An “absurdist reality show”?

Ars Technica senior editor Sam Axon, who loved the film, describes it as “an absurdist reality show” or a “post-postmodern comedy rather than an interesting documentary” that is “more for fans of Nathan Fielder than for people interested in Theranos.” Fair enough. But it has been marketed as a documentary. That label carries certain expectations. Yes, Fielder and Oppenheim are deliberately (and skillfully) thwarting those expectations, but to what end? Savvy consumers already know that documentaries frame their subjects in specific ways. Gibney, for one, unapologetically makes documentaries that espouse his personal point of view, rejecting the so-called “view from nowhere”—i.e., the illusion of objectivity. And reality TV has been around for decades. We know it’s innately performative, and that cameras subtly alter human behavior, blurring the boundary between truth and fiction. This is not a novel insight.
Fielder makes a show of approaching his subject with an open mind in order to be more “objective,” but there are plenty of details that Fielder omits to better shape his preferred narrative. For instance, Evans claimed they took a private jet to the Texas federal prison, whereas the film shows them driving there. More significantly, it’s clear Fielder deeply dislikes Evans (by the end of filming, the feeling was mutual), which is why he deliberately features moments that portray Evans as a controlling, manipulative, and almost comically vain Silicon Valley bro.
By comparison, Holmes is treated with kid gloves. This is not the smart, savvy, high-powered businesswoman who graced magazine covers and wowed tech reporters with her rosy vision of a diagnostic future free of anxiety-inducing blood draws. Even whistleblower Tyler Shultz has said this version of Holmes seems “broken.” But she’s still a very good liar.
Shultz points out in an article for STAT News that Holmes and Evans were living in the $125 million Green Gables estate just prior to filming. They moved to a smaller, average-looking rented condo on the beach for the duration of the shoot (which still rents for around $28,000 a month)—a strategy Holmes employed before when being profiled by journalists. And the disassembled Theranos blood testing device Holmes displays for the cameras—in the scene that triggered the “can” vs. “could” discussion—is not the correct device, per Shultz:
That was not the device I worked with 12 hours a day, not the device we hid from regulators, not the device that constantly failed quality controls, not the device we used to knowingly give patients inaccurate medical results. The device she showed Fielder on the kitchen table was not the reason she went to prison. Elizabeth showed him a future version of the Theranos product that was never completed and never used in order to lead Fielder down this BS semantic rabbit hole and to trick him into litigating the entirely wrong thing.
Did Fielder catch the misdirection? Was he taken in by the subterfuge, like so many before him? Or is he willfully ignoring those aspects because they don’t suit his purposes? I’ll take Gibney’s transparent subjectivity any day over Fielder’s ambiguous gamesmanship.
You Can See Everything is obsessed with whether Holmes is lying, believes her own lies, or even understands what lying entails. Perhaps it’s not that black and white. I’m willing to grant that Holmes’ tears at having to leave her newborn child to serve her sentence are genuine; any mother would be heartbroken. But it also serves her broader purpose of crafting a more sympathetic narrative. The portrait that emerges is one of Holmes as the victim of yet another controlling, abusive man. It’s her entire legal defense during her trial, re-created here for Fielder’s (and our) benefit, with Evans taking on the scapegoat role of Holmes’ former business and romantic partner, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, currently serving a 12-year sentence for his part in the Theranos debacle.
Fielder has built his entire brand around the unreliable narrator trope, while Oppenheim has been accused of misleading his subjects while making a 2017 short for The New York Times, so it’s fair to say both men might have a complicated relationship with the truth. Perhaps Holmes got the “documentarians” she deserved, and this is a match made in heaven. One can’t rule out the possibility that she and Evans were in on the game from the start and that the entire film is an elaborate performance piece, manufactured for our post-truth consumption: ‘Haha, look at these people trying to out-manipulate each other for the cameras, like contestants on the latest reality show.’ Are you not entertained?
The cynical nihilism of it all is exhausting, and ultimately the joke is on us. Facts matter. Accountability matters. Even in a world awash in deep fakes and misinformation, there are still some truths that can be known, no matter how doggedly Fielder and Oppenheim try to muddy the waters. They want us to believe that Elizabeth Holmes is “unknowable and everything is ambiguous,” as Carreyrou—who, unlike me, loved the film and thinks it should win the Oscar for best picture—recently wrote on X. “She went after Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung with everything she had. I was threatened with litigation on a daily basis for months on end. It was a ruthless cover-up of a breathtaking fraud, and she was at the controls. Just a little context for those who have forgotten or didn’t follow the original story.”
In the grand scheme of things, nobody cares what the science-and-culture writer at Ars Technica thinks about this film. I am firmly in the minority with my assessment, and I’m good with that. Oppenheim and Fielder will rake in box-office millions and collect a bunch of prestigious awards, including a possible Oscar. Holmes will serve her time—in fact, she’ll be eligible for a halfway house next year—and Evans is already hard at work raising capital for a new biomedical startup. Holmes will once again try to rehabilitate her image by spinning some new variation on how she did nothing wrong, the device really does work, and she is the victim here. It’s the only story she knows how to tell.
But we don’t have to keep falling for it.
You Can See Everything is now playing in theaters.
Jennifer is a senior writer at Ars Technica with a particular focus on where science meets culture, covering everything from physics and related interdisciplinary topics to her favorite films and TV series. Jennifer lives in Baltimore with her spouse, physicist Sean M. Carroll, and their two cats, Ariel and Caliban.

Ethiopia acquires Russian fighter jets and air defence systems amid war in Tigray
- Published
Ethiopia has received 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, as fighting intensified in the northern Tigray region neighbouring Eritrea.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who is attending the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, described the acquisition as a "milestone" that would boost Ethiopia's defence capacity.
He said Ethiopia and Russia had agreed on the deal several years ago and the warplanes had come ahead of schedule. He also said that Ethiopia had plans to acquire four S-400 air defence systems from Moscow.
The Ethiopian leader said the military hardware was essential to protect the country from external threats.
Abiy, who described Russian President Vladimir Putin, "as a close friend of Ethiopia", said Ethiopia had now become the first country in sub‑Saharan Africa to own this kind of "advanced combat technology".
"If we fail to build this capability, surviving as a country in our region will become difficult. Countries with sufficient preparation are not easily defied," he said.
Russia and Ethiopia have signed several military agreements in recent years, including a deal in 2021 to train and improve technology for the military.
- How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia 
  - Published2 October
Abiy explained that Ethiopia signed an agreement with Russia several years ago to procure the Su‑35 jets and S‑400 systems, citing global air force trends and security threats facing the country.
The Su‑35, he noted, was equipped for both air‑to‑air and air‑to‑ground combat, with the ability to detect and neutralize incoming cruise missiles at distances of up to 200km (124 miles).
Military intelligence analyst Qalaab Segatu told BBC Amharic that Ethiopia's acquisition of additional warplanes was a key indication that "it was preparing for possible wars with other countries, not just internal conflicts".
According to him, the jets are highly manoeuvrable and capable of covering large areas, with radars capable of ensuring air superiority and long-range scanning.
When combined, the fighter jets and air defence systems "create a significant capability to protect and defend major cities and critical infrastructure such as the Renaissance Dam, providing key strategic air superiority", Qalaab said.
Abiy said in addition to the advanced capabilities of the aircraft from Russia, the use of drones was equally important in strengthening deterrence.
Ethiopia has extensively used military drones, including those sourced from Turkey and China, in recent conflicts.
"We need to build capacity not only with drones, but also with the fourth generation capabilities of the Su 30 and Su 35 [aircraft]," Abiy said.
The latest acquisition of military hardware from Russia comes after the current conflict in northern Tigray started last month between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which it denies.
Tensions between the two countries have also persisted as Abiy terms Ethiopia's lack of direct sea access an "existential question", which Eritrea views as a direct threat to its sovereignty.
Eritrea gained independence in 1993 after a decades-long war with Ethiopia, with the latter losing access to the sea.

On 22 October 2026, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur acknowledged that face-offs with Chinese forces had occurred at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border. On 23 October 2026, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal stated that the situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) becomes “disturbed” when Chinese troops deviate from established patrolling patterns.
Amid this, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows residents of Arunachal Pradesh fighting Chinese soldiers. The post also alleges that soldiers from the region have been called to Delhi. Let’s verify the claim in this article.
Claim: The video shows residents of Arunachal Pradesh fighting with Chinese soldiers in October 2026.
Fact: The video dates back to 23 May 2025 and shows a protest against the proposed Siang Dam project in Beging village, Siang district, Arunachal Pradesh, not residents fighting Chinese soldiers in October 2026. Arunachal Pradesh Police officer Sangay Tenzin confirmed to Factly that the uniformed personnel in the video are police officers and identified the officer seen in the video as DySP Toguam Gongo. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a Facebook post dated 23 May 2025 featuring the same video. This confirms that the video predates and is unrelated to the reported face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops along the Arunachal Pradesh border in October 2026. According to the post, the Anti-Dam Party of Siang and Upper Siang districts organised an indefinite sit-in protest in Beging village, Siang district, where NHPC has proposed the Siang Dam project. Approximately 400 people participated in the protest. During the protest, a group of angry activists set fire to the village’s suspension bridge, partially damaging it. The protest was later called off following negotiations with officials.
Upon closely examining the clearer version of the video, we noticed that the police officer’s uniform bears the Arunachal Pradesh Police Service (APPS) badge on the shoulder and the Arunachal Pradesh Police logo.
We also found several videos uploaded (here, here, and here) by local media outlets in May 2025 featuring visuals similar to those in the viral video. Their captions described the footage as showing a protest against the proposed dam in Beging village, Siang district, on 23 May 2025.
We contacted Arunachal Pradesh Police officer Sangay Tenzin, who appeared in media reports. He confirmed to Factly that the uniformed personnel in the video are Arunachal Pradesh Police officers, not Chinese soldiers. He said he was present at the protest against the proposed dam in Beging village, Siang district, in May 2025, along with DySP Toguam Gongo, whom he identified as the officer seen in the viral video. At the time, Tenzin was posted as DySP (Headquarters), Siang, while Gongo was DySP (Law and Order), Siang. Both have since been transferred to other districts.
To sum up, this video shows a confrontation between residents of Arunachal Pradesh and police during a 2025 protest, not a fight with Chinese soldiers in October 2026.

Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.
“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”
After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”
Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.
The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.
Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.
Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.
“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”
Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.
Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.
Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.
He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.
“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”
The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.
Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.
“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

In the future, you won’t be able to use Reddit without logging in.
Reddit CEO Steve Huffman confirmed the impending change in a letter (PDF) to shareholders today about Q3 performance. He said that Reddit is shifting “to a logged-in-only experience,” adding:
Moving to primarily logged-in will ensure our users have the best Reddit experience possible, and can find the content and communities most relevant to them. It is better for our business because we will have more signals for ads targeting, and being logged-in leads to higher engagement generally. It also allows us to protect access to Reddit’s extremely valuable corpus of data, and helps us better adapt to emerging regulations around the world.
Huffman also said that the login requirement will help Reddit better retain new users.
Reddit will start testing the login requirement in “select,” non-US markets in Q4. The company will use those tests to decide what a logged-in-only Reddit will look like “globally,” per Huffman.
“Pretty much all of the major ad-based platforms have gone through this transition. We are excited and moving quickly,” the CEO added, noting Reddit’s intent to become a “direct daily habit for every Internet user.”
The impending requirement comes as Reddit search referral traffic “was down meaningfully in Q3,” Huffman wrote. The largest hit came from logged-out and web traffic, and the overall trend has continued into Q4.
“During October, we have seen that search traffic has dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week. If this rate of decline continues, current trends would suggest that total DAUqs [or daily active unique users] could fall in Q4, by a low-double-digit percentage from our current base of 130 million DAUqs,” Huffman wrote.

Trillions of bacteria living in the human gut may play a role in Parkinson’s disease, a brain disorder that causes tremors, stiffness, and slowed movement, according to a new study involving patients from Keralam.
Researchers from the Cochin University of Science and Technology (CUSAT) and the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST), Thiruvananthapuram, found significant differences between the gut bacteria of Parkinson’s patients and those of healthy individuals. The findings were published online in npj Parkinson’s Disease, an international scientific journal.
Parkinson’s disease occurs when nerve cells in the brain that produce dopamine, a chemical that helps control movement, gradually die. Scientists have long suspected that the gut and brain communicate continuously, and that an imbalance in gut bacteria could contribute to inflammation affecting the brain. Studies have shown that non-motor symptoms, including constipation and other gastrointestinal problems, can appear years before the tremors begin in Parkinson’s patients.
The study involved 65 Parkinson’s patients attending SCTIMST’s Comprehensive Care Centre for Movement Disorders and 65 healthy individuals, most of whom were the patients’ spouses. Spouses were included as healthy individuals for comparison, as they were more likely to share similar diets and living conditions.
Metagenomic sequencing
Researchers analysed stool samples using metagenomic sequencing (16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing), a technique that identifies the bacteria present and helps assess their potential functions in the gut. They found higher levels of bacteria potentially associated with inflammation and lower levels of beneficial bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids, which help maintain the gut lining healthy and regulate the immune system, in Parkinson’s patients.
The researchers suggest that the shift in bacterial communities could weaken the gut barrier and allow inflammation to spread.
“The study found that differences in the abundances of these bacteria were strongly associated with disease severity and other clinical features of Parkinson’s disease,” said Baby Chakrapani P. S., director of the Centre for Neuroscience and assistant professor in the Department of Biotechnology at CUSAT. “The findings also suggest that gut bacteria may be linked to disease progression through their influence on processes involving dopamine, glutamate, and GABA, chemicals that play important roles in brain function.”
Funded by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the study was conducted by Aneesa P. A., a research associate at CUSAT, under the supervision of Mr. Chakrapani and Dr. Syam Krishnan of SCTIMST.
Gut bacterial composition is influenced by factors such as diet, age, sex, and lifestyle. Differences in these factors, as well as genetics, could explain why studies in different populations have reported inconsistent associations between particular bacteria and Parkinson’s disease.
According to the researchers, this is the first study in an Indian population to integrate gut microbiome composition with its functional role in Parkinson’s disease. The findings could help future research into simple tests for early diagnosis of the disease and treatments aimed at restoring gut health.

Centre open to amending DPDP Act rules or the law itself to address media concerns over its impact on press freedom, days after Supreme Court agreed to hear challenge
NEW DELHI: Centre Friday said it is open to changing the rules of Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and, if necessary, the law itself to eliminate the possibility of its application becoming an impediment for journalists and media houses.Senior officials at the ministry for electronics & information technology said that sections of the law, which have been flagged as violative of the constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of speech and expression, are applicable to data fiduciaries and they are not for journalists."This law is only on data fiduciaries-those who keep and control data. Journalists and media houses do not come under this category," When told about the worry among journalists that DPDP Act does not expressly exempt media houses, he said, "The rules can always be amended to allay any concern on that count. The rules have the same power as the law. If necessary, we can go a step further to change the law itself."The DPDP Act has been been justified in citing citizen's right to privacy, the need to protect data and in placing obligations on data fiduciaries.
Centre's reaction came days after the apex court agreed to examine a plea filed by Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) which represents 21 of India's leading news media organisations and challenged the validity of various provisions of the act and rules framed under it.
The association alleged that the law was violative of the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression and threatened the full spectrum of journalistic activity.Officials said that the the concern about the DPDP act becoming an impediment for journalists will be addressed by carving out exemptions for them in the rules and, if necessary, in the law itself.I&B minister Ashwini Vaishnav said on Friday that Section 7 of the DPDP Act is for data fiduciaries like banks, telecom providers and insurance companies and media does not come within its ambit. "This govt is committed to uphold the constitutionally guaranteed rights to freedom and expression". Section 7 says that "the personal data of a data principal may be processed by a data fiduciary (a) for the specified purpose for which the Data Principal has voluntarily provided her personal data... and in respect of which she has not indicated... that she does not consent to the use of her personal data."

The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.
Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK, standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” he said in the post. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
Myanmar’s military has held the Nobel peace prize laureate in almost total seclusion since the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”.
On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year.
Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

Buddha-linked holy relics to be taken to Arunachal for exposition from Oct 31-Nov 21
Tawang, Sacred Piprahwa relics linked with Lord Buddha are set to be brought to Arunachal Pradesh for a three-week exposition in the northeast state starting with Tawang on October 31, officials said on Friday.
Currently housed at the National Museum in Delhi, the holy relics will be on display at the iconic Tawang Memorial till November 1, following the inauguration of the exposition on Saturday, and will then be taken to Bomdila and Namsai, reflecting Arunachal Pradesh's rich Buddhist traditions.
Union Minister of Culture and Tourism, Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, is scheduled to participate in the inaugural ceremony at the historic Gaden Namgyal Lhatse , the culture ministry said.
The ministry is hosting the exposition of the Holy Relics of Shakyamuni Buddha, in collaboration with the government of Arunachal Pradesh, the International Buddhist Confederation and the National Museum, from October 31 to November 21, it said.
After ceremonial observances at the museum on the night of October 30, the relics are planned to be taken to the Air Force Station, Palam, for onward transportation to Arunachal Pradesh, the officials said.
As per the proposed movement itinerary, the holy relics are scheduled to depart from Palam in the early hours of October 31 by a special Indian Air Force aircraft and reach the Air Force Station, Borjhar, Guwahati, before being transported by helicopter to Tawang, they said.
Upon arrival, the holy relics will be received with due religious ceremony and reverence.
They will thereafter be taken to the Tawang Monastery for installation and the inaugural ceremony, scheduled for October 31 morning.
A further inaugural function, together with the opening of the associated exposition and exhibition, is scheduled for November 1, with Arunachal Chief Minister Pema Khandu as the chief guest, the ministry said.
The exposition will coincide with the last day of International Tourism Mart 2026 being hosted by the tourism ministry in Tawang from October 29-31.
On Friday, several ITM delegates visited the Tawang monastery and experienced the rich architectural and cultural heritage of the centuries-old Buddhist site.
PTI also visited the monastery on Friday morning and interacted with some of the monks there.
Preparations are underway for the exposition at the monastery, which is also a popular tourist destination.
"The holy relics were last time brought here in 2013 when Tawang hosted it. We feel deeply honoured to host it again. The Holy Relics of Shakyamuni Buddha hold great reverence for us. His exalted statue graces the central hall of our monastery," the monk told PTI here.
The occasion coincides with the observance of Lhabab Duchen, a significant festival in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition commemorating the Buddha's descent from the heavenly realm. The exposition will thus bring together religious observance, cultural heritage and public participation in a spiritually meaningful setting, the official said.
The movement and installation of the holy relics are being planned with particular attention to their sanctity, security and conservation requirements. The Ministry of Culture is coordinating with the Ministry of Defence, Indian Air Force, the government of Arunachal Pradesh, the National Museum and other agencies concerned for the necessary operational arrangements, they said.
Piprahwa, present-day Siddharthnagar district, Uttar Pradesh, occupies a prominent place in the archaeological history of Buddhism. In 1898, William Claxton Peppé excavated a stupa at the site and discovered reliquaries containing bone fragments and precious objects, bringing international attention to the historical and religious significance of the discovery.
Subsequently, the Archaeological Survey of India conducted further excavations between 1971 and 1977 under the supervision of archaeologist K M Srivastava. Excavations at deeper levels revealed two additional reliquary caskets containing ancient bone relics traditionally associated with Lord Buddha, the culture ministry said.
The larger casket contained 12 sacred bone fragments, while the smaller casket contained 10, making a total of 22 sacred relics recovered during these excavations. Of these, 20 are preserved at the National Museum, New Delhi, and two at the Indian Museum, Kolkata.
The relics, comprising ancient osteological material, are regarded as exceptionally rare and are accorded profound religious reverence by Buddhist communities. Their historical and archaeological importance is accompanied by a deep spiritual significance rooted in the long-established Buddhist tradition of relic veneration.
On November 8, the holy relics are scheduled to be ferried from Tawang to Rupa by helicopter and thereafter, by road to Bomdila. The itinerary includes ceremonial reception at Upper Gompa before their installation at Lower Gompa, the officials said.
On November 14, the holy relics will be transported from Bomdila to Rupa by road and thereafter, by helicopter to Nalung Helipad, Namsai. They will be taken to the Golden Pagoda for the exposition.
Following the conclusion of public darshan at Namsai, the holy relics are scheduled to return to the National Museum on November 21 via Tezu Airport and Air Force Station, Palam.
The timings and movement arrangements will remain subject to operational, weather and security considerations, the officials said.
The holy relics being taken to Arunachal Pradesh originate from Piprahwa in present-day Siddharthnagar district, an archaeological site associated with ancient Kapilavastu and the Shakya tradition of Lord Buddha.

For a genuine fright this Halloween, you can turn your gaze to the southern border, where ravenous, flesh-eating maggots are festering and have taken to eating people’s pets.
This week, the country’s New World Screwworm (NWS) infestation spread to a third state, Arizona, which joins New Mexico and Texas in being plagued by the horrifying parasites. To date, 74 animal cases have been identified in the US since the flies re-invaded the country in June.
The flies lay hundreds of eggs in wounds and moist orifices of animals, and the resulting voracious maggots feast on their victims. The maggots resemble screws and tortuously bore and twist into living flesh, causing severe, sometimes fatal wounds, before dropping to the ground to develop into adults.
Because of their ability to ravage livestock, the flies were eliminated from the country in the 1960s through aerial releases of sterile male flies, which thwart successful breeding. For years, they were held at bay using a biological barrier along the Darién Gap at the border of Panama and Colombia. But the barrier was breached in 2022, and the flies have made their way back to the US through Central America.
No one is safe
While they are largely seen as a threat to the livestock industry, they can also devastate wildlife, domestic pets, and in rarer cases, humans. According to the latest data from Mexico’s Ministry of Health, the country has confirmed 806 cases of human screwworm infestations since the flies reemerged. Nine people died from the savage maggots.

Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.
Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.
Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”
The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.
“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.
Neither Binance or law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers, but researchers say there are overlaps with previous cryptocurrency attacks from TraderTraitor. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.
The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.
Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations—often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit.
Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible.
“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” the company says in a statement. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”
“These folks in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance organizations,” Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “TraderTraitor seems to focus on these larger operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations.”
TRM and Chainalysis have initially linked the attack to TraderTraitor and say the determinations are based on their analysis of both on-chain and off-chain activity. “The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit, which had been attributed to North Korean actors,” a research blog from Chainalysis says.
“Binance says the attack began with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Targeting crypto company staff is a TraderTraitor hallmark,” Elliptic’s Robinson says. “The attacker funded their wallet through Tornado Cash and rehearsed the attack in advance, as in Bybit.”
While around $3 billion of cryptocurrency was initially frozen in the aftermath of the attack, it is likely those behind it could still potentially take away huge sums as not all of the stolen crypto can be frozen. Research from Chainalysis says the company is seeing money “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that thousands of transactions being quickly processed indicates that they are using “automation to obscure the trail of funds.”
Elliptic’s Robinson says that around $2.8 billion, or around 44 percent of the total amount stolen, has been frozen by crypto companies and exchanges so far, with almost all of this being stablecoins. “The remaining $3.3 billion is mostly Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, which no one can freeze,” Robinson says. “It can only be stopped when it reaches an exchange or other service. Some will be caught over the coming months, but I don’t expect the frozen share to rise much further.”
