ICE activity is surging ahead of midterms. So is voter turnout.
Very early on Wednesday morning, Dover, N.J., Councilwoman Sandra Wittner started getting messages about immigration agents. A dozen or more were gathering outside a Walgreens, according to the messages she was getting. Throughout the day, neighbors in north New Jersey saw a spike in Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity.
And New Jersey is not alone. In the weeks ahead of the midterms, various cities and states across the country are reporting a notable rise in ICE activity, according to reports gathered by NPR and its member stations.
"The tactics that the administration has been deploying in communities really appear to be designed to try to intimidate voters," says Wendy Weiser of the Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law School. Despite that, early turnout is surging.
"There was definitely a lot of apprehension and fear," Wittner recalls. "We just really weren't sure if something huge was about to happen. People were not feeling very comfortable or safe."
Wittner is not sure who was detained or where, which is unsurprising: these days it's difficult to report on ICE crackdowns as they happen, because the Department of Homeland Security no longer publicly shares timely information on its operations.
NPR wrote to the agency to ask if there has been a recent surge. It responded: "ICE agents uphold our nation's immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day."
And yet NPR and its member stations have received tips from rural Illinois, Oregon, Detroit and California about surges in ICE enforcement, throughout October.
An official within New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office who was not authorized to speak publicly confirmed that they have noted a surge in ICE activity in the city.
"We're certainly witnessing an uptick in activity, and have been since the summer," says a member of a volunteer group of neighbors in New York. She asked that NPR not use her name, as she is worried about retaliation. Her group goes to the scene where an ICE operation is happening, documents it, reminds those being detained of their rights, and alerts neighbors.
"In the past few weeks we've seen numerous large operations, or what we call cluster raids, multiple agents going to one spot and then the next," she said.
On the other side of the country, Oregon Public Broadcasting reporter Troy Brynelson has reported on a similar trend. "What we were seeing in early October and what we've seen continue, at least anecdotally throughout this month, is that ICE activity has really picked up in Portland." Brynelson says it seems to be concentrated in commercial areas. "I'd say it's a noticeable uptick compared to what we've seen over the summer."
Juan Proaño of the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), a civil rights organization says he's concerned because this is happening so close to the midterm elections. "It's not about ICE at the actual polling station, it's ICE at the perimeter of the polling station," he says.
"Mass enforcement actions could be away from the polls, but with social media and the news, it could be enough to dissuade somebody from actually going out to vote."
Weiser of the Brennan Center says there's no indication the raids are affecting turnout. On the contrary, she says there has been a surge in early voting in minority communities across the country. "The good news is: it isn't working. Americans are tuning this out and we are not seeing a significant impact on participation. And we are actually seeing huge surges in participation in communities of color, and in Latino communities, and in all the communities that have been targeted by ICE and DHS."
Even so, she says that intimidation at the polls is illegal, and should be reported.

MGM Healthcare organised a three-km umbrella walkathon, ‘Stride for Stroke’, in Chennai on Thursday to mark World Stroke Day. More than 400 people, including stroke survivors, participated in the event, which was flagged off by actor Ramya Subramanian.

Roopesh Kumar, Director of Neurosurgery, MGM Healthcare, stressed the importance of recognising warning signs such as facial drooping, weakness on one side of the body, and difficulty speaking. Early treatment could help minimise the risks, he said. .

Haiti announces new election dates as 2,000 Salvadoran troops help fight gangs
Haiti’s government has announced new election dates as police and soldiers, backed by over 2,000 troops from El Salvador, fight gangs
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Haiti’s government has announced new election dates as police and soldiers backed by the recent arrival of more than 2,000 troops from El Salvador fight gangs.
The Provisional Electoral Council said late Wednesday that the first round of general elections will be held next July 18 and the second round on Oct. 4.
Haiti has not held elections in more than a decade and is run by an unelected prime minister. The presidency has been vacant since President Jovenel Moïse was killed in 2021.
The council said it expects to publish the final candidate list, including those running for the presidency or the Senate, by mid-January, with May 20 marking the end of voter registration.
The first round of elections was initially scheduled for Dec. 13, but was delayed by gang violence in Haiti’s central region and in Port-au-Prince. Four aviation technicians from El Salvador working with a U.N.-backed gang suppression force went missing on Oct. 18 in the capital after coming under attack.
In response, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti to help rescue the four technicians, who the Haitian government says were abducted.
El Salvador’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement late Wednesday that Bukele had spoken with Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé about the security operation to rescue the technicians.
Meanwhile, Haiti’s government issued a statement saying the two leaders are reinforcing cooperation within the framework of the U.N.-backed gang suppression force.
Experts have questioned exactly what role the Salvadoran troops are playing in Haiti.
Romain Le Cour, head of the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said their rules of engagement, chain of command, objectives and duration “remain opaque.” He questioned what kind of coordination they might have with the gang suppression force, Haitian police and Vectus Global, the private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince.
“Are we witnessing yet another model of deployment, parallel to the multilateral framework? The role of the United States, which supported and facilitated this deployment, also deserves scrutiny,” he said.
Le Cour said the number of Salvadoran troops in Haiti will surpass that of personnel in the gang suppression force, raising questions about the future of the U.N.-backed force.
“What does that mean for its authority, its coherence and its future?”
He added: “the most basic question remains unanswered: why were the Salvadoran technicians in a gang-controlled neighborhood in the first place?”
Le Cour and others also raised concerns about the safety of Haitian civilians caught in a gun battle between Haitian gangs and the international forces.
On Wednesday, Doctors Without Borders issued a statement calling on “the authorities and all parties involved to spare civilians and ensure access to health care facilities for all the wounded and sick, without distinction.”
The aid agency said it treated 30 patients injured by gunfire or drone explosions from Oct. 18-26, and that it took some of the wounded several hours to reach hospitals run by Doctors Without Borders.
“Roads and bridges are blocked, and any travel is extremely risky,” said Davina Hayles, Doctors Without Borders head of mission in Haiti. “In a capital city where the health care system has collapsed and many facilities are closed, it is essential to ensure there is access to functioning health care facilities like ours.”
More than 5,700 people have been killed or wounded in Haiti from January to mid-September, according to the U.N. Those recently killed include two Haitians who worked for the Norwegian Refugee Council.
“We call on all parties concerned, including Haitian authorities as well as the international community, to do everything in their power to protect civilians, uphold international law, and prevent further violence,” the council said in a statement Thursday. “Neither the Haitian society nor the outside world can tolerate that civilians, including aid workers, are killed with impunity.”

- In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, the Alaska Senate race was embroiled in controversy as a claim circulated that Democrats engaged in ballot-stacking, referring to an election tactic where political parties recruit additional candidates to draw votes away from an opponent
- Alaska Democrats allegedly pushed a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan to run for Senate in order to confuse voters and direct votes away from Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent. Snopes readers asked us to determine the veracity of this claim and the legality of such a tactic.
- The rumor stems from a New York Times investigation based on the claims of an ex-employee of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, interviews with dozens of people involved and a review of communications and documents. We have no reason to doubt the veracity of the Times' reporting. However, because we were unable to view the evidence or obtain additional confirmation from people involved, we cannot confirm its claims as of this writing.
- Snopes concluded that even if Peltola's team engaged in ballot-stacking, it's not unprecedented. Republicans have also employed the tactic during elections. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche also said that such actions "should be" illegal but stopped short of saying they are. The Alaska Supreme Court has permitted the independent candidate Sullivan to run on Nov. 3.
- Election expert John Fortier told Snopes that while people have been prosecuted for deceiving voters, there is no specific law related to the process of ballot-stacking.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Peltola's and incumbent senator's campaigns, as well as independent candidate Sullivan and members of the team allegedly involved in the stacking plan, and await responses.
In an investigation published Oct. 28, The New York Times reported that staffers for Alaska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola spent months recruiting candidates named Dan Sullivan in order to peel votes from incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Political parties often employ the election tactic, referred to as "ballot-stacking," to confuse voters by deliberately recruiting additional candidates to run with the goal of drawing votes away from an opponent.
In Alaska, a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan, whom a Democratic operative associated with Peltola's team allegedly recruited, is on the ballot, alongside Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan. President Donald Trump has called Peltola's alleged actions a "fraud on the American public." Additionally, the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit to block or delay the election certification if the incumbent were to lose the senate race.
Snopes readers asked us to look into the legality of ballot-stacking as an election tactic, as well as the veracity of the claim that Peltola's staffers tried to recruit multiple Dan Sullivans to join the Senate race. Readers also wanted to know whether the DOJ could block the election from being certified if the Republican candidate lost.
Below we break down everything we know about the controversy and ballot-stacking during elections:
Did Peltola's team carry out ballot-stacking?
The New York Times spoke to Elisa Rios, a former staffer and campaign manager for Peltola who was recently fired. Rios claimed top campaign aides instructed her to find as many people named "Dan Sullivan" as they could in Alaska and convince them to run for Senate, causing confusion among voters and possibly costing the incumbent senator crucial votes.
The Times reported that it reviewed text messages and conducted numerous interviews with Rios and 12 people who participated in the alleged plan, knew about the plan or were would-be candidates. Shortly before the story was published, Rios attempted to retract her statements to the Times, the newspaper reported. She was planning to file a wrongful-termination lawsuit against the Peltola campaign. The Times kept her statements in the story.
The Peltola campaign denied being involved in Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy. Jim Lottsfeldt, a local political consultant aligned with super PACs supporting Peltola, said Rios was a source of "disgruntled, anti-Mary Peltola stuff that I think is often not true." The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee also denied participating in such a project, but the Times said it had reviewed texts and documents showing otherwise.
Rios claimed a Democrat operative named Jerid Kurtz — who reportedly posed as a man named "Zane" and approached people to attempt to convince them to run in or to drop out of the race — made contact with Dan J. Sullivan and described him as amenable to running if it would help Peltola.  Kurtz is an Ohio native, according to the Times, and would reach out to people under the alias with an email that included the word "buckeye." Ohio is known as the Buckeye State.  
Rios also alleged that Jacquelyn Lopez, an attorney for the Peltola campaign, was involved in efforts to create a "right-wing state party" that could challenge the incumbent Republican senator.
We have no reason to doubt the veracity of the Times' reporting. However, because we were unable to view the evidence or obtain additional confirmation from people involved, we cannot confirm its claims as of this writing.
Snopes reached out to an individual we believe to be Rios via Facebook and will update this story if we receive a response We have also reached out to Lopez but did not receive a response by the time of publication. We were unable to contact Kurtz, who has removed his social media pages.
Additionally, we contacted Peltola's campaign to learn more and will update this story accordingly.
Ultimately, Dan J. Sullivan is allowed to run in the Senate election,
Who is Dan J. Sullivan and is he allowed to run?
Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, lives in the small fishing community of Petersburg, according to the Times. He is contesting the Nov. 3 senate election with no party affiliation, though he initially registered to run as a Republican. Sullivan has maintained publicly that he entered the Senate race of his own volition, though Rios contended that he was contacted by Kurtz and expressed a desire to help Peltola's campaign.
We reached out to Sullivan to learn more about the motivations behind his candidacy. We will update this story if we receive a response.
As of June 26, Sullivan is legally permitted to run in the election — something that the Peltola campaign and its affiliates celebrated, according to the Times' report — though the election board initially attempted to block him.
On June 15, the Alaska Division of Elections announced that Sullivan was ineligible to participate and would be removed from the ballot because his filing was "for the purpose of confusing or misleading voters." Carol Beecher, the elections division director, wrote in a letter (emphasis ours):
You requested to access the ballot under the name "Dan Sullivan" even though it appears from Division records that you have never registered to vote or sought ballot access under this name. Our records indicate that you are registered to vote under the name "Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr." That you chose the occasion of your declaration of candidacy for U.S. Senate to seek ballot access under a name you have not used in your interactions with the Division suggests—and in combination with the additional facts I outline in this letter leads me to conclude—that you are seeking to confuse yourself with another candidate in the race, the incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan, rather than distinguish yourself from him. Indeed, you yourself appeared to be confused when you initially emailed the Division asking to be listed on the ballot as "Dan S. Sullivan." "S" is Senator Sullivan's middle initial, not yours.
She added, in a likely reference to Kurtz:
A political consultant you have admitted is working with your campaign is a known longtime supporter of Democratic candidates including the primary Democratic challenger to Senator Sullivan. This consultant's work on your behalf is, in isolation, innocuous. Alongside the other facts I have catalogued in this letter, however, it suggests a determined effort and a deliberate attempt to use the similarity of your name to confuse Alaska voters in the upcoming primary election.
Upon appeal, on June 26, the Alaska Supreme Court permitted Sullivan to appear on the ballot, though it did not give its reasoning. Alaskan Republican officials made the decision about how Sullivan was to appear on the ballot, and determined he would be listed without a party affiliation while the incumbent senator would be listed as a Republican. Alaskan voters can vote for both men if they are confused between the two, as the election employs a ranked-choice system. 
Is ballot-stacking illegal?
Generally, ballot-stacking as an election tactic is not illegal. In a Fox News interview, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche called the practice fraud. When asked whether the practice was illegal, Blanche said "it should be" but stopped short of saying it actually was.
The Times investigation also noted that "ballot-stacking tactics are common in politics and generally considered legal."
For example, in 2024, according to an Alaska News Source report, a registered Democrat named Eric Hafner ran for Alaska's U.S. House seat, even though he was incarcerated in a federal prison in New York and did not even live in Alaska. (Hafner had been sentenced to 20 years in prison for making death threats to judges, police officers and others.)
The Alaska Beacon noted that while the Democratic Party sued to keep Hafner off the ballot, the Republican Party sought to keep him on it. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled in Hafner's favor and the Republican candidate defeated Peltola for the House seat. Hafner's campaign advertising was also reportedly backed by a Republican campaign group.
Also in 2024, a pro-Peltola PAC ran ads for a third-party candidate after Democratic strategists saw the tactic as favorable to Peltola.
John Fortier, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank, told Snopes over the phone that there is no specific law against adding similar-sounding names to ballots as an election tactic. However, there have been cases where people were prosecuted on grounds of deceiving voters, Fortier said, like cases filed against groups accused of making deceptive "robocalls" to voters to spread false information about election dates.
For example, in 2011, a campaign manager for Republican former Maryland Gov. Robert Ehrlich was convicted of two counts of conspiracy to violate election laws and two counts of election fraud. He orchestrated a scheme of robocalls targeting Black Democratic voters by informing them that Democratic Gov. Martin O' Malley had already won the election as of 6 p.m. on Election Day 2010, and thus attempted to deter them from going to the polls.
We also found a 2020 case in Florida where a local Republican Party chairman was found guilty of a misdemeanor campaign finance violation through a scheme in which he planned to use a so-called ghost candidate to siphon votes away from the Republican candidates' competitor.
Can DOJ delay or block election certification process?
On Oct. 22, the DOJ filed a complaint against the state of Alaska, Beecher, the state election board and the state ballot counting review board, saying the sole purpose of Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy was to "benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan." The lawsuit sought to delay or block Alaska from certifying its election results if the Republican candidate lost.
Fortier told Snopes that the DOJ complaint did not have a "real leg to stand on [as] the grounds were not really clear." He said, generally speaking, it is uncommon for election certification to be delayed or overturned, and even more uncommon for federal actions to be imposed on a state's election. The DOJ complaint appeared to be geared towards "broadly raising the issue [of ballot-stacking] and putting it back into people's minds," he added.
The U.S. Constitution allows states to control their own elections, so the DOJ lawsuit may have little merit in the long run. Additionally, Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means it could take weeks to finalize a result.
The state argued thst the DOJ lawsuit had "no legal basis," adding that "delaying certification of Alaska's election results—but only if a particular candidate does not win—would interfere with state election administration and threaten election integrity." The state also noted that the ballots now clearly distinguish the two candidates, who are now listed as "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr." with no party affiliation, while the incumbent is listed as "Dan S. Sullivan."
The state's response said:
If any voter remains confused, Alaska law allows voters to receive assistance from others. And if the voter is still uncertain, he can rank both Sullivans as his first and second choices under Alaska's ranked-choice voting system so that his vote will count for either Sullivan over any other candidate.
Will it affect the election?
Some Alaskans say such political tactics will do little to change their views. An Alaska Public Media report featured interviews with Alaskans on both sides of the aisle. One registered Republican said he was still voting for Peltola and that Rios' claims were likely because she was a disgruntled former employee.
Another voter said, "Voters are intelligent and can figure out how to rank and can figure out which Dan Sullivan is their person."
Some Petersburg locals also described Dan J. Sullivan as a man of "high character" and did not believe the Times' account of him working with Democrats behind the scenes.
In sum …
While The New York Times' reporting indicates Democrats in Alaska may have engaged in political skullduggery, ballot-stacking appears to be a common tactic employed many times by both sides over the years with minor repercussions. Even the U.S. attorney general said such a practice "should be" illegal but did not assert it was.
As of this writing, both Sullivans are on the ballot for the Nov. 3 Senate election in Alaska.

Chennai-based stroke medicine expert Sivarajan Thandeswaran has called for certification of Indian hospitals to distinguish them as ‘stroke-ready’ so that people do not waste time in seeking treatment.
“Hospitals in India have to apply for and obtain NABH or JCI certification; instead, a proper government legislation making it mandatory for patients to be taken to and treated at comprehensive stroke centres, as done in the West, will improve stroke care,” said a senior consultant in Stroke Medicine, General Internal Medicine and Gerontology, at Kauvery Hospital in Alwarpet on Wednesday.
He was speaking at a webinar on ‘The Golden Hour: Every Minute Matters, Every Life Counts’, presented by Kauvery Hospital in association with The Hindu to mark World Stroke Day, observed annually on October 29.
He was joined by Harish R. Kamath, consultant neurologist, Kauvery Hosur. The experts stressed on the need for timely access to care as time is the most crucial factor to salvage the brain. Stroke is the second leading cause of death and, therefore, treatment in the window period of 4.5 hours is critical.
Treatment of stroke has transformed tremendously, and families need to be aware, Dr. Thandeswaran added.
In his presentation, Dr. Kamath explained the symptoms of stroke, including loss of balance, blurring vision, facial asymmetry, weakness in arms, and slurring speech. He said 1.8 million new stroke cases are added every year and 7.25 million deaths due to stroke occur every year.
Dr. Thandeswaran said that while big city hospitals have facilities for scanning, imaging, and treatment, including thrombolysis (dissolving blood clots with medicine) and thrombectomy (removing clot through surgery), in remote areas, telemedicine and video calls were being used in identifying stroke patients and transferring them to Comprehensive Stroke Centres, where advanced services and specialist teams are available.
The doctors discussed lifestyle-related risks, including poor dietary habits, physical inactivity, and inadequate sleep.
“People should take ownership of their health through routine check-ups for better treatment outcomes,” Dr. Thandeswaran suggested.

A former Bangladesh air force officer was found dead near Turag River in Dhaka on Wednesday, weeks after his podcast questioning allegations linking him to a video purportedly showing former prime minister 
Sheikh Hasina
 fleeing the country in August 2024.
The 28-year-old former flight lieutenant Tahsif Souri had gone missing a day before his body was recovered. Police said an inquest report found no external injury marks on his body, though blood was seen coming out of his nose.
His body was sent to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College for an autopsy.
Souri had been "compulsorily retired" from service about a year after the fall of the Hasina government.
His death has brought renewed attention to a podcast interview in which he spoke about allegations that he had recorded and circulated footage of Hasina leaving Bangladesh on August 5, 2024.
The interview resurfaced following the recovery of his body.
What ex-Bangladesh officer said about allegations
During the interview as cited by the Dhaka Tribune, the host referred to a media report alleging that footage of Hasina leaving the country had been recorded at Kurmitola Airport and circulated by Souri. The report had also reportedly linked him to an investigation into the alleged involvement of the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), within the Bangladesh air force.
Responding to the allegations, Souri said the report had claimed that flight lieutenant Rifat Ashrafi recorded the video and that he had circulated it. He questioned the evidence behind the claim that he had shared the footage.
“Even if I recorded the video or circulated it, what proof do they have? I want to ask that,” he said.
Asked whether the allegations had led to his dismissal from the air force, Souri said this was possible but declined to disclose details of the events at the time.
“I cannot disclose everything, and there are things I am unable to discuss. I think they did this because of these allegations,” he said.
Souri also said he faced social embarrassment and harassment after the report was published, claiming its headline and presentation had created a misleading impression of him among readers.
He rejected allegations of RAW's involvement within the air force, saying: “If I were linked to RAW, why would I be in Bangladesh? If I were linked to RAW, why would I speak publicly?”
He described the allegation as “a very ridiculous claim”.
Souri further claimed that the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) directorate had said he had no such involvement. However, no detailed documents supporting the claim were presented during the interview.
Asked whether he had appealed against his discharge from the air force, Souri said he had not and was uncertain whether he would do so in the future.
He also expressed frustration over the withholding of his passport, describing it as a violation of his democratic rights.
“They had withheld my passport, which is my democratic right. I am deeply upset about this. I suffered for two years,” he said, adding that he had since recovered the passport.
Souri's interview prompted the military's public relations directorate, ISPR, to reiterate its August 4, 2025, statement. It had denied reports that action against Souri and flight lieutenant Rifat Ashrafi was linked to allegations that the officers had recorded and shared the video showing Hasina fleeing the country.
During the podcast, Souri dismissed as propaganda a 2024 media report claiming he was an agent of RAW. However, he neither confirmed nor denied his alleged links to the video.
Souri's father, KM Enayetul Karim Helal, told reporters that an acquaintance, Dwip, had taken his son out on Tuesday evening.
"Tahsif sent his mother a message round 1:30am Wednesday, saying he would return home. But he never did" said Helal.
Bangladesh home minister Salahuddin Ahmed told reporters that he would comment after the initial probe and autopsy findings. He did not respond when asked whether Souri had shot the video.
Meanwhile, Ashraful Alam Khokan, a former aide of Hasina, questioned whether Souri had been deliberately targeted through media reports.
"Was Tahsif deliberately portrayed in the media as an agent of RAW with the intention of getting him killed? "At the time, however, his activities were reportedly aligned with those who seized power in July," he said, referring to the Muhammad Yunus-led government.

Smiling for camera, filming Himalayas: Man's final moments before chopper crash
A smile for the camera and a glimpse of the snow-covered Himalayas were among the last videos 41-year-old Pratap Bachihalli Ningaraju sent his family before the helicopter he was travelling in crashed near Joshimath. All six people on board, including the pilot, died. The crash has also renewed concerns over helicopter safety during the Char Dham pilgrimage.
A smile for the camera before take-off, then a view of the snow-covered Himalayas. These were the last two videos 41-year-old Pratap Bachihalli Ningaraju sent to his family from inside the helicopter on Friday, as it flew from Badrinath, one of Hinduism’s most sacred pilgrimage sites, perched nearly 11,000 feet above sea level, to Sahastradhara, near Dehra Dun.
The first video captured Pratap smiling at the camera. The second offered a glimpse of the snow-clad mountains outside. Sent at around 1.12 pm, they would be his last messages to his family.
Less than two minutes later, the helicopter lost contact. At around 2.20 pm, its mangled remains were spotted in a village near Joshimath, its destination.
Pratap and five others, including the pilot, were declared dead. Pratap and the four other passengers -- Arun Salunkhe, Sudhir K, HS Nataraj and Shankargowda VB -- were all from Karnataka. The pilot, Captain Himanshu Sabharwal, 48, was from Delhi. Salunkhe, 44, was an inspector with the Bengaluru Police's Central Crime Branch.
The privately operated helicopter, operated by Trans Bharat Aviation, lost contact less than two minutes after take-off, Chamoli Superintendent of Police Surjit Singh Panwar said.
The helicopter, bearing call sign VT-HCX, was flying over the Joshimath valley when communication was lost. The Uttarakhand Civil Aviation Development Authority (UCADA) said its tracking system also stopped receiving the helicopter's location.
According to the District Emergency Operations Centre (DEOC), an Army Signal Centre team spotted the helicopter in the Hathi Parvat area. Smoke was seen rising from it as it rapidly lost altitude.
The bodies of the pilot and the five passengers were found near the wreckage in Chai village. However, officials said they could not be brought back immediately because of darkness and the difficult terrain. Additional District Magistrate Vivek Prakash said the bodies would be taken to Joshimath town on Saturday, where post-mortems would be conducted.
SEARCH AND RESCUE OPERATION
Soon after receiving information about the helicopter's disappearance, joint teams of the police, State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and Army were dispatched from Pandukeshwar and Jyotirmath to search for it, SP Panwar said. Drone teams were also deployed from the district headquarters in Gopeshwar.
The DEOC said an aerial reconnaissance of the crash site was carried out using one recce helicopter and one Retriever helicopter of UCADA. An SDRF team was also dispatched from Sahastradhara.
Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami expressed grief over the loss of lives and directed officials to conduct a detailed investigation into the cause of the crash. He also asked the district administration to extend all possible assistance to the families of the deceased and ensure that relief arrangements were made promptly.
Dhami later held a review meeting and instructed officials to carry out rescue and relief operations on a war footing, using all available resources.
FLEET GROUNDED, PROBE ORDERED
The India-based Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) will probe the crash. A senior official said an investigation team had left for the site.
UCADA CEO Prateek Jain told PTI that the entire fleet of Trans Bharat Aviation Pvt Ltd had been grounded as a precautionary measure.
The crash site is around 45 km from the Badrinath shrine. A helicopter journey from Badrinath to Dehradun takes about an hour, while the road distance is around 326 km.
AVIATION SAFETY CONCERNS IN CHAR DHAM SECTOR
The crash comes amid concerns over helicopter safety in Uttarakhand's Char Dham sector. More than 21.55 lakh pilgrims have visited Badrinath since the shrine's portals opened in April this year. As many as 87 pilgrims visiting the shrine have died during the period.
Badrinath is one of the four shrines that make up Uttarakhand's Char Dham circuit, along with Yamunotri, Gangotri and Kedarnath. Helicopter services for the pilgrimage are usually offered in packages covering two or all four shrines. Packages covering two shrines cost around Rs 1 lakh to Rs 1.15 lakh per person. In both types of packages, Badrinath is the final destination before the helicopter returns to Dehradun.
The government told the Rajya Sabha in July last year that 12 accidents involving registered helicopter operators had occurred between 2020 and 2025, killing 30 people. Seven of those accidents took place in Uttarakhand.
Minister of State for Civil Aviation Murlidhar Mohol said the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) had initiated additional surveillance and safety audits of helicopter operations during the Char Dham Yatra.
An AAIB analysis recorded nine occurrences in the Char Dham sector between 2015 and 2025 — eight accidents and one serious incident. At least one accident or serious incident was reported every year from 2022 onwards.
There were four accidents in 2024, two of them fatal, the highest number recorded in a single year, the AAIB said.

France has released its Global Health Strategy for 2023-2027, in Lyon today, in the presence of three French Ministers, the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, the Minister of Health and Prevention, the Minister of Higher Education and Research, and WHO’s Director-General.
As a lead player for shaping global health policies, France has called on national and international stakeholders to support building a new global health architecture towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and in particular SDG3, focused on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all, at all ages.
The new Health Strategy aims to help reduce health inequalities and strengthen the One Health approach to better prevent and prepare for future global health emergencies. It urges the global community to address the health consequences of climate change and the environmental impact on health systems.
To underscore WHO’s and France strong collaboration and in recognition of France’s pivotal global health role, Dr Tedros travelled to France to join the launch event.
“France was a founding member of WHO in 1948 and has been a strong friend to WHO throughout the 75 years since then,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health, and the new Global Health Strategy will enhance that role. It aligns well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, empower and perform for health.”
France shares key health priorities with WHO, adopting a crosscutting approach and prioritizing universal health coverage (UHC) as part of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda. France also provides support for transformative initiatives at WHO such as the WHO Academy and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) which the Ministers visited today.
Dr Tedros addressed the audiences at the Academy and IARC together with Ms Catherine Colonna, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention, and Ms Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research.
"The World Health Organization, whose 74th anniversary we are celebrating today, must continue to play a central and driving role,” said Ms Catherine Colonna, the French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “France will continue to support the WHO and its ambitious governance and financing reforms."
"France is also committed alongside the WHO Academy through several partnership with universities, research institutes, and public health institutions," remarked Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research. "Our goal is to enrich the learners' experience through a diversified training portfolio within the Academy."
"The launch of this Global Health Strategy is the perfect opportunity to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the WHO. The Organization plays a central role in global health, and we must continue to support it," said Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention. "This is why, I am announcing today, France is keen to host, in the first quarter of 2024, in partnership with the WHO, the first international financing conference for the fight against meningitis."
The 2023-2027 French Strategy for Global Health is the fruit of collaboration involving a wide range of French actors: public agencies, civil society organizations, higher education and research organizations, scientific institutions, foundations, organizations of human, animal and environmental health specialists, local government bodies and the private sector. They will all be represented within a monitoring committee to track the Strategy’s implementation and progress.
From left to right: Minister of Health and Prevention H.E. Aurélien Rousseau, WHO’s Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs H.E. Catherine Colonna, and Minister of Higher Education and Research, H.E. Sylvie Retailleau.

Keralam Health Minister K. Muraleedharan on Friday said the government would take further action after receiving a report from an expert committee probing the allegations that expired doses of Remdesivir were administered to Nipah patients in previous years.
However, critical care specialist Dr A S Anoop Kumar, who treated several Nipah patients at a private hospital, said that patients who died due to Nipah were not administered doses of Remdesivir.
Former Health Minister Veena George said that allegations raised by Mr. Muraleedharan are suspicious as the medicine has an expiry period of 2.5 to 5 years.
In a reply to a submission by Congress MLA Mathew Kuzhalnadan in the Assembly on Thursday, Mr. Muraleedharan said that Remdesivir procured in 2021 had an expiry date of May 2023 but might have been administered to patients admitted to Kozhikode Medical College till 2025.
Speaking to reporters in Kozhikode, Mr. Muraleedharan said the information presented to the Assembly was based on reports from responsible officials of the Health Department and that he would not make further comments until the expert committee submitted its findings.
The government would investigate whether the deaths of Nipah patients were linked to the administration of expired medicine and whether other patients who received the drug had suffered any adverse effects, Mr Muraleedharan said.
“There are several doubts regarding the medicine, including whether it was administered after its expiry date. We will investigate and take a decision,” he said.
The Minister clarified that there were no concerns about the quality or efficacy of Remdesivir itself and that the issue under investigation was whether expired doses had been administered to patients.
Recalling the procurement of the drug during the Nipah outbreak after the UDF government came to power, he said efforts to source it from different parts of the country had failed as the available stocks in Mumbai had expired.
Subsequently, the Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) informed the government that the medicine was available in Bahrain, following which it was procured within 48 hours, he said.
He said patients who received the medicine within its validity period had recovered and asserted that the controversy concerned its expiry date rather than the drug’s efficacy.
Mr. Muraleedharan said the expert committee headed by Dr R Aravind, head of the Infectious Diseases department at Thiruvananthapuram Medical College, would conduct an impartial examination without any preconceived conclusions.
The probe would also examine how the medicine was procured and supplied, the role of intermediaries and the functioning of KMSCL.
The government would investigate whether any agents were involved in the procurement process, he said.
The Minister also said the Kozhikode Medical College superintendent had informed him that the packaging of the Remdesivir medicine listed an expiry date but did not mention its manufacturing date. Both details are normally required on medicine packaging, and the discrepancy would be examined, he said.
“Further decisions on the issues would be taken after receiving the expert committee’s findings,” he said.

Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by the global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk, third-party website.
The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.
“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”
A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.”
“We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations,” an Accenture spokesperson tells WIRED. When pressed, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that there had been what could be characterized as an incident.
The Accenture employee is alleged to have connected a secure production environment to their personal Claude account so as to allow an AI agent to write and deploy code. Claude is currently barred from being used by DOD staff. (Anthropic directed WIRED to the company’s usage policy, which instructs users not to use its products to “interfere with the operation of military bases and related infrastructure” or to “bypass security controls such as authentication systems, end point protection, or monitoring tools without authorization.”)
The Accenture employee’s AI agent ran on the DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Sources indicate that despite the security risks posed by the AI coding agent, Accenture employees did not treat the incident as severe or urgent. DOD employees and federal contractors are required to report any cybersecurity incident within 72 hours of its discovery, but sources indicate Accenture did not initially report the breach to the government at all.
“We are in a conflict with Iran right now,” says the employee, noting that Iran has attempted to hack several federal agencies and parts of US infrastructure. “It’s the worst time to be having this kind of cavalier attitude.”

Accenture currently has more than $3.5 billion in contracts with the federal government, nearly $605 million of which are with the DOD. The company also contracts with other federal agencies, such as the Department of Education, the General Services Administration, and the Department of Energy, among others. Earlier this month, the Federal Bureau of Investigation found that an Accenture contractor failed to patch a vulnerability that led to the hacking group ShinyHunters getting access to the details of thousands of the Bureau’s employees. The FBI removed that contractor in early October.
Matt Triner, founder of Hunter Strategy, a Washington, DC-based IT consulting company, says that the issue exemplifies the conflicting demands government contractors face more broadly. “Organizations are often punished for reporting incidents like this, even though it’s the right and legal thing to do,” says Triner. In many cases, he says, a company could lose government contracts by admitting they’ve had a security breach, though he says that an incident like the one described is “absolutely one that would need to be reported.”
Triner also notes that the increasing pressure on contractors to deliver projects faster and at a lower price point is at odds with prioritizing safety and security. “Unfortunately, everyone is operating in a system where there are competing rules and incentives, and that existed before AI, but now it’s the same problem on speed,” says Triner.
The coding environment accessed by the Accenture contractor is run on the Non-classified Internet Protocol Router Network (NIPRNet), a DOD network used for unclassified information. While it does connect to the internet—contractors and employees can access their emails and web browsers through the network—it is heavily secured.
According to the source, in order to automate the process of writing code and spinning up cloud servers, the contractor gave their login credentials to the Claude agent. This gave the agent administrative access and allowed it to bypass the security controls enforced through the normal login process. The AI agent—which was not only writing code but also committing it or saving the code into the system on behalf of the Accenture employee—needed to connect out to the internet to perform its tasks. In doing so, it appears to have sent the contractor’s login credentials, passwords, and a map of NIPRNet out to a third-party website.
WIRED is declining to name the third-party website so as to protect the system from further vulnerability, but the National Institute of Standards and Technology has previously identified it as high risk because it has a vulnerability that could let hackers inject instructions into an AI coding agent to steal credentials.
The system the AI agent accessed contained CUI. “Information from a CUI environment is not supposed to leave that infrastructure,” says the source. “There is no insight about what happened to the information, including the login credentials, after it was sent to [that service], whether it’s been retained”
Depending on the agency and its work, CUI can include anything from personally identifiable information to proprietary business or contracting information. According to the DOD’s website, CUI can include information on “the securing and safeguarding of explosives, hazardous chemicals, or pipelines,” documentation related to the designs of “military or space equipment or technology,” and “the exact location and quantities of radioactive material.”
Distinct from the actual data, a map of it could be incredibly valuable to a hacker. “Once an attacker understands how those things fit together, even if those things are public information, what is sensitive is how we are putting those things together and turning that into actionable intelligence,” says Triner.
While a map might not get a hacker into a system, he says, it could help an adversary move faster once they do have access and “help an attacker understand where the crown jewels are.”
Jake Williams, a former NSA hacker and faculty at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy, says that an AI agent running code in NIPRNet presents a “huge problem, and there are huge national security impacts.”
Williams notes that while individual pieces of data or information might be considered CUI, “when that unclassified information is aggregated, that can become classified itself.” For instance, the location of certain hazardous materials might be CUI, as might be information about the vulnerability of the facilities that house them. Combined, however, they could reveal information that would be kept classified.
But this is not the only way classified information may have been put at risk. Frequently, tools and code are tested in NIPRNet before being deployed into more sensitive systems like the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet), the military’s secured network for classified information, and Joint Worldwide Intelligence Communications System (JWICS), a secure intranet for top secret information. Both SIPRNet and JWICS are air gapped, a security measure that means they are not connected to any outside networks. On a practical level, that means SIPRNet and JWICS would be extremely difficult for a hacker to access remotely.
But with the login credentials exfiltrated by an AI agent, a hacker could access NIPRNet and insert a backdoor or other malicious code into a tool or system. Without proper review, this code could end up deployed in one of the air-gapped systems.
“The code could operate completely normally in NIPR and do something malicious and undisclosed in a SIPR network, that is 100 percent possible,” says Williams. Exfiltrating data out of these networks would be difficult, he adds, but malicious code could be used to attack the systems from the inside. “I think the most likely thing would be some kind of distributed denial of service attack,” he says.
Triner says that even something more subtle, such as slowing down intelligence operations and activities, could cause damage and make users lose trust in a tool, even once the problem is fixed.
As vibe coding, or prompting an AI assistant to write the code for a product described by an engineer, is becoming more common, vetting code is becoming more of a challenge. AI is capable of generating code at a volume that far surpasses human productivity, making it time-consuming and difficult to vet.
“When you’re using an agent, you have no idea of the supply chain or even the inference chain of what has ultimately generated the code,” says Williams. “A lot of the code that these LLMs were trained on is itself vulnerable, and they can regurgitate the same kinds of architecture and architectural issues that we see in other code.”
The government does have a way to identify flawed code in NIPRNet. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) scans code for bugs and flaws before allowing it to run. But Williams notes that a hacker-inserted “backdoor is not a vulnerability, even if we may not want it there,” and therefore would likely fly under the radar of SAST’s detection. SAST also does not usually identify structural issues in the logic chain of how code is created.
There’s no indication that hackers were able to get into a classified or top-secret system. Still, Williams says, the incident should raise significant alarms. “Architecturally, any information about NIPR that you can’t see through open-source intelligence, DOD considers a close hold regardless of whether something touches a classified network,” he says.
This is not the first time the DOD has been made vulnerable because of AI-related issues. Last year, ProPublica revealed that Microsoft was using “digital escorts” on its projects with the federal government, wherein American employees with security clearances would be overseeing code written by outsourced workers in China. Experts who spoke to ProPublica said that the program presented a particular security risk because the American employees were often not able to vet the code themselves, leaving openings for malicious code to be inserted unknowingly into government systems.

The Indian Institute of Technology Bombay on Friday said its researchers have developed a low-cost device that can screen for anaemia and sickle cell disease using a drop of blood.
A research team from the Department of Chemical Engineering, led by Mahesh Tirumkudulu, has developed a simple, low-cost point-of-care approach that uses the length of a blood smear (the distance that a drop of blood spreads across a glass slide) to detect anaemia, and detect and monitor treatment for sickle cell disease. IIT Bombay said.
Prof Tirumkudulu's team built their own automated device to have a uniform method of creating a smear. Under these controlled conditions, the researchers observed that blood from different people gives different smear lengths, and this difference holds useful information.
Prof. Tirumkudulu explained that more viscous blood spreads less easily and, therefore, produces a shorter and thicker smear under the same conditions.
Once the team confirmed that the method could sense small differences in blood viscosity, they decided to investigate whether those differences could help identify disease. It was found that anaemia lowers red blood cell concentration and haemoglobin, while sickle cell disease makes red blood cells rigid.
The researchers said their patented automated smearing device can be manufactured cost-effectively. Also, the test itself requires only a pipette, glass slides, an inexpensive chemical, vials for the sickling treatment, and a ruler or imaging device to measure smear length, they added.
"This makes our technique particularly useful in places where conventional diagnostic laboratories are difficult to access, and it doesn't require any special expertise to use," said Dr. Mahrukh Mir, a former PhD scholar in Prof Tirumkudulu's lab, and the first author of the study.
The researchers pointed out that blood viscosity cutoffs vary for various groups of people because certain genetic differences affect how blood reacts when oxygen levels drop.
Also, the anaemia test could miss identifying some patients when the usual link between viscosity and anaemia does not hold, such as in a rare condition called hyperviscosity syndrome, where blood plasma is unusually thick.
Currently, the technology is licensed to Rheoheme Private Limited, an IIT Bombay startup, and the team is now working with the National Institute for Research in Tribal Health, Jabalpur, in Madhya Pradesh and All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Nagpur, toward regulatory approval, while exploring extending the device to measure clotting time and glucose levels.
"Our initial aim was to understand the physics of spreading blood drop, and that led to the medical applications," added Prof Tirumkudulu.

A mother’s knowledge, attitude and feeding practices can significantly influence a child’s willingness to try new foods, which highlights the need for stronger nutrition counselling for caregivers during early childhood, according to a new study by researchers at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN).
Reluctance to try unfamiliar or diverse foods studied
The study, published in the Journal of Nutritional Science, examined food neophobia, a condition in which children are reluctant to try unfamiliar or diverse foods. Such behaviour can limit dietary variety and potentially affect nutritional health during crucial years of growth.
Researchers assessed 150 mother-child pairs from Addagutta in Hyderabad between August and October 2025 focusing on children aged two- seven years and explored how maternal feeding practices were associated with food neophobia and children’s nutritional status.
Findings
The findings revealed that nearly 77% of children showed moderate levels of food neophobia, while 11.3% displayed high levels and 12% had low levels. Boys recorded slightly higher food neophobia scores than girls, although the differences were not statistically significant.
Nutritional status-food acceptance link
The study also found a link between nutritional status and food acceptance. Children suffering from wasting were more likely to exhibit higher food neophobia scores than those with normal nutritional status, suggesting that reluctance to try new foods may be associated with poorer dietary outcomes.
Nutrition knowledge an important factor
Researchers observed that maternal knowledge, attitudes and practices played an important role. Children whose mothers demonstrated moderate levels of nutrition-related knowledge and positive feeding practices had lower food neophobia scores than those whose mothers had lower scores.
Karthikeyan Ramanujam, Scientist-C at ICMR-NIN and lead author of the study, said the findings underscore the importance of everyday feeding behaviours. He suggested that caregivers should repeatedly offer a variety of foods without pressure, create positive mealtime experiences and respond supportively when children reject unfamiliar foods.
ICMR-NIN Director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings offer an opportunity to strengthen behavioural feeding counselling through existing government programmes such as the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) and POSHAN Abhiyaan.
Researchers cautioned that the study was limited to a single urban low-income community and a relatively small sample size. They noted that, as a cross-sectional study, it identifies associations but cannot establish direct cause-and-effect relationships, as per a press release.

Booking an Uber, Ola or a Rapido takes a few taps. But keeping thousands of cars available, drivers earning and vehicles maintained requires an entire operation behind the scenes. Gurugram-based Carrum Mobility has built its business around that responsibility. Founded in 2024 by Karan Jain, who previously cofounded self-drive rental startup Revv, Carrum emerged after CarDekho acquired Revv in 2023. Conversations with former colleagues at Uber convinced Jain that managing organised fleets could become a significant opportunity in India's ride-hailing market. Since its inception, Carrum has grown into a sizable fleet operator with 5,500 vehicles on its books, all the while remaining profitable, according to Jain. The startup has also received $17 Mn funding from Uber this year alone. How Carrum Makes Money From Its Fleet Carrum's biggest strength is its partnership with Uber. It claims to be India's largest supplier of Uber Black vehicles. By managing vehicles and drivers across Uber's Go, Premium and Black services, the startup gets access to a large pool of ride demand without having to build its own customer-facing app. Its job is to keep cars running, drivers earning and vehicles productive. This is also where Carrum's business model shines the most. Many drivers want to earn through ride-hailing but cannot afford to buy a car or take on the cost of maintaining one. Carrum helps bridge that gap by managing vehicles and driver partners. The model has helped Carrum build a network of thousands of drivers and vehicles in a relatively short period. Here’s a snapshot of its operations: Driver network: Carrum has a base of 28,000+ driver partners Ride volumes: Its fleet facilitates 35,000+ rides a day and 1 Mn+ rides a month Fleet mix: Uber Go vehicles account for an estimated 65–70% of its fleet, while a little over 20% comprises Uber Black vehicles Revenue contribution: Uber Black contributes around 28% of Carrum's revenue. Each Black vehicle generates around ₹1 Lakh a month, compared with ₹65,000 for an Uber Go vehicle, according to Jain. Keeping The Engines Running Managing thousands of vehicles requires more than simply putting drivers behind the wheel. Carrum uses technology to track vehicle performance, coordinate maintenance, manage driver onboarding and handle financial settlements. It also uses data analytics, including heat maps and recommendations on where and when to log in, to help drivers find more ride opportunities. The aim is to keep vehicles on the road for longer, reduce downtime and improve the earnings generated by each car. The more productively Carrum's fleet operates, the better it can spread the cost of maintenance, financing and other operations across its rides. Drivers also pay an onboarding fee to Carrum, which helps the company recover some of the costs of bringing new drivers into the network amid high churn. Jain estimates that revenue is split roughly 60:40 between drivers and Carrum. The company uses its share to cover vehicle maintenance, financing and other fleet-related expenses, while drivers bear fuel costs. For Carrum, Uber provides the demand that keeps its fleet moving, while its own technology and operations determine how efficiently it can serve that demand. The fleet-management model is already competitive. Everest Fleet, Uber India's largest overall fleet partner, reports over 23,500 vehicles. Globally, Moove operates a similar mobility infrastructure model. In42 Take: Carrum Needs To Drive Solo Carrum claims to have been profitable since its first month of operations, reporting a PAT of ₹6.5 Cr on operating revenue of ₹233 Cr in FY26. It aims to double both figures in the ongoing fiscal year while expanding its fleet to 7,700 vehicles. However, growth and profitability alone do not guarantee a sustainable business, as the bigger concern is customer concentration. Uber is Carrum's biggest source of business, and any change in Uber's fleet requirements or commercial terms could affect Carrum's business. Then, the startup has no plans to partner with rival ride-hailing platforms. Instead, it is considering adjacent services such as chauffeur-driven cars and employee transport. These could diversify its revenue, but would require new customers, fresh partnerships and a different operating playbook. Uber's presence in these segments could also leave Carrum facing the same dependency problem. For now, Carrum has shown that it can build a profitable fleet business around Uber. What remains unproven is its independent growth. So, can Carrum turn its Uber-led growth into a sustainable business without depending on a single customer?

The IT ministry (MeitY) has proposed a consent-based framework to facilitate data sharing for training AI models in India. Called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI training, the framework aims to help startups, businesses and academic institutions access large-scale, India-specific datasets to develop AI models while protecting citizens' privacy and ensuring compliance with the DPDP Act. The DEPA for AI training also proposes a techno-legal architecture to enable organisations to collaborate on AI model training without directly transferring underlying datasets. With this, the ministry aims to foster access to datasets for researchers and businesses looking to train AI models. The guidelines have been formulated in collaboration with think tank iSPIRT. Explaining The New Proposed Framework The proposed architecture builds on India’s existing DEPA framework, which already supports consent-based data sharing through initiatives such as Account Aggregator. The new framework encompasses the following technical pillars: Confidential Clean Rooms: Secure computing environments where organisations can collaborate on data processing and AI model training without exposing the underlying datasets to one another Differential Privacy: A privacy-preserving technique used to ensure that individual-level information cannot be identified or extracted from an aggregate dataset Electronic Contracts: Machine-readable agreements that define and enforce data-sharing conditions, including permitted uses, data protection and security requirements Zero-Trust Security: An approach where every access request is authenticated and authorised, with encryption, continuous monitoring and auditing to protect data The proposed framework also defines key stakeholders for enabling safe sharing of data for training AI models: Training Data Providers (TDPs): Organisations that make their data accessible through the framework. For instance: banks, hospitals, government agencies Training Data Consumers (TDCs): Startups, enterprises, researchers and individuals seeking access to datasets to train AI models Data Collectives or Data Collabs: Intermediaries that aggregate, standardise, and organise data from various sources and define data-sharing policies and governance rules for participants Under the DEPA framework, TDPs would first register their datasets on a data exchange platform after anonymising and encrypting them. The datasets would then be tagged with metadata and cryptographic identifiers for traceability. TDCs can then request a dataset for their specific use cases, and an electronic contract system checks their requests against data-sharing policies and governance rules before granting access. Once access is given, the model is then trained within a secure data environment using differential privacy methods, ensuring that the raw data remains inaccessible to consumers. The framework also proposes that trained models must undergo independent checks for bias, fairness, security, safety and explainability. Only models that pass receive approval for pilot deployment and scaling. Even after deployment, the oversight will continue in the interest of long-term trust and accountability. In line with this, the framework will ensure that TDCs remain subject to continuous monitoring, periodic reviews, and traceability of the model’s outputs back to the data and contracts used in its training. Govt’s Focus On AI Governance The launch of the new DEPA framework for AI training comes soon after TRAI also released draft guidelines on the responsible use of AI in telecom networks and service delivery. The telecom regulator has sought inputs from stakeholders by November 27. As per TRAI, its draft guidelines are rooted in the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines. The centre had earlier released these guidelines to focus on fostering innovation and safe development and deployment of AI offerings, while mitigating risks posed by the technology. A few weeks ago, union IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw had also said that the centre will release a consultation paper for regulation on AI safety and security within a month. Earlier reports had also hinted that the Centre was looking at formulating a new framework for AI regulation.

Trading has resumed on Polymarket’s flagship international platform after a hack that drained money from the wallets of some traders.
A third-party vendor based in the United Kingdom was breached, not the prediction market’s website itself. Law enforcement in the UK have been notified of the incident, the company said. Trading was initially paused while the company investigated for several hours.
On X, prominent traders complained that they had lost money; Blockchain analytics firm Bubblemaps reported that around 700 users appear affected, with approximately $2.7 million stolen. Polymarket declined to comment when WIRED asked how many traders were impacted by the breach and how much money was lost, but said it will refund impacted traders.
The hack did not impact users on Polymarket US, the company’s newer platform for people within the United States. Polymarket runs two separate prediction markets; Polymarket US operates as a federally regulated financial exchange within the country, while the flagship Polymarket is a cryptocurrency-based platform that is banned in the United States and a number of other countries.
This is not the first time that Polymarket traders have experienced security woes. In June 2026, Polymarket experienced another breach, which resulted in over $2 million in losses for impacted traders.
The company has been a lightning rod for controversy since its 2020 launch. In the past few years, it has been the center of several high-profile alleged insider trading incidents resulting in arrests. One case involved a special forces soldier accused of wagering on the capture of Venezuela’s former leader; another involved a Google employee who allegedly used confidential information to make millions. In both cases, the suspects have pleaded not guilty.
Polymarket recently raised $1 billion in August 2026, with a fundraising round led by 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. It is now valued at $21 billion.
