Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.
In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).
Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.
“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.
Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.
South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.
However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.
Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.
Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.
South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.
In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.
The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.
Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.
Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.
The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.
For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.
The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.
However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.
Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.
“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.
“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”
Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.
“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”
In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.
While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

Human rights lawyer couple sentenced to 10 years' prison in Pakistan
- Published
A Pakistani anti-terrorism court has sentenced human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha to 10 years in prison, over an alleged security breach during a cricket tour in 2024.
The couple were accused of removing road barriers and obstructing police officers in Islamabad - charges that both have denied.
Mazari and Chattha were previously sentenced to up to 17 years in prison for social media posts criticising the military.
Pakistan's Supreme Court had suspended those sentences in August, but police re-arrested the couple before they could be released. They have been imprisoned in Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail for the past several months.
This latest case concerns an incident on 25 October 2024, when England's cricket team was touring Pakistan.
Prosecutors accused Mazari and Chattha of removing barriers from a road designated for the team's security convoy and obstructing police officers at Zero Point, a major cloverleaf road junction in Islamabad.
They were each sentenced to 10 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Act, as well as additional one-year and two-year terms for obstructing and using force against public servants. All sentences will run concurrently.
The court also fined each of them 200,000 Pakistani Rupees (£541:$723).
In statements recorded during the trial, the couple described themselves as "prisoners of conscience" who had faced state persecution.
"I am being punished for not only supporting my wife's work and activism, but for choosing this path of resisting injustice as our life journey together," Chatta said in his statement to Dawn News.
The couple had earlier said that they were "being made an example to further cement the chilling effect against those who stand (or want to stand) against tyranny, oppression, and injustice".
Amnesty International has criticised the proceedings, saying the couple were denied an open and fair trial.
"These convictions are an indictment of Pakistan's justice system." said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International's Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact.
"Imaan and Hadi are being targeted solely because of their refusal to stop their fearless human rights work and for exercising their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly."
The organisation also raised concerns that the trial had been moved inside the prison, where Mazari and Chattha were kept behind a cage-like structure during hearings.
The couple have faced several criminal cases in recent months.
They have been in custody since 23 January, when they were arrested in a separate case involving an alleged altercation outside the Islamabad High Court. A day later, they were sentenced to up to 17 years in prison under Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act over social media posts critical of the military.
Pakistan's Supreme Court suspended those sentences and granted them bail on 17 September - but they were arrested again the same day in connection with a separate case over a protest in March 2025, in which they were accused of chanting "anti-government slogans" and "blocking roads".
Mazari and Chattha are prominent human rights lawyers who have represented activists, journalists and marginalised communities subjected to enforced disappearances.
Mazari's mother, Shireen Mazari, is a former human rights minister who served in the government of former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan.
The couple's convictions have long drawn criticism from international human rights organisations, which have raised concerns about the treatment of lawyers and activists in Pakistan.

US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears
- Published
US stocks have continued to slide as concerns continue to intensify over the increasing costs of the artificial intelligence (AI) build out.
Shares in Intel continued their overnight slide into early trading on Friday, falling as much as 30% after the chip maker warned of a weaker computer market even as it plans to increase spending on AI.
Amazon shares fell as far as 6% before recovering after its reported earnings on Thursday evening fell short of investors' expectations.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange opened on Friday at its lowest level in more than two months, down 2.5%, as other tech stocks including Reddit and Roblox continued to fall.
The losses follow the value of Google owner Alphabet plunging by more than $500bn on Thursday after it revealed its own AI summaries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.
Alphabet stock continued to fall in early trading, down 1% after Thursday's massive slide.
The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere, with Intel on track to lose more than $130bn in value after its earnings update rattled investors.
On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year, and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.
"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.
In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.
Amazon on Thursday revealed the company was also spending more cash that it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.
Shares in Amazon recovered slightly from the overnight fall but were still down about 1.6% in Friday trading.
Reddit stock was down by 26%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.
Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by nearly 20%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.
Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.
Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.
He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".
"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."

Akai teased its new MPC Sample Key on Instagram earlier this week, and said it plans to open-source its software so the modding community can hack it to their hearts’ delight. While there’s no word yet on when the device will launch or how much it will cost, The Verge has received exclusive images of the upcoming instrument that offer some details about its feature set.
Exclusive details about Akai’s MPC Sample Key
The open-source MPC Sample Key won’t be focused on chopping up drum breaks.
While the Sample Key shares many of the same controls as the MPC Sample — including the three context-sensitive encoders, a large main encoder — it seems designed for pitched sample playback, rather than chopping up drums. In fact, the “chop” button from the MPC Sample is missing entirely from the Sample Key.
The dedicated pitch and mod wheels are another clue there. But there are also buttons for changing the octave range of the 25-key keyboard, as well as ones labeled “chord” and “arp.” Presumably, those enable a chord playback mode and an arpeggiator. While using an arpeggiator to play back drum samples can be a fun way to create rhythms, it’s more commonly used for melodic and bass parts. And a chord mode would be basically useless for drums. Those options also appear to replace the chop function from the standard MPC Sample.
There also appears to be a dedicated looper that could be useful for live performance and layering sounds. And, instead of the Flex Beat effects from the original MPC Sample, there’s something called “Swarm.” Though what that is isn’t exactly clear at the moment.
Like the first entry in the Sample series, the Key has a built-in mic and speaker for all-in-one music production. While we haven’t gotten a glimpse at the back panel yet, the config options on the front suggest that, in addition to MIDI, the Sample Key will have CV outs for integrating with modular synths.
Correction October 30th: The MPC Sample Key is 25 keys, not 37.

The Indian Air Force (IAF) on Sunday, October 25, celebrated the 104th birthday of Wing Commander Cecil Barretto (Retd), honouring a military career spanning World War II, the 1947–48 Kashmir War and the formative years of the Air Force's Dental Branch. At 104, Barretto, a recipient of the Vishisht Seva Medal (VSM), represents a remarkable chapter in India's military history. Having begun his career in the Army Dental Corps in February 1945, he went on to become one of the two pioneering officers who helped establish the IAF's Dental Branch in 1956. On October 25, 2026, a team from the Airmen Training School (ATS), Belagavi, accompanied by Air Vice Marshal SJ Nanodkar (Retd), president of the Air Force Association's Goa Branch, visited Barretto at his residence in Goa and felicitated him in the presence of his family. "Once an Air Warrior, Always an Air Warrior!" the IAF's Training Command said in a post, describing the gesture as a reaffirmation of the force's commitment to honouring its veterans and celebrating their legacy. According to the Bharat Rakshak Indian Air Force Database, Barretto was born on October 25, 1922. His service number was 5232 and he served in the Dental Branch. He retired from the Air Force on December 16, 1975, as per the database. His military career, however, began much earlier. Barretto was commissioned into the Army Dental Corps in February 1945, during the final phase of the Second World War. According to his service record and the accompanying Vishisht Seva Medal citation reproduced in the Bharat Rakshak database, he was initially posted to No. 4 Army Dental Centre in Rawalpindi. He was subsequently appointed Officer-in-Charge of No. 35 Indian Army Dental Centre, attached to the 14 Indian Division, where he served until the end of the war. The citation notes that he carried out dental inspections and treatment among troops with an exceptional sense of duty, ensuring that no man-days were lost. His service continued after India's Independence. Barretto was posted to Jammu and Kashmir as Officer-in-Charge of No. 8 Military Dental Centre when Indian Army troops were inducted to fight Pakistani raiders during the 1947–48 India-Pakistan conflict. The citation praised his devotion to duty and efficiency during this period. One of Barretto's most significant contributions came in 1956, when the Indian Air Force established its Dental Branch on March 31. Two officers from the Army Dental Corps, Major JM Rao and Major C Barretto, were seconded to the Air Force to help establish the new branch. The existing Military Dental Centres at Palam and Jalahalli were transferred to the IAF and redesignated as No. 1 and No. 2 Air Force Dental Centres, respectively. While Rao took charge of the centre at Palam, Barretto commanded the centre at Jalahalli. Their IAF service numbers were 5231 and 5232, respectively. Both officers were part of the branch's formative years and are regarded as its founding officers. Barretto subsequently served at several Air Force stations, eventually commanding the Military Dental Centre at Panaji, Goa. His responsibilities extended beyond Air Force personnel. According to his VSM citation, he was also called upon to provide dental care to the Army and other service personnel stationed there. The citation described his professional skills and conduct as highly appreciated by Air Force personnel and their families, adding that he had rendered distinguished service of a high order. Barretto's distinguished military service was recognised with the Vishisht Seva Medal. The Bharat Rakshak database reproduces the Government of India's Gazette citation for the award, dated January 26, 1976. The citation highlighted his exceptional sense of duty during World War II, his service in Jammu and Kashmir after Independence, and his contributions to the Air Force after being seconded to it. It also praised his professional competence, devotion and selflessness while serving military personnel across different stations. Barretto's military legacy extends beyond his own career. According to aviation historian Anchit Gupta, Barretto was one of four brothers who rose to senior ranks in the Indian Armed Forces. His siblings included two Brigadiers and a Lieutenant General. The family also has a historical connection to Mahatma Gandhi. Their father, Dr Cristovam da Gama Barretto, was Gandhi's dentist at Wardha, Gupta noted. Reflecting on the veteran's 104th birthday, Gupta described him as potentially “the oldest surviving IAF officer and welcomed the Air Force's gesture of honouring one of its pioneers.” At 104, Barretto's life stands as a tribute to a generation of military personnel who served through the Second World War, India's Independence and the early decades of the country's military evolution. From treating troops during wartime to helping establish an important branch of the Indian Air Force, his career remains an enduring part of India's military heritage. Cape Town set for classic finale – what does history suggest could happen?
- Published
Third Test, Cape Town (day four of five)
South Africa 329 & 387: Mulder 115, Rickelton 101
Australia 429: Inglis 102; Harmer 4-104
Australia need 288 to win
A gripping series has the finale it deserves.
Having effectively began day four on 40-4, South Africa batted on and on against Australia in Cape Town to move from a position where defeat looked likely to one where a series victory is a real possibility.
In being bowled out for 387 in the final over - with Ryan Rickelton making 101 and Wiaan Mulder last man out for a brilliant 115 - South Africa set the tourists a target of 288 for victory.
WinViz - the tool analysts CricViz use to predict such results - gives the hosts a 54% chance of victory.
If only things were that simple…
History a good omen for Australia
Australia's target is such that should they chase it on day five, it would be the second-highest fourth-innings chase in the 62 previous Tests on this famous ground.
The highest? That's a good omen for Australia.
They chased 331 for a four-wicket win in an epic Test against the Proteas in 2002, when Ricky Ponting hit a brilliant 100 not out.
There have been five other scores above 288 in the fourth innings at Newlands - all of which were made in defeats or when salvaging a draw.
For much of the afternoon and evening sessions, as Australia's bowlers tired, this surface appeared flat enough to score.
When Rickelton and Mulder applied themselves, few opportunities were created. They were able to progress to their third and fourth Test centuries respectively.
It took a run out to end Rickelton's knock, after which Marco Jansen pulled to deep square leg and Gerald Coetzee was also run out - three dismissals down to batter error in a collapse of 4-61, which left South Africa nine down and 251 runs ahead.
That Mulder and number 11 Kagiso Rabada flogged 36 before the close, suggested run-scoring is not impossible.
Pitch turning more but batters more secure
None of those late runs were made under the pressure of a chase, however.
The wicket of Simon Harmer in the final session, bowled shouldering arms by a ball from Nathan Lyon which turned back sharply showed the difficulty ahead.
Harmer dismissed Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Josh Inglis and Alex Carey in Australia's first innings - all recognised batters.
The 37-year-old Essex legend, who once considered playing for England, will be crucial.
As ever in such scenarios, the pitch will play its part.
The PitchViz rating - CricViz's way of assessing the difficulty of a surface - jumped to 6.6 in the final session, comfortably the highest (thus most difficult) rating of the Test.
After settling down in the morning, the ball, as would be expected as a Test progresses, was turning significantly more in the final session than at any point across the previous four days.
Interestingly, however, South Africa's false shot percentage was just 11% across day four, a drop from 18% on day three.
Uneven bounce has not yet been a factor but one ball to Rickelton shortly after tea also shot low.
Head the key man?
Intrigue is added by the fact that whoever wins this Test will end the series top of the International Cricket Council's Test rankings.
One man appears to likely to play a huge part in the outcome.
Faced with a target of 205 in the first Ashes Test almost a year ago, Australia opener Head thrashed a sensational 123 from 83 balls to turn a tricky chase into a riotous charge to victory over England.
There was a time, between 2008 and 2019, when Australia had a poor record in situations such as these.
In that period they failed in 14 of their 17 fourth-innings chases when set targets between 200 and 350.
That has changed in recent years, however, with Cummins' men having pulled off pursuits of 282 and 279 since 2023, in addition to the Perth victory last year.
Few sides have been better in key moments in the modern era. Saturday will provide another chance for Australia to deliver under pressure.

The recent conversation over the merchant discount rate on select UPI transactions raised the question of who pays for the digital convenience that millions of people enjoy. Hospitals may soon face a similar problem for strengthening their privacy even if no separate “privacy charge” appears on a patient’s bill.
Protecting digital patient information will require secure systems, trained personnel, and continuous compliance. Parliament enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023 in response to this need. The Act consists of 44 sections in nine chapters plus one Schedule. The government notified its Rules on November 13, 2025, with the Sections pertaining to provisions for consent managers set to kick in from November 13, 2026. The rest of the substantive obligations will start to apply from May 13, 2027.
Unusually difficult places
The Act is a general framework to protect digital personal data across sectors, including healthcare. In healthcare, the Act recognises that clinical consent and data consent are different. For example, a person agreeing to undergo a medical scan does not automatically mean they have agreed to every later use of the same scan, no matter how useful the hospital or doctors deem the scan data to be. While facilitating this distinction, the Act also makes room for data-processing during emergencies and specific medico-legal and public health situations.
Under the DPDP Act, the patient is the data principal (or owner) and the hospital — which usually decides why and how some information will be used — is the data fiduciary. Some external software, cloud, and/or data-processing company will serve as the data processor.
That said, hospitals are unusually difficult places in which to ensure compliance with a general data-protection law. Unlike banks or regional transport offices, hospitals continuously create information of an intimate nature. For example, healthcare workers record a patient’s clinical notes, nursing observations, diagnostics and laboratory results, ventilator readings, and prescriptions — all within hours.
At the same time, several professionals will need to access different parts of that record at different times. If access is too tightly controlled, patient care may suffer; on the other hand, unrestricted access can result in significant breaches of privacy. So the Act needs to facilitate the lawful processing of consent with reasonable security safeguards, grievance handling processes, and of course the correction or erasure of data where permissible.
Failure to take reasonable safeguards can attract a penalty of up to ₹250 crore.
Compliance costs
In the same vein, compliance requires hospital information systems with role-based access, facility to encrypt or mask data as necessary, systems to generate and preserve audit logs, backups, vendor contracts, breach response protocols, staff training, and a clearly identified person who is responsible for data governance.
Entities designated data fiduciaries must also appoint a statutory data protection officer, and smaller hospitals will need a privacy or data management lead in practice.
Further, information rarely stays within the hospital, since a cashless claim can send diagnoses and reports to an insurer or a third party administrator. Laboratories, radiology platforms, cloud vendors, and telemedicine services will create additional routes for the same record. Even low-cost WhatsApp-based workflows that became popular because they were convenient will have to be examined for compliance and security.
Healthcare may therefore need specific DPDP provisions, either explicitly or eventually as a separate Act, to cover sector-specific uniqueness, such as small hospitals and large hospitals separately, as clinical care is more than a commercial transaction.
Lesson from Chandigarh
U.S. estimates show the cost of complying with the famed Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, to be around $5 per patient a year in 2008. Estimates for 2025 suggest the cost of $498 per affected record.
In a 2023 study, researchers from India and Norway estimated that adding an integrated information and communications system to an urban primary health centre (PHC) would expand the centre’s annual economic budget by 17.7%. But when the researchers applied the same model across 400 PHCs, the incremental cost fell to about 6% per PHC. The reason: common development and infrastructure costs were shared.
The finding offers an important policy clue: the government should not expect every small hospital, diagnostic centre, and/or PHC to independently purchase the same privacy tools, legal templates, and so on.
That said, the harder problem is that India has legislated faster than it has trained the people who must make the law work. Medical education teaches confidentiality and ethics, but there is no uniform DPDP-oriented National Medical Commission curriculum or standard course materials that span medicine, nursing, allied health, hospital administration, and healthcare IT training.
The vendor side faces the same problem: behind every software workflow is a human being who configures access, checks claims, handles support or views data. And an untrained person handling data in a hospital can pave the way for a major breach due so little as to one leaked password. So data literacy has to become a core healthcare competency.
Building an ecosystem
The National Health Accounts 2022-23 released this year estimated the out-of-pocket expenses on healthcare to be 43.4% of total health expenditure. There is a nontrivial chance that the new costs of complying with the DPDP Act will be passed on to patients as well.
Ahead of the November 13 date, the Indian government should step in by enabling a shared infrastructure through the Unified Health Interface of the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. It could provide model consent and vendor agreements with affordable cybersecurity support, and healthcare-specific implementation standards.
User data is routinely commoditised today, and passing a law assuming compliance and waiting for complaints or litigation will not suffice. As the DPDP Act comes into effect, the government must finance, build, and sustain an ecosystem that allows every health worker to comply and patients to be able to better access care.

Census 2027 population enumeration to span up to 50 days, with 40 questions including caste, Aadhaar and voter ID details
NEW DELHI: The population enumeration phase of Census 2027 will last longer than in past census exercises, with its duration spanning nearly one-and-a-half months from Jan 10 to Feb 28, including the 15-day self-enumeration window, as against the earlier Phase-2 duration of 20 days, conventionally running from Feb 9-28.Sources told TOI that the house-to-house population enumeration schedule announced earlier for poll-bound states of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Goa and Punjab also spans 35 days. While plant-derived kababs may still struggle to replicate the taste and texture of meat from a tandoori joint, they may contain relatively more protein in a form that the body can absorb, according to a study presented on Monday (October 26, 2026).
In a collaboration between the CSIR–Institute of Himalayan Bioresource Technology (CSIR-IHBT), Palampur, and the Good Food Institute (GFI) India, a non-profit that promotes alternative proteins such as plant-based, fermentation-derived and cultivated meat, scientists investigated whether protein bioavailability (meaning protein in a form that’s nutritively useful to the body) of traditional meat was the same as that of plant-based meat.
Tests on five cooked plant-based products — two burger patties, a nugget and two seekh kebabs — showed higher bioavailability percentages than their chicken counterparts, according to the findings presented at a press conference on Monday (October 26). The plant-based kebabs scored 80.8% and 86.1% against 38.8% for chicken. The nugget scored 61.2% against 43.4%, and the patties recorded about 57% and 58% against 21.2%.
The findings do not mean plant-based meat is healthier, but only that they are nutritively comparable, as ‘healthier’ is a subjective term, Dr. Padma Ishwarya, senior scientist at GFI India, told The Hindu. “It’s too much of a vague term. It’s too broad a term…for health, we need to do further studies.”
The chicken products held more crude protein and released more amino acids, the building blocks of protein, during digestion, and Dr. Ishwarya said more products and samples would be tested in the next phase.
The work has not yet been published as a journal paper. “It is a report that is hosted on our website, but it is very much peer-reviewed,” Dr. Ishwarya said in a conversation with The Hindu. Two experts reviewed it, she said, and it was an overview and that detailed manuscripts would follow.
The team used an in vitro method that simulated digestion in a laboratory. Samples went through a two-minute salivary phase, then a stomach phase with digestive enzymes at pH 2 to 3, and then an intestinal phase. The method follows INFOGEST, an internationally harmonised protocol, Dr. Ishwarya said.
The team added an ultrafiltration membrane chosen to mimic the pore size of the human intestine. Whatever passed through the membrane was deemed bioavailable, and only free amino acids were measured. Each sample was adjusted to start with 40 milligrammes of protein.
Animal studies remain the gold standard, she said, but are tedious and require ethical clearances. The simulated method is faster and more reproducible. The team plans to conduct tests across laboratories next year so that NABL-accredited labs can use the method.
Plant-based meat, Dr. Ishwarya said, is made “specifically for biomimicking animal-derived meat”, unlike crisps or cereals, which are plant-based foods. It is made from soya, pea or wheat gluten, mostly soya, and shaped by extrusion, a process in which material is pushed through a die under heat and pressure. She said it contains no synthetic chemicals beyond ingredients such as spices and texturisers.
The study examined only protein. An earlier analysis in 2024 of about 120 products in the Indian market, she said, found that saturated fat and sodium levels were comparable to those in animal-derived products, leaving room for reduction. Plant-based products also supplied dietary fibre, which animal-derived products do not.

- The claim that rapper Nicki Minaj is not a United States citizen is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from X and TikTok posts claiming that even though Minaj is expressing her support for U.S. President Donald Trump and encouraging voters to support Republicans in the midterm elections, she herself cannot vote.

As rapper Nicki Minaj expressed her support for U.S. President Donald Trump and joined him at a Republican campaign rally in late October, many people questioned (archived) her own citizenship status.
Numerous posts (archived) claimed that while Minaj called on voters to support Republican candidates in the midterm elections, she herself cannot vote because she isn't a citizen.
One X user wrote, "The GOP is telling people to 'vote red' with Nicki Minaj as the messenger. Problem is, she can't even vote. She's not a U.S. citizen."
Minaj wrote in a Jan. 28 X post that she was "finalizing" her citizenship paperwork. In the same post, she suggested she was a lawful permanent resident, commonly known as a green-card holder. Noncitizens, including permanent legal residents, cannot vote in federal or state elections and most local elections.
Since a person's immigration record is not publicly available, we were unable to confirm Minaj's immigration status using primary evidence as of this writing.
We also reached out to her record label, the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to learn more, and will update this story if we receive responses. Until then, we leave this claim unrated.
On Jan. 28, Minaj wrote on X:
Residency? Residency? The cope is coping. 😅
Finalizing that citizenship paperwork as we speak as per MY wonderful, gracious, charming President. 
Thanks to the petition. 📋 
I wouldn't have done it without you. 
Oh CitizenNIKA you are thee moment
Gold Trump card free of charge
Minaj was referring to the Trump administration's "gold card" visa, which guarantees foreigners U.S. residency for a $1 million fee. In January, The New York Times reported that, per a Department of Homeland Security official, Minaj has been a legal permanent resident in the U.S. for over two decades, meaning she likely would not need to apply for a gold card.
In a 2024 TikTok livestream, Minaj said she was "not a citizen" despite paying "millions of dollars" in taxes.
In 2018, while posting about children in immigration detention centers, Minaj said on Facebook that she "came to this country as an illegal immigrant @ 5 years old." She was born in Trinidad and Tobago. In the same post, she wrote, "Please stop this. Can you try to imagine the terror & panic these kids feel right now?" 
Citizenship applications can take around 12 months to process and timing varies based on the applicant's primary city of residence. Assuming Minaj uses Los Angeles as her primary residence, where she has a home, the process could take more than a year, according to processing times on USCIS website. Given that she has a close relationship with Trump, it is possible her application could be expedited.
On Oct. 25, White House communications director Steven Cheung posted a video of Minaj in Air Force One, pretending to be the new White House press secretary and praising Trump.
For further reading, Snopes has reported on the unsupported rumor that Minaj was the only "Trump gold card" visa recipient, and the claim that her husband is a registered sex offender.

Marvin R. Shanken, the longtime editor and publisher of Wine Spectator magazine who was instrumental in elevating the profile of American wine business, died Thursday in Manhattan. He was 83.
Shanken started his career in 1972 when he bought a small industry newsletter named Impact, which became a key resource for the wine and spirits industries. He purchased the struggling Wine Spectator newspaper in 1979, which he turned into a glossy magazine with more than 100,000 subscribers.
Wine Spectator became a key educational tool to help consumers become more familiar with the beverage, and contributed significantly to raising the status of the Napa Valley wine region. Wine Spectator articles utilized the 100 point wine rating system, which made buying fine bottles much more approachable for the general audience.
Shanken also founded the magazine Cigar Aficionado and purchased Food Arts and Malt Advocate, which was renamed Whisky Advocate. Other publications he founded through his M. Shanken Communications include Market Watch and Shanken News Daily.
“He helped educate millions of Americans on the joys and virtues of wine, and tirelessly encouraged and pushed winemakers to produce the best for their customers,” Wine Spectator wrote in its obituary.
Among his many milestones were establishing Wine Spectator’s Restaurant Awards program, taking over the long-running Wine Experience weekend to bring producers together with consumers and creating the Wine Spectator Scholarship Foundation.
“It was an extremely influential publication that, along with Robert Parker, actually affected the way wine was made. Wine Spectator could make wineries halfway around the world change the way they made wine,” W. Blake Gray of the website Wine-Searcher told the New York Times.
Born in New Haven, Connecticut, Shanken studied business at the U. of Miami, then received an MBA from American U. in Washington.
He started off working in investment banking on Wall Street, during which time he was sent to California to help finance a vineyard purchase. This led to him developing a strong interest in wine and the industry. He pivoted his career to running the Impact newsletter, encouraged by its reception from alcoholic beverage wholesalers. At the time, there was very little substantial reporting on the wine business.
After he bought the struggling Wine Spectator newspaper, he relocated the offices from San Diego to San Francisco and became editor. The magazine expanded to cover travel, cooking, restaurants and collecting, and recently celebrated its 50th anniversary.
Shanken is survived by his wife, Hazel Rudy, daughters Jessica, Allison and Samantha, four grandchildren and two sisters.

Greenland opens new international airport to lure tourists
Greenland has opened a new international airport, seeking to lure visitors from around the world as the Arctic island looks toward eventual independence from Denmark
ILULISSAT, Greenland -- ILULISSAT, Greenland (AP) — Greenland has opened a new international airport, seeking to lure visitors from around the world as the Arctic island looks toward eventual independence from Denmark.
Thursday's inaugural international flight between Copenhagen, Denmark, and Ilulissat, Greenland, was part of the island government's efforts to grow its tourism industry to boost and diversify an economy still reliant on fishing.
Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described the new airport as “one of the biggest investments” in the island’s history. Nielsen was one of 169 passengers on Thursday's 4.5-hour flight on an Airbus A330neo. An Associated Press journalist also took the flight, operated by government-owned Air Greenland, as part of a trip organized by tourism agency Visit Greenland, for this story.
“If Greenland wants to be independent, we need to have a strong foundation, both economically and in terms of industry and business,” Nielsen told the AP before the plane departed.
The strategic island, home to roughly 56,000 people, has been a focus of U.S. President Donald Trump since his first term, when he initially expressed his desire to acquire Greenland. His repeated threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a NATO ally, during his second term prompted months of tensions with other NATO allies. In September, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
“There’s no doubt that it has been a shadow over the entire Kingdom of Denmark, but especially Greenland,” said Danish Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard, who also took the inaugural flight. “The opening of this new international airport marks, I think, hope and optimism.”
Ilulissat, known as the "City of Icebergs," sits along the island's western coast and is home to some 5,000 people. Greenland's third-largest city is also one of the island's most-visited destinations. More than 550 kilometers (342 miles) north of the capital, Nuuk, its tourism offerings range from sled dog tours to icefjord cruises in picturesque Disko Bay, known for its towering icebergs.
Previously, travelers reaching Ilulissat had to arrive by cruise ship, take a small plane from Iceland or fly to one of Greenland’s international hubs and connect to smaller aircraft. There are no road connections from other big towns.
For decades, Greenland’s main international aviation gateways were former U.S. military air bases, distant echoes of World War II, in Kangerlussuaq and Narsarsuaq. Locals and international visitors had to land there before catching smaller aircraft to the island's major towns, including Ilulissat and Nuuk. That changed in late 2024, when an international airport opened in Nuuk.
United Airlines last year began a new seasonal route between Nuuk and Newark, New Jersey. The inaugural flight was the first direct from the U.S. to Greenland by an American airline.
The Ilulissat airport, meanwhile, has a 5,000-square-meter (53,820 square feet) terminal and a new 2,200-meter (1.37-mile) runway, long enough to accommodate larger passenger aircraft. Air Greenland has committed to as many as six weekly flights between Copenhagen and Ilulissat during next year’s peak summer months, and Icelandair will also fly large jets from its Keflavik hub. Jens R. Lauridsen, CEO of Greenland Airports, said the company is also hoping to lure airlines in the U.S. and mainland Europe to serve Ilulissat.
“It’s quite wonderful that you can go directly right now,” said Kirsten Berthelsen, a 35-year-old Ilulissat resident and student who booked a ticket for Thursday's flight without realizing it was the inaugural service. “Sometimes it’s quite difficult to travel from Nuuk and to other countries.”
While the number of international visitors to Greenland has grown by at least 65% since 2018, reaching almost 150,000 in 2024, the expected travel boom has yet to materialize. In 2024, tourism accounted for less than 5% of the territory's GDP. Infrastructure, including hotel capacity, remains limited.
Aalborg University associate professor Carina Ren, who specializes in Arctic tourism, said some U.S. tourists were even deterred from visiting the island because of the recent Trump standoff, with a few canceling their flights.
“I’ve heard of people canceling their bookings, but also others canceling because they were afraid that perhaps they would not be welcomed,” she said, adding that many Americans still visit, particularly on cruise ships.
Even so, there are some local concerns about mass tourism and potential damage to Greenland’s fragile nature.
Palle Jerimiassen, a former regional mayor, said he fears the city's environment, population and infrastructure may be overwhelmed by too many visitors.
“How many can we invite?” he said. “We are welcoming all the tourists, it’s a possibility to earn some new money."
He added: "But we have to be careful.”

China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party
- Published
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.
What is a plenum?
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.
What is on the agenda this year?
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

Philippine police obtain warrant to search Thomas Markle's devices
- Published
Philippine police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from the former home of Thomas Markle, father of the Duchess of Sussex.
Earlier this month, it was reported that hundreds of images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Thomas Markle Sr, 82, had been found at the property in the Philippines.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week. However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.
Thomas Markle Sr, who is now in the US, has strongly denied the allegations made by his son, describing them as "sick lies".
Cebu Regional Prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that Thomas Markle Jr was "adamant" that the case should be investigated, and that he felt his father "has to answer for it".
Last week, the Sun on Sunday reported that Thomas Markle Sr's ex-wife, Roslyn Loveless, had sent a letter to the Metropolitan Police about the 2019 allegations, which was shared with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex at the time.
Loveless, who has since died, is the mother of Meghan's two half-siblings. She divorced Thomas Markle Sr. in 1975, before he married the duchess's mother.
The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a statement shared on Friday, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".
Speaking to the Sun, Thomas Markle Jr also apologised to Meghan for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement, and said he had "been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years".
Thomas Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May.
He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.
The police say they must identify how the material was obtained before they can consider any criminal charges.
Campaigners describe Cebu as a known hotspot for the sexual exploitation of children, and authorities say they take any such allegations very seriously.

King Charles III arrives in Guyana as part of official nine-day Caribbean trip
King Charles III has landed in the South American country of Guyana, a former British colony that was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the Caribbean during the colonial era
GEORGETOWN, Guyana -- GEORGETOWN, Guyana (AP) — King Charles III arrived Thursday in Guyana, a former British colony that was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the Caribbean during the colonial era.
Charles landed in the South American country following an invitation from Guyanese President Irfaan Ali, who has publicly requested an apology as some Caribbean leaders press for slavery reparations.
Charles, who is on a nine-day official trip in the Caribbean, descended from the plane in a tan suit and greeted Ali, who was wearing an all-ivory Jodhpuri suit.
Guyana is a diverse country of some 840,000 people that recently became one of the world’s largest offshore oil producers after massive oil deposits were discovered off its coast more than a decade ago.
About 36% of Guyana’s population is Black while 50% is East Indian, descended from indentured servants from India brought to the South American country after slavery was abolished.
Charles last visited Guyana in 2000 as a prince.
He is scheduled to meet with Ali, business owners and elected leaders of Amerindian villages known as “toshaos” during his two-day stay in Guyana.
Hilary Beckles, head of the Caribbean Reparations Commission, said at a recent press conference that the region has never been better prepared to confront Britain and the monarchy about its links to slavery.
“The region is mobilized, the governments are mobilized," he said.
The commission was established by regional governments to make Britain and other former European slave-trading nations pay reparations for their role.
In a recent interview with ITV News, Ali said Charles has “rightfully recognized slavery as the darkest days in human history.”
“Moving to the apology is the next step,” he added. “You exploited the region. You destroyed lives. You created underdevelopment.”
The British government has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.
Charles was previously in the Bahamas and is scheduled to arrive Friday in Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting and meet with leaders of 56 member states. Talks are expected to focus on climate, trade and development, but some Caribbean leaders have said slavery reparations should dominate conversations.

Extreme drought driven by an historic El Niño is affecting as many as 8 million people in Papua New Guinea, causing a cascade of issues from shortages of food and water, to electricity scarcity and schooling disruption.
An influential coalition that includes churches, trade unions and business groups has said the Pacific nation is in the midst of a “national crisis”, but there appears to be “no coordinated plan to protect vulnerable communities from the worsening impacts of El Niño.”
Residents and community leaders have told the Guardian that rivers and creeks have dried up and family food gardens – a vital source of food and income for many – have shrivelled. Schools and health facilities are being forced to close early because they lack sufficient water to provide basic services.
Emilly Meren, humanitarian projects manager at CARE International in PNG, said in rural highland areas families were rationing food to one meal a day – while food insecurity was leading to localised disputes between families.
“For women and girls, they are expected to do more to support their families,” she said, yet they were “the last to eat because they have to serve others first”.
“They have to travel three to four hours to source water and food and are exposed to a heightened risk of harassment. We are hearing stories of transactional sex happening in the community – exchanging sex for money or for food.”
The El Niño climate pattern is gaining strength in the tropical Pacific with forecasts suggesting it will be the strongest ever recorded with its impacts worsened by global heating.
Some parts of PNG have had less than a quarter of their usual rainfall since August.
The PNG National Weather Service declared the onset of El Niño in June but Kasis Inape, the service’s assistant director, said at that point, much of the country was already in drought and about 8 million people had been affected.
Inape said PNG was one of the wettest places in the world with rain fed by warm tropical waters, but the El Niño had seen those waters shift east “and we’re starved of rain”.
“Because we’re a rain-fed country, a lot of our people are subsistence farmers and they depend just on rainfall to survive and to feed themselves,” he said.
PNG’s wet season is between November and April and Inape said while some short term relief was forecasted, there were concerns El Niño would shorten the season.
“The place is so dry – just two months of rain is not enough to allow crops to grow and water levels to be comfortable,” Inape said.
In Morobe province’s Bulolo district, smaller rivers have dried up leaving families without access to water for drinking, cooking and washing.
Resident Theophil Zarack said many schools and health centres were operating for only half a day, with some clinics no longer accepting inpatients due to a lack of available water.
Martha Zureno, a resident in Leklu village, said: “All our rivers have dried up, including the one behind my house. Now, my children and I have to walk for miles every afternoon to fetch water for cooking and drinking from the other side.
“We have a well that we dug ourselves, but we only use that water for washing. All the crops in our gardens have dried up and died, and we cannot grow anything now.”
Zureno said that most of the local residents depend on panning for gold to earn an income, but without water, “even that has become increasingly difficult”.
Meanwhile, a destructive hailstorm in parts of Enga province earlier this month – not blamed directly on El Niño – buried sweet potatoes under ice, exacerbating the food scarcity issue, according to George Iki, president of the Sambe Unity Development Association.
In the capital Port Moresby, PNG Power has begun planned electricity blackouts after falling dam levels cut hydropower generation and said disruptions could continue for up to 10 months. The company was working to manage dam releases to protect the city’s water supply.
Peter Aitsi, a prominent PNG business figure and co-chair of the Community Coalition Against Corruption, said the government needed to carry out “proper assessments” of the unfurling impacts, particularly on rural communities.
Last month the group called the drought situation a “national crisis”, but according to Aitsi, urban centres have been mostly shielded from the impacts. That could change, however, with electricity blackouts and a shortage of fresh food from drought-stricken areas, he said.
Aitsi said the capital had been covered in a smoke haze in the past week from fires elsewhere on the island, and in Indonesia to the west, that scientists say have been fuelled by El Niño.
Prime minister James Marape has directed provincial and district authorities to prepare for a prolonged dry season, saying his government was examining financial arrangements to support disaster responses.
“Cabinet is looking at tailoring provisions of our financial instructions to make sure that districts and provinces are assisted to respond to disasters as they happen where appropriate,” Marape said.

Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150 mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards South Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85 mph (140 km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of over 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150 mph (240 km/h), with winds gusting over 185 mph (296 km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100 mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150 mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

My father, John Staley, who has died aged 88, was field director for Oxfam in south India and Sri Lanka during the late 1960s and early 70s, when he was responsible for Oxfam’s funding of several hundred local, national and international voluntary agencies.
His role included aid administration, policy formulation, project appraisal, recommendations for funding, disaster relief and liaison with government and non-government organisations. He led Oxfam’s response in India to a drought in Maharashtra in 1973, which fed more than 20,000 people as part of a work-for-food programme, and was made MBE in 1974 for services to the Indian people.
 
John was born in Epsom, Surrey, the only child of Robert, a doctor, and Sylvia, a housewife. He went to Marlborough college in Wiltshire, and then, after national service, to Cambridge University, where he studied natural sciences and economics (1957-61).
At Cambridge he met Elizabeth Pott, and they discovered a shared love of travelling on an overland expedition to Pakistan with friends. They married in 1962 and did PhDs together at the University of the Punjab in Lahore, studying the economics and geography of mountain communities in northern Pakistan.
In 1966 they returned to the UK, where they finished their PhDs and where John did some freelance lecturing at the Commonwealth Institute, the Pakistan Society and the Royal Central Asian Society before taking up his field director post at Oxfam in 1967.
John eventually became research director for Oxfam in India (1975-76), and during that time discovered the concept of experience-based training, by which small groups of people learn about the behaviour of groups and organisations from their own analysis of their experience of the group.
In 1976 he and some Indian colleagues founded Search, an organisation that developed and used these experience-based training methods to train people in development work in India. He was seconded by Oxfam to Search from 1976 to 1980, and then, in 1982, returned to the UK to become a lecturer and later senior lecturer in development studies at Selly Oak Colleges in Birmingham – remaining there until his retirement in 1999.
 
Thereafter he wrote, travelled, took part in his local U3A in Great Malvern, Worcestershire, and cared for his garden and a small local wood that he and Elizabeth bought as a retirement project. Over the years John wrote three books, Words for My Brother (1982), People in Development (also 1982), and Enticing the Learning (2008).
 
Elizabeth died in 2019. John is survived by their children, Eleanor, Joanna and me, and grandchildren Isabelle and Freddie.

Rumors that the U.S. Department of Defense gave a high-value contract to a foreign pharmaceutical company to produce "ketamine wafers" for the military circulated in October.
People on social media alleged the product was being developed by Singapore-based iX Biopharma and was called Wafermine, described as a "small ketamine wafer that dissolves under the tongue and delivers the drug through the mucous membrane without injection."
The claim gained enough popularity that Snopes readers reached out to us via email and asked us to investigate.
The claim was true, according to multiple documents from iX Biopharma. Neither the company nor the Pentagon has responded to Snopes' request for comment, but we will update this article if we hear back.
On Feb. 12, the company issued a news release and announcement from the board of directors about the contract with the Department of Defense. "The U.S. government will provide $40,954,914 in funding to support the development of Wafermine," the announcement read.
IX Biopharma described Wafermine as the "world's first patented sublingual racemic ketamine wafer being developed for acute moderate to severe pain" which can be administered without an injection. The news of the announcement was added to the company's newsroom website on Feb. 12.
The announcement added that the "contract was awarded to the Company under a sole-source procurement process, meaning the U.S. government determined that the Company was uniquely capable of delivering the required product within the required timelines."
The contract was celebrated in the company's 2026 annual report, released in September, which called the DOD's investment its "defining event of the year" and said it "anchored" the company's entry into the U.S. healthcare market.
The report clarified that the development of Wafermine is intended for the U.S. military "to deploy on the battlefield and include in its standard issue medical sets, kits and outfits."
A 2019 study showed that as the use of ketamine in U.S. combat operations increased from 2010-19, use of opiates decreased.
Deployment of a new product like Wafermine would usually be subject to full approval by the Food and Drug Administration before release, but on Sept. 3, the Department of Health and Human Services made an Emergency Use Authorization declaration, available to read on the Federal Register.
The declaration cited a determination made by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in July which declared a current or "significant potential" of a military emergency.
The HHS declaration read, in part:
On July 15, 2026 the Secretary of War determined, pursuant to sec. 564(b)(1)(B) of the FD&C Act, that there is a military emergency, or a significant potential for a military emergency, involving a heightened risk to U.S. military forces of an attack with a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear agent or agents; or an attack by an agent or agents that may cause, or are otherwise associated with, an imminently life-threatening and specific risk to U.S. military forces (including agents of military combat such as firearms, projectiles, and explosive devices). Injuries arising from these attacks may cause U.S. military forces to experience moderate to severe acute pain and place them at risk of developing life-threatening hemodynamic instability, including shock or respiratory distress.
In sum, an EUA would allow Wafermine to be expedited for use on the battlefield despite not yet having full approval from the FDA.
IX Biopharma announced the move toward an EUA in September, writing that "circumstances exist for the FDA to consider Wafermine for EUA. Before the Declaration, supply of Wafermine to US military personnel would have required full FDA approval. With the statutory precondition under section 564 now satisfied, a regulatory route exists, subject to the FDA granting an EUA."
The company said it planned on filing its EUA before the end of the year.
In October, Politico reported that iX Biopharma's Nevada-based manufacturing partner, Orion Specialty Labs, was not yet licensed by the state pharmacy board to operate.
IX Biopharma's annual report stated Orion had "ordered specialised manufacturing equipment" and that it "relocated our manufacturing equipment from Australia to Orion's facility to accelerate the production readiness."

India’s development story over the past decade has been one of infrastructure: highways, metro lines, electrification and digital public platforms, each treated as a foundation for growth that requires public investment and planning. One foundation on which every household and economy depends has not received the same attention: care.
Everyone needs care at some point in life. How care is organised shapes people’s opportunities, well-being and participation in society and the economy. When services are absent, families, and women most of all, bear the cost in unpaid work, lost earnings, and narrower opportunities.
In the Periodic Labour Force Survey 2025, 44.4% of women outside the labour force cited childcare and homemaking as the main reason for staying out of the labour force. India’s Time Use Survey 2024 found that 41% of women aged 15–59 provided unpaid care, spending an average of 140 minutes a day on it. Expanding access to affordable, quality care services can give women greater freedom to pursue employment, leisure and participation in public life. With an ageing population, the need for accessible care services will only grow.
Yet care rarely features in India’s growth strategy. For a Viksit Bharat 2047, the question is not only how to expand women’s economic participation, but how to build the care system that makes such participation possible. The Anganwadi network, strengthened through Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, anchors early childhood care and nutrition. Palna, under Mission Shakti, supports crèches, while Mission Vatsalya, social security and provisions for persons with disabilities and senior citizens address other needs. The challenge is architecture, not ambition. Four gaps stand out.
First, fragmentation. Care is split across multiple Ministries, from women and child development to housing and urban affairs. Each runs valuable programmes, but without a common framework. This can leave gaps such as crèches that close before factory shifts end or eldercare needs that fall outside of existing schemes.
Second, coverage. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) estimates that 9–10 million women in low-income urban households need childcare. Similarly for eldercare, 24% of older persons face limitations in daily activities, while national data on service availability and coverage remain limited.
Third, the workforce. Care depends on frontline workers; from Anganwadi workers to home-based caregivers and domestic workers — many of whom remain inadequately remunerated or engaged on an honorary basis. Building on NITI Aayog’s proposals, clear standards, certification, decent working conditions, social protection and career pathways would recognise care as skilled and paid work.
Finally, financing and norms. Care is still budgeted as welfare rather than investment, and workplace policies assume that caregiving is women’s work. The Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister (EAC-PM) recommends statutory paid paternity leave in the private sector.
Comparable economies are building their own care ecosystems. Colombia’s 2025 National Care Policy brings 34 government entities under one framework. Brazil’s 2024 National Care Policy and 2025 National Care Plan set up inter-Ministerial committees to steer implementation. In Nepal, care mapping was used to fund care pilots.
The way forward
In India, NITI Aayog’s Reimagining Care: Strategies for Empowering Caregivers in Viksit Bharat@2047 report proposes a National Caregiving Council to strengthen coordination. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is consulting States and Union Territories; its May 2026 national workshop discussed a National Care Economy Mission with inter-Ministerial governance, aligned financing and shared data. State-level care roadmaps can make this practical. States can map needs, services and demographic trends, identify gaps in childcare, eldercare and disability support, and prepare costed plans with clear responsibilities.
Building on UNDP’s research and lessons from UN Women’s TransformCare initiative in more than 50 countries, the two agencies are supporting this agenda under government leadership, from mapping care services and skilling care workers to backing women-led childcare enterprises with the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and Women Entrepreneurship Platform.
India has the programmes, policy vision and evidence. On this International Day of Care and Support, the task is to connect them, finance them and hold them to account: to build care the way India builds infrastructure.
Shoko Ishikawa is Country Representative, UN Women India; Angela Lusigi is Resident Representative, UNDP India
