An unpublished government report on feral deer shows Australia is failing in its efforts to stop the spread of what one advocate warns could become “Australia’s next feral pig”.
The five years from 2020-2025 over which the national feral deer action plan was assessed covers a period in which the famously elusive species has increasingly encroached upon major cities, leading to more frequent encounters – including a memorable occasion in which two men in various degrees of undress were fined after becoming lost in the bush when they were spooked by deer while nude sunbathing.
The report says deer, one of the country’s “most rapidly increasing invasive pests”, have both increased in numbers and spread in territory, costing more than $91m in production loss and management time every year.
Deakin University’s Prof Euan Ritchie, president of the Australian Mammal Society, said he was “not at all” surprised by this year’s national vertebrate pest management report card.
“This report shows that governments are failing miserably to invest enough to control deer populations and the severe impacts that they can have on agriculture, native wildlife and the environment, road safety and culturally significant sites,” Ritchie said.
“This is what sustained failure to act sufficiently results in.”
Six species of feral deer are established in Australia – chital, fallow, hog, red, rusa and sambar – with well-established populations across south-eastern Australia, where densities are highest. There are smaller, more localised populations in South and Western Australia and the Northern Territory.
The report card, produced by the National Vertebrate Pest Coordinators, shows every state and territory is failing or floundering in their efforts to control feral deer – with one notable exception. South Australia, which launched an ambitious statewide eradication plan in 2022, received a green in all four categories assessed under the traffic light system of marking. The report showed – with high confidence – that the state had decreased the abundance, distribution and environmental and agricultural impacts of deer.
New South Wales and Tasmania were given reds in all four categories, while Queensland and the ACT both received three reds and a yellow. No jurisdiction but SA received a single green pass mark.
Invasive Species Council advocacy manager Reece Pianta said the report confirmed what land managers had been seeing on the ground for some years. In May 2025, the council released footage and images that it said showed the Gold Coast “under feral deer siege”.
Pianta said the report, leaked to his organisation, points to “a long-term systemic underfunding of deer control”. He said deer did not have the recognition of other more notorious invasives, but controlling them was every bit as necessary.
“Deer are the next feral pig,” he said. “The difference with deer is that an intervention now could make a significant difference to the population numbers and contain, or even reverse, that spread.”
While Pianta said deer “probably can’t be eradicated” from the entire continent, he said South Australia’s “A+” report score showed it was possible to do so in some states and territories, while others would require a long-term effort to contain the spread of deer and mitigate their impacts.
Adelaide University Environment Institute director Prof Andrew Lowe said the report was a “good news story” for his state that rang true with what he was seeing on the ground.
Lowe, who is also member of the Hills and Fleurieu Landscape Board, which is involved in managing deer, said SA grappled with its “massive problem with deer” in earnest from 2022, after an agricultural impact estimate showed the $36m worth of damage done every year by deer there was set to increase to $241m by 2031.
But although deer had “massively declined” in the few years since a $4m eradication program began, Lowe said deer were seeking refuge on the fringes of urban areas, where culling was more expensive. He said functional eradication of deer from SA would take about another $10m over 10 years.
The cost of inaction, though, was of a different magnitude.
“If we don’t do that, then the population will go up again and we’re going to be in the same situation,” Lowe said. “So $10m versus $240m – do the math.”

China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified, taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress which happens every five years and, is expected to be held in the second half of 2027. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party, making him the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong.
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

Along with the rest of the world, we at Ars are mourning Sir Patrick Stewart—the beloved award-winning actor best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise—who died yesterday at the age of 86.
A statement released by Stewart’s representatives said:
We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia. He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.
Born in Yorkshire, England, in 1940, the acting bug bit Stewart at the age of 12, when his English teacher handed out scripts for Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice and asked young Patrick to read the part of Shylock—a role the adult Stewart would later play for the Royal Shakespeare Theater (RSC), among many other parts. His signature bald head emerged early, around 19, thanks to alopecia. He briefly worked as a cub reporter and a furniture salesman before winning a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theater School, and he landed his first professional role in 1959, playing a marooned pirate in a production of Treasure Island for the Lincoln Repertory Company.
Stewart worked regularly in theater and on British television, and his big break came in his late 40s. The actor was conducting master classes on Shakespeare at the University of California, Los Angeles, when a TV producer developing TNG heard him lecture and thought he would make a perfect captain for the Enterprise-D. Creator Gene Roddenberry wasn’t initially keen on the choice, but Stewart’s audition changed his mind. The rest is television history.
On Instagram, fellow thespian Sir Ian McKellen—who first met Stewart when both were young actors with the RSC and co-starred as Magneto in the X-Men films—recalled the day Stewart told him about the Star Trek offer.
“’But Patrick, think of your stage career in the UK,'” McKellen recalled saying. “‘Do you really want to risk—getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?’ Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did.”
Stewart himself never expressed anything but pride in the role. “For huge numbers of people, I will always be Jean-Luc Picard, and that’s fine,” he told The Independent in 2003. “I really believe we created an admirable individual.”
TNG ended in 1994, but it wasn’t long before Stewart created another iconic role, starring as Professor Charles Xavier in 2000’s X-Men, alongside McKellen as Magneto. He reprised the role in six more films and voiced the character in multiple video games.
He was a serious actor who never took himself too seriously, relishing Shakespeare, Ibsen, and Beckett but also throwing himself into comedic TV appearances on Saturday Night Live, The Daily Show (he was a “special correspondent” for several segments in 2012), and Sesame Street. Who could forget his timeless “Soliloquy on B,” channeling Hamlet? Or his daily readings of Shakespearean sonnets that helped us all get through the COVID-19 pandemic? He voiced Napoleon in 1999’s Animal Farm, CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock on American Dad and, earlier this year, Sir Nitchfield in the delightful Sheep Detectives.
In between acting gigs, Stewart found time for charity work, advocating for such causes as domestic violence prevention and PTSD awareness among members of the armed forces, drawing on his own childhood being raised by an abusive father. All of this made Stewart one of the most beloved actors of our time. Tributes to Stewart are all over social media today, as celebrities and regular folk alike reflect on everything the actor’s work has meant to them over the years, including these heartfelt words from his lifelong friend McKellen:
Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.
Ars staffers share their own reminiscences about Stewart and what he meant to them below.
Ken Fisher, founder and editor-in-chief:
I had the good fortune to literally bump into Sir Patrick Stewart outside Bond 45 in Midtown Manhattan (when it was on 45th Street). I was coming out of the restaurant with a couple of colleagues one evening when I turned right into him. When my eyes met his, I entered a state of total confusion. I knew he loved and even played Broadway, but it didn’t register why he was here, right next to me.
Fortunately, I recovered—but then, for some unknown reason, I said in a pirate voice, “Scuse muh, Capt’n!” But he didn’t miss a beat, smiled, and took a posture of “after you good sir!” I immediately chuckled like a fool and then added that I loved his work both on and off the stage. He thanked me, and we kept on rolling. I am thankful to this day that I didn’t say something corny like “two to beam up.”
What struck me about the exchange was that, as brief as it was, he did not appear annoyed in the slightest. And while I know he is a world-class actor, he also seemed genuinely appreciative of the comment. I am grateful today that I got to share my appreciation with him, awkward though it was.

Eric Berger, senior space editor:
Warmth. Humanity. Decency. Honesty. Integrity. Intellectualism. These are but a few of the traits I associate with Captain Jean-Luc Picard. At a time when our leadership in the United States, and many other countries around the world, regularly showcases the opposite of these characteristics, is it any wonder that we dearly miss the captain of the Enterprise-D? Picard first graced our TV screens in the late 1980s, a super impressionable time for me. As a result, for a time, that is how I expected most leaders would behave. Alas, no.
I’m sure everyone has their favorite Picard scenes, but for me it came at the very end of The Next Generation; we had all gotten to know and love the bridge crew so well, and it felt so bittersweet that it all was ending. There was Jean-Luc, who had maintained his professional distance for seven years, joining his crew at the poker table. And now, not just the series is over, but so too is the era in which Patrick Stewart was alive and making the world a better place. It’s a little darker outside.
Kyle Orland, senior gaming editor:
With Patrick Stewart’s death, there will be plenty of people remembering all of the Star Trek: The Next Generation moments when he ably portrayed Captain Picard as the moral and diplomatic core of the show. And for sure, Stewart’s meaty and memorable monologues in episodes like The Drumhead, The First Duty, Darmok, Chain of Command, and more will be long remembered by sci-fi fans and studied by actors honing their craft.
But the most lasting Captain Picard moments for me are often the ones where Stewart got to let his hair down (so to speak) and show some rare emotional vulnerability in what was usually such a composed and professional character.
It’s these smaller emotional character moments—and Stewart’s ability to make so much of them—that added depth and roundness to Captain Picard’s character over the years. And that continued all the way up to Next Generation‘s very final moments, where Stewart captures the wistfulness and regret of Picard finally deciding to join the senior staff poker game. “Five card stud, nothing wild… and the sky’s the limit.”
Jeremy Hsu, technology reporter:
As a very casual Star Trek viewer, I only really began to grasp the depth of Patrick Stewart’s acting when I became enthralled by the silver screen chemistry between him and co-star Ian McKellen in the X-Men film franchise. The love-hate relationship and emotional vulnerability that Stewart and McKellen instilled in their roles as old-friends-turned-rivals has resonated with me throughout the years, and I still have deep appreciation for how the actors’ real-life friendship grew from that acting experience.
I also count myself extremely fortunate to have seen Stewart and McKellen perform together in a Broadway stage revival of the play Waiting for Godot in 2014. I’m sad they won’t be performing together again, but whenever they had the opportunity, they shone brightly indeed.
Jacob May, copy editor:
Hope and altruism are central themes in Stewart’s iconic roles, and they resonated most with me during one of my lowest moments.
Ever the one to inspire, Stewart’s role as Professor X in many X-Men films encouraged people and mutants to see the best in themselves and in each other. In 2014’s Days of Future Past, his pep talk extended to new ears: a younger, disillusioned version of himself (played by James McAvoy), and he may have well been speaking to me, too. Professor X’s telepathic abilities transcend space, time, and reality—don’t question it too much.
Upon the film’s release, I was freshly laid off from my hometown newspaper after the copy desk saw its numbers cut in half. (What was already a skeleton crew became less than that.) It wasn’t lost on me that being a cynic and malcontent was partly why I wasn’t picked to remain at the paper. In my late 20s, I questioned many of the decisions that set me on my journalism path, unsure what would happen to my career.
The younger Charles Xavier finds himself in a similar spot: angry with himself, with other people, and with the general state of things—and he’s seemingly out of a job. The older Professor X reminds his younger self that people can overcome their self-defeating flaws. “Just because someone stumbles and loses their way doesn’t mean they’re lost forever.”
Younger Chuck laments being tormented by people’s accounts of their pain, something a person who reads the news for a living can relate to. I try to unplug from Cerebro—er, my computer—when I’m off the clock. Xavier doesn’t have that luxury. The constant voices have driven him to despair and left him increasingly jaded.
But older Xavier calls him out, saying it’s his own mindset that’s holding him back. “We need you to hope again,” he says.
Therein lies the answer to Xavier’s malady: hope. And, as it turns out, the advice was also applicable to a young journalist in a crumbling industry. Incidentally, Stewart also found himself at a career crossroads as a young man, though he wasn’t too far along a chosen path, according to the Hollywood Reporter.
At 15, he got a job at the local newspaper, The Dewsbury Reporter, where he was tasked with interviewing bereaved family members when someone in town died. Journalism turned out not to be his passion, and he spent much of his free time with drama groups. His editor finally told him he had to choose between acting and journalism—and he quit on the spot.
Maybe if I had an Englishman’s commanding baritone, I would have made the same choice.

Ryan Whitwam, senior technology reporter:
Patrick Stewart was a prolific actor, but I will always associate him most with Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek: The Next Generation, a show that made a real impression on me as a nerdy kid. It was refreshing to see a leader who valued science and reason—someone who didn’t immediately reach for their phaser. Despite the sometimes silly sci-fi subject matter, Stewart never seemed like he was too good to be spouting technobabble, even though he was famously skeptical of the role at first. Stewart’s portrayal of Picard elevated the series and helped it to age into a classic that I (and I’m sure many of you) still enjoy.
I also appreciate that he took so many different roles in movies and TV during his post-Trek career. Whenever I saw Patrick Stewart pop up on my screen or heard his voice unexpectedly come out of a cartoon character, it was a reminder of how happy TNG made me over the years. I’ll miss that, and I’ll miss knowing that Patrick Stewart is out there being a kind, thoughtful guy off screen.
Lee Hutchinson, senior technology editor:
The version of Patrick Stewart that lives in my head will most often be the noble starship captain who taught us life lessons every Friday night at 7 pm on channel 39. But while Stewart was obviously fantastic at portraying Picard’s stentorian and often stuffy formality, I was surprised when I discovered that the man behind the uniform was… surprisingly hilarious.
I tuned into his early 1994 Saturday Night Live appearance expecting an endless series of Trek riffs, but what I got instead was a sketch about an erotic cake shop run by a weirdly scatological baker. My confusion gave way to giggles—it was a one-note joke, but the image of Stewart in an apron talking about “sexy cakes” has stuck in my head for decades. He committed to it every bit as hard as he committed to following the Prime Directive, and at 16, it made me realize that anyone who could go from “The first duty of a Starfleet officer is to the truth!” to that and sell them both with equal intensity and sincerity was not a one-note actor. This was a man with a hell of a lot of range!
The performance that brought me the most joy, though, was his turn on Ricky Gervais’ Extras, where he played a version of himself as an actor, delivering career advice to Gervais. The scene is a masterclass in expectation subversion, something Stewart often seemed to revel in. I won’t spoil it for the two or three readers who still haven’t had the pleasure, but I will say that to this day my wife and I still say, “I’ve seen everything, I’ve seen it all!” at each other regularly in conversation.
Farewell, Sir Patrick. You gave us so much. Thank you.
Jason Marlin, technical director:
Like many Gen Xers, I grew up loving the original Star Trek series. But The Next Generation held a special place in my heart. From the moment it premiered, I was captivated by the mind-bending concepts it explored. Jean-Luc Picard quickly became one of my favorite characters. I admired his intelligence, leadership, and moral integrity. He was the quintessential Starfleet captain, and he made balding cool in a way only Michael Jordan could rival.
Years later, I discovered what would become my favorite Patrick Stewart performance: his formidable portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge on Broadway and in the 1999 adaptation of A Christmas Carol.
For me, the movie remains the definitive version of Dickens’ classic, and watching it has become a cherished family holiday tradition. During the COVID lockdowns, we eagerly tuned in to Stewart’s readings of Shakespeare, and of course, his solo multipart rendition of A Christmas Carol. A roaring fire, some warm drinks, and his perfect Shakespearean accent made everything seem right with the world.
Sir Patrick Stewart will be greatly missed in the Marlin household.
Nick Indge, senior technology reporter:
Growing up in the US, raised by Brits, there was something quietly thrilling about seeing a Yorkshireman handed the captain’s chair. Better still, it made TNG legitimate in the eyes of my parents—a classically trained Shakespearean actor wouldn’t be involved in anything unserious, surely. As I came of age in 2000, there he was again as Professor X. Of course he was. Who else could it have possibly been? Beyond the roles, though, he just seemed to be a genuinely good man, the Mr. Rogers and Weird Al tier of human being. And when the world was upside down at the height of COVID, there he was, reading me a daily sonnet.
Jennifer is a senior writer at Ars Technica with a particular focus on where science meets culture, covering everything from physics and related interdisciplinary topics to her favorite films and TV series. Early voting in the U.S. midterm elections is underway. Voters are deciding which party will control Congress, as well as numerous state legislatures and governors' offices. Snopes' fact-checkers are flagging rumors surrounding the election, debunking false statements by candidates and suspicious voter fraud claims with nonpartisan research and expert sources. Join our effort to keep this election fact-focused by becoming a Snopes member.
- A long-standing, unproven voter fraud theory claims that some voters receive multiple ballots, allowing them to vote more than once.
- The theory is not supported by evidence. We found no documented examples of voters receiving multiple ballots and casting multiple votes on a large-enough scale to skew election results.
- There can be legitimate reasons why voters receive or turn in multiple ballots in a single election, and it is not uncommon for voters to receive more than one ballot both as a result of a mistake or on purpose. In cases where extra ballots mistakenly get sent to voters, elections officials have multiple ways to ensure they count only one vote per person.
- Ballots are also extremely difficult to copy, meaning large-scale fraud using copied ballots would be near-impossible to carry out. Election officials would likely catch attempts at fraud during the canvassing process if the number of returned ballots was higher than the number of registered voters.
- Tammy Patrick, the chief programs officer at the National Association of Election Officials, an association that trains and certifies election and voter registration officials, encouraged voters with doubts about how officials certify and count ballots to engage with the system to understand how its many safeguards work.
In October, Tulare County, California, said on Facebook (archived) that some voters may have received "duplicate vote-by-mail packets" for the Nov. 3 midterm election.
The Sacramento Bee — citing Michelle Baldwin, the county's registrar of voters — reported that a printing vendor had mistakenly printed and sent extra ballots to 7,791 voters.
The incident in Tulare County appeared to play into a long-standing theory of fraud: namely, that some voters receive multiple ballots, allowing them to vote multiple times in the same election and skew results in favor of a particular party or candidate.
One X user reacting to news about voters in California receiving extra ballots wrote (archived): "Shocker… We've been talking about receiving multiple ballots every election cycle since 2018 and how big a problem it is, only to be told we're wrong or lying by internet 'fact checkers.'"
The X user above was correct that voters receiving multiple ballots is a known election phenomenon. In the run-up to the 2026 midterms, election officials in Michigan and California addressed the issue in local media. The Bipartisan Policy Center, a nonprofit organization, discussed the issue in a February report on voting by mail.
However, we found no documented examples of voters receiving multiple ballots and casting multiple votes on a large-enough scale to skew election results. There can be legitimate reasons why voters receive or turn in multiple ballots in a single election. Some incidents, such as the one in Tulare County, can be attributed to human error. Other times, election officials might send a second ballot if the first contained an error. Either way, officials have well-established safeguards in place that prevent voters from voting more than once.
Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer at the National Association of Election Officials, an association that trains and certifies election and voter registration officials, told Snopes the data does not support claims that fraudsters are using multiple ballots per voter to skew election results, mainly because it would be extremely difficult to pull off such a scheme. Patrick said:
There's a saying, "Is the juice worth the squeeze?" And in this case, it isn't. When we think about voters being able to vote multiple times because, that is what it comes down to here: Is there anyone who is being able to vote more than once in a jurisdiction because they got more than one ballot? That does not happen.
Because there was no documented proof of fraudsters skewing elections by issuing multiple ballots to individual voters, we leave this claim unrated.
Tracking 'extra' ballots in 2026 cycle
Using the National Association of Election Officials' "Electionline" project, which collects news articles on various topics related to elections, we found at least 10 reports across eight states of voters receiving more than one ballot ahead of the 2026 midterms where election officials did not intend to send the extra ballot.
- Local media in California reported on Oct. 24 that at least 15,000 voters in Fresno County could have received an extra ballot. The county's registrar of voters, James Kus, reportedly said sending out extra ballots was a "common issue" that often happened after voters updated their information on the voting register.
- In Tulare County, California, 7,791 voters received an extra ballot. Officials said this was due to a vendor error.
- Local media in Kane County, Illinois, on the outskirts of Chicago, reported that elections officials had sent "about 2,000" extra ballots to voters due to "processing issues" with the clerk's ballot-printing machine.
- In Athens-Clarke County, Georgia, 1,154 voters received extra ballots as a result of "an error in a mailing list."
- More than 600 voters in Warren County, Iowa, reportedly received an extra ballot. Election officials had not given a reason why at the time of this writing.
- Officials in Weber County, Utah, reportedly sent up to 167 voters an extra ballot due to a "miscalibrated envelope stuffing machine."
- Officials in Imperial County, California, said around 160 voters were affected by a "mailing error" that issued them an extra ballot.
- Local media in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, reported that due to "a communication issue between the county and state while files were prepared," 157 voters received an extra ballot.
- Election officials in Pueblo County, Colorado, said that some homeowners received more than one ballot to vote on a special tax issue. Officials said anyone who received more than one ballot should call the elections office as they may not have received them in error.
- Officials in Pleasant Prairie, Wisconsin, said Oct. 27 that some voters may have received extra ballots due to an error by a village employee helping to prepare absentee ballots.
While the instances of officials sending extra ballots to voters recorded above were almost all the result of mistakes, there were also legitimate reasons why a voter might receive an extra ballot.
For example, Patrick said that election officials might send out a second ballot if the first contained a mistake. She said it was then up to election officials "to make sure that the security protocols are there and are followed" so voters who received more than one ballot got only one vote.
'Extra' ballot does not mean extra vote
In all the cases above, officials emphasized that safeguards during the vote-counting process mean that just because a voter received an extra ballot did not mean they got an extra vote.
For example, the elections-focused nonprofit news organization Votebeat reported in May that election officials in Wisconsin and other states print individual barcodes on ballots that tie them to a particular voter. If an official scans a barcode tied to a voter who has already voted, the vote-counting system will reject the second ballot.
In Pennsylvania, Westmoreland County Commissioner Doug Chew reportedly told the Latrobe Bulletin that officials would use a barcode system to ensure that their vote-counting system would reject a potential second ballot from the same voter.
Patrick told Snopes that other protections such as signature verification keep voters from submitting an absentee ballot and also voting in person. Election officials use those same protections to ensure that the system counts only one absentee ballot per person.
In addition to barcodes and signature verification, Patrick said the ballots themselves were very specific and individualized, meaning fraudulent attempts to mass-copy ballots and sway elections would be extremely difficult to pull off. She said:
The ballots themselves have pretty specific card stock, they have very specific timing marks down the side that allow for them to be tabulated. It's not the case that there's one ballot that everybody gets. In Maricopa County, they literally have upwards of 10,000 different ballot styles. So, knowing which ballot style each individual voter gets is tied to the ballot style, it's very specific, so even if you were to go out and take your sample ballot and duplicate it somehow, it doesn't matter, that's not an official ballot, it's not going to go through the tabulator. It's never going to get to that point in the process because it has to first be authenticated before it even makes it that far into the building.
Aside from ballots being difficult to copy, adding a significant number of ballots to a count would not go unnoticed. As part of the election certification process, officials will canvass — meaning count — absentee ballots and compare them with the known number of voters. A significantly higher number of returned ballots than voters would raise the alarm on fraud.
Patrick warned against automatically assuming election fraud if one person turned in multiple ballots at a polling station or drop box. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, at least 35 states allowed voters to nominate a person other than themselves to turn in their ballot, meaning some voters might legitimately hand in more than one ballot.
Engage with system to quell concerns, expert says
Despite there being no documented incidents of election fraud via illegal ballot duplication, prominent politicians such as U.S. President Donald Trump have shared the unproven theory. However, as we outlined above, election officials have multiple safeguards in place that are effective at ensuring that any one voter gets only one vote.
Patrick suggested that the best thing worried voters could do was to engage with the system.
It's important to understand all the safeguards that are in place all along the path. To talk to your neighbors that work at the elections office, or who are poll workers. To go down and take a tour the next time there is a town hall and ask questions and see how it actually works.
She said, "When you have questions, elections officials are there with the answers and they want you to understand your process and your elections and to have confidence in it," but added that voters should not "try and 'test the system'" by submitting more than one ballot if they received multiple, "because that's criminal and you'll get caught, so you don't want to do that!"
For further reading, Snopes has covered a number of claims related to the 2026 elections.

Bluesky now has a dedicated 'moderation inbox'
The beta feature makes it easier to stay on top of reports and account strikes.
Bluesky is rolling out a new feature today that will allow users to track the platform's various moderation actions in one place. The new "moderation inbox" is available in beta through the Bluesky app, and collects reports you've filed about other users and posts, actions taken against your account and your overall standing on the platform.
You can enable the moderation inbox by turning on beta features in the Bluesky app's Settings menu, and then finding the inbox under the Moderation tools menu. Bluesky says the inbox will start empty, even if you've already received a strike, but will fill up as you file reports about posts and Bluesky takes action against your account or applies labels to your posts. The inbox also lets you appeal most of Bluesky's decisions directly through the app, though suspensions still have to be handled at the login screen.
Bluesky says the goal for the feature is to make it easier to communicate with users. The company has previously shared moderation decisions over email, which it says made it difficult to reach people using Bluesky on independent servers, and often meant that when it did email, it was only for serious decisions. The inbox allows anyone who uses the Bluesky app to be contacted with a notification and lets the company share each step of the moderation process without cluttering anyone's email inbox.
Bluesky has earned a reputation for offering robust blocking tools that make it easier for users to moderate their own feeds, but the company's own approach to moderation has drawn criticism. In 2025, The Guardian reported that Bluesky's automated spam system regularly deactivated the accounts of Palestinians crowdfunding for supplies on the platform, which critics said treated people like bots. Users similarly took issue with the company's moderation of posts dealing with the assassination of Charlie Kirk. Clearer in-app notices and appeals might have softened some of the backlash.
Alongside the moderation inbox, Bluesky's latest update also adds an optional widget users can place on their home screen that displays trending topics.

India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.
Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.
At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.
Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

On 22 October 2026, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur acknowledged that face-offs with Chinese forces had occurred at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border. On 23 October 2026, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal stated that the situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) becomes “disturbed” when Chinese troops deviate from established patrolling patterns.
Amid these developments, several videos are being circulated on social media (here, here, and here), purportedly showing clashes between Indian and Chinese troops along the Arunachal Pradesh border, including claims of an Indian soldier’s capture and alleged attempts by Chinese troops to cross the border. Let’s verify the claims made in these posts in this article.
Claim: The videos show clashes between Indian and Chinese troops along the Arunachal Pradesh border in October 2026.
Fact: None of the viral videos shows the reported India–China border face-offs in October 2026. The first and third videos were circulating on social media by December 2025, while the second features footage filmed on 28 September 2021, as reported by CNN. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
During our investigation, we found several social media posts (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals dating back to December 2025. This confirms that the viral video predates the reported India–China border tensions in October 2026 and is unrelated to the recent developments. These posts allege that an Indian soldier suffering from diabetes and altitude-related health complications fainted while on duty near the Line of Actual Control (LAC). Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) personnel provided him with first aid and medical assistance before safely handing him over to his own unit. The posts portray the incident as a humanitarian gesture amid India–China border tensions.
A News18 Hindi report published on 16 December 2025, featuring a screenshot of the viral video, claimed that Chinese soldiers had assisted an unconscious Indian soldier. While highlighting the humanitarian aspect, the report also noted scepticism over the video, particularly why the soldier’s legs appeared to be tied, raising questions about whether the incident was a genuine humanitarian gesture or an attempt by China to improve its image.
However, we could not independently verify the video’s origin or the context in which it was recorded. The available evidence indicates that the video predates the October 2026 border face-offs. At the time of writing, the Indian Army had issued no statement confirming the capture of any Indian soldier during these incidents.
Video 2
During our investigation, we found that the viral video predates the reported India–China border tensions in October 2026 and is unrelated to the recent developments. The video has been online at least since December 2022.
A CNN report published on 15 December 2022 featuring the same visuals stated that the footage was filmed on 28 September 2021. According to CNN, a serving Indian military officer familiar with clashes along the India–China border confirmed that the video was recorded in Arunachal Pradesh, near the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border between the two countries.
Video 3
During our investigation, we found several social media posts (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals dating back to December 2025. This confirms that the viral video predates the reported India–China border tensions in October 2026 and is unrelated to the recent developments. These posts claimed that the video shows Indian soldiers beating Chinese troops allegedly attempting to infiltrate Arunachal Pradesh, describing it as an old border clash.
An X post by the Indian Army’s Fact Check Unit debunking the viral video stated that the footage was unauthenticated and was falsely presented as a recent October 2026 confrontation, creating rumours and confusion about the situation along the LAC. It also warned that old videos are often circulated as recent incidents and urged citizens to avoid sharing unverified footage and rely on official sources for updates.
To sum up, none of these viral videos shows the India–China border face-offs in October 2026.

Manisha Bhanwala created history in Astana, Kazakhstan, on Friday as she became the first-ever Indian woman to win a gold medal at the Wrestling World Championships.
The 29-year-old Manisha came from behind to defeat USA’s Abigail Nette 8-6 in a thrilling 59kg final.
Manisha overcame her disappointing performance in the 57kg weight class at the Asian Games in Japan to give a dominating performance in the non-Olympic category.
Manisha began her campaign with a ‘Victory By Fall’ over Canada’s Laurence Beauregard in the round of 16. In the quarterfinals, the Indian took down Mongolia’s Bolortuya Khurelkhuu with a 6-0 scoreline. In the semifinals, the wrestler from Haryana defeated local favourite Altyn Shagayeva via technical superiority.
In the final, Manisha suffered an early setback as Nette quickly executed a four-point move. The Indian challenged that call only to lose and give another point to the American. A caution against Manisha extended Nette’s advantage to 6-0. But Manisha got a stepout before the break to get one point on board.
In the second period, Manisha started her comeback with a takedown against Nette. The 28-year-old American challenged arguing that the referee had whistled to stop the bout. The unsuccessful challenge awarded one more point to Manisha and position in par terre.
From 6-4, Manisha managed to turn Nette using a gut-wrench for two points. She even tried holding the American for the fall but could not execute it.
At 6-6, Nette was still ahead based on the criterion of a bigger scoring move and tried to run down the clock. However, Manisha scored another takedown and held on to her 8-6 lead to create history.
Manisha is only the second Indian wrestler after Sushil Kumar (66kg, 2010 Moscow) to win the gold medal at the prestigious tournament.
At the ongoing edition, Manisha is the fourth Indian medallist in women’s wrestling after Neelam Sirohi (silver, 50kg), Kajal Dhochak (silver, 76kg) and Tanu Sharma (bronze, 72kg).
In men’s freestyle, Vicky (97kg) was beaten 10-0 by Iranian superstar Hassan Yazdani in the repechage round.
Three others, Nikhil (61kg), Pushpender Dalal (86kg) and Jaspooran Singh (125kg), moved into repechage rounds.

New Delhi/Bengaluru: India on Friday showcased a system that allows companies and researchers to train artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms on sensitive data held by hospitals, banks and government agencies without the information leaving those institutions or being exposed to them. The Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training framework was launched by the ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY) and developed primarily by iSPIRT, a volunteer-led technology think-tank that has contributed to the development of India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and India Stack, a set of digital public infrastructure systems that enable services such as digital identity (Aadhaar), payments and the secure sharing of data (DigiLocker). Depa’s central idea is to bring AI models to the data, rather than move the data to researchers, a senior government official said at the framework’s unveiling in Bengaluru on Friday. To be sure, Depa itself is not new. In 2020, NITI Aayog, the government's top policy think-tank, introduced it as a framework that allows citizens to securely share their data with their consent. The new framework, developed by iSPIRT, extends this approach to training AI models on sensitive data belonging to millions of people without requiring the data to leave the institutions that hold it. Consultations on Depa for AI will begin in the coming weeks, before it is brought under a legal framework, a process which could take years, the stakeholders confirmed. Depa comes as India prepares to implement its first data privacy law, the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, in the coming months. Meanwhile, several lawsuits involving AI platforms and their use of proprietary data remain sub judice. The official cited earlier called the approach “a democratic third way” between the US, where companies buy data in commercial deals—and China, where the state pools it. Industry stakeholders called the framework potentially crucial for effective training of domain-specific AI models, applications and products. “While the framework could be potentially vital, the real use cases could be for startups like Sarvam and others seeking to build domain-specific AI for healthcare, education, critical communications and others. But, the crucial aspect would be to build a trust framework before that, and also validating the quality of vast tranches of sensitive data—both of which are difficult to establish,” said Jibu Elias, India lead for responsible computing at global open-source internet body, Mozilla Foundation. Under Depa, data remains with its owner, while a “sealed room”, which is a secure computing environment, runs only what an authorised digital contract permits. No one can access the data inside, not even the company operating the system, according to the launch presentation. A developer ssends in an AI model and receives only the trained model or, in cases such as a loan application, the decision itself. On Friday, early pilots of the framework were demonstrated. In one such trial, a bank that has been testing the approach since March 2026 identified which customers of a fintech qualified for its credit cards before seeking anyone's consent, and then requested permission only from those who had a real offer. The pilot handled more than 2 million requests in two weeks. In another pilot, hospitals and a health-tech startup are training a tumour-detection model on MRI scans the startup never sees. Ajay K Sood, principal scientific adviser to the government, Meity secretary S. Krishnan, iSpirt co-founder Sharad Sharma, and representatives from HDFC Bank, Sarvam and Emergent AI, among others, attended the event. The framework, the stakeholders said, could be key as hospitals and banks rarely share data. They make little money from it and risk fines of up to ₹250 crore under India’s data protection law, if it leaks. India's existing consent-based data-sharing framework “solves the individual consent problem brilliantly, but it is not able to solve the collective problem,” a banking executive said, citing fraud that spans multiple banks as an example. For now, Depa’s day-to-day management is expected to be handled by Samyog, a new industry group “powered by iSpirt.” Its website says it will register participants, provide standard contracts, and resolve disputes. Its board includes Sharma, and several leaders helped write the handbook. The site does not say Samyog is government-appointed. Executives at iSpirt said that data owners, like hospitals and banks, would be paid each time their data is used. But, the handbook only says that payment methods “will be explored.” It also does not specify who would be liable if data were to leak from a sealed room. The framework is not legally binding, and officials did not say if or when it might be. The path forward includes pilots in finance and healthcare and regulatory sandboxes where companies test models under supervision. Binding rules are more likely to come from sectoral regulators than through a new law, as was the case with India's account aggregator system, which took five years to move from RBI rule-making to launch. Much also depends on the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, whose main rules take effect in May 2027. India also continues to explore a dedicated AI legislation, while also debating if AI platforms need a completely new definition of how they are protected under law, Mint reported Wednesday. He's been a tinkerer of machines and PCs since childhood, a habit he was thrilled to convert into his profession. This has led him to fascinating experiences of technologies around the world, which is what keeps him hooked to his job.

Shouvik likes to believe that he is one of the few technology journalists in India who can also code. He has also been writing about the rise of AI well before it became a household name, and has met some of the most fascinating people over the years through his work.

Population census begins January 25, barring poll-bound states and snow-covered regions
The population census will be conducted from January 25 to February 28, 2027.
Census 2027 is set to be held across most of India from January 25 to February 28, 2027, the Census Commissioner announced on Friday. The population enumeration will however not include poll-bound states and snow-bound regions. The reference date for the census shall be 00:00 hours of March 1, 2027, the official notification read.
The census will not cover Manipur, Goa, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Uttarakhand as assembly elections are due in these states and union territories early next year.
Ladakh and the snow-bound non-synchronous areas of Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir will also not be surveyed during this period.
A notification issued by Mritunjay Kumar Narayan, Registrar General of India (RGI) and Census Commissioner, stated that the "revisional round" of population census will be conducted from March 1, 2027, to March 5, 2027.
Before the door-to-door census begins on January 25, citizens will be given the option to self-enumerate between January 10, 2027, and January 24, 2027.
The census, the eighth since Independence, is being conducted in two phases: house listing and housing census, and population enumeration.
The decennial exercise, scheduled for 2021, was postponed due to the Covid-19 outbreak. The Union Cabinet approved ₹11,718 crore for conducting the census, which will be the biggest headcount exercise.
The Centre has deferred house-listing operations for Census 2027 in Manipur, a notification issued by the RGI said last month.
India's last census was conducted in 2011 with a headcount of 1.21 billion people, including 62.32 crore males and 58.75 crore females. The country had 24.95 crore households at that time.

On Friday, the CEO of the company behind the doomed Odyssey cruise ship apologized to residents, many of whom are now stranded in Cambodia. Hours later, that apology was gone.
Villa Vie Residences CEO and founding partner Kathy Villalba sent Odyssey residents a message on Circle, the ship’s internal messaging platform, saying she was sorry for the "pain, the loss, and the uncertainty" they face after the voyage came to an abrupt halt this week.
Villa Vie had promised residents of its 509-cabin ship a chance to live permanently at sea and circumnavigate the world every three-and-a-half years. On Tuesday morning, residents were given only a few hours' notice to disembark.
Business Insider reviewed screenshots of the memo, which was deleted hours after it was posted. Three Villa Vie residents with access to Circle confirmed the memo's contents and that it was no longer visible.
In it, Villalba said the media attention had become "overwhelming" and that she had been advised to refrain from making further public comments.
Villalba and Villa Vie did not respond to requests for comment on the memo or why it was deleted.
Read more of our reporting on the Villa Vie Odyssey
In the apology note, Villalba said the company was still in talks with potential investors and expressed hope that a resident-led initiative to buy the ship would succeed.

Dear Residents, I owe all of you a message, and I am sorry if it has taken me this long to find the words. I think part of me has been in denial that this could really be happening. Even now, we continue to speak with potential investors, holding on to whatever hope remains because I simply cannot imagine letting this dream go. The media attention has become overwhelming, to the point that reporters are now contacting our families, including people who have nothing to do with the company. On the advice of counsel, I have been asked to refrain from making further public comments, particularly as even conversations within Circle are no longer private. But I couldn't remain silent without telling you how deeply sorry I am for the pain, the loss, and the uncertainty so many of you are facing. I know so many of you are hurting, scared, and angry, and I wish more than anything that I could take that pain away. For nearly two years, this wasn't just a business to me. It was my entire life. I poured my heart, my soul, and everything I had into it The ship was my baby, but it was your home, and in so many ways, all of you became my family. I care for this community as though it were my own children, through the good days and the difficult ones. My team used to call me the "Resident Wikipedia," because I knew all of you by name and by story. That meant so much to me, because getting to know each of you individually was the best part of all of this. The thought of losing it leaves a hole in my heart that I cannot begin to describe. Thank you for believing in two ordinary people with an extraordinary dream. Together, we created something truly special. We traveled the world, built friendships, shared laughter and tears, and experienced a way of life that so few people ever get to know. I still don't want this to be the end. I sincerely hope the resident initiative succeeds, and we stand ready to assist wherever we reasonably can to help preserve the lifestyle you have all grown to love. Please know that we love and care about each and every one of you. Through the good and the bad, even through the disagreements and disappointments, that has never changed. Above all, I hope everyone is safe, supported, and looking after one another during this incredibly difficult time. From the bottom of my heart, thank you for being part of this dream. With love, Kathy <3

Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he also commented on AI’s impact on math, Altman said:
Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.
“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.
But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”
Whether Altman meant your gaming PC or developers working with something like the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box or the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, the outcome is the same. Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years. And the billions they’re willing to lay out for chips is why the laptops, phones, and other tech you use are getting more expensive right now.

“If the public is drifting away from government hospitals and being pushed into the clutches of the corporate healthcare system, it is undeniably because politicians and governments lack genuine sincerity,” said 115 citizens and activists in an open letter to Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy and Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha.
The letter accused successive governments of failing to strengthen public healthcare, alleging that the lack of basic amenities in government hospitals is driving patients towards private healthcare.
Gaps in basic facilities
The letter highlights concerns over drinking water facilities, toilets, sanitation and the maintenance of infrastructure at major government hospitals in Hyderabad, including Osmania General Hospital, Gandhi Hospital, Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS), Niloufer Hospital and Petlaburj Maternity Hospital.
The signatories — comprising social activists, academics, writers, journalists, teachers and other citizens — questioned whether the government’s promises to improve public healthcare translated into better conditions for patients.
Is the problem a lack of medical expertise or basic facilities?
The signatories argued that the challenges confronting government hospitals cannot be viewed solely through the lens of shortages of doctors and other medical personnel. The signatories acknowledged that healthcare workers were already working under considerable pressure, but said the absence of basic amenities was adding to the difficulties faced by patients.
“Government hospitals have experienced doctors, medical staff and research capabilities, but inadequate facilities are undermining the healthcare experience,” they added.
Referring to Osmania, Gandhi, NIMS, Niloufer and Petlaburj hospitals, the signatories questioned why patients should have to endure difficult conditions to access treatment when the institutions were expected to provide essential public healthcare services.
When basic amenities become a question of dignity
They have identified clean drinking water, functional toilets and proper sanitation as among the most pressing requirements in public hospitals. Questioning the government’s responsibility for maintaining these facilities, the signatories asked whether patients should be held responsible for unhygienic conditions and unpleasant odours in hospital toilets, arguing that the responsibility for maintenance rested with the authorities.
They said patients who could afford private healthcare might choose to seek treatment elsewhere, but those unable to bear the additional expense were left with fewer options.
Should hospital maintenance be handed over to private entities?
The signatories also cautioned the government against transferring responsibility for maintaining basic hospital amenities to corporate entities under the banner of public participation as doing so would impose an additional financial burden on patients. They called for the government to take responsibility for improving existing infrastructure and ensuring that essential facilities were properly maintained.
They further questioned the emphasis placed on changing photographs on walls and ambulances after a government assumes office, arguing that the same attention should be directed towards providing basic amenities in hospitals.
A call for a Right to Health law
Beyond immediate improvements to hospital infrastructure, the signatories urged the Telangana government to introduce a strong Right to Health law through consultations with people’s organisations and public. They called for a broader effort to strengthen the public health and medical system so that ordinary citizens would not be compelled to abandon government hospitals because of inadequate facilities.

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

Mushroom murderer fails to overturn convictions in Australian court challenge
- Published
Australia's mushroom killer has failed to overturn her murder convictions on appeal, with the court also ruling that she never be released from prison.
Erin Patterson, 52, was found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023. Her life sentence included a non-parole period of 33 years.
In Victoria's Court of Appeal on Friday, three judges threw out her appeal against her convictions and agreed with the prosecution that her sentence was inadequate, as it allowed for the possibility of freedom.
Patterson's crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms," they said.
"We have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period," Justice Stephen McLeish told the court, on the panel's behalf.
After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms.
Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.
He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.
Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.
Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face.
She promptly launched an appeal against her convictions, with her legal team in August arguing seven grounds for her appeal.
They claimed a hotel booking mishap - which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media - was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial.
They also argued certain pieces of evidence shown to the jury were irrelevant and prejudicial - such as cell tower data suggesting Patterson visited areas where death cap mushrooms might be found and Facebook posts where she complained about her in-laws.
Meanwhile, the judge wrongly blocked other evidence that would have demonstrated the mother-of-two's long-time hobby of mushroom foraging, they said.
The defence team also asserted that the prosecution's five-day cross-examination of Patterson was "unfair and oppressive", and that the Crown was inconsistent in its arguments about a motive.
On Friday, the appeal judges dismissed all seven grounds.
Patterson has 28 days to decide if she will seek to convince the High Court of Australia to hear another appeal over the case.

Hong Kong Leader Apologizes for Deadly Fire and Blames Construction Industry
John Lee, the city’s chief executive, said his housing secretary would step down, but he vehemently defended the government.
Hong Kong’s leader apologized on Thursday for a deadly fire last year and said his housing secretary had resigned, in an effort to offer accountability for a disaster that drew outrage and created a political challenge for his Beijing-backed government.
“The fire brought sadness and misery to us,” said John Lee, Hong Kong’s chief executive, at a news conference. Flanked by seven other officials, Mr. Lee bowed to the assembled media and added, “I apologize.”
The gesture was notable coming from a government that was quick to crack down on expression in the weeks after the deadly fire, which killed 168 people at the Wang Fuk Court housing complex in northern Hong Kong last November. But Mr. Lee also vehemently defended the government in a testy question-and-answer session on Thursday as he was asked, several times, about his own accountability.
The resignation of the housing secretary, Winnie Ho, was the first by a senior official following months of questions over the culpability of Hong Kong’s leaders. Mr. Lee stopped short of blaming her directly, adding that “the fire did not involve any personal wrongdoing by the secretary,” but said that she should “bear political responsibility.”
He primarily blamed collusion and corruption in the construction industry for the fire, saying that construction insiders with connections to organized crime groups known as triads had been responsible for shoddy repair work that led up to it. Mr. Lee said the government would hold criminally accountable anyone who was found guilty of rigging a construction bid.
The seven buildings that burned in the blaze had been undergoing government-mandated repairs and were shrouded in netting that was later found to be substandard. The authorities said the netting and polystyrene foam that was used to protect windows was responsible for the rapid spread of the fire, which burned with such intensity that it took thousands of firefighters two days to put out the blaze.

The Delhi Police had posted a video on their X handle on October 25, which urged citizens to not burn crackers this Diwali. Along with a meme video, the post was captioned: “This festive season, let tails wag, not tuck. Say NO to crackers, YES to a greener Diwali.”
Soon after the post was made, social media users had predicted that it would be removed soon. Incidentally, just within a few hours of the post being made, the Delhi Police removed it from X.
While Delhi Police did not issue any clarification as to why the post was taken down, several X users wondered whether the reason behind the post being taken down was perhaps the purported pressure from the BJP-led central government.
Alt News co-founder Mohammad Zubair had also remarked on Delhi Police’s post, before it was taken down, with the caption: “This tweet will soon be deleted due to political pressure.”
Another X user, Jeevansh Arya, shared a screen grab of the Delhi Police’s post and questioned whether it would be deleted.

The official handle of Indian Youth Congress also questioned the logic behind the retreat of the Delhi Police.
Administrative Indecision in The Past
This is, however, not the first time that the Delhi administration retracted its position during Diwali regarding firecrackers. Over the past two years, Delhi’s authorities and the courts have attempted to take a strong stance against firecrackers due to the city’s severe air pollution, but they have often backtracked on their decisions.
Ahead of Diwali 2024, the Delhi government imposed a complete ban on the manufacture, sale, storage and bursting of all firecrackers until January 1, 2025. The Supreme Court later criticised the poor enforcement of the ban and suggested that the government consider making it permanent. In December 2024, the Delhi government told the court that it had imposed a year-round ban on firecrackers.
However, the position changed soon. In April 2025, the Supreme Court refused to relax the ban, but in October it allowed green crackers to be sold and used in Delhi-NCR for a limited period during Diwali. The court said these crackers had to meet standards set by the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), and allowed their use only during specified hours. The Delhi government and the Centre supported the relaxation.
In effect, the authorities moved from a complete ban on firecrackers to allowing a limited category of green crackers, despite earlier court observations that even green crackers could not be considered a comprehensive solution to Delhi’s pollution problem.
Delhi Pays The Price
Delhi’s air quality worsened sharply during Diwali 2025, with the city’s AQI (Air Quality Index) reaching almost 500, falling under the hazardous category. Firecracker bursting was followed by a dramatic rise in PM2.5 and PM10 levels.
According to a Times of India report, between 9 pm and 10 pm on Diwali 2025, the PM 2.5 concentration of Delhi’s Nehru Nagar region saw a spike from 679 micrograms per cubic metre to 1,763µg/m³. The report also mentioned that the peak PM2.5 concentration was more than 29 times the national daily limit of 60 µg/m³ and around 118 times the World Health Organization’s recommended daily guideline.
Pollution Concerns Framed as Anti-Hindu
Following Diwali last year, Alt News had written about the Right-wing supporters in the country interpreting complaints on the detrimental environmental effects of bursting firecrackers as an “attack against Hindutva” itself.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee had posted a video on his X page asking his audience to desist from burning firecrackers. Right-wing social media users immediately began sharing images of firecrackers that they had apparently hoarded. While some questioned Rathee’s stake in it, others indulged in whataboutery and asked whether he had shown environmental concerns on Bakrid. Certain users went to the extent of mockingly comparing the extreme pollution levels in India to the genocide in Gaza.
Similarly, when BJP leader Subramaniam Swamy wrote on X, “Exploding fire crackers after 10 pm today is a criminal offence. Police should crackdown on them”, Right-wing influencer Chandan Sharma (Hindutva Knight/@HPhobiaWatch) targeted Swamy’s daughter, The Hindu’s Diplomatic Editor, Suhasini Haidar, using obscene language for being married to a Muslim man.
Several Right-wing accounts, such as @NamitaBalyan, @AchAnkurArya, and @JaipurDialogues, posted photos showing the firecrackers and the knight sky shrouded in smog, ultimately dismissing grave environmental concerns under the garb of protecting Hindu festivals.

From her own Barbie doll to bench - how Ellie Kildunne slipped from Red Roses' XV
- Published
She's the poster girl. She's the former World Player of the Year. She came second at BBC Sports Personality of the Year. She lit up the 2025 Rugby World Cup. She's even got her own Barbie doll.
So why didn't Ellie Kildunne start for England against the USA on Friday night?
First of all she is human, let's not forget that.
We're all allowed ups and downs. It's just that Kildunne's dip comes with the large spotlight of her being the Red Roses' household name.
None of her team-mates come close to her popularity with fans both in and outside rugby union with her 239,000 Instagram followers. Her face and name are used for clicks by all the media, present company included.
However, if you follow the sport and watch her play, no-one is undroppable.
England suffered their first loss in four years to end their 41-Test unbeaten streak in Toronto against Canada. In that fixture and their previous match with the same opposition in Exeter, Kildunne, 27, was a target for the opposition. She was never given space, defenders stepped up, her arms were pulled and balls were spilt.
When England head coach John Mitchell benched her after England's loss in Toronto he was clear that "it isn't disputed that she adds huge value".
However, he went on to add: "She's just going through a difficult period at the moment, and it's important for us to help her through that.
"She wants to become consistent as well, and she'll get back. It's also important to create competition and to recognise that you have to become more consistent, especially when you're competing in the Red Roses.
"So it's really important to reinforce the behaviours that we think are necessary to our game, and that goes for everyone."
The key word we can take from that is "consistent" - mainly because Mitchell said it twice.
Kildunne remains one of the world's most phenomenal players when it comes to gainline success and metres gained.
Much of this is due to poor opposition defence, but her statistics show a decline over the past three seasons at international level.
It seems almost harsh to highlight as these are numbers other players could only dream of but she's also gone from beating an average of six defenders a game in 2024, to 4.2 in 2026.
Kildunne has also conceded more penalties in 2026 than either of the previous two years. Some of these statistics, althought not all, are mirrored in her PWR performances last season.
While Canada are not alone, it does appear they are one of the best teams at dealing with Kildunne's threats.
In their drawn match in Exeter, Kildunne made 17 carries for 47 metres, an average of 2.8m, which is well below her usual standards. In Toronto she had the ball turned over twice - that was her joint-most in any England game.
Emma Sing now appears to have some purchase on the England 15 shirt and it is well deserved. She is a different full-back to Kildunne, which is a bonus for the Red Roses.
Sing has three PWR titles with her club side Gloucester-Hartpury and has been one of their most reliable players throughout that period. She has got a monster boot round the park and off the tee and, while Sing might not score the same worldies we have seen from Kildunne, her highlights reel is none too shabby.
On Sing's starting selection in Ottawa, Mitchell was happy to explain the players' differences: "They play quite differently. So we're very fortunate to have two very good full-backs. But you know, Emma's been sitting in the in the wings in this particular phase of our campaign.
"She was intermittent through injury for a long period of time. So she's in a really good physical place, and she's worked really, really hard. So I think it's time to give her an opportunity."
