It is a bit crass, but if you only follow men's rugby, Kildunne is a bit more Marcus Smith, while Sing is a bit more Freddie Steward - they are just different players.
Add to that, Sing was brought up on a Devon sheep farm and is not a huge fan of the media spotlight. That is not to say that Kildunne has coveted it, but she is far more comfortable in the media space.
You also must tip your hat to Kildunne and how she has managed herself with her new-found fame. After England beat New Zealand at Allianz Stadium in September, she spent an hour signing autographs and doing selfies to an unrelenting, screaming chorus of "Ellie, Ellie, Ellie".
Managing your own needs as an athlete and the increasing demands of fans is not an easy circle to square.
So where does Kildunne go from here? That is actually the most exciting bit.
No-one with a spiral bomb like she produced in the 2025 Rugby World Cup final is going to fade into the shadows. She is an incredible athlete and rugby player, so the expectation is that, much like Doctor Who, she will just regenerate.
Kildunne 2.0 could end up spending more time on the wing for England initially, but you can only see her fighting for a shirt and getting better.

Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasrin, who is currently living in Kolkata, on October 20, Tuesday, wrote on Facebook that although Leftists in West Bengal organise bookstalls during Durga Puja, such stalls are absent during other ‘religious’ festivals such as Christmas and Eid. She questioned why Leftists choose not to sell books promoting ‘atheism’ during other religious festivals, but instead promote them only during a Hindu festival.
In her post, she wrote (translated from Bengali), “Someone asked, “Have you ever seen Leftists selling books on atheism to Muslims near an Eidgah on Eid? Have you ever seen them selling books by Richard Dawkins or Christopher Hitchens to people attending Christmas prayers on Christmas Day? Then, quite naturally, the question arises: why do they want to sell books on atheism specifically at Hindu Durga Puja pandals?” What answer do the Leftists of Kolkata have to this question?”
This post has garnered over 7,000 likes and 1,300 reshares, and garnered significant traction, although she had disabled the comment section of the Facebook post.
Nasrin, who has been in exile since leaving Bangladesh in 1994 amid death threats and protests over her writings critical of the ‘dogmas’ of Islam, was forced to leave Kolkata in 2007 following violent protests against her autobiography ‘Dwikhandito’ and pressure on the then CPI(M)-led Left Front government.
She remained unable to return to West Bengal for nearly 19 years, with successive CPI(M) and Trinamool Congress (TMC) governments in power. However, in July 2026, following the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) coming to power in the state, Nasrin returned to Kolkata and was publicly welcomed and celebrated by sections of the Right-wing BJP-RSS ecosystem.
Against this backdrop, her recent Facebook post questioned what she portrayed as the Left’s selective promotion of atheism. Moreover, her statement comes on the heels of state authorities demolishing and damaging certain bookstalls set up by Left parties near Jadavpur’s 8b bus stand on October 17.
Fact Check
Alt News found several social media posts and news reports that refute Nasrin’s claim that the bookstalls are exclusively set up during Durga Puja.
The Students’ Federation of India (SFI) and the Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI) have been organising a bookstall near Park Street, where Christmas is celebrated in Kolkata, for at least 10 years. Prominent Left leader Biman Bose has also visited the stall. The bookstall has been featured on the social media handles of SFI, DYFI, CPI(M) and other affliated organisations, and has also been covered by the media. The Telegraph reported the setting up of the bookstall at Park Street for the first time in 2016, Alt News also founds images of stalls from 2017, 2022, 2024.

Similarly, the SFI-DYFI local committee in the Khidderpore area of Kolkata organised a bookstall during Eid this year. Khidderpore has historically been home to a significant Muslim population. The bookstall was organised for two days and was featured on the Facebook page of the CPI(M) Kolkata Port Assembly Committee.

Further, Nasrin claimed that the Leftist bookstalls only sell books promoting atheism. However, the images on social media, posted by people who bought books from hundreds of these stalls, clearly show a vast array of books from across genres being sold in these stalls.
An Alt News correspondent visited the CPI(M) bookstall set up near Jadavpur 8B bus stand and encountered a diverse section of books, ranging from Bengali classics, poetry, history among others. Books on Ramkrishna and Vivekananda were also available at the stall.
CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh made a video, interviewing a woman who visited the stall and described herself as a devotee of spiritual leader Lalon Fakir. In the video, she shared her book haul which comprised books on Lalon Fakir, and other Hindu spiritual leaders like Nityananda Mahaprabhu, and even a cook book.
CPI(M) leader Sudip Sengupta, who is in charge of the 8B bookstall regularly posted pictures of the stall on his Facebook page. In one such image, physician Dr. Arjun Dasgupta was seen holding a book on Swami Vivekananda, along with a book on the Second World War.
According to Dasgupta, apart from Leftist books, the stall also contains books such as Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s Anandamath. “I was looking at some old pictures my family took at the Jadavpur 8B stall, and I could see Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s books behind me. His books include ‘Anandamath’, which has the song ‘Vande Mataram’. So it is simply not true that these stalls only sell books promoting atheism. These stalls are part of Bengal’s culture, and anyone who loves books should stand against efforts to shut them down,” said Dasgupta.
“We Bengalis feel that a book is a book, whether it is sold at an ISKCON stall or a CPI(M) stall. We love books and naturally gather around any stall that sells them. When we were children, these stalls introduced many of us to great books from around the world. I vividly remember my father buying me a copy of ‘Ispat’, the Bengali translation of Nikolai Ostrovsky’s ‘How the Steel Was Tempered’. I think thousands of people like me have similar memories,” he added.
Similarly, the Rashbehari-1 area committee of the CPI(M) set up a book stall near the Kalighat temple during Durga Puja. Images of the stall show stacks of books ranging from Bengali children’s classics such as Thakurmar Jhuli to literary works including ‘Ichhamati’ by Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay, ‘Kapalkundala’ by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, ‘Grihadaha’ and ‘Devdas’ by Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay, among others. Books on Maa Sarada, and books written by Rabindranath Tagore were also visible at the stall.
Thus, the findings above show that Nasrin’s claim that Leftists organise bookstalls only during Hindu festivals such as Durga Puja is false, as there is documented evidence of Left organisations organising bookstalls during both Eid and Christmas. Her claim that books exclusively on atheism are sold at the stalls is also false, as there is documented evidence of books of various genres being sold across Left bookstalls.

The Indian Patent Office has rejected a patent application filed by the U.S.-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development (TB Alliance) for the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL), a six-month, all-oral treatment regimen for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
The Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust and Third World Network (TWN) welcomed the development.
Recommended by the WHO for eligible people, BPaL offers a shorter course of treatment than older, longer regimens, reducing the burden of treatment on patients and their families.
“Only those who have been treated for TB know what it feels like to go through more than a year of antibiotics with painful injections. Access to a shorter, oral and effective treatment can mean returning to work, caring for their families and rebuilding their lives”, explained Loon Gangte of DNP+.
The decision follows two pre-grant oppositions filed in 2020—one by Eldred Tellis (Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust) and Ganesh Acharya, with support from the Lawyers’ Collective and Médécins Sans Frontières Access Campaign, and the other by the Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), with support from TWN.
The opponents challenged the patent application on the grounds that the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, as well as its use in a shorter treatment regimen, had already been disclosed in scientific research and clinical trials dating back to 2015. They argued that combining these known medicines did not constitute an inventive step warranting a new patent monopoly.
The Opposition invoked key safeguards under India’s Patents Act, including Section 3(d), which restricts patents on new uses of known substances, Section 3(e), which excludes mere admixtures, and Section 3(i), which excludes methods of medical treatment. The opponents further argued that the application failed to sufficiently disclose the claimed invention. All four grounds were upheld by the Indian Patent Office.
India has the world’s largest tuberculosis burden. According to WHO estimates, approximately 2.71 million people developed TB in the country in 2024, accounting for a quarter of global cases, with an incidence rate of 187 per 1,00,000 people. Civil society groups are also demanding that the TB Alliance stop the pursuit of proprietary rights over BPaL in other countries.
“Having received public and philanthropic support to develop pretomanid, one of BPaL’s components, they should not be applying for a patent, let alone over frivolous secondary patents on its combination with the other two known medicines,” said Mr. Tellis.
In light of the weak claims by the TB Alliance, Prathibha Sivasubramanian, senior researcher at TWN, endorsed the call for the waiving of patents. “The Indian Patent Office’s decision should serve as a clear signal to the TB Alliance to voluntarily surrender granted patents and to withdraw all corresponding pending applications in other jurisdictions. TB Alliance should also publish its pretomanid licence agreements,” she said.
Patents on the BPaL combination have been granted in 11 countries and are set to expire in 2036: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Bulgaria, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, South Africa, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

Sporadic gunfire sends Ethiopians fleeing into Kenya as trucks remain stuck at border
Gunfire was heard from the Ethiopian border town of Moyale as civilians continue to flee into Kenya to escape violence from a regional dispute
MOYALE, Kenya -- Sporadic gunfire could be heard coming from the Ethiopian border town of Moyale on Friday as Ethiopian civilians continued fleeing into Kenya to escape violence stemming from a regional dispute.
Cargo trucks were stranded on both sides of the border as tensions persisted between leaders of the Oromia and Somali regional states of Ethiopia.
An Associated Press reporter in Moyale, Kenya, recorded gunfire coming from the Ethiopian side of the border and reported hearing sporadic gunfire daily since Oct. 22.
Up to an estimated 50,000 people have crossed into Kenya, the U.N. refugee agency said Wednesday, citing local authorities, up from 36,000 reported Tuesday. Registration and verification were continuing, the agency said.
Benedict Munywoki, deputy county commissioner for Moyale Sub-County, said Thursday that some of those fleeing Ethiopia were staying in town rather than in camps, making an accurate count difficult.
“The initial number of people who are in camps and also integrated into the community is still growing day by day,” he said.
The U.N. refugee agency, the International Organization for Migration and the Kenya Red Cross were working to provide medical care, food and shelter.
At a camp established by the Kenya Red Cross, people cooked food in large pots over wood fires Thursday while health workers weighed children and measured their upper arms to check for malnutrition.
Seifu Negash, an Ethiopian doctor who fled into Kenya, was volunteering with the Kenya Red Cross to treat fellow refugees.
“The war, it started suddenly then we were displaced from that area,” Seifu said, describing difficulties both in Ethiopia and after crossing the border.
Residents have been opening their homes to people fleeing the violence.
“When they arrive we welcome them and give them a place to stay and sleep,” Moyale resident Galgallo Jarso said Monday. “We are giving them food and when they fall sick we take them to hospital.”
Local leaders in Kenya’s Marsabit County have appealed for support, warning that the arrivals could overwhelm communities already struggling with food and water shortages.
The conflict monitoring organization ACLED traced the latest fighting to an Oct. 18 confrontation over the opening of a Somali regional administration office and the raising of its flag in a disputed part of Ethiopian Moyale.
The Ethiopian town is divided between the Oromia and Somali regional administrations. The fighting is rooted in a longstanding boundary dispute between the Borana, who are Oromo, and the Garre, who are Somali, according to ACLED’s senior East Africa analyst, Jalale Getachew Birru.
A 13-year-old Oromo girl was killed in the initial confrontation, although accounts differ over the circumstances, the analyst said. Fighting subsequently spread to other communities, involving regional police and local militias.
ACLED said fighting appeared to have subsided Wednesday, although tensions remained high.
The violence has also raised security concerns in Kenya. Kenyan police reported last week that a woman was wounded in the neck by a bullet in Moyale. Police did not identify where the shot came from.
The border dispute comes as Ethiopia faces separate conflicts elsewhere. In northern Tigray, rebels have vowed to keep fighting after losing control of the regional capital, Mekelle, earlier this month.
Elsewhere in Oromia, the Ethiopian Orthodox Church said two attacks killed at least 60 Orthodox Christians on Oct. 20 and 24. Regional authorities blamed the Oromo Liberation Army, whose leader has previously denied targeting civilians.
Those attacks occurred in different districts from the Moyale fighting.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front and the Oromo Liberation Army are among seven groups that formed the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival in September, seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government from power.
___
Kazziha reported from Nairobi, Kenya. Nicholas Komu contributed to this report from Nairobi.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
- Published
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.
Anti-corruption purges continue
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.
Who are the key figures purged?
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violating [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."
Xi's plans for the future
Analysts believe one reason for the increased empahsis on discipline – which many interpret as loyalty – is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder Communist China.
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."

A stroke is an urgent situation where either the flow of blood to the brain is cut off, or there is a rupture of the blood vessels in the brain. Oxygen and glucose are the two elements essential for brain activity. Interruption of their supply results in impairment of brain activity and eventual damage of brain tissues -- and this damage occurs in minutes. The first few hours of a stroke, therefore, determine how damaged the brain can become.
Types of strokes
Strokes can be categorised into ischemic strokes and haemorrhagic strokes. In ischemic strokes, the stroke occurs due to the blocking of an artery by a blood clot. In haemorrhagic strokes, there is a rupture of the blood vessel, which leads to blood in the brain tissue. Regardless of the type of stroke, the result is damage to the brain tissue, which can result in vital body functions including speaking, movement, vision, memory and coordination becoming impaired.
An ischemic stroke is accompanied by oxygen starvation of the affected brain tissue. Due to insufficient energy resources, brain cells cannot function normally. The chemical composition of the brain cells, therefore, changes, which results in the accumulation of toxic substances that harm brain cells and other structures. With continued oxygen starvation, cells continue to deteriorate. The damage, however, does not occur uniformly. In the central area of the brain (core) where oxygen starvation is critical, damage can occur rapidly and irreversibly. Around this area, there is a zone called the ischemic penumbra. Here, even if blood flow is low, brain cells can survive for a certain period of time. They can be saved if blood flow is restored promptly.
The effect of bleeding in a haemorrhagic stroke is brought about by the leaking of blood into the brain when there is a rupture of a blood vessel. This may lead to injury of brain cells, and also interfere with proper blood and cerebral spinal fluid flow in the brain.
The first few hours
There are only so many minutes that the brain can withstand interrupted blood flow. Brain cells (neurons) begins to undergo irreversible damage within 3 to 5 minutes of interrupted blood flow. With each minute that goes by, 1.9 million neurons, i.e. 32 neurons per second, die due to lack of oxygenation, which is why we emphasise that ‘time is brain’. The first few hours are critical since at this point, one needs to assess what kind of stroke it is and start appropriate treatment.
In some cases of ischemic stroke, intravenous thrombolysis, the administration of drugs that dissolve the clot within the blood vessels, might be given in the first 4.5 hours after symptoms develop. In some patients with large vessel blockage, there might be indications for mechanical thrombectomy. In simple terms, a mechanical thrombectomy involves the removal of the clot using special equipment, and it might be done up to 24 hours after the patient was last seen without symptoms. In cases of haemorrhagic strokes, others strategies must be employed: this includes blood pressure control, correction of the consequences of taking blood thinners, management of intracranial pressure, and surgical procedures, where necessary.
Not all patients automatically qualify for all interventions. There are other issues that have to be taken into account, including the patient’s medical status, imaging studies, timing of stroke symptoms, and dangers involved in the therapy. Even some of those who come after these time windows, can still be eligible for certain treatment procedures after imaging is done.
How brain function is affected
The effects of a stroke vary, depending on the site and degree of damage within the brain. Movement centres can be damaged leading to weakness or paralysis that usually affects one side of the body. Speech centres could be damaged causing speech problems and comprehension difficulties or trouble reading and writing. A stroke involving the visual pathways leads to a sudden loss of vision or partial visual fields. If the cerebellum or the brainstem is involved, there could be a problem with dizziness, poor coordination, problems swallowing, double vision or loss of balance. There could also be memory, attention and decision-making problems and problems with emotional regulation.
It is important to know and understand these symptoms since sometimes a stroke occurs without the characteristic facial drooping or arm weakness of the disease.
Recognising warning signs
The BE FAST method is an effective means of identifying the symptoms of a stroke:
- B – Balance: Sudden loss of balance, dizziness or difficulty walking
- E – Eyes: Sudden blurred vision, double vision or loss of vision
- F – Face: One side of the face is drooping or numb
- A – Arms: One arm is weak or dropping down
- S – Speech: Slurred speech
- T – Time: Call for help immediately
Sudden changes in vision, lack of balance, confusion or even a severe headache without apparent reason might be symptoms of a stroke as well. Disappearing symptoms within a minute or two shouldn’t be considered harmless and require immediate medical examination.
After the golden hour
The ‘golden hour’ is significant to preserve as much of brain function as possible and to ensure best possible outcomes, but this does not mean medical professionals cease working after this window is over. Medical teams will continue monitoring the condition of the patient, controlling blood pressure and preventing additional harm to him or her. In case the condition of the patient becomes satisfactory, it is likely that he or she will be offered physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy and cognitive therapy.
It is worth noting that every stroke patient has his or her own path to recovery, which depends greatly on the level of injuries, the affected area of the brain, timely assistance and the patient’s health in general. For all individuals, however, it is important to understand how the brain functions, remember the signs of a stroke and seek timely help for oneself or a loved one.
(Dr. B. K. Madhusudhan is lead consultant – neurology, Aster RV Hospital, Bengaluru. madhusudhan.bk@asterhospital.in)

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

A dispute over whether a newly purchased iPhone can be brought into India without paying customs duty has put Kochi airport in the spotlight. An NRI passenger from Kozhikode, identified as Ajas Muhamad, was booked by the Nedumbassery police after refusing to pay a duty demand of nearly ₹30,000 on an iPhone 18 Pro he had purchased in Dubai. The disagreement was not simply about the amount being charged. It centred on how customs rules distinguish between personal belongings and newly purchased goods brought into India from abroad. Ajas maintained that the phone was meant for his personal use and argued that carrying two devices should not automatically make one liable for duty. Customs officials, however, reportedly took the view that the newly purchased phone did not qualify for the exemption applicable to used personal effects. Ajas arrived at Nedumbassery airport from the UAE in October, carrying a new iPhone 18 Pro as well as an older phone he had been using. According to reports, customs officials questioned him about the new device and informed him that he would have to pay customs duty to take it out of the airport. The amount reportedly demanded was between ₹20,000 and ₹30,000. Ajas refused to pay, saying the phone was for his own use. He also claimed that other passengers arriving on the same flight had faced similar demands. After the disagreement escalated, Ajas staged a sit-in protest at the airport. CISF personnel intervened and escorted him away from the customs area. Customs officials subsequently filed a complaint alleging that he had obstructed them from performing their duties. The Nedumbassery police registered a case against him. Ajas left the phone in customs custody and said he would challenge the decision legally. The dispute has drawn attention to the Baggage Rules, 2026, which came into force on 2 February. Under these rules, eligible Indian residents, tourists of Indian origin and certain foreign nationals are entitled to a general duty-free allowance of ₹75,000 when arriving by air. The rules also allow used personal effects required for daily necessities of life to be brought into India without duty. However, this does not mean every newly purchased electronic item is automatically exempt simply because the passenger intends to use it personally. The rules define personal effects as articles, new or used, that a passenger may reasonably require for personal use during a journey, excluding goods brought in for commercial purposes. But the specific duty-free provision for personal effects refers to used items required for daily necessities. New purchases are also subject to the general allowance and other applicable conditions. This is where the Kochi dispute becomes complicated. Ajas reportedly bought the iPhone in Dubai for around Dh5,950, a value above the ₹75,000 general allowance. Customs officials appear to have treated the new device as a dutiable purchase, while Ajas has questioned why it should not qualify as a personal-use item. The rules do not set a simple blanket limit of one mobile phone per passenger. However, carrying a device for personal use does not, by itself, really settle whether it qualifies for duty-free clearance. The incident has since triggered debate among NRIs and frequent international travellers, many of whom have shared similar experiences at airport customs counters. BJP veteran RK Sinha dies at 75; party leaders, RSS pay tribute
Sinha died at his residence in Noida after a brief illness, family sources said.
Several BJP leaders, Union ministers and the RSS on Friday condoled the death of party veteran and former Rajya Sabha MP Ravindra Kishore Sinha, aged 75, recalling his contributions to the organisation, journalism, industry and social service.
Sinha died at his residence in Noida after a brief illness, family sources said.
BJP national president Nitin Nabin paid floral tributes to Sinha at AIIMS and said his contribution to the BJP since its formative years, as well as his role in giving SIS a global identity and generating employment in the security sector, would always be remembered.
The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) also condoled Sinha's death.
In a condolence message jointly issued by RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat and general secretary Dattatreya Hosabale, the organisation said Sinha's contribution to giving a new identity to the private security services industry, nation-building, social work and the media world would be remembered.
The BJP president said, "His contribution to the expansion of the organisation since the founding days of the BJP will always be remembered. Along with giving SIS global recognition from Patna, he also played an important role in job creation in the security sector."
Describing Sinha as a guiding figure for the Chitransh community, Nabin said he always stood by people in their moments of happiness and grief.
"For me too, he was like a guardian, and his demise is a personal loss," he said, adding that Sinha's simplicity, dedication to the organisation and society, and affection for party workers would always be remembered.
In its condolence message, the RSS said, "The demise of renowned social worker and former Rajya Sabha MP Ravindra Kishore Sinha has caused a loss to the public sector. His contribution to giving a new identity to the private security services industry, service to the nation, social work and the media world will be remembered.
"The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh offers its heartfelt tribute to him. We pray to God to grant the departed soul a place at his sacred feet and provide strength to the bereaved family," it added.
Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath expressed profound grief over Sinha's demise.
He said, "Mr Sinha's invaluable contribution to social service and the organisation can never be forgotten. May Prabhu Shri Ram grant the departed noble soul a place at his holy feet and give the bereaved family members the strength to bear this immense grief."
Union Minister for Road, Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari also expressed grief over Sinha's demise, recalling his contribution to strengthening the party and his journey as an entrepreneur.
"The news of the demise of R K Sinha ji, senior leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party and former Rajya Sabha MP, is extremely heartbreaking," he said.
"I shared a close bond with him. His journey as an entrepreneur, from zero to success in his industry, is remarkable. As a successful entrepreneur and a personality dedicated to ideology, he will always remain a source of inspiration for all party workers," Gadkari said in a condolence message.
BJP national general secretary Smriti Irani also condoled his death, describing it as extremely heartbreaking. She said Sinha's work in journalism, social service, industry and politics would always be remembered.
She also recalled his dedication to the organisation and his efforts towards the rehabilitation and employment generation for ex-servicemen.
BJP national general secretary Harish Dwivedi expressed deep grief over Sinha's demise, saying the news of his death after a prolonged illness had left him saddened. "His demise has left our hearts deeply anguished and sorrowful," he said.
Senior BJP leader Ravi Shankar Prasad also condoled Sinha's death. He prayed for peace to the departed soul and strength to the bereaved family to overcome the loss.
Born in Bihar and educated in Patna, Sinha began his career as a journalist with a Hindi newspaper and started SIS Enterprises, the country's largest private security firm, in the late 1970s, roping in a large number of ex-servicemen who had retired after the Bangladesh war.
The business, which is now said to be worth thousands of crore, gained instant success, especially in the "coal belt" of what was then south Bihar and now comprises Jharkhand.
Known to be ideologically inclined towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh since his days as a student, Sinha is counted among the founding members of the BJP, and he was elected to the Rajya Sabha in 2014 and also became a member of the party's national executive committee.

The Osmania General Hospital (OGH) in Hyderabad has established a dedicated gender-affirming surgery service in the government healthcare sector in Telangana, marking a step towards improving access to specialised healthcare for transgender persons.
The Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery has introduced the service through a multidisciplinary team of specialists from plastic surgery, anaesthesiology, endocrinology, urology, gynaecology and psychiatry, along with nursing staff and other healthcare professionals. The initiative has been developed over the past eight months, said doctors.
The team has successfully performed several procedures for transgender people, including frontal bossing reduction, autologous fat grafting for breast augmentation, breast augmentation using implants, penile inversion vaginoplasty and bilateral nipple-areola complex-sparing mastectomy. Breast implants have also been facilitated through letters of credit under the Chief Minister’s Relief Fund (CMRF).
The initiative aims to provide safe, accessible and affordable gender-affirming surgical care within the public healthcare system, particularly for individuals who face financial and logistical barriers to accessing specialised procedures.
The service follows a multidisciplinary approach, with emphasis on patient evaluation, individualised surgical planning, perioperative care and post-operative follow-up. The hospital has also received support from the Queer Badhu Parents Association, whose president, Mukunda Mala, helped facilitate the renovation of a three-bed ward for transgender patients recovering from surgery, said Dr P. Lakshmi, Professor and Head of Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.
The hospital plans to expand the range of gender-affirming procedures offered and further strengthen the multidisciplinary programme. The initiative is expected to help more transgender people access specialised surgical care through the government healthcare system while promoting inclusive, dignified and comprehensive healthcare.

Syrians struggle with soaring prices as crisis challenges post-Assad recovery
- Published
Last month, protests erupted in squares and streets across Syria. People burned tyres, blocked roads and chanted slogans, angry at the government's decision to raise fuel prices again. It was the largest show of discontent yet since President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power two years ago.
Speaking on a Syrian TV channel, a man said he still supported the authorities but that his situation had deteriorated to the point where he could no longer afford to buy bread. "Honestly," another said, "we have begun to fear what kind of new decision each morning will bring".
The increase was the latest in a series of measures people blame for a growing cost-of-living crisis. For many Syrians, life, financially, has worsened since rebels led by Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad, ending five decades of his family's brutal rule and more than 13 years of a devastating civil war.
Catapulted to the presidency, Sharaa has, since then, led Syria's transition and efforts to revive a broken economy after a long period of mismanagement, isolation and conflict.
There was never any doubt about how challenging this would be. But as they celebrated Assad's overthrow and their new freedoms, Syrians, perhaps unrealistically, hoped things would quickly improve. That, however, has not materialised, and the handling of the economy has frustrated many here.
From essential bills to basic items, the cost of virtually everything has gone up. And many saw a further and unexpected rise in fuel prices as a sign of a government out of touch with its country.
"We don't want roundabouts. Every day they build a new roundabout. People stood by you and are still with you," another protester said, addressing Sharaa, "but this will [make] things explode".
Days later, amid calls for further demonstrations, the increase was revoked.
In a suburb of Damascus, I joined Fatima Saleh Eid at an open-air market for her weekly shop. At 50, she works as a cleaner to help support her family.
"We've suffered a lot," she said. Her husband had recently been hired by a ceramic factory after a year unemployed. He is among the lucky ones, as many are struggling to find work. In some streets, men gather in the hope of meeting someone offering a day job; often, they wait in vain.
Since coming to power, the government has slashed long-held subsidies as part of an austerity drive. The price of bread, a Syrian staple, has increased tenfold. Fuel prices are now in line with the international average, which has put pressure on farmers and made transportation more expensive, while the cost of electricity has gone up several hundred per cent for some.
The authorities, in response, have adjusted public sector wages, including pensions; unsurprisingly, the effect of the additional pay for people has been lost as prices keep rising.
"We eat more sparingly now. We can't afford chicken anymore nor meat. We only eat vegetables but even [that is] expensive," Fatima said. "Inshallah [God willing] things will get cheaper."
As she spoke, around a dozen people, of all ages, gathered around us. Nobody disagreed. One elderly man also said he had stopped eating meat. Another, in his 20s, told me his family were no longer able to pay the medicine for his father, who had a heart condition. One young woman said she and her four children could only afford to have a proper meal every two days.

Marwan Bashour, a 68-year-old pensioner, said his monthly pay was around $90 (£70), which is the public sector minimum wage. "It's not enough at all," he said.
The United Nations Development Programme said 90% of Syrians were in poverty last year.
Marwan told me how he made ends meet.
"Sometimes I borrow money, sometimes I sell things from my house," he said, "like an old pot or plates that we never used, gifts that were given to us. I've even had to sell furniture".
There have been other pressures too. Like many Syrians, Marwan used to rely on help from aid agencies. But, for him, that has stopped, as organisations have been forced to cut back services because of funding cuts.
Syria has also not been immune to the impact of the US-Iran war. The government said the fuel increase that led to the protests was, in part, due to the pressure on energy markets because of the conflict.
I met another pensioner, Nabil al-Remhein, who is 63. None of his four adult children could find work. "We're now having only one meal a day. It's tragic," he said. His face looked tired. "It isn't only me. It's the entire population. We're all hungry... We're suffocating under rising costs."
Nabil took me to his house, in a poor area of narrow alleys and modest buildings. There, I met his wife. She was doing her chores in the dark.
"I'm afraid of the electricity bill," Nabil said. "We've cut back on lighting up the house and we [also] turn off the fridge for about five hours a day".
Still, their latest bill was about a third of the family's income. He has not paid it.
Dr Haid Haid, a Syrian columnist and consulting fellow at the London-based think tank Chatham House, said a "significant portion of the population" was worse off than before Assad's fall.
The economic crisis, he told me, was "one of the most dangerous issues" for the government, and that some of it was of its own making.
"Part of [the crisis] is related to the lack of [financial] resources and the legacy left by the former regime," he said.
"But it's also the direct impact of the new policies that are moving [Syria] towards a liberal and free-market sort of economy, which don't take into account the impact on people".
A spokesman for the Syrian economy and industry ministry told me no-one was available for an interview.
Sharaa has, of course, scored some important gains.
International sanctions imposed in the Assad-era have been lifted, and the US has removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
Security remains volatile and a source of concern, but the country feels more stable.
And the president continues to consolidate his power and, earlier this year, retook the resource-rich north-east from a Kurdish-led militia. (The Druze still control areas in the south, where they want to create an autonomous state; Israel occupies parts of the south-west.)
But real economic recovery is yet to happen. Large parts of Syria remain in ruins after a war that killed half a million people and displaced half of the population.
Unable to afford rent, many families live in partially destroyed buildings. The World Bank says reconstruction costs are estimated at $216bn and, without foreign help and investment, it will be impossible for Syrians to rebuild.
Samir Aita, a Syrian economist who heads the Circle of Arab Economists, a Paris-based independent think-tank, said the crisis was a "combination of policies with the [government] not managing expectations and creating unrealistic hopes".
When I asked him about how he felt about the future, he said: "It's unsustainable. If they don't change, I fear chaos."
Exhausted after years of conflict, Syrians, left with almost no choice, remain hopeful.
Abu Mahmoud, a cab driver, told me: "They inherited the country bankrupt, so people need to be patient. Things don't happen overnight."

Missing man’s body found in Najafgarh drain; 2 held for killing him over minor’s rape in 2021
During interrogation, the duo said they killed the man, whom they already knew, as an act of revenge, after he allegedly raped a minor girl, a relative of one of the arrested persons, in 2021
The decomposed body of a 32-year-old man, who was missing since Sunday, was found with a head injury and bricks tied to it in southwest Delhi’s Najafgarh drain Wednesday evening, police said on Friday. Two men were arrested on Thursday in connection with the murder.
During interrogation, the duo said they killed the man, whom they already knew, as an act of revenge, after he allegedly raped a minor girl, a relative of one of the arrested persons, in 2021.
The arrested men first strangled the victim, then hit his head with a brick before tying them to his body and throwing it into the drain, police said.
Deputy commissioner of police (DCP) (Dwarka) Kushal Pal Singh said that on Wednesday evening, the Chhawla police station received a call regarding a human body lying in the Najafgarh drain near Badusarai village The caller told police that he was returning home after work when he spotted the body in the drain.

“Upon inspection, it appeared that the victim had sustained an injury to the rear side of his head, allegedly caused by a heavy object. Bricks were also found tied to the body, apparently to prevent it from floating to the surface. Local enquiry helped us establish the victim’s identity as Vikram Singh, a 32-year-old resident of Badusarai village,” said DCP Singh. Police said Vikram had been missing since October 25.
After failing to ascertain his whereabouts, his family filed a complaint at the Chhawla police station two days later. A case under section 140(3) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) was registered.
It was found during a probe that local street vendors from Vikram’s Badusarai village in Chhawla had seen him with two men, Praveen alias Bholu (30), and Sagar (26), of the same village near the drain around 9:30pm on October 24. After scanning CCTV footage in the area, the duo’s presence near the drain on that night was confirmed.
“We took Praveen and Sagar into custody, interrogated them, and confronted them with eyewitnesses and digital evidence after which they confessed to killing Vikram. Praveen disclosed that Vikram in 2021 had allegedly raped a minor girl who was his relative. A protection of children from sexual offences (POCSO) Act case was registered, Vikram was arrested and sent to jail. However, he came out on bail after a few months. Since the trial of the case is still continuing, Praveen was enraged over the delayed justice and planned to kill Vikram,” said an investigator, asking not to be identified.

On October 24, Praveen and Sagar allegedly lured Vikram near the drain on the pretext of having a liquor party. When Vikram was heavily drunk, Sagar allegedly asked Praveen to kill him and take his revenge, the officer said.
“The two strangled Vikram. When he became unconscious, Praveen picked up a brick and hit his head. After confirming that Vikram was dead, the two put some broken bricks in his trouser’s pockets and also tied bricks to his legs using the shirt he was wearing. Thereafter, they threw the body into the drain and returned home. The murder happened around midnight,” added the officer.

Two people have been arrested in connection with the killing of a male cheetah cub at the Kuno National Park, officials said on Friday (October 30, 2026).
A senior wildlife official told The Hindu that two people had been arrested after questioning. “The arrest has been made by a special task force formed for the purpose under the Arms Act, after which the accused were produced before a court. They are currently in police remand, and we will take custody soon,” the official said, requesting anonymity.
“The case will be solved very soon, and we will reveal everything in a day or two. At the moment, multiple teams are at work,” the official said adding that more than five forest personnel had been suspended.
Another senior wildlife official, however, said that the two persons had been detained on Thursday (October 29) evening while the weapon, believed to be a country-made bharmar gun, is yet to be recovered.
“Several people in villages near the spot where the cub was found have been questioned so far and based on that two locals were detained last night [Thursday]. They were arrested today. Searches have also been conducted in the area to find the gun,” the official said, adding that the accused were being questioned about the circumstances of the incident and the firearm used.
Earlier on Thursday (October 29), officials had said that investigating teams have been scanning a large area, mapping the cub’s movement over 15-20 days based on its tracking radio-collar.
The probe is being led by a four-member special task force formed by the State Government along with the State Tiger Strike Force
Officials suspect that the weapon used in the shooting is “a country-made bharmar gun”, a traditional single-shot, muzzle-loading smoothbore firearm that is popular is the rural and forest parts of the region.
The 19-month-old cub, KNG22, an offspring of South African cheetah Nirva, had been found with five gunshot injuries in Sheopur forest division on October 25 and died during treatment on October 27 in Jabalpur. This was the first instance of a cheetah being shot since Project Cheetah, a reintroduction programme for the species, was launched in September, 2022.

Page turners have been the latest item to have as an e-reader user, but while Kobo launched a remote last year, Kindle had yet to have one—until now.
Kindle announced the release of the Kindle Click, its first Bluetooth page-turning remote, in early October, and it's finally available to buy. It's a huge improvement over third-party devices that required you to have one part of the device on your Kindle so it could tap and turn the page for you, and a remote in your hand. The worst part was not just that it blocked some of the screen, but that you had to track the battery life of two separate pieces.
The Kindle Click solves these complaints, and while it launched on the same date as the new Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft, it's backward compatible with Kindle models from 2024. It's easy to set up: Just go into your device settings, click on Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and then Bluetooth devices to sync your Kindle Click. I tried it with both a 2024 Kindle and a 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, and both devices were able to find the Click almost instantly and start working.
The Click has two buttons on the main body that move forward and backward and will move around a page you're on, too (but won't select a book for you; it'll just move through your library or homepage). There are also two buttons on the right side that let you adjust screen brightness, which is a fantastic convenience. There's also an included lanyard to attach it to your wrist. It's great to pair with a Kindle stand of any kind so you can prop up your Kindle and turn the page without lifting a finger.
Some Charger Options
If you're getting a new Kindle, you might not be thrilled to discover you need to provide your own charging block to charge it. And if you haven't already switched over your home's collection of wall chargers to USB-C, you'll be especially frustrated when you open the box and find only a USB-C cord. If you're in the market for a new wall charger to pair with your Kindle, these are a couple of our favorites.
Looking to charge on the go? You shouldn't need to with a Kindle's long battery life. But in case you're a serial battery drainer, you can try these portable power banks we love. If neither of these suit you, check out our complete guide to the Best Power Banks.
Kindle Adornments
While everything else in this guide serves a protective or convenience purpose, this section features items with a singular purpose: fun. Here are a few I've liked adding to my Kindle.
Kindle Bags and Sleeves
Looking for a bag to tote your Kindle around? These carriers have you covered with a specific size and special pockets designed to safely store your device. Sure, you could throw your Kindle in any old bag, but these will keep it secure and prevent scratches from your keys. If you'd rather use the bag you have but want a separate sleeve to keep it safe, we've got ideas for that too.
Still Need a Kindle?
If you're reading this guide and actually are still in need of a Kindle, we've got an entire guide to the best Kindles to buy and why. The newest models are (for the most part) the smartest buy, unless the older 2024 models are on sale.

Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
- Published
Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologised and ended its merchandise partnership with a controversial Japanese TV show after drawing backlash in China.
Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative.
The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show.
Sanrio said it terminated its collaboration with Vivant after determining that it "contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio's core values".
"Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people," Sanrio said in the statement late on Wednesday.
"We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects."
China-Japan ties have plunged to their lowest point in years, since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last November sparked a diplomatic firestorm.
Responding to a question in parliament, Takaichi suggested that Japan would activate its self-defence force if China attacked Taiwan.
Beijing has since been heaping pressure on Tokyo, from restricting rare earth exports to curbing tourism and even reclaiming its pandas.
Takaichi told parliament earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and planned to watch them over the year-end holidays.
State-run Global Times took aim at Sanrio on Wednesday, saying the hugely popular cat character "should not dance with Japan's right wing".
Sanrio "stands to lose far more than short-term sales" by collaborating with "anti-China content", the Global Times article said. "The trust and emotional bond it has built up over a long time will also suffer."
When asked about Sanrio's scrapped partnership with Vivant on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry said the incident should "serve as a warning to the international community and discerning people in Japan".
Hello Kitty is not the only internationally beloved figure to have faced such wrath in China in recent days.
Earlier this week, several Chinese brands dropped French footballer Kylian Mbappé over comments he had made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong - which he has since apologised for.
Vivant is about a Japanese salaryman who finds himself entangled in an international web of crime and espionage.
Its first season, which aired in 2023, was set in a fictional Central Asian country. Its second season, which premiered in July, features Chinese agents torturing a Japanese spy by cutting his fingers and stabbing his abdomen.
Chinese state outlets, including CCTV, argued that these tactics "highly overlap" with those historically used by Japanese troops against the Chinese, and that the drama "distorts the truth".
Masamine Ryuho, the president of Vivant's TV network TBS, said on Wednesday that the show was completely fictional and had no intentions of "disparaging any particular country".

Nissan has a new version of its best-selling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested back in February. Most of the hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid.
That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V. Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars’ gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiast irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for.
Series hybrids
Under the hood, with its crisp shut line and slim horizontal lights that give me something of a Range Rover vibe, there’s a 1.5 L, three-cylinder turbocharged direct-injection engine that generates 148 hp (110 kW). It only revs to 5,200 rpm because it’s optimized to charge the battery, not cope with the various loads of an engine connected to a gearbox and the wheels. That also allows the engine to operate at a rather impressive 42 percent thermal efficiency—we would need to look at Formula 1 engines to find higher.
This charges a 1.67 kWh lithium-ion traction battery that has been optimized for its charge and discharge ability, which in turn powers a pair of electric motors. At the front axle sits a 202 hp (150 kW), 243 lb-ft (330 Nm) permanent synchronous magnet motor, at the rear another PSM providing 134 hp (100 kW) and 144 lb-ft (195 Nm), although given the battery’s limitations, combined power output is 225 hp (168 kW). And as you would expect, the motors will regeneratively brake under deceleration to return as much energy to the battery for reuse as possible.

If re-elected, BJP will implement Uniform Civil Code in UP: Amit Shah
Targeting Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Amit Shah said, “Your party will not form the government in Uttar Pradesh for the next 30 years."
Union home minister Amit Shah on Friday said the BJP would implement the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in Uttar Pradesh if voted back to power, while predicting that the Samajwadi Party would remain out of power in the state for the next 30 years.
Addressing the BJP Uttar Pradesh unit's State Working Committee meeting, Shah said, “This time, when the government comes to power, UCC will be implemented in Uttar Pradesh. UCC has already been implemented in many states.”
Targeting Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Shah said, “Akhilesh Babu, mark my words, your party will not form the government in Uttar Pradesh for the next 30 years. The people will not forgive even your third generation.”
Also Read: BJP’s state-by-state push for UCC raises a key question: Is it ‘uniform’ code?
UCC debate
Shah's announcement comes amid renewed calls by BJP leaders for the implementation of UCC across the country, with party leaders in several states backing a common set of civil laws.
Recently, Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma called for the implementation of the UCC nationwide, arguing that Muslim women were among those most affected by its absence. He said a common law was necessary to address issues such as polygamy and pointed out that the UCC had already been notified in Assam.
"The UCC has already been notified in Assam and should be implemented nationwide," Sarma said in Basti district of Uttar Pradesh. He also said Muslim women suffer the most in the absence of such a law, news agency PTI reported.
The remarks followed comments by former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Karol, who on Thursday described the UCC as the need of the hour and said a central civil code should be in place to bring uniformity to the law.
He was addressing the National Legal Dialogue on Article 44 and UCC, organised by the Bharat Collective Foundation. Karol acknowledged that there could be differing views on the subject but maintained that a common civil code should be in place.
Meanwhile, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari recently said his government would introduce stringent laws against "love jihad" and "land jihad" within six months and implement the UCC in the state, along the lines of Uttarakhand and Gujarat.
Talking about the Uniform Civil Code, the chief minister said West Bengal would follow Uttarakhand and Gujarat in implementing a Uniform Civil Code.
"Give us six months, will also bring stringent laws against love and land jihad," he told the gathering.
The West Bengal government has constituted a high-level committee headed by former Supreme Court judge Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai to examine a draft Uniform Civil Code (UCC) for the state.
According to a government notification, the West Bengal UCC Bill aims to standardise civil laws across all communities on matters concerning marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption. The UCC was one of the key poll promises of the BJP in the 2026 Assembly elections.
