New Delhi, Oct 30: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has today released draft ‘Guidelines on Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Telecommunication Networks and Provision of Telecommunication Services’ for stakeholders’ comments.
In February 2026, the Government of India released the ‘India AI Governance Guidelines’ with the goal to harness the transformative potential of artificial intelligence for inclusive development and global competitiveness, while addressing risks it may pose to individuals and society. The guidelines are anchored in seven guiding sutras or principles — Trust is the Foundation, People First, Innovation over Restraint, Fairness & Equity, Accountability, Understandable by Design, and Safety, Resilience & Sustainability. Part 4 of the guidelines provides practical guidance for industry actors and regulators to increase clarity, predictability and accountability in the ecosystem.
The telecommunication sector constitutes a significant part of India’s digital infrastructure. Today, the telecommunication sector supports connectivity for the public, delivery of public and essential e-services, conduct of trade and commerce, and secure and resilient functioning of the country’s critical information infrastructure. It is critical not only for social, economic and commercial activities but also for national security and emergency response in the country.
At present, AI is increasingly being integrated into telecommunication networks and provision of telecommunication services. With a view to ensuring consistent and responsible implementation of the India AI Governance Guidelines in the telecommunication sector, and to increase clarity, predictability and accountability in the ecosystem, TRAI has decided to frame guidelines on responsible use of AI in telecommunication networks and provision of telecommunication services after following stakeholders’ consultation.
In this regard, a draft of the Guidelines on Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Telecommunication Networks and Provision of Telecommunication Services has been placed on TRAI’s website (www.trai.gov.in) for seeking inputs from stakeholders. Written comments on the draft guidelines are invited from stakeholders by 27.11.2026
The comments may be sent, preferably in electronic form to Shri Akhilesh Kumar Trivedi, Advisor (Networks, Spectrum & Licensing), TRAI, at [email protected]. For any clarification/ information, Shri Akhilesh Kumar Trivedi, Advisor (Networks, Spectrum & Licensing), TRAI may be contacted at Telephone Number +91-11-20907758.

Fragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to coins and a child’s necklace, have been found tucked away in a wooden wardrobe sealed off for almost 2,000 years in the ruins of Pompeii.
The artifacts provide an intimate glimpse of daily life in the ancient Roman city before it was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The wardrobe was discovered in a room of a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, which was one of the most bustling streets in Pompeii.
The items inside included tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner and a bronze lantern.
But the most intriguing relic was a necklace featuring more than 20 small charms crafted from various materials and representing several deities, including depictions of the gods Bes and Mercury.
The type of necklace, known as a crepundia, was traditionally worn by children. Its decorative charms rattled to help parents keep track of their children and could also help them be identified.
“A crepundia had a very special function,” said Gabriel Zuchtriegel, the director of Pompeii archaeological park.
“It was a reminder of their parents who perhaps lived far away … it was very typical of this society of people, who were often displaced. Many people moved around in the Mediterranean area and tended to carry personal objects with them.”
The wardrobe contained other items including 38 bronze coins, cooking pots and a wooden box with lead weights, suggesting that someone who lived in the home was a tradesperson.
The fact that money and personal objects were left behind could point to the owners having to flee the eruption at short notice, Zuchtriegel said.
Archaeologists also found the fragmented skeletons of two mice inside an amphora that had been kept in a storage area of the home.
The home had previously been associated with a person called Cornelius Maximus owing to the discovery of inscriptions, which are no longer visible. Its facade was first excavated in 1912, but experts are only now delving into some of its rooms as part of a wider restoration project.
There are also excavations under way at the Villa of the Mysteries in a suburb of Pompeii, which also first came to light in the early 20th century.
“It’s never been completely excavated, so we kind of want to finish the job,” said Zuchtriegel. “What’s interesting is that we’re not excavating in the part where the owners lived and where great frescoes are to be expected, but in the servants’ quarters.
“So what we hope to find there is more insight into the daily life and economy of those who were somehow in the shadow of history. The majority of the inhabitants in the Villa of the Mysteries were actually servants.”
Excavations at Pompeii regularly yield discoveries from the ruins of the ancient city. In 2025, a large and sophisticated thermal bath complex, which was thought to have been used by its owner to woo well-heeled guests, was found during excavations of a home on Via di Nola in Regio IX, a wealthy district of the city.
A home containing a cramped bakery, where enslaved people were believed to have been imprisoned and made to produce bread, was found in the same district in 2023.

World champion Jepchirchir fails drugs test
- Published
Olympic and World Championships marathon gold medallist Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for EPO.
Kenyan Jepchirchir provided the sample prior to winning the Sydney Marathon on 30 August 2026.
The 33-year-old clocked a time of two hours, 18 minutes and 31 seconds to win in Sydney.
EPO, or erythropoietin, is a natural substance produced within the kidneys that stimulates the creation of new red blood cells.
If injected, it is only detectable in the urine or blood for a short window of time, and increases the amount of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles, in the blood stream.
Jepchirchir became the Olympic women's marathon champion at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics and returned to the Japanese capital to win the World Championships in September 2025.
She broke the women's half-marathon world record in 2017 and on three occasions in 2020.
In addition to Sydney, her other major wins came at the New York Marathon in 2021, the Boston Marathon in 2022 and the London Marathon in 2024.
Jepchirchir won the Sydney race, which became the seventh world major in 2025, by more than three minutes from compatriot Irene Chepet Cheptai.
She provided the sample which tested positive for EPO while in Kenya prior to the race.

Isro successfully launches NVS-03 satellite to strengthen India's NavIC navigation system, improve civilian access
Besides enabling navigation, the atomic clock also provides precise timekeeping.
The Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro) on Friday successfully launched NVS-03, India's next-generation navigation satellite, in a major boost to the country's indigenous navigation capabilities.
The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) carrying the satellite lifted off from the second launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR). NVS-03 is a crucial addition to the Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) system, India's answer to GPS.
Also Read | Isro NVS-03 satellite launch: The science and setbacks behind NavIC, India’s version of GPS
How NavIC's new satellite will improve civilian navigation
The satellite carries an indigenous Rubidium atomic clock developed by the Space Applications Centre and will transmit signals in the L1, L5 and S bands. The inclusion of the L1 band makes the satellite compatible with modern civilian smartphone chipsets and wearable devices.
Besides enabling navigation, the atomic clock also provides precise timekeeping. Banks, stock exchanges and the armed forces rely on accurate time, and even small differences between time sources can affect their operations. India has also been working to establish an independent ground-based timekeeping system.
In June 2025, the government said it would stop relying on GPS, which is used by US government, for maintaining Indian Standard Time (IST) and switch to five atomic clocks installed in Guwahati, Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Faridabad and Bhubaneswar. It said the clocks had been tested and that the system would become operational soon. Banks and businesses would be required to use the system once it was operational.

Delhivery swung to a consolidated net profit of ₹40.6 Cr in Q2 FY27 from a ₹50.5 Cr loss a year earlier, while operating revenue grew 19.8% YoY.
Operating revenue growth outpaced the 14.2% increase in total expenses, helping the logistics company turn profitable despite a decline in other income.
The company’s board approved an investment of up to ₹36 Cr in wholly owned subsidiary Delhivery Fintech Distribution to fund its operational and business requirements.
Logistics company Delhivery reported a consolidated net profit of ₹40.6 Cr in the September quarter of FY27 (Q2) from a loss of ₹50.5 Cr in the year-ago period, supported by revenue growth outpacing the increase in expenses. Sequentially, profit increased 27.4% from ₹31.9 Cr, while operating revenue grew 4.6% from ₹2,930.7 Cr.
Operating revenue rose 19.8% YoY and 4.6% QoQ to ₹3,066.4 Cr during the quarter under review. Other income fell 27.8% YoY to ₹66.6 Cr from ₹92.2 Cr. Including this, Delhivery’s total income stood at ₹3,133 Cr as against ₹2,651.5 Cr a year earlier.
The company’s total expenses increased 14.2% YoY to ₹3,093 Cr from ₹2,708.1 Cr. Freight, handling, and servicing costs, its largest expense head, rose 19.1% to ₹2,195.1 Cr from ₹1,842.9 Cr.
The company reported a pre-tax profit of ₹39 Cr against a pre-tax loss of ₹53.2 Cr in Q2 FY26. A net tax credit of ₹1.6 Cr took its net profit to ₹40.6 Cr. Alongside the results, Delhivery’s board approved an equity investment of up to ₹36 Cr in Delhivery Fintech Distribution, in one or more tranches, to support the subsidiary’s operational and business requirements.

The Madhya Pradesh Government has constituted a five-member committee to investigate claims that at least 10 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Madhya Pradesh's Dewas district, officials said on Sunday (October 25, 2026).
The panel will submit its report within 15 days, they said.
Ujjain divisional Commissioner constituted the committee after conflicting claims over the deaths.
Some villagers have claimed that at least 10 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Dewas district between September 27 and October 16.
The district administration had earlier dismissed the claims as false and misleading. It later said viscera samples of two deceased persons have been sent to a forensic science laboratory (FSL) for examination. The cause of death would become clear after the reports are received, it added.
The administration said 10 persons died in Chandana village between October 1 and 15, but denied that any of the deaths was caused by spurious liquor. It attributed the deaths to old age, common illnesses, brain haemorrhage and "deterioration of health due to excessive alcohol consumption".
Ujjain Additional District Magistrate Pratham Kaushik will head the probe committee, which includes Mandsaur Additional Superintendent of Police Ramsanehi Mishra, Ratlam Sub-Divisional Police Officer Lekhraj Meena, Ujjain divisional flying squad Deputy Excise Commissioner Harshvardhan Rai and Regional Director of Public Health and Medical Education Dr Deepak Kumar Pippal.
The panel will conduct a detailed and impartial inquiry into the causes and circumstances of the deaths, along with the related technical and administrative aspects, and submit a factual report within 15 days, according to the Ujjain divisional Commissioner's order.
Madhya Pradesh Congress president Jitu Patwari has claimed that 22 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Chandana, Binjana and adjoining areas over the past month, while at least 40 people suffered damage to their eyesight.
The Opposition party leader has accused the administration of concealing the deaths and shielding the "liquor mafia".

The six-month, all-oral regimen is recommended by the World Health Organisation (WHO) for eligible patients with certain forms of drug-resistant tuberculosis.
BPaL — bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid — provides a shorter, more effective treatment for people with highly drug-resistant tuberculosis, for whom older regimens could involve 18–24 months of treatment, multiple medicines and, in some cases, painful injections.

Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.
A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.
During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.
Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.
A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

India’s spin bowling coach Sairaj Bahutule said senior spinners Kuldeep Yadav and Varun Chakravarthy are well aware that they might not get opportunities in the ongoing T20I series against New Zealand despite being part of the squad, as the team management continues to stick with its preferred bowling combination.
The two spinners remained on the sidelines for a fourth straight game as India’s bowling attack endured a torrid outing, conceding 259 for seven in an 87-run defeat. India though has an unassailable 3-1 lead with a game to go in Hamilton.
Bahutule, however, said both players understood the realities of team selection and continued to work hard behind the scenes, remaining prepared for an opportunity.
“I think more than anything, they (Kuldeep and Varun) are well prepared to play. But the combination, it’s very important to understand that they might not get that opportunity. They are very much aware of it,” Bahutule said at the post-match press conference.
“At the same time, they keep working behind the doors. Whenever they are needed, in fact, they will be ready for it. I think it’s a question of giving them the opportunity,” said Bahutule.
The spin bowling coach expressed hope that the two spinners would get a chance in the next game or the upcoming One-Day Internationals.
“Hopefully, in the next game and the coming one-dayers, they (Chakravarthy is not part of the ODI squad) will get the opportunity.”
Explaining the team’s approach towards its spin bowling options, Bahutule said they have been encouraged to attack but pointed out that defensive bowling could also serve an attacking purpose depending on the match situation.
He highlighted Axar Patel’s ability to deliver in the PowerPlay and adapt to different overs while also underlining the readiness of Kuldeep and Varun to bowl at various stages of an innings.
“I think we encourage our bowlers to attack. Sometimes being defensive can also be an attacking role. You know what I mean? So, there are different situations which we need to handle. Axar is somebody who bowls in the PowerPlay and whichever over he’s given, he executes it very well.
“When you have Varun as well as Kuldeep in the wings, they too are ready to bowl at any stage. They play a different role in conditions like this. But there is a lot of clarity given to them in terms of what is expected from them.”
Bahutule also spoke about the possibility of using Abhishek Sharma as a bowling option, revealing that the left-handed batter regularly works on his left-arm spin bowling during practice sessions.
“Abhishek keeps practising. He is somebody who, in the nets, keeps working on his bowling. He always tries to contribute through his bowling. But it’s all about the captain’s instinct on the ground. He has to go according to that.
“Sometimes, you get a chance. You can get a chance by looking at the conditions. But they are very much prepared. In any situation, I think the opportunity will be given. They will surely go there and execute their skills.”
The bowling coach also addressed India’s struggles at Eden Park, where the dimensions of the ground presented a particular challenge. With short boundaries making it easier for batters to target the ropes, the venue demanded precise execution and a clear understanding of the dimensions from the bowlers.
Asked whether India’s batters had tried too hard while dealing with the ground’s dimensions, Bahutule acknowledged that Eden Park was a challenging venue but insisted that the team was clear about its strengths and intended approach here.
“You could say that. Because Eden Park, obviously, it’s a challenging ground in terms of dimensions. But I think we were very clear as to what we wanted to do. We were clear in terms of our strengths. And we wanted to execute our skills to whatever we could really work towards. But it didn’t happen.”
Despite the heavy defeat, Bahutule maintained that India has adapted well to different pitches and conditions in the preceding matches. He said the team would reassess its combination before the next game at Hamilton, leaving the possibility of changes open.
“I think today was a different day. I think we played really good cricket in the last three games. Different pitches, different conditions is something which we really learned to adapt to. That’s what the effort was, but it didn’t happen.
“We will go to the next venue and decide as to what combination would be ideal. They might get an opportunity, but let’s see how it turns out at Hamilton.”

Despite an overall decline in tobacco consumption, disadvantaged and rural populations in India and the U.S. continue to be disproportionately affected, according to a comparative analysis presented at a national pulmonary diseases conference here.
The analysis highlighted that smokeless tobacco and bidis remain major concerns in India, while cigarettes and e-cigarettes remain public health challenges in the US.
The paper, titled "Two Countries, Two Tobacco Epidemics, One Hidden Inequality", was presented on October 25 by Akanksha Anand, assistant professor at Morgan State University's School of Community Health and Policy in the US, during the 28th National Conference on Pulmonary Diseases (NAPCON) concluded on Sunday.
The study examined tobacco-use patterns and disparities using national survey data from both countries, highlighting the role of gender, income, education and geographical location in tobacco exposure.
According to the Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS), tobacco use among adults aged 15 and above in India declined from 34.6 % in 2009-10 to 28.6% in 2016-17.
However, smokeless tobacco remained a major concern, with a prevalence of 21.4 % in 2016-17, nearly twice the 10.7 per cent prevalence of smoked tobacco.
The National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21) showed that 38%of men and 8.9 % of women used tobacco.
The rural-urban divide was particularly significant, with 42.7 %of rural men reporting tobacco use, compared with 28.8 % of urban men.
Among women, tobacco use stood at 10.5 % in rural areas against 5.5 % in urban areas.
The presentation noted that focusing only on cigarette smoking could overlook substantial tobacco exposure through bidis, smokeless tobacco and other products.
It also highlighted the risks associated with secondhand smoke.
In the US, data from the 2024 National Health Interview Survey showed that 9.9 %of adults smoked cigarettes, while 7 % reported using e-cigarettes.
Cigarette use was considerably higher in non-metropolitan areas at 15.4 %, compared with 8 % in central metropolitan counties.
Similarly, e-cigarette use stood at 9.2 % in non-metropolitan areas against 6.1 % in central metropolitan counties.
The analysis found that while tobacco products differed between the two countries, social and geographical inequalities remained common challenges.
Gender, wealth, education and geographical location were important factors influencing tobacco use in India, while rural residence, education and age played significant roles in the U.S.
The presentation highlighted the need for targeted public health interventions to address tobacco use among vulnerable populations and reduce associated respiratory health risks.
It also cautioned that the figures were drawn from surveys conducted in different years using different methodologies and should not be treated as directly comparable.
The analysis was based on published national estimates rather than an original combined analysis of individual-level survey data.

Pakistani human rights lawyer and activist Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her husband, fellow lawyer Hadi Ali Chattha, have been sentenced to 10 years in prison each by an anti-terrorism court in Pakistan. The verdict, delivered on 29 October, 2026, relates to an incident in Islamabad in October 2024, when the couple allegedly removed road barriers placed along a route secured for the visiting England cricket team. The case has attracted considerable attention because Mazari is a prominent human rights lawyer known for representing people who have faced alleged abuses by state agencies, including journalists, activists and members of minority communities. She has also been a vocal critic of Pakistan's military establishment and its record on human rights. The couple have denied the charges and described themselves as prisoners of conscience, alleging that the proceedings are connected to their human rights work. The latest sentence is also not their first encounter with the Pakistani justice system this year. They were previously sentenced to 17 years in a separate case involving social media posts, before Pakistan's Supreme Court suspended those sentences in September. Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir is a Pakistani lawyer and human rights activist who has built a public profile through her work on cases involving alleged human rights violations, enforced disappearances and the treatment of political activists. She has represented people from different sections of Pakistani society, including journalists, political activists and families seeking information about relatives allegedly detained by security agencies. Her work has also focused on the rights of religious and ethnic minorities, women's rights and freedom of expression. Mazari is the daughter of Shireen Mazari, a former Pakistani federal minister for human rights who served in Imran Khan's government. Her mother has also been a prominent political figure and a vocal critic of the treatment of political opponents in Pakistan. Over the years, Imaan has become known for speaking openly about alleged abuses by the country's security establishment. Her public statements and legal work have frequently brought her into conflict with the authorities. Her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, is also a lawyer and human rights advocate. The two have worked in the legal field and have faced criminal proceedings together. Their work has received international recognition. In 2026, the Ludovic-Trarieux International Human Rights Prize was jointly awarded to Mazari and Chattha for their work defending human rights and the rule of law. The latest case dates back to October 2024, when England's cricket team was touring Pakistan. Security arrangements had been put in place in Islamabad, including roadblocks and barriers along routes designated for the visiting team. According to the prosecution, Mazari and Chattha removed some of these barriers, obstructed police personnel and interfered with security arrangements. Authorities alleged that their actions put the visiting cricket team's security at risk and could have encouraged public unrest. The couple disputed the prosecution's version of events. Mazari maintained that they had been stopped by police at a roadblock while she was trying to reach court to represent a client. The case was registered at Islamabad's Kohsar police station in March 2025. The couple were subsequently charged under provisions of the Pakistan Penal Code and the Anti-Terrorism Act. They pleaded not guilty when the trial began. The proceedings eventually took place inside Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail, with the court recording statements from seven prosecution witnesses. On 29 October, 2026, Anti-Terrorism Court judge Tahir Abbas Sipra sentenced both Mazari and Chattha to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment each under Section 7(h) of Pakistan's Anti-Terrorism Act. They were also convicted under two provisions of the Pakistan Penal Code. The court handed them one-year sentences under Section 186 for obstructing public servants and two-year sentences under Section 353 for assaulting or using criminal force against public servants. The additional sentences will run concurrently with the 10-year terms. The court also imposed fines under the different provisions. In its reasoning, the court said the incident put the England cricket team's security at risk and indicated an intention to create a sense of terror. However, the judgement also described the actual incident as an apparently ordinary case involving the removal of a barrier. The sentencing has triggered criticism from human rights organisations, lawyers and activists, who have questioned the severity of the punishment and the fairness of the proceedings. Mazari and Chattha have maintained that they are being targeted because of their work as human rights lawyers and their criticism of Pakistan's powerful military establishment. In their defence, they argued that the case was intended to discourage people from speaking against alleged state excesses. Their family has also raised concerns about the trial. Shireen Mazari described the proceedings as a sham trial, alleging that the couple were not allowed to defend themselves through their own lawyer and were not provided with important legal documents. Amnesty International condemned the convictions, arguing that anti-terrorism provisions were being used to punish the couple for their human rights advocacy. The organisation also raised concerns about their right to a fair trial. The authorities, however, have proceeded with the prosecution, maintaining that the case concerns the disruption of security arrangements during an international cricket team's visit. An important part of the controversy is that the 10-year sentence is separate from another criminal case involving the couple. In January 2026, Mazari and Chattha were sentenced to 17 years in prison each in a case involving their social media posts. The prosecution alleged that their online statements promoted an anti-state narrative and violated provisions of Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act. The convictions attracted criticism from international human rights organisations and United Nations experts, who raised concerns about freedom of expression and the use of cybercrime laws against government critics. The couple challenged the convictions. On September 17, Pakistan's Supreme Court suspended their sentences and ordered their release while their appeals were pending before the Islamabad High Court. However, their release was short-lived. Islamabad police arrested them again within hours, this time in connection with the separate cricket security breach case. The 29 October verdict has now resulted in another 10-year prison sentence for each of them. For now, the couple remain at the centre of a legal and political controversy in Pakistan. Their supporters view the convictions as part of a wider pattern of pressure on lawyers and activists challenging state institutions, while the prosecution maintains that the case concerns a breach of security arrangements. That enthusiasm often spills into her work, adding personality, urgency, and a touch of chaos that keeps her writing alive. Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
- Published
Kenya is grappling with its first ever outbreak of Ebola, a disease which neighbouring countries, such as Uganda and Democratic Republic of Congo, are used to dealing with.
Nine cases have now been confirmed including its first patient, who travelled from DR Congo and died two weeks ago.
Four relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner have now tested positive, meaning they are all linked to him.
But concerns are rising that the virus could start spreading further, even as the government has sought to assure citizens.
The US has warned it citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Should Kenyans be concerned?
Kenyans have been expressing their concerns that the disease could spread more widely.
More than 4,000 people have died since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
The latest outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kenyans raised questions from the outset, about how the first patient was able to spend time in the region worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. He died days after his arrival in Kenya.
As a regional transport hub, the risk of the outbreak spreading is a big concern.
The doctors' union in Kenya has expressed concerns at "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenya's main airport.
Dennis Miskellah, the union representative, told the BBC that border and port facilities were grossly understaffed.
However, Health Director-General Patrick Amoth on Tuesday evening sought to reassure people, saying that the eight patients were all improving and responding well to treatment.
What is being done to stop it spreading?
When the first case was announced, the authorities urged people not to panic, assuring them of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
Kenya has since introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from 10 countries it considers to be at high risk: DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
The government has additionally designated treatment and isolation facilities across the country, and health workers have been trained to deal with the disease.
Amoth also said that a dedicated laboratory had been set up at the Kenyatta National Hospital Infectious Disease Unit to handle Ebola tests, to ensure that the hospital's laboratory was not contaminated.
In Kenya, 134 out of 135 people listed as contacts of the first patient remain in quarantine. That means about 99% of the contacts have been traced and isolated, in order to prevent Ebola from spreading to the wider population.
That all of those infected so far had links to the first victim shows Kenya's early response is working, according to the International Rescue Committee.
The government is also working with international partners, including Africa CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), to support its response, including surveillance, communication and community engagement.
A toll-free emergency hotline, 719, has been provided to the public to report suspected symptoms.
Is Kenya prepared in case it starts spreading further?
Amoth said that none of the contacts of the first patients had showed symptoms before going into quarantine "and therefore the potential to spread to another person is very minimal, literally non-existent".
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Despite that, Kenya's health ministry says nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola at the national and local levels, besides the facilities that have been designated to handle the virus.
The ministry has urged people to remain calm and vigilant. It has also asked Kenyans not to stigmatise people identified as contacts of Ebola cases.
The ministry, along with the WHO, have produced posters to help people understand Ebola and support its containment. One message reads: "Stop stigma, choose support. Stigma can discourage people from reporting symptoms or cooperating with response teams."
In addition, the government has procured supplies of protective equipment.
Is enough being done to protect health workers?
Not according to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Union (KMPDU).
With three health workers and a hospital cleaner among those infected, questions have been asked as to whether the government could do more to protect workers.
Health workers and carers can face a higher risk of Ebola infection because caring for infected patients may bring them into contact with blood and other bodily fluids.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Dennis Miskellah, the KMPDU deputy secretary general, told the BBC that protective equipment must be provided to hospitals so that they are fully protected, especially in case patients with symptoms do not declare that they have been in areas with Ebola.
He suggests the government ought to conduct proper health education to destigmatise the virus, so that people do not seek to hide their symptoms.
The International Rescue Committee has also called for continued funding for contact tracing, border screening and training of frontline health workers in Kenya.
Will there be any restrictions, like a travel ban?
Kenya remains open with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.
Despite confirming the eight cases, the authorities have explicitly ruled out a national lockdown or general travel ban for Kenyans.
The US on Monday issued an advisory asking citizens to reconsider travelling to the country over Ebola concerns. Other countries have issued health alerts, including the UK, which warned its citizens that they may encounter enhanced health screening, and Canada, which has asked citizens to monitor their health for 21 days.
No country has issued an outright ban against their nationals visiting Kenya, nor have Kenyans been blocked from entering other countries over Ebola fears.
Has business and tourism been affected?
Analysts have raised concerns over the potential impact of public health fears on international travel and tourism but there is no evidence this has happened yet.
But the situation could change if the outbreak were to spread into the wider population.
How many Kenyans are there in DR Congo?
The exact number of Kenyans living in the DR Congo is not clear.
A report authored last year by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think-tank put the number of Kenyans living in eastern DR Congo at about 2,500, including about 50 investors. It also noted that there were about four times as many Congolese living in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, alone.
The Kenyan embassy in the Congolese capital, Kinshasa, which represents Kenya's interests in four countries - DR Congo, Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville and Gabon - has in the past urged Kenyans living in the region to formally register so that it is able to serve them better.
How have neighbouring countries responded?
Several countries in the region have announced tightening of surveillance measures and enhanced screening for visitors.
One man who came into contact with the man who died in Kenya is under quarantine in Somalia and samples have been sent to Kenya for testing.
Somalia has also said it was taking precautionary measures, including enhancing surveillance measures at border points "given the evolving regional situation and the movement of people between countries".
The suspected case in Somalia had travelled through Ethiopia, which has also said it had tightened surveillance to prevent an outbreak
In Tanzania, visitors are expected to undergo daily health monitoring for 21 days, through an automated tracking system, which was announced after Kenya confirmed multiple cases of Ebola infections.
Uganda said after Kenya's first Ebola case that it was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health".
The Kenyan businessman had travelled through Uganda on his way home from DR Congo.
Uganda had reported two Ebola deaths shortly after the outbreak was reported in DR Congo, but the WHO has since declared it to be free of the disease.
On Tuesday, Nigeria confirmed a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda to Abuja. Nigeria is the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East and Central Africa.
Ugandan health officials say the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business before passing through Uganda in early October.
The health ministry stressed she did not have symptoms while transiting through Uganda and only developed them after arriving in Abuja.

Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.
In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.
Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.
The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.
Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.
Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.
“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”
Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.
“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.
In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment.
Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.
Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

What it takes to turn a 5-room HDB flat into a private dining pizzeria
A shared love of pizza has turned into a home-based business. Limited space, demanding schedules and contrasting working styles are now tests David Shen and Sheralyn Tay must navigate, as captured by On The Red Dot.
SINGAPORE: A married couple are busy preparing a pizza dinner for eight guests in their Yishun flat when they receive a last-minute request: Can they accommodate a ninth guest?
“Easy-peasy,” the husband says. The look on his wife’s face says otherwise.
“No, it’s not, okay? We have to move a lot of things,” Sheralyn Tay counters before bustling to reset the table.
As her stress level rises, hubby David Shen languidly brings out a stool from their household shelter. “Sheralyn gets a little bit nervous when it comes to a little bit of last-minute changes,” he says. “But you know, that’s life.”
This is not just another day in married life, however, for the couple, both 45. For two years, they have welcomed paying guests to their five-room flat through their private dining business, PXZA, which they juggle with their day jobs.
And it takes more than pizza-making skills to pull off these dinners. With home-based business regulations preventing them from hiring external help, the couple must handle everything themselves — with limited kitchen space and limited time between each course they serve.
On this evening, they are debuting a new pizza flavour, Coney Dog, which added a couple of hours to their preparation. With a last-minute extra guest and their different working styles, can they keep their 12-course pizza dinner on track?
On The Red Dot’s Hustle In My HDB returns for a second season to follow Singaporeans like them and explore how they navigate constraints and family life while running businesses in their homes.
“I’M OBSESSED WITH PIZZA”
Shen and Tay’s home-based pizzeria has its origins in the pandemic, when Shen was craving Neapolitan-style pizza — which is best eaten fresh from the oven and not as a takeaway, the couple agree.
So they borrowed an oven from a friend and tried making it themselves. Those early attempts were “quite terrible”, Tay recalls. But they persisted, testing their dough about three times a week, with friends sampling the results.
WATCH: We turned our HDB flat into a pizza private dining space in Singapore (14:46)
Eventually, one friend wanted to bring along his family for a meal, offering to pay and suggesting that the couple host private dinners. Thus they created PXZA, with omakase-style dining and menus featuring the freshest ingredients they can source.
It is a passion project fuelled by their shared love of pizza.
“I’m obsessed with pizza. I’m obsessed with the dough,” says Shen, a marketing consultant, who sees their private dinner parties as a way of building a community of “pizza fanatics”.
Tay, who runs an editorial consultancy and co-owns a fashion brand, has always found joy in cooking and in hosting others. “I love feeding people, and David loves making pizza,” she says.
But the pursuit of their shared passion requires good time management. Even as they both mainly work from home, their pizza preparations must fit around their day jobs.
To ease the workload on dinner days, which are Fridays and Saturdays, they get their toppings and other ingredients ready in advance.
Saturdays are especially hectic for Tay, who may start work at her fashion brand’s studio or workshop at 8am and return home at 3pm or 4pm, with not long to go before guests arrive.
“When I come home, it’s bang, bang, bang,” she says. “Get things done.”
FROM “FRIDGE JENGA” TO MISSHAPEN PIZZA
Meal prep is only part of the challenge. PXZA’s ingredients occupy about 60 per cent of the couple’s fridge and freezer, leaving Tay to play what she calls “fridge Jenga” to fit in their own meals too.
Kitchen counter space is also limited. Shen sometimes moves his dough to the air-conditioned living room to keep it cool and free up space, while using ice during mixing to prevent it rising too quickly in Singapore’s heat and humidity.
The couple have divided the work according to their strengths.
Shen makes the dough and bakes the pizzas. He uses Excel spreadsheets for dough-making, which he says involves “a bit of chemistry”. But when it comes to toppings and flavours, he prefers to be “a bit more spontaneous (and) creative”.
Tay, meanwhile, brings structure and consistency to his ideas by managing inventory, the planning and written recipes. “He’s a fly-by-the-seat-of-his-pants kind of guy — things will just work out,” she says. “Who makes it work out? I do, right?”
She also takes charge of the plating and hosting. And she decides which of his “crazy ideas” make the cut, often rejecting dishes that are difficult to prepare ahead of time or to reproduce consistently, for example.
She saw potential in his Coney Dog pizza, however, and agreed to it despite the hours needed to prepare its chilli con carne base. “It’s also very fun to be playing around with new things,” acknowledges Tay.
She appreciates how he pushes her beyond her comfort zone. His calmness can also soothe her nerves, like when he told her before the dinner where they debuted their new pizza: “Deep breath, dear.”
Shen, in turn, credits her with getting things “back on the rails” with her practical approach. When a misshapen pizza emerged from the oven, for example, she arranged the slices to make it look rounder before serving it.
Even with their differences to iron out after more than two decades together, she sees this as a natural part of getting things done rather than “a bad thing” to avoid.
They work through their disagreements while planning each meal so they can focus on serving guests. Once dinner service begins, she says, “we’re a team — we work together”.
FOR THE FUN OF IT, NOT THE FUNDS FROM IT
With teamwork, the couple successfully accommodated their extra guest and served all 12 courses, which meant Tay could breathe a “huge sigh of relief”. Their new pizza, which Shen termed “a labour of love”, was also well-received.
Given the effort involved, with hours spent preparing and hosting each dinner, and the quality of the ingredients, Tay thinks the S$100 they charge per person is reasonable.
PXZA is not their main income source, and they have no plans to change that.
“Revenue isn’t really the most important thing for us,” says Shen. He calls their home-based business “a hobby that funds itself”, whose earnings pay for better ingredients, kitchen equipment and other “toys” they might not otherwise buy.
They rely on word of mouth for custom rather than actively marketing the venture. Although they aim to host two dinners weekly, work and social engagements mean they may take bookings for fewer than half the slots each month.
Even then they see a need to improve the way they manage the workload. Tay handles most of the grocery shopping and the scheduling, and Shen acknowledges that he could take on more to ease her stress.
“I hope that he steps up a bit more,” Tay concurs.
Storage space is another aspect that may need addressing. They are considering a minor renovation to add more cupboards to their living room.
They have also discussed collaborating with friends who run restaurants, although such projects would have to fit with their existing commitments.
Opening their own restaurant, meanwhile, is not on the cards for now. Shen prefers to focus on making “great pizzas” rather than managing profit and loss, while Tay values the freedom from overheads, staff wages and other business obligations.
“It’d be nice to continue to welcome people into our home and feed them,” she says. “There’s nothing better than making people feel happy.”
And how long may that continue? “As long as it remains fun,” says Shen.

Google fixes an annoying Photos bug that hid edited images from other apps
Hey, that's not what Magic Eraser is supposed to do!
Google has finally fixed an irritating bug that Android users were running into when they tried to access pictures they edited in Google Photos. Over the summer, some folks found that these snaps were missing from the image picker in other apps, such as messaging and social media services.
Saving an edited image as a copy rather than overwriting the original was said to work. But for those who preferred to only have the edited version of a photo and ditch the original, this could have been an annoyance.
It took Google some time to squash this bug but, according to APK Mirror founder Artem Russakovskii and 9to5Google, the issue is resolved. Your edited images should at last be free from Google Photos purgatory.
This isn't the only major Google Photos bug that popped up recently. Last month, Google acknowledged an issue with the app that made the Share, Edit, Add to and Trash buttons on the bottom of the screen unresponsive on certain devices after a user made an edit. Within a day or so, the company resolved that issue, as Android Authority reported at the time.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

Nearly 40% of patients seeking neurological care at the casualty in NIMHANS are patients, with as many as 705 cases reported every month. As the number of patients requiring emergency neurological care remains a concern, a hub-and-spoke model linking NIMHANS with the Karnataka Institute of Medical Sciences and Research Institute (KMCRI) in Hubballi is helping extend specialised stroke treatment to northern Karnataka.
The initiative aims to ensure that patients receive prompt assessment and treatment closer to home, particularly during the critical first few hours after a stroke. KMCRI manages around 100 to 120 stroke patients a month under the collaborative model, with teleconsultation and coordinated treatment protocols helping doctors make time-sensitive decisions. World Stroke Day is observed on October 29.
Girish B. Kulkarni, professor of Neurology and head of the stroke unit at NIMHANS, said early recognition of symptoms, rapid transportation to a stroke-ready hospital and timely treatment were essential to improving outcomes.
‘Every Minute Counts’
“This year’s theme, ‘Every Minute Counts’, highlights the importance of recognising stroke symptoms early and ensuring that patients reach hospitals that are equipped to provide appropriate treatment without delay,” he said.
Dr. Kulkarni said around 1,700 patients attended the neurological casualty services at NIMHANS every month, of whom 705 were stroke patients. The institute administers intravenous thrombolysis to around five to eight patients and performs about five to nine endovascular thrombectomies every month.
To northern districts
Under the hub-and-spoke model, NIMHANS serves as the central specialised centre, while KMCRI in Hubballi is developing its capacity to evaluate and treat acute stroke patients in the region. Teleconsultation and structured coordination between the institutions help doctors assess patients and initiate appropriate treatment without waiting for a transfer to Bengaluru.
Amruth, professor and head of the Department of Neurology at KMCRI, said the centre was managing an average of 100 to 120 stroke cases a month.
“Through structured coordination and teleconsultation mechanisms with NIMHANS, patients arriving at our centre receive immediate medical management and targeted interventions,” he said.
The model is particularly relevant for patients in northern Karnataka, for whom travelling to Bengaluru during a medical emergency can consume valuable time. Stroke treatment is highly time-sensitive, and delays in diagnosis and intervention can increase the risk of death or long-term disability.
The KMCRI spoke centre has begun evaluating stroke patients and providing intravenous thrombolysis. A dual-plane digital subtraction angiography (DSA) machine has also been installed at the centre, with endovascular thrombectomy services expected to be introduced soon, Dr. Amruth said.
Thrombolysis involves administering clot-dissolving medication to eligible patients with an ischaemic stroke, which occurs when a blood vessel supplying the brain is blocked. Endovascular thrombectomy is a procedure in which doctors remove a clot from a blocked blood vessel using specialised equipment. The choice of treatment depends on the type of stroke, imaging findings, the time since symptom onset and the patient’s clinical condition, Dr. Kulkarni said.
‘BE FAST’
Dr. Kulkarni said improving public awareness was the first step in reducing delays in stroke treatment. He said the acronym BE FAST can help people recognise the signs of a stroke: B for sudden loss of balance, E for eye or vision disturbances, F for facial drooping, A for arm weakness, and S for speech difficulties. The final letter, T, underscores the need to seek timely medical help and act immediately.
Sudden onset of any of these symptoms should prompt immediate medical attention. Patients should not wait to see whether the symptoms improve or attempt to manage them at home. They should recognise the warning signs and seek emergency medical attention immediately rather than wait for symptoms to subside, he added.

- Twitch streamer and left-leaning political commentator Hasan Piker has filed a defamation lawsuit against conservative commentator Scott Jennings, seeking $72.5 million.
- The lawsuit pertains to a heavily edited video that Jennings reposted in August, to which he added his own commentary falsely presenting the clip as Piker saying he had a "plan of returning our country to lynchings," as well as that Piker "is out there calling for Black people to be lynched." The text of Jennings' post also falsely claimed, not as a direct quote, that Piker indicated "the USA should resume lynchings against black people."
- As Snopes previously reported, a full review of Piker's unedited remarks about lynchings confirmed he was sarcastically mimicking other people's opinions. The video's fragmented excerpts from three different streams presented Piker's words without full context, and in some cases out of order. As such, it was misleading.
- Piker's complaint, filed Oct. 27 in a U.S. district court in Washington, D.C., cites Snopes' reporting. The complaint accurately says Jennings had not responded to our email, in which we asked whether he researched the original clips from Piker's past streams and if he wished to provide further comment.
- We once again emailed Jennings and Piker for comment. A statement from one of Piker's attorneys appears later in this article.
On Oct. 27, Bloomberg Law reported that Twitch streamer and left-leaning political commentator Hasan Piker — who campaigned for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Party's U.S. Senate candidate in Michigan — had sued conservative commentator Scott Jennings, seeking $72.5 million for alleged defamation.
The lawsuit concerns a heavily edited 41-second video that Jennings shared in his own commentary video (archived) on Aug. 11. The edited clip shows Piker appearing to make several offensive statements targeting Black people, such as, "I don't give a f*** what Black people care about," and mentions going "back to a better time when lynchings were happening." Others (archived) shared the video, as well.
In Jennings' commentary, he falsely claimed the video shows Piker saying he had a "plan of returning our country to lynchings," as well as that Piker "is out there calling for Black people to be lynched." The text of Jennings' post also falsely claimed, though not as a direct quote, that Piker said "the USA should resume lynchings against black people."
The edited clip consists of genuine sentence fragments stitched together from three of Piker's streams out of context and out of order, twisting their original import. In one of the original streams, Piker's remarks on lynchings were sarcastic reactions to a user's chat comment and opinions expressed by someone else in a separate video.
A review of Piker's full, unedited remarks found he was speaking of a desire to prioritize winning elections over concentrating on matters that he believed resulted in past electoral losses.
Piker's complaint, filed Oct. 27 in a U.S. district court in Washington, D.C., alleges two counts of defamation and one count of false light, claiming Jennings "knew the portrayal was false or acted with reckless disregard for its falsity," as well as that, as a result, "Piker has suffered injury to his reputation, public humiliation, emotional distress, mental anguish, and damage to his professional interests."
Piker is seeking $27.5 million in compensatory damages, $45 million in punitive damages, attorneys' fees and other relief.
The complaint cites Snopes' reporting from August, specifically on pages 5, 29 and 30, including accurately stating that Jennings had not responded to our email in which we asked whether he researched the original clips from Piker's past streams and if he wished to provide further comment.
Piker spoke about the lawsuit during his stream on Oct. 27, saying Jennings "certainly messed up" and that the case was about "truth in the media." He added of Republican commentators, "I don't think you should be able to get away with lying like this, and if I don't put a stop to it they're going to continue maliciously defaming others as they have done so this entire time."
Daniel Watkins, one of several attorneys representing Piker, emailed Snopes the following statement:
Scott Jennings accused Hasan Piker of calling for Black Americans to be lynched. That is an extraordinary accusation. And it was a lie. Jennings took a manipulated video, put words in Hasan's mouth that he never spoke, and then held those words up as proof of something Hasan never said or believed. There is something especially disgraceful about exploiting this country's history of racial terror to destroy another man's reputation. Scott Jennings has every right to disagree with Hasan Piker. He has no right to invent what Hasan said. We brought this case because the truth matters, reputation matters, and there comes a point when lying must have consequences.
Snopes once again emailed Jennings and Piker for comment about the lawsuit and will update this article if we receive further information.
Transcript of the edited video
Days prior to Jennings' post, the National Republican Senatorial Committee posted (archived) the same video compilation.
The transcript, featuring heavily edited excerpts from three different streams, reads as follows:
I don't give a f*** what Black people care about. [cut] Aw, "Black people care about this. Black people care about that." Like, shut the f*** up. That's not how politics works.
[cut]
"Oh, well, Hasan, how dare you. Like it or not, Black people care about this issue." It's like, it's such a f***ing stupid stance.
[cut]
Any other Black folk want to engage in radical activist language in this f***ing chat? Suck my f***ing c***.
[cut]
Yes, dude. It's because I'm racist. That's why. It's because I'm racist, dude. [cut] "Go back to a better time when lynchings were happening. This is what I like as a Black man." [cut] "Why are you always doing too much with Black people? Leave them alone. I wanna go back to lynching. Like, I get it but [cut] relax. Man, shut the f*** up, ok? God damn." [cut] You got me. [cut] Ok, you got me. Because I'm a [cut] racist person.
In August, NRSC spokesperson Bernadette Breslin did not directly answer our question of whether the organization researched the clips, but she did label Piker as "a communist fanboy and terrorist sympathizer who glorifies racism and violence." She also cited the Anti-Defamation League's page warning of Piker's past rhetoric and shared other examples of alleged inflammatory remarks.
In Snopes' original report, we presented our investigation of all three clips with transcripts as follows:
The first clips in the 41-second video, with Piker saying, "I don't give a f*** what Black people care about," came from his July 30, 2024, stream.
The pertinent moment, beginning at the 4:10:48 mark, shows him watching a campaign speech featuring then-Vice President Kamala Harris, who was running for president at the time. He reads out loud a chat user's comment that says, "Like it or not, Black people care about the border." He then makes an opinionated point about avoiding what he believed to be failed strategies to winning elections (bolding reflects remarks from edited video):

Moments later, Piker continues making remarks about the same subject. He previously addressed the same comments from the 2024 video in an early 2026 stream.
June 2025
The second clip in the 41-second video was from Piker's June 25, 2025, stream.
Beginning at the 3:16:28 mark, Piker reads out loud a user's chat message saying, "With all due respect, you don't know Black people." Piker responds to that user, "With all due respect, I know polling."
